Bhūtarāja. 35) Or, it may mean "the king of kings" in the sense of a Piśācarāja. 36) Or, it may mean "the king of kings" in the sense of a Yakṣarāja. 37) Or, it may
An attendant and servant of Vaiśravaṇa, with tears welling within him and his throat choked with sobs, brooded for a long time over even an unknown matter, reflecting:
"Of what kind [of being]?"— [namely], one who is the cause of producing the flower called *ketaka*.
Because they arise during the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*). Now, he explains why, at the mere sight of a cloud, there is internal weeping and meditation for him:
"Even for one who is happy and not separated [from his beloved], the mind [is affected] at the sight of a cloud—that is, at the sight of the rainy season."

How much more so when the beloved person, who longs for an embrace around one's neck, is far away— a state that causes one's conduct to change, brings about delusion, and is filled with intense longing?
The meaning is: when even those who are well-settled feel longing upon seeing that the rainy season has arrived, what need is there to mention the case of those separated from their lovers?
It refers to one for whom the very embrace of the neck constitutes the object of their affection and desire.
The rainy season (*varṣā*) is that in which clouds are perceived;
it is a state fallen from its own nature, characterized by a different mode of being. (3) — Dākṣiṇāvarta.
"Having somehow stood before him"—

the intention is that, desiring to have the cloud convey his own message to his beloved, the lover, though tormented by passion, stood before the cloud with great effort in order to offer it a welcome and so forth for that purpose.

The reading is *kautukādhānahetoḥ*. *Kautuka* means eagerness regarding the object of desire (*kāma*). The meaning is "for the purpose of bestowing curiosity. Yādava states: "Kautuka is used for the absence of an object, for a hand-thread, for curiosity, for desire, and for what is known as auspiciousness. The reading *ketukādhānahetoḥ* means "for the purpose of the conception of embryos" (*ketukānāṃ garbhādhānahetoḥ*).

It is said that there would be a certain purpose; one should understand that this [purpose] would not otherwise be an utterly praiseworthy qualification. Regarding the qualification "for the sake of creating curiosity," the meaning is that he became subject to another's will by forgetting the task at hand—such as the welcome for the cloud—which was situated within his heart's desire.
It has been stated as the cause.
"With suppressed tears" means with tears held within; "on account of his authority" indicates that he is an attendant of the King of Kings.

The connection is that he "meditated for a long time" (ciraṃ dadhyau). He meditated, that is, he reflected. Due to delusion (*moha*), his mind was devoid of sensory objects; hence, the verb *dhyai* is used here without an expressed object.
"Happy ones" means those possessing the causes of happiness; that is to say, those whose beloved persons are present.
Overpowered by the longing for a different way of life.

Regarding the phrase "the person longing for an embrace around the neck": the meaning is that when the beloved person, out of fear of hearing the thundering of clouds during the rainy season, requests to embrace the husband's neck.
The reading is "tasyāśleṣapraṇayini jana" (the person longing for his embrace). "Tasya" means of that Yakṣa. "Dūrasaṃsthe" means situated at a distance. || 3 ||
Which reading is correct, *kaṇṭhśleṣa* or *tasyāśleṣa*? Mallinātha [prefers] *tasya*.

*Rājan* means a Yakṣa. According to the *Viśvakośa*, *rājan* is used for a lord, a king, the moon, a Yakṣa, a Kṣatriya, and Śakra. *Rājarāja* is the king of kings, namely Kubera. According to the *Amarakośa*, *rājarāja* is the Lord of Wealth (*Dhanādhipa*). [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied after [words ending in] *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*.
Thus ends the suffix *ṭac*.
His attendant Yakṣa,
with tears suppressed within— meaning, with his tears held back because of his *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) nature— [remained].

The term *kautuka* refers to the cause for producing longing (*abhilāṣa*), which is the reason for instilling curiosity; for the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *kautuka* may denote longing, a festival, jesting, or a spectacle."
The meaning is: "before that cloud," by some means or other, with great effort;
for [the lexicon] Ujjvala states: "The indeclinables *katham* and so forth are used even when there is a desire to express a cause for knowledge, etc.;
*katham* and so forth, as well as *tathāpi*, are used in the senses of intensity of effort and abundance."
Having stood for a long time, he meditated; that is, he reflected. This is from the root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking," used in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "until the subsiding of all mental fluctuations."
He states the cause of the transformation with the words "meghāloke":

when there is the appearance of clouds— that is, upon seeing clouds— the mind (cetas) of even those who are happy, even those joined with beloved ones and the like, has its state (vṛtti)— its activity— altered.
It becomes otherwise;
that is to say, it undergoes a transformation.
Toward a person who is longing for an embrace of the neck and seeking a neck-embrace.
When he is situated far away—that is, when he remains at a great distance—what more need be said?

The meaning is: what need is there to speak further regarding those separated from their beloveds? The implication is that for those in separation, the sight of a cloud serves as an intensifier (*uddīpana*) of their longing.
This is the figure of speech *arthāntaranyāsa*. As stated by Daṇḍin:
"That should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa*, which, having introduced some matter (*vastu*), is the presentation of another matter capable of establishing it. (Kāvyādarśa 2.361) || 3 ||
The commentary on this is *Sumativijaya*.
For a long time, a yakṣa was a follower and servant of Dhanadadeva, the king of kings.
He reflected for a long time and became filled with anxiety.
Having done what? Having somehow, with great difficulty, due to the weakness caused by the pain of separation, stood before that cloud.
Of what nature was he? He was one whose purpose was the planting of *ketaka* flowers.
Of what nature was the follower? He had tears within due to grief, and his voice was faltering.
For this reason— because even the heart of one who is happy and accompanied by his wife undergoes a change, becoming contrary [to its usual state] upon the sight of clouds— that is,
when it becomes filled with intense longing for a person who is affectionate and eager for an embrace around the neck.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "When the characteristics of a woman are situated at a great distance, what more need be said?"
"He meditated" (dadhyau). This is the form derived from the root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking," using the *liṭ* (perfect) tense in the remote past.
Regarding the word *ketakādhānahetoḥ*: "ketaka" refers to the *ketakī* flower; "ādhāna" means production or manifestation;
thus, "ketakādhāna" is the production of *ketakas*. "Ketakādhānahetu" is the cause of that production.
The sense is that, indeed, the *ketakī* blooms during the rainy season.
"Antar" means within; he whose tears (bāṣpa) are within, that is, in the heart (hṛdaya), is "antarbāṣpaḥ. Regarding "megha": the sight (āloka) or perception of a cloud is "meghālokaḥ";
[the term refers to] in that sight of a cloud. || 3 ||
When the monsoon was near, he— seeking a means to sustain the life of his beloved and wishing to send news consisting of his own welfare by means of a cloud—
to that messenger for whom he had prepared an offering of fresh *kuṭaja* flowers:
Being pleased, he uttered words preceded by affection, saying, "Welcome."
In the sky (Da); in the mind (Da, Ma); for the sake of the purpose (Da, Su). VALL:
Then that Guhyaka addressed a welcome to that cloud: "It is auspicious."
"Welcome to you," he said;
those words preceded by affection and characterized by joy, such as "Welcome," are as follows:
"Are you well? Is it all well with you in every respect? Please rest."
"Let this place be purified.
Of what nature was he? He was one who, by means of a cloud (*jīmūta*), intended to send—or cause to be brought—news (*vārttā*) consisting of his own welfare and auspicious state. For he...
He entreats for the sustenance of his beloved’s life, which is the very support for his own survival;
for from the attainment of a husband's welfare, the recovery of those most dear arises.
To what sort of him? To him for whom an offering (argha) has been prepared with fresh kutaja flowers.
Because worship was performed [for him], for this very reason he is pleased. "The day of tranquility in the month of Āṣāḍha" has the same meaning as that which was stated.

"In the sky being near" (*pratyāsanne nabhasi*) is what is restated. *Nabhas* refers to the month of Śrāvaṇa. Alternatively, some explain it as "in the sky (*nabhasi*) being near," meaning as if situated close by because it is densely covered with clouds (*jaladaniścitatvāt*).

The cloud itself conveys the news in the sky; for it brings [the news] while producing joy. The causative suffix (ṇic) arises in the sense that "by means of joy, it will cause [the news] to be taken away."
Then, by the rule *ḷṭ śeṣe ca* and because of the word *ca*, the *ḷṭ* (future) is used when there is a verb denoting an action as the object (*upapada*).
The meaning is that he spoke words of welcome in order to cause [the guest] to proceed.
Regarding the phrase "by Jīmūta," it is according to what is prescribed in the alternative case by the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām*.
Agency. "To him" means: that which one intends through an action is the recipient (*sampradāna*); such is the definition of the recipient. (4)
"Near to the right-turning [breath]" means:
when the mind— the internal organ— is near, established in its natural state, yet the heart is agitated by meditation.
The meaning is "when [the moon] has become established.

Regarding the reading *pratyāsanne nabhasi*, the word *nabhas* denotes the month of Śrāvaṇa; this is according to the statement of Amarasimha: "Nabhaḥ means the sky, and nabhaḥ and nabhā mean the month of Śrāvaṇa. At that time...

It should be understood that it is improper to delay, setting aside the Āṣāḍha month already at hand. Furthermore, the statement "close your eyes and pass the other four months in the month of Śrāvaṇa" would be unreasonable.

Others, however, say: the word *nabhas* denotes the rainy season; thus, his thought occurs even before the rainy season begins, as he intends to cause his own departure to be conveyed by the cloud for the sake of sustaining the life of his beloved when the time of the rains has arrived. That...

"Even though it was inconsistent," thus [the text says], because it indicates the consideration of immediate action by stating that the Guhyaka, disregarding [the inconsistency] out of eagerness, made that request.
For the sake of supporting the life of her beloved, with the purpose of preserving the life of her beloved.
By Jīmūta: it should be understood that the mention of the name of the subject under discussion without the pronoun *tat* occurs because of its intervention by another sentence.
The occurrence; the event.
"With *kuṭaja* flowers. According to Halāyudha, the *kuṭaja* is the *girimallikā*.
It should be understood that the mention of *kuṭaja* flowers is made because they belong to the rainy season (*vārṣika*).

The reading is *kalpitārghāḥ*. [This means] for the purpose of the prescribed rite of worship (*pūjāvidhi*). According to Amara: "In the sense of price or in the rite of worship, it is called *argha*. The expression beginning with *prīti-* refers to words expressing the affection of those worthy of worship.
The term *pradhānavacana* means "a welcome," that is, a beautiful arrival or coming; by this, the word *svāgata* is intended. || 4 ||
Mallinātha: Now, having composed his inner mind, what did he do? To this he says:
"pratyāsanne" (when [the time] was near).
That yakṣa; the meaning is "he who reflected for a long time.
"In the sky" means in the month of Śrāvaṇa. According to Amara, "nabhas" means the sky and "śrāvaṇa" or "nabhā" refers to the month of Śrāvaṇa.
"In the vicinity" means immediately following Āṣāḍha; the sense is that it has arrived.
This is because he, seeking the support for his beloved’s life, [fears] the rainy season, as it generates the pain of separation.

The meaning is that, according to the maxim "it is better to prevent the arising of a misfortune than to remedy it once it has arisen," he desired to devise a means for his beloved to sustain her life even before [the danger occurred].
A *jīmūta* is a bundle, a binding of cloth or fabric for water—that is, for living beings (*jīvana*).

It is a valid form according to the rule of the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Rudra states: "The word *mūta* may also mean a binding of cloth. By that *jīmūta*, the cloud, acting as the instrument, [one sends] one's own message consisting of well-being.
*Vārttām* refers to activity (*pravṛtti*) characterized by one's own welfare; according to Amarasimha, "news" (*vārttā*), "activity" (*pravṛtti*), and "event" (*vṛttānta*) are synonyms.

*Hārayiṣyan* means "intending to cause to reach" or "intending to convey. The suffix *ḷṭ* (the future tense marker) is applied here because of the word *ca* in the rule *ḷṭ śeṣe ca*, which allows for the *ḷṭ* suffix when another action is subordinate to the purpose of the primary action.
The sense is that action for the sake of livelihood must be performed by one who bestows livelihood;

since the designation of "object" (karman) is optional according to the rule *hṛkror anyatarasyām*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the alternative where it is treated as the agent (kartṛ).
With fresh and newly blossomed *kuṭaja* flowers— *kuṭaja* and *girimallikā* being synonyms according to Halāyudha—
and with *girimallikā*s.
To him for whom the *argha*— the ritual procedure of offering— is prepared, fashioned, and performed.
"Argha refers to price as well as the ritual procedure of worship," according to Amara.
To that Jīmūta; since the recipient is expressed as such, the fourth case (caturthī) is used according to the rule that "the mention of the action must also be made.
That [act] in which the words are preceded by affection—that is, words characterized by affection.
With words headed by joy,
he spoke a welcome— meaning a pleasant arrival and a greeting of welcome— with delight;
that is to say, he inquired after his well-being.
However, the Master has here proposed the superior reading *manasi pratyāsanne*,
meaning "when [the mind] has become proximate, that is, when it has returned to its natural state.
As for the contradiction with his own previous reading that he himself pointed out, we [have addressed it as follows].
This is resolved simply by reconciling the alternative reading "on the first day of Āṣāḍha. || 4 ||
This is the commentary on the *Sumativijaya*:
What did that Yakṣa do while his internal organ (mind) was not composed?
He addressed that cloud with a welcome, inquiring after its well-being;
for what reason? Because the Yakṣa was pleased and satisfied, thinking, "My task shall be accomplished."
To him who was such? To him for whom the *argha* offering had been prepared—that is, for whom worship had been performed—with fresh, newly blossomed *kuṭaja* flowers produced from the *kuṭaja* tree.
What was that yakṣa about to do?
By means of a cloud (*jīmūta*), he intended to send—meaning to deliver—a report concerning his own auspicious state from his side;
for what purpose? For the sake of providing a support for his beloved’s life—that is, for the sake of his own wife.
For the sake of protecting one's life.
Under what condition? When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived and is near at hand.
Of what nature was the welcome? A speech headed by affection—a charming utterance characterized by love.
Such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
*Kalpitāya* means "to him for whom an *argha*—consisting of the offering of flowers and so forth—has been prepared (*kalpita*) or fashioned (*racita*).
Thus, it means "to him for whom the *argha* has been prepared."
"Śrāvaṇa is the month of Nabhas," according to Hemacandra.

"Having the life of the beloved—that is, one's own wife—as its support" means that which has that very thing as its basis, its object, or its purpose; thus, it is "that which has the life of the beloved as its support. (4)
"Where is a cloud— a mere conjunction of smoke, light, water, and wind—
and where are the meanings of a message, which must be delivered by living beings with keen senses?
Thinking thus, the Guhyaka, disregarding his anxiety, made his request to him.
For those afflicted by desire are wretched in their longing toward both sentient and insentient beings.
°arthas Da; and sandeśāś ca (Da); prakṛti° Ma, Su; VALL:
Now, one might ask, "How can a cloud, being insentient, act as a messenger? To this he says:

The Guhyaka, a being of merit, out of eagerness and under the sway of longing, thus—without reckoning or reflecting—begged and entreated that cloud. He asked: "Where is the cloud, and where are the matters of the message, the subjects of the news?"
A cloud, for its part, is merely a collection of smoke, light, water, and wind;
indeed, clouds composed of smoke and the like are insentient.
The meanings of messages, however, are conveyed by human beings—living creatures endowed with clever senses and sharp faculties.
They are to be attained; they can be led [to him], but not by those devoid of intelligence.
To the question "How then did he fail to reflect upon this?", he says:
Because those who are afflicted by desire, tormented by the snare of passion (*madana*), become wretched in their entreaties toward both sentient and insentient beings, such as lions and trees.
"Indeed, they are not capable of distinguishing between what is their proper object and what is not"—thus, by this artful turn of phrase, the poet sets aside his own fault. || 5 ||

Having raised the doubt that it would be difficult for a cloud— which is devoid of consciousness— to carry out the matter known as the delivery of the message to Dakṣiṇāvarta, he refutes it with the verse beginning "dhūma... (smoke).
"Sannipāta" means a collection.
"Sandeśārtha" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the message itself is the purpose"; some read it as "sandeśāśca."
"With sharp instruments" means with keen faculties (*indriya*). *Kha*, *akṣa*, *indriya*, and *srotas* are synonyms;

*hṛṣīka* and *karaṇa* are also considered such, according to Halāyudha. [The word] "eagerly" (*autsukya*) is used because of being intent upon a desired object; for one who is intent upon a desired object is called "eager" (*utsuka*).
"Amara" (immortal) is the connection, meaning "not reckoning" [the aforementioned]. A *guhyaka* is so called because he hides (*gūhate*) his treasure; [this refers to] the *yakṣas*.

This is the name of the action because it involves concealing the treasure of Vaiśravaṇa. Alternatively, the words *yakṣa* and *guhyaka* also apply to the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada). Thus, Yādava [states]: "The *yakṣas* and *guhyakas* are also the Giver of Wealth. Therefore, by means of the word *guhyaka*, which denotes Vaiśravaṇa...
Because it is appropriate to designate him by the name of his Yakṣa attendants, he is called a Guhyaka.
Therefore, even though there is a distinction between a Yakṣa and a Guhyaka, one should understand that no contradiction arises with the term "Guhyaka" when considering the phrase "the Yakṣa Cakra."

The term "yayāca" (who begged) is used with reference to what will be stated hereafter. Those who are "praṇayakṛpaṇāḥ" (miserable in their affection) are base in their begging. Their baseness consists in the failure to abandon what has been seen [as flawed].

Here, the locative case in "cetaneṣvacetaneṣu" (among sentient and insentient beings) denotes the object; for although one could have simply said "even among insentient things," the inclusion of both "sentient and insentient" is intended to refer to the sequence beginning with smoke, light, water, and wind.

It should be understood that this was done in accordance with what was introduced immediately prior: the insentient subject under discussion, and the sentient subject subsequently introduced by the words "by those with efficient instruments. || 5 ||

In response to the inquiry, "O Mallinātha, how can one set about causing an object that is to be accomplished by consciousness to be performed by something insentient? the poet provides the answer with the verse beginning "dhūma... (the smoke).
Smoke, light, water, and wind—their conjunction is the cloud; where is it? Being insentient, it is incapable of conveying a message.

"With mature faculties" means with capable sense organs (*indriya*). According to Amara, "faculty" (*karaṇa*) refers to that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*), and it applies to the field (*kṣetra*), the limbs, and the sense organs.
"By living beings" means by sentient beings (*cetana*). According to Amara, "a living being" (*prāṇin*) is a sentient person who is subject to birth.
"Prāpaṇīyāḥ" means those who are to be reached. "Sandeśāḥ" refers to those things which are being communicated; where are those very objects?
Thus, because of the application toward desired objects due to eagerness and so forth, it is "intent upon a desired object. Intent upon a desired object.
"Utsuka" means "eager," according to Amara.
Without counting [the cost] and without reflecting, the Guhyaka Yakṣa entreated— that is, he made a request of— that cloud.
The root *yāc* is used in the sense of begging.
For indeed, those afflicted by desire and tormented by passion—whether sentient or insentient—are naturally wretched and inherently base regarding those objects.
The meaning is that for those blinded by desire, because they lack the discrimination between what is appropriate and inappropriate, an insentient thing making a request is not contradictory.
Here, the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous) arises from the union of two discordant things, namely the cloud and the message (*meghasaṃdeśa*). That...
It has been said:
"Where there is the production of a contradictory effect, or where there is misfortune, or where there is a mismatched union—that is the *viṣama* (incongruity) ornament; it is of three kinds."
And that [simile] is enlivened by the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroborative generalization), because it is introduced in the fourth quarter precisely as its support. || 5 ||
This is the commentary on the *Sumativijaya*:
the *guhyaka* Yakṣa requested— that is, made a petition— to that cloud.

What was the Guhyaka doing? He was acting in the manner about to be described, out of eagerness—that is, due to being agitated by longing—and thus failing to take account of it, meaning he did not reflect upon it.
He asks, "How so? [The answer is: Where is the cloud, and where are the matters of the message—the words of the message?
The word "where" indicates a vast difference.

Of what nature is the cloud? It is a conjunction of smoke, light, water, and wind—a collection of smoke, fire, water, and air—because these elements, beginning with smoke, have attained a state of unification within the cloud.

Of what nature are the contents of the message? They are those things to be conveyed, capable of being delivered by living beings, that is, by human beings. By what kind of living beings? By those with efficient organs, that is, those endowed with all the sense faculties.

For this reason (*hi yasmāt*), people afflicted by desire (*kāmārta*)—tormented by sensual pleasures—are "naturally wretched" (*prakṛtikṛpaṇa*); that is, they are deficient by nature (*prakṛtyā*), by their very essence (*svabhāvena*). They are "naturally wretched" in the sense that they are devoid of the thorough knowledge of the nature of both sentient and insentient things. This is the logical connection (*anvaya*).

Regarding "dhūma" (smoke): smoke, light, water, and wind—these are smoke, light, water, and wind; [the compound refers to] those [elements], namely smoke, light, water, and wind. "Jyotis" (light) means fire.
"Paṭubhiḥ" means those whose instruments—the sense organs—are sharp, that is, endowed with capacity;
by them, "paṭukaraṇaiḥ. "Kāmārtāḥ" means afflicted or tormented by desire; those tormented by passion. "Madanapīḍitāḥ" means those tormented by the god of love.
People do not speak [of this] before one who possesses consciousness; or rather, the sense is that it is spoken of before one who possesses consciousness. 5.
Born in the world-renowned lineage of the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds, I know you to be the natural agent for Indra, able to assume any form at will;
therefore, by the power of fate, I have come to you as a suppliant, though my kinsmen dwell afar.
A request made to one of superior virtue is better, even if it fails, than one made to a base person that succeeds in obtaining its desire.
[The commentary] says: "Puṣkalā" (Da); "Moghā" (Da, Su).
[The author] speaks of that very same request preceded by flattery.

Since I know you to be such as this, I have come to you with a request; for what kind [of person] are you? You were born in the lineage and family of the Puṣkarāvartakas, the clouds of universal dissolution—this is a statement regarding your noble birth.

Likewise, there is a description of the power of Maghavan Indra as consisting of both constituent persons (*prakṛti-puruṣa*) and ministerial persons (*amātya-puruṣa*). For among the constituent elements, the ministers are the most prominent;
and for Indra, the clouds alone are the performers of his pleasure.
Or, the term *prakṛtipuruṣa* means that he (the king) is both the source (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*) among the constituent elements.
For these seven—the sovereign, the minister, the realm, the treasury, the fort, the army, and the ally—are the seven constituents; thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs. (Manu 9.294)

"Kāmarūpa" means pleasing or having a form according to one's own will, due to the manifold forms of clouds; he will say this very thing later: "having made myself into a cloud of flowers. Therefore, by the power of fate, I am a kinsman from afar, with my wife not present, [staying] with you.
The petitioner has become one who possesses the object of his request;
if I am thus endowed with such qualities, then why should there be such a solicitation directed toward me?
To this he says:

Because a request made to a person of superior qualities— one who is distinguished by lineage and other virtues— is better (varaṃ), meaning more auspicious, even if it is barren or fruitless, since it does not bring shame; but it is not so when made to one who is base or inferior, even if the desired object is obtained.

Even when there is a difference in grammatical gender, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs because of the introduction of the general category, as in the expression "a single well is better than a hundred pits," and so forth.
Now Dakṣiṇāvarta makes a request preceded by praise, saying: "He has been born."
Certain clouds, such as the Puṣkalāvartakas, remain stationary.
[The term] "puruṣa" refers to the person situated among the constituent elements (prakṛti) such as the ministers and so forth.
"Kāmarūpin" means one whose form is subject to will; this is an epithet.

For the purpose of going to Durgā and other such places, he will say: "Therefore, you should follow the northern direction, beautiful in its horizontal extent," and "Having gone, immediately assume the form of a young elephant.
By this, there is the recognition of his noble birth and his power.

*Arthitva* means a request. By virtue of fate, one becomes a "distant kinsman" (*dūrabandhu*), meaning one whose wife is far away. According to the etymology "one who binds is a *bandhu*," the word *bandhu* refers here to the wife, who is the object of attachment.
By the word "friend" (*suhṛt*), which is a synonym for "kinsman" (*bandhu*), even a wife is included.
Furthermore: "A son is the foremost among those who are dear; a wife is the best among friends;
Mount Meru is the greatest of mountains; and Madhusūdana is the supreme among gods. Thus it is said.
*Mogha* means vain, useless, or purposeless.

*Varam* means slightly dear; however, when used in the sense of "taking refuge in the best," one should say *varaḥ*. In this regard, Amarasimha states: "In the masculine, *varaḥ* [is used] for a boon or a god; in the sense of 'best,' it is used in three genders; and in the neuter, it means slightly dear."

Thus [it is said in Pāṇini 3.3.174]. With the intention that she becomes unpleasant due to failure to obtain [what was requested], it is said "slightly pleasing" (*manākpriya*). The syntactical connection is: "In the case of a base person, even a request that has attained its desired object is not excellent. (6)
"O Mallinātha, it has been born," [he said].

"O Megha, you who are known in the worlds (*bhuvaneṣu vidite*). Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of a completed action (*bhūtārtha*) with the word *niṣṭhā*. However, if it were intended to convey the present tense according to the rule beginning with "matibuddhi...
(Pāṇini 3.2.188), then by the rule "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67), the word *bhuvana* would necessarily be in the genitive case; consequently, a compound (*samāsa*) would not be possible.
It would be so, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini] stating "and with a word ending in a *kta*-suffix, when honor is expressed" (P. 2.2.12; cf. 3.2.102, 3.2.188, 2.3.67).
[There are] certain excellent clouds, namely the Puṣkaras and the Āvartakas. Of these...
"Born in a lineage"; this means born of a great family.
"Kāmarūpa" means one whose form is subject to will; the sense is that it is capable of moving through difficult terrains and the like. I know him to be the principal personage of Maghavan (Indra).
By reason of his being born of a great lineage and possessing such qualities, he is under the power of fate—that is, dependent on destiny.
"Vidhi" refers to a rule or destiny (Amara);
"vaśam" means dependent or under control (Viśva).
One whose wife is far away is "dūrabhandu"; such as I am, separated from my wife, [I have come] to you.
He has become a petitioner.
Now, one might object: "In the case of a beggar's request, what use is there for the excellence of the qualities of the object being requested?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that even when a request is made by chance, there is simply no fault of insignificance.
He says that "exertion" (upayoga) is "begging.

Even if begging toward a person of superior qualities—that is, one possessing greater virtues—is fruitless and ineffective, it is still better as a slight source of pleasure; for such a person is pleasing because of the abundance of their virtues.

The sense is that because begging is fruitless, there is only slight affection. In the case of an inferior person—one devoid of merit—even a request that has attained its object and is thus successful is not "excellent" (*vara*);
the meaning is that it does not even constitute slight affection. *Vara*, when preceded by *deva*, means a boon.
"Śreṣṭha" is used in three genders; as a neuter noun, it means "slightly pleasing," according to Amara.
This is the figure of speech *preyas* (the pleasant), vitalized by the figure of speech *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration). As it was stated by Daṇḍin:
"The *preyas* is the narration of that which is more dear."
It is very clear that this [conclusion] in the first three quarters of the verse is supported by the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different fact) situated in the fourth quarter. || 6 ||
*Sumativijaya* is its commentary:
"O Cloud! You who were born and produced in the lineage of the *puṣkarāvartaka* clouds."
I know you. In what kind of lineage? One renowned throughout the world, famous in the three worlds.
Of what nature are you? You are the primordial person (prakṛtipuruṣa), the primary being of Maghavan, that is, Indra.
Furthermore, of what nature are you? You are one who can assume any form at will (kāmarūpa), acting according to your own desire or possessing whatever form you wish.
O Cloud, for that reason, by the power of destiny and the force of karma, I have become a petitioner and a beggar with respect to you.
How am I? I am one whose kinsmen are far away, having my own wife situated at a distance.

For this reason, a request or petition made to a superior person— one who possesses abundant virtues— is better, even if it is fruitless and ineffective; whereas a request or petition made to a base person is not better, even if its desires are attained and it is successful.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).
It is better to employ the neuter gender when there is a desire to express a general sense.
*Arthitva* is the state of being a seeker (*arthin*).
One whose kinsmen are far away (*dūrabandhu*) is one for whom the relatives characterized by a wife are distant.
One whose kinsmen are far away. || 6 ||
O cloud, you are the refuge for those who are tormented; therefore, carry this message from me—separated from my beloved by the wrath of the Lord of Wealth—to her.
Your destination is the city named Alakā, the residence of the lords of the Yakṣas.
The palaces are washed by the moonlight from the head of Hara situated in the outer gardens.
And he says that it is not proper for you not to accept our request: *Vall*.

O Payoda (cloud), since you become a refuge for those tormented by heat through your gift of water, therefore carry, bring, and deliver my message— the news— to my beloved, who is likewise tormented by separation.
The phrase "of one agitated by the anger of the Lord of Wealth" (dhanapati-krodha-vileṣitasya) serves to demonstrate his state of intense suffering.
He asks, "Where must I go? and replies:
"The city named Alakā, the abode of the lords of the Guhyakas—that is where you must go; that is your destination."
And he says that it is not difficult to know:
"In an outer garden, in the grove of Kailāsa. That is, it is both external and a garden;
the palaces situated there have been washed by the moonlight upon the head of Hara who dwells therein.
On which day even the palaces were washed;
[this is an example of] the suffix *ta* used in the sense of the agent of the action, according to Pāṇini 3.4.71.
In response to the inquiry, "What is your request, O Dākṣiṇāvarta?", he says: "Of those who are tormented."
[This refers] to those tormented by the heat [of the sun] and those tormented by desire.
Now, is it not the case that for those tormented by desire, the sight of a cloud is contradictory? For it has been said:
"When a person is intent on embracing one's neck, what need is there to mention when they are far away? Therefore...

How is the meaning "of those tormented by desire" to be understood? It is said: for the cloud, indeed, through the instigation of beloveds who have gone abroad, brings about the union of those separated ones with their beloveds and thereby removes the torment of those couples; therefore, you belong to those who are tormented.
It has been said, "for refuge. He will say later, "he who hastens the multitudes. The syntactical connection is: "O Hari, [deliver] my message to my beloved.
Where does that beloved reside? What is the name of that place, and what are its characteristics?
Regarding the requirement for a destination, he says "gantavya" (to be gone to).
"Alakā" is the name [of the city]; the word "nāma" is used in the sense of renown.
It belongs to the lords of the yakṣas, that is, the chiefs of the yakṣas.
By the phrase "the palace washed by the moonlight from the head of Hara situated in the outer garden," the defining characteristic is stated.
Here, some [maintain that] it is in the Alakā garden of the Supreme Lord residing on Kailāsa.
Considering it inappropriate for [the city] to be situated in Caitraratha, they explain it thus:

the term "garden" (udyāna) is intended here to refer to the area outside of Alakā, which is located on the slopes of Kailāsa. For the word "garden" may apply both to an exit and to a distinct type of forest.
This is because of the statement of Amarasiṃha: "The purpose [is the reason]. || 7 ||
"O Mallinātha,
[the commentary on] the verse beginning with 'santaptānām'..."

O cloud, you are the fever for those who are tormented by the heat of the sun or inflamed by the distress of separation from their loved ones during exile; "santāpa" and "sañjvara" are synonyms, according to Amara.

You are a refuge through the gift of rain for those exhausted by the heat, and a protector through your longing for their own homes for those who have gone abroad; "refuge" (śaraṇa) refers to a house or a protector,
according to Amara.

Therefore, for that reason, carry my message—the news—to my beloved, who has been separated from me by the wrath of Dhanapati (Kubera) and deprived of her; that is to say, deliver it to my beloved. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here in the sense of a general relationship.
The meaning is that by carrying our message, he shall dispel our distress.
To the question of where she resides or what distinguishes that place, he says:
"to be gone to" (*gantavya*).
That which exists outside is "external" (*bāhya*). [The suffix] *yañ* is applied according to the rule *bahir-deva-pañcajanebhyaś-ca*. Thus, it is "external" (*bāhya*).

It is described as such because its palaces—the dwellings of the wealthy—are washed clean and rendered spotless by the moonlight upon the head of Hara (Śiva) as he stays in the garden; "harmya" and similar terms denote the residences of the rich, according to Amara. By this, the distinguishing characteristic [of the city] is stated.
The city named Alakā, renowned as Alakā, is the abode and dwelling place of the lords of the Yakṣas;
it is to be gone to by you—the meaning is that you must go there. The genitive case is used according to the rule "kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā" (Pāṇini 2.3.71). ||7||
*Sumativijaya* provides the commentary on this:
O *payoda*, cloud, you [are the refuge] for people tormented by the heat of summer.
You are my refuge. For that reason, carry—bring—to my beloved wife my message in the form of news concerning me;
for me, who have been separated by the anger of the Lord of Wealth (Dhanapati).
Of that which has been separated [from the compound]:

"O Cloud, there is a place of residence, a dwelling-place named Alakā, belonging to you—the lords of the Yakṣas—which is to be gone to. Alternatively, "Alakā is to be gone to by you. [This is used] in the sense of the locative case.
The third case [is used] due to its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛt*).
What is it? Dwelling, that is, residence.
Of whom? Of the lords of the Yakṣas.
Of what nature was Alakā? Its palaces were washed by the moonlight of Śiva, who resides in the outer gardens; such is the grammatical construction.
"Dhanapati" means one who has been separated or parted from Dhanapati due to his anger;
[the phrase] "dhanapatikrodhaviśleṣitasya" refers to one who has been separated by that anger of Dhanapati.
"Bāhyodyāna" refers to Mahādeva, who resides in the outer garden; [the phrase] "tacchirasī" means upon his head.

"Candrikā" means moonlight; "bāhyodyānasthitaharaśiraścandrikādhautaharmyā" refers to that [city] whose palaces (*harmyāni*)—meaning houses—are washed white by the moonlight from the head of Hara (Śiva) situated in the outer garden. The plural number is used because of the rule *gurāvekaśca* ("the singular may be used for a group").
As you ascend the path of the wind, the wives of travelers, their tresses disheveled, will gaze upon you with renewed hope;
for who, when you are thus equipped, would neglect a wife distressed by separation?
There would be no other person like me who lives dependent on others. || 8 ||
O travelers' wives separated from their lovers, you are taking heart as you behold the sky, which has risen up like the path of the wind.
They will see [the clouds] by lifting up their faces;
for, gaining confidence through the arising of certainty, they take heart, thinking:
"This cloud has risen; here, our lords of life must surely be present."
"One must come"—why is hope placed in the mere sight of him? He says:
when you have girded yourself and made the effort [to go], who would neglect his beloved, who is distressed by separation?
He would have been separated [from her], had there not been another person such as he. Of what sort was he? One like me, whose livelihood is dependent on others.
Alternatively, the connection here is: "What other person would neglect his wife? For men, sporting with their beloveds who are under their own control, pass the rainy season.
Words such as "sannaddha" (equipped) and others are used figuratively in such contexts.
"O Dākṣiṇāvarta, if you prepare yourself for my task, it will not be a source of consolation for me alone, but for other people as well"— with this intention, he said to you: "tvām."
"Mounted," it is said.
The path of the wind is the sky.
"With their tresses uplifted" refers to the lifting up of the hair because it hangs from the cheeks due to separation from their beloveds.
"From confidence" (*pratyayāt*) means from the trust [arising] at the arrival of the beloved.

Regarding the reading *āśvasatyaḥ*, it is a form devoid of the *num* augment. Here, some [grammarians] derive [the word] from the root *kṣamūṣ* (to endure) by applying the rule for *ṣit* roots—namely, *ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.104)—to effect the *ṣit* operation.

Since the *ṣit* designation in the rule *kṣamūṛ* (Pāṇini 1.3.60) is established as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that operations based on the *gaṇa*-lists are not invariably applicable, for this very reason, in the expression *na viśvaset pūrvavirodhine*, the *luṅ* suffix does not occur after *śap*;
likewise, in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, it is said: *āśvaseyur niśācarāḥ*.
Therefore, some explain that the reading should include the augment *num*, as in *āśvasantyaḥ*.

That is not correct; for the form is established even otherwise. In this case, the establishment of the form occurs precisely by relying on the fact that the operation of the *gaṇa* [of roots] is non-eternal (*anitya*).
Enough with this detailed discussion; he speaks what is logical.
"Sannaddhe" means one who has equipped himself [for battle] and is intent on returning from his expedition.
"Virahavidhurām" means afflicted by separation; that is to say, distressed by separation and fallen into the hardship of separation.
Regarding the word *vidhura*, Yādava states: "The word *vidhura* may mean one whose wife is gone, as well as one who is distressed or separated."

"Another" means even one who is unlike me, even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the word *anya*, Yādava states: "The word *anya* [is used] in the senses of 'different' and 'unlike'. "This person like me" means "like myself.
Just as my own livelihood is dependent on others, so too is that of the ordinary person.
The meaning is: even one whose livelihood is dependent on others would not do so; for who, while you are prepared, would neglect his wife? || 8 ||
Mallinātha says: "The consolation of the wives of travelers is a secondary benefit for you who have set out for my sake"; thus he says, "You... [and so forth].

When you have ascended the sky, the path of the wind, those travelers go along their paths— the suffix *ṣkan* is applied here according to the rule *pathaḥ ṣkan*. Their wives are those whose husbands are away on a journey (*proṣitabhartṛkāḥ*).

"From confidence" (*pratyayāt*) means from the trust [inspired] by the arrival of their beloveds. According to Amara, *pratyaya* is used in the senses of dependence, oath, knowledge, cause, and trust. "Confident" (*āśvasantaḥ*) means those who have placed their trust; this is derived from the root *śvas* with the suffix *śatṛ*, according to the rule *ugitaśca*.
The suffix *ṅip*.

Likewise, having raised their forelocks so that their curls hang down, and holding the tips of their locks up in order to extend their vision, the women will gaze; the meaning is that they will look with extreme longing.
Regarding how travelers will proceed upon my arrival, he says:
"For indeed, when you are armored and engaged [in battle], who would neglect a wife distressed and helpless by separation? The meaning is: no one at all."

The meaning is that even another person, distinct from me, who— like me— is dependent for his livelihood upon others and whose life is sustained by others, would not remain indifferent; for indeed, no one who is independent would ever neglect such a situation.

Here, the figure of speech is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth). As it has been stated: "Where there is a mutual support between cause and effect, or between the general and the particular, that is illustrated as *arthāntaranyāsa*," according to its definition.
The summary of the victory of this commentary.
O cloud, the wives of travelers behold you.
In what state are you? Ascended—that is, mounted—into the path of the wind, which is the sky.
In what state are the wives of the travelers? With the ends of their tresses raised up.
With their hair standing on end,

what are the wives of travelers doing? They are taking heart— that is, they are becoming composed— out of conviction and certainty that, with the arrival of the clouds, their husband will surely return.
The meaning is this: O cloud, what person would neglect— that is, abandon— a wife distressed by separation, tormented by the pain of being apart from her husband?

Under what condition? When you, the cloud, have become prepared—that is, when lightning, thunder, and so forth have arisen—then, O cloud, no other person either, like me, would be one whose livelihood is dependent on another; that is, he would not be subject to fate. This is the syntactical connection.
The figure of speech is *vyatireka* (contrast).

Regarding the term *udgṛhītā*: those [women] by whom the ends—the tips—of the *alakas*, that is, the locks of hair, have been *udgṛhītāḥ*, meaning raised upward; these are *udgṛhītālakāntāḥ*. This refers to women separated from their lovers (*virahiṇī*).
The sense is that because there is no tying of the hair, they are those whose hair is unbound (*agranthitakeśāntāḥ*).
One whose livelihood (*vṛttiḥ*), meaning subsistence (*ājīvikā*), is dependent on another—that is, under the control of another—is "one whose livelihood is dependent on others" (*parādhīnavṛttiḥ*).
The sense is that he is dependent upon wealth.

"Pathikānāṃ vanitāḥ striyaḥ" means "pathikavanitāḥ," which signifies the wives of travelers. The word *pratyaya* has multiple meanings, such as confidence, oath, knowledge, certainty, and so forth. (8)
Take leave of this lofty mountain, your dear friend, whose slopes are marked by the footprints of the Lord of the Raghus— footprints worthy of adoration by men;
for it is by coming into contact with him from time to time that you attain excellence at every stage of your growth.
He sheds warm tears born of long separation, manifesting his affection for you.
Now, Valli generally states the instruction.
Embracing this mountain Citrakūṭa, bid it farewell with longing and look upon it for a long time;
for mountains are the dear friends and beloved companions of the clouds.
Therefore, because of their arising, the friend is made to linger at the time of departure.
Of what nature is this [mountain]? It is lofty and high;
furthermore, it is marked—that is, impressed—with the footprints of Rāma, which are worthy of worship by all people. This is a statement regarding its sanctity.
He describes the duty of a friend:
that mountain, at all times— specifically at every occasion of union— having attained union with you,
sheds the heat of tears born of long separation.
The manifestation of affection occurs; the meaning is "he who feels affection."
For mountains indeed become moistened by the rain from the clouds and emit vapor;
this very thing constitutes friendship—that upon seeing a friend after a long time, tears and affection arise.
[In the phrase] "āpṛcchasva," the *ātmanepada* ending is used according to the rule *āṅi nupracchyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.21).
"Priyasakhaḥ" means "he who is dear and a friend. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.91 (*rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*).
The expression "having reached a state of union" refers to the priority of the shedding of tears.
Or [it is] dependent upon the act of affection. || 9 ||
"O Dākṣiṇāvarta,
take your leave."

"Take leave of him" means "honor him" or "pay him respect. The *ātmanepada* ending is used here because of the Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.3.21, which prescribes it for the roots *pra-cch* and *nū* when preceded by the prefix *ā*. According to Amara, *ā-pracchana* means "greeting," "welcoming," or "honoring."

By the question "I am going there," the intention is to express that worship [is due]. He says, "by men who are not barren," to show that this mountain must be honored not only because of its friendship with you, but also because it is occupied by distinguished persons.
Marked by its movement; upon the ridges of the mountain ranges.
To the question, "How is it known that he has friendship with me?
he says: "O Time! O Time! For every year, this is the season for the meeting of friends.
The intended meaning is as follows: *snehavyaktiḥ* means the manifestation of affection;
*bāṣpa* refers to both steam and tears, for Yādava states that *bāṣpa* denotes tears, water, and smoke; *uṣṇam* means "hot," in the sense of being hot due to arising from long separation.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Upon attaining union with you, he sheds hot tears born of long separation; thus, the manifestation of his affection occurs.
Here, a certain friend, seeing a friend who has arrived from afar—

The meaning is that, by shedding tears heated by long separation, he manifests his affection; this is to be understood as being conveyed through the poetic figure of *khaṇḍaśleṣa* (partial punning). || 12 || — Mallinātha.
"Take your leave," he said.

"Priyaṃ sakhāyaṃ priyasakham" [is the analysis]; the suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaḥ ṭac. "Tuṅgam" means elevated. By the footprints of the Lord of the Raghus (Rāma)—which are worthy of being honored by men and which are to be worshipped—[the mountain is adorned] upon its ridges (*mekhalāsu*), that is, its slopes (*kaṭakeṣu*). Now...

*Mekhalā* [means] at the place of the hips, on the peak-like ridge of the waist; Yādava says it means "the binding of the loins. *Aṅkitam* means marked or characterized. Thus, because of friendship, greatness, and purity—
Worthy of honor:

O virtuous one, having embraced this mountain Citrakūṭādri, bid it farewell with the address "I am going," and thus pay it homage. [The terms] *āmantraṇa* (addressing), *sabhājana* (honoring), and *āpracchana* (taking leave) are used here.

Amaras: The reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed by the *vārttika* "An addition [should be made] for the roots *nṛ* and *pracch* with the prefix *ā*" (Pāṇini 1.3.21 vārttika). [The question is: "Does time fulfill the state of friendship? At every time, that is, at every rainy season (*prāvṛṭkāla*), it is also the time for meeting with friends.
By the word *kāla* (time), you express repetition; having come into contact (*saṃyogam*) or union with the heat born of long separation— the *bāṣpa*,
which according to the *Viśvakośa* refers to both eye-water and vapor— he, that mountain, was shedding it.

The manifestation of affection (*snehavyakti*) is the emergence of love (*premāvirbhāva*). For it is the nature of those who are affectionate that tears fall when they are reunited after a long separation; such is the meaning. (12) —9— Sumativijaya.

The commentary on this: O cloud, having embraced—meaning having closely approached and joined with—this mountain, Rāmagiri, you should bid it farewell, that is, speak with it. O cloud, at the proper time, meaning during the rainy season.
Affection becomes manifest; love is revealed.
Having done what? Having reached, that is, having attained, union—that is, conjunction—with you, O Mountain.
What were you doing? Shedding hot tears born of long separation—that is, arising from a long period of parting.
Of what nature was the mountain? Your dear friend, your beloved companion.
Furthermore, of what nature was the mountain? Lofty, that is, very high.
Furthermore, of what nature was the mountain? Marked by the footprints of the Lord of the Raghus, signified by the feet of Śrī Rāmacandra.
In what? In the girdles, that is, in the sunken parts.

Of what kind were the footprints of the Lord of the Raghus? Venerable to men; the genitive case is used here in the sense of the agent of the action (of being venerable). They are praiseworthy by men.
Such is the grammatical connection (anvaya).
The repetition "kāle kāle" (at every moment) is used for emphasis (*vīpsā*). By saying "at every moment," it is merely indicated that the affection is of long standing.
"Sneha" refers to the manifestation, the becoming manifest, or the particularity of affection—that is, love.
The manifestation of affection (*snehavyakti*). "After a long time" (*cireti*) means born from a long separation (*ciravirahaja*).
The sense is that just as another person, being pained by the sorrow of separation, sheds warm tears upon meeting their beloved, so too does the cloud.
The poetic figure is *svabhāvokti* (description of inherent nature). 13.
-9- The favorable breeze pushes you along very gently, and this cātaka bird, longing for water, warbles sweetly on your left.
Surely, the cranes— long accustomed to their young and now forming their rows—
will attend upon you in the sky, who are so pleasing to the eye.
°kṣamaparicayās Da, °kṣaṇaparicayās Ma, °kṣaṇaparicayāt Su; °subhagās Da; VALL.
And he spoke thus, providing encouragement by describing auspicious omens: "You shall not be alone."
Just as this beauty is perceived, so shall the cranes in the sky certainly serve and take refuge in you, who are so pleasing to the eye;
for what reason? Because the favorable wind impels you very gently.
Just as this cātaka bird or peacock warbles sweetly—
whether on the left side or staying on the right, speaking charmingly— and is greedy for water, longing for water.
From the sight of the rain-clouds in the monsoon, the cranes too will arrive;
this is the nature of the rainy season.
Of what sort are they? They are those whose acquaintance has become firm through the act of conception.
For it is the report that they will become pregnant by the thundering of the clouds;
they have formed garlands and arranged themselves in rows.
The doubling [of the word] in "mandaṃ mandam" is used to express intensity. 10.
"O Dākṣiṇāvarta,
by this omen, it is intended that before you even behold my beloved,
a reunion with your own dear one shall occur," he said very softly.
"It pushes."
In this case, the favorable nature of the gentle breeze is the cause. Likewise, Varāhamihira states regarding a great expedition:
"One who has cast up fire, dust, leaves, birds, umbrellas, banners, and fans..."
A wind that is foul-smelling, causes exhaustion from the discharge of ichor by elephants, or arises from clods of earth being thrown together, brings misfortune;
whereas a wind that is desirable, auspicious, follows one on a journey, requires little effort, is refreshing, fragrant, moves clockwise, and is substantial, bestows success. Thus it is said.
And it has been said:
"Because of the favorability of the wind, it portends the fulfillment of one's prayers" (Raghuvamśa 1.42).
In the phrase "and the wind," the word "and" (ca) indicates another cause, namely, the favorability of the crow.
It is collected [as follows]. The word *yathā* denotes similarity (*sādṛśya*). Similarity is the correspondence between cause and effect.
As Yādava says: "The meanings of *yathā* are similarity, fitness, repetition, and non-transgression. Now...
Alternatively, the word *yathā* is used in the sense of *yasmāt* (because). The means of proof (*pramāṇa*) must be sought.
The meaning is: "Just as a favorable breeze pushes you very gently, so too shall there be union with the female crane."

"Vāma" means situated on the left side. The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is to be understood according to the manner previously stated. "Nadati" means it makes a sound. "Madhuram" means pleasant to hear.
Regarding "sagandha," Halāyudha states: "Sagandha is desired as a kinsman."
One should appoint as ministers those who have served one's father and grandfather, because they have been tested in times of adversity.
For they do not abandon him even when he acts improperly, due to their shared lineage (*sagandhatvāt*).
Kauṭilya employs the word *sagandha* in reference to kinsmen; here too, the word *yathā* [is used] in the same sense.
This is to be added: regarding the cry of a cātaka bird perched on the left side as being an omen for a journey, Varāhamihira states in the *Yogayātrā*:
"The *cucundarī*, the female pig, the jackal, the *śyāmā*, the *gallī*, the *piṅgalikā*, and the *anyapuṣṭā* [are likewise considered]."
Female house-lizards are auspicious, as are those known as male and those that are birds.

Thus; it should be understood that by this [verse], the male *cātaka* bird is also included by the word "puṃs" (male). Likewise, in the *Mahāyātrā*, that same Varāhamihira prohibits the cry of the *cātaka* with reference to a specific time.
"But pigs, dogs, wolves, and the like are not to be accepted in Bhādrapada; lotuses, goats, and krauñca birds in Śarad; and elephants and cātaka birds in Śrāvaṇa.
Thus, because of the prohibition regarding specific times, the cry of the cātaka serves as the causal factor [for the rite] at a time that is not prohibited.
It is understood as follows: due to its association with that which is capable of conceiving an embryo (*garbha*), the word *garbha* denotes a living being residing within the womb.
[The word *garbha* is used for] a chamber, food, fire, a son, the seed of a jackfruit, and the belly.

And regarding "kukṣisthajantau," Yādava [states that] the word *kṣama* denotes capability. Amara [says]: "The words *kṣiti*, *kṣānti*, and *kṣamā* denote patience; *kṣama* is used in three genders for what is capable and for what is beneficial. Thus, it means "familiarity capable of [ensuring] conception" (*garbhādhāna-śakta-paricaya*), from which [the phrase is derived].
This is because it is well known that the crane conceives through union with the cloud.
Furthermore, there is the observation of a sign [in the *Rāmāyaṇa* 4.28.26]: "The row of cranes, longing for the clouds, flies about and appears utterly bewildered."
"Nūnam" signifies certainty; according to Amara, "nūnam" is used for conjecture as well as certainty.
It also suggests the meanings "having formed rows" and "having bound garlands of flowers. Furthermore, this qualifying term "delightful to the eyes" applies to the cranes (*balākā*).
This is the mark of the Meghapriyā-samādhi. "In the sky" means in the atmosphere; by this, a secluded place is also implied. — Mallinātha, verses 9–10.
He says "very slowly, very slowly" because even auspicious signs are being seen by you.

"Favorable" (anukūlaḥ) means the wind blows toward you "very gently" (mandaṃ mandam); the sense here is "extremely gently. In this case, the repetition must somehow be justified as being for the sake of emphasis (vīpsā). However, if one were to rely on the rule *prakāre guṇavacanasya*, then by treating it as a *karmadhāraya*-like compound...

When the *luk* elision occurs, the form would be *mandamandam*. Vāmana expresses this very point by stating that in the case of *mandamandam*, there is reduplication for the sake of indicating the manner (*prakāra*).
For example, it means "similarly" or "in accordance with the future result. As, for instance:
"Yādava states that *sādṛśya* (similarity), *yogyatva* (fitness), *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution), and *anatikrama* (non-transgression) [are the meanings of the prefix *sa-*].
It means "it pushes" or "it impels. Some say that this term *sagandhaḥ* means "proud" (*sagarvaḥ*) or "related" (*sambandhī*).
Regarding both [meanings], it is stated: "*gandhaḥ* [is used] in the sense of sulphur (*gandhaka*), fragrance (*āmoda*), a trace (*leśa*), as well as relationship (*sambandha*) and pride (*garva*)."
"Viśvaḥ": O Lord, your *vāma*—that which resides in the left portion—is indeed *vāma*. According to the *Śabdārṇava*, the word *vāma* may mean "crooked," "charming," "left," or "moving to the left."
The *cātaka*, a specific kind of bird, also warbles—that is, it utters—sweet and pleasant sounds.
These two omens are present; he says "garbha" because another omen will also occur. *Garbha* refers to a creature residing within the womb. For when the fire that nourishes the embryo [is present]...
Regarding the phrase "in the pleasure, in the jackfruit thorn, in the womb, and in the creature dwelling in the womb," the Yādavas [explain] that its *ādhāna*—
its production— is itself the festival (*kṣaṇa-utsava*). The sense is that this is because it is a cause of pleasure.
According to Amara, the word *kṣaṇa* denotes a specific time or a festival during a state of inactivity.

For that reason—due to familiarity, that is, through repeated practice—in the sky (*khe*), they have formed a continuous line (*ābaddhamālā*) near you for the sake of the pleasure of conception (*garbhādhāna*). They have arranged themselves in rows in your vicinity.
This is the meaning. And it is said in the *Karṇodaya*: "The female cranes, forming circles all around in the sky through their connection with the clouds, bear the embryo.
The female crane (*balākā*) [beholds] you, who are pleasing to the eyes and have seen her beloved.
They will surely resort to the truth.

The auspiciousness indicated by favorable winds, the cries of cātakas, and the sight of cranes is observed in the treatises on omens (śakuna-śāstra); however, it has not been recorded here for fear of prolixity. || 10 ||
This is the commentary on the *Sumativijaya*:
O cloud, the wind— meaning the breeze— blows very gently, that is, slowly and by degrees, upon you.
In that same manner, this *cātaka* bird, standing on your left side, utters sweet and pleasing words; it cries out from the right. Of what nature is the wind? It is favorable, following behind you.
In what state is the *cātaka*? It is full of pride and joy due to its attainment of water.
O Cloud, surely (*nūnam*)—meaning with certainty—the female cranes (*balākā*), the wives of the *baka* birds, will serve you in the sky (*kha*).
In what manner do they serve you? You who are "delightful to the eyes" (*nayanasubhagam*), providing pleasure to the sight.
Why? Because of the familiarity with the moment of conception—that is, the occasion of taking up the embryo.
This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
In this poem, two *ca* particles indicate simultaneity.

Regarding the word *balākā*: they are called *balākās* because they go (*akanti*) with a curved (*vakra*) motion due to their strength (*bala*), namely youth and pride; the root for this word is *aka*, meaning "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*). (Dhātupāṭha 1.829)

"At the time of conception" (*garbhe*) means at the moment of the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*); "from that which has acquaintance with it for a mere moment" refers to that [moment] characterized by contact for only an instant.
For in the rainy season, the festival of conception occurs every year precisely upon the arrival of the clouds.

For those wives of the cranes, it was so because of long-standing familiarity; indeed, for women, the conception of a child is a great festival.
