You shall see your brother’s wife unharmed and her gait unhindered;
for the bond of hope generally restrains the heart of women, which is like a flower and prone to wither instantly upon separation.
Then, [it is] mostly similar; for indeed, Da; even one whose life-force is similar, Da; it protects, Ma, Su;
VALL.
And he says that your affliction will not be in vain:

You behold that wife of your brother, the spouse of your friend, certainly unharmed and as if immortal. Of what sort is she? She is intent on counting the days. How much time has passed? How much [more remains]?
"Remaining"—this refers to her being intent on counting [the days] until the limit. Because she is a devoted wife with a single husband; that is, one whose husband is alone.
If she is such as this, then how is it that she is "unharmed"? To this he says:

Because, when separated from their beloveds, the hope that women place in them generally restrains and sustains their hearts; since that heart is like a flower, it is for this very reason prone to immediate falling—that is, on the verge of perishing at that very moment. Such being the case...
It is sustained by hope, thinking: "Surely there will be a reunion with our beloved again. This bond of hope is like a literal tethering rope.
Just as the snare of a spider—the weaving of its threads—obstructs even a dry flower driven by the wind;
the word "ca" (and) serves for conjunction in reference to the preceding sentence, as it does elsewhere. *Praṇaya* means affection, love, or longing.
In the word *ekapatnīm*, the suffixes *ṅīp* and *nañ* are permanently excluded by [Pāṇini 4.1.35] *sapatny-ādiṣu*.
In the word *bhrātṛjāyā*, the absence of elision (*aluk*) [of the genitive case-ending] as prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.3.23] *ṛto vidyā-yoni-sambandhebhyaḥ* is to be considered problematic.
"And that [conch] must necessarily be one that spirals to the right."

It was said that she might not have perished in my absence because she was intent on counting the days and because the duration of our separation was fixed; let her live as she pleases. However, if her virtue were to be compromised, your request would become futile.

Anticipating this objection, he says "ekapatnīm. The term *ekapatnī* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who has no rival wife" (*asapatnīkā*) and is worthy of being a wife (*patnī*) through her connection with the sacrifice.
Because she possesses both the state of having no rival wife and the status of a wife, there is no violation of her virtuous character (*śīla*).
This is the intended meaning. Therefore, she is "unharmed" (avyāpannām).
You are one whose movement is unimpeded (avihatagatiḥ), meaning your gait is free from obstacles.
By this [description], the prohibition against looking at another's wife does not apply to you here, as she is your brother’s wife.

It has been said that she is "the wife of your brother. Indeed, women are by nature of tender hearts; therefore, suspecting how she could have lived for such a long time by merely counting the days, he says: "Hope..."

And so forth. "The bond of hope" (*āśābandha*) refers to the longing that "if my beloved lives, there will be a reunion with him at another time. By the term "bond of hope," the metaphorical identification (*samādhi*) with shackles is intended.
It is called "ruṇaddhi" (it obstructs) because the function of a bolt will be described later.

"Kusumasadṛśaprāṇam" means having life-force like a flower, or strength like a flower. Regarding the word *prāṇa*, Keśavasvāmin states: "In the masculine gender, *prāṇa* denotes wind, strength, the earth, and the vital breath. For [life] is generally like a flower.
Some read "aṅganānām" (of women). The reading is "sadyaḥpātapraṇayī"; it means having the habit of praying for an immediate fall [into his arms] at the time of separation. —10–11— Mallinātha.
And her destruction or a lapse in her vow would not render your effort fruitless;
thus he says, "And her... and so forth.
She was intent—meaning absorbed and devoted—to counting the days remaining until the end of the monsoon; for Amara states that *tatpara* means "absorbed" or "devoted.
For this very reason, she was unharmed—that is, not dead—at the conclusion of the curse.
The meaning is that they live in the hope of my return.
"Ekapatnīm" means one who has but a single husband; that is to say, a devoted wife (*pativratā*). The feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the nasal *n* are applied according to the rule "nityaṃ sapatnyādiṣu."
"Bhrātṛjāyām" means the wife of one's brother; the intention is that she is as free from suspicion as a brother, and thus worthy of being looked upon. "Tām" refers to her, my beloved.

Being one whose movement is unimpeded and whose course is uninterrupted, you will certainly see—that is, you will indeed behold it. For "āśā" signifies both direction and thirst; thus says Yādava: "Āśā [denotes] direction and thirst."
That by which one is bound is a "bond" (*bandha*), meaning a fetter; that is to say, a stalk. "The bond of hope" (*āśābandha*) refers to hope itself as the agent of binding.
"Affectionate" means endowed with love, and for that very reason, it is "like a flower," meaning delicate.

For this very reason, in separation—that is, in the absence of the beloved—the heart (or life) of women is prone to immediate collapse; for the *Śabdārṇava* states that "heart" (*hṛdaya*) may refer to life, the mind, the chest, intention, or what is dear. Generally, it obstructs [the flow of life].
It obstructs. This is the *arthāntaranyāsa* [figure of speech].
—11— This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.

Furthermore, O Megha, you will certainly and inevitably see—that is, behold—that brother’s wife, the husband’s consort. In what state is she? She is intent upon counting the days, being attentive to the calculation of the days.
Furthermore, of what nature was she? A virtuous woman with but one husband.
Furthermore, of what nature was she? Unimpaired, that is, living.
Of what nature were you? With unimpeded movement, or with movement unerring, by virtue of the wind.
For this reason— that is, because the bond of hope generally, or for the most part, restrains and sustains the hearts and minds of women from death caused by separation—
what is it? It is the bond of hope.

Under what condition? When there is separation—that is, when there is a parting from their husbands. Of what nature is the heart of women? It is like a flower—equal to a blossom, as delicate as a flower.
Furthermore, of what nature is the heart? It is "sadyaḥpāti," meaning having the quality of falling immediately. Again, of what nature is it? It is "praṇayi," meaning endowed with affection.
Such is the grammatical construction.
"Divaseti": *divasagaṇanātatparām* means "intent on counting the days";
[the compound refers to] her who is intent on counting the days.
"Eketi": *ekapatnī* means "she whose husband is only one," namely, myself.

Pāṇini [states in 4.1.32]: "The augment *nuK* is applied after the words *antarvat* and *pativat*, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ī*. Thus, it is *avyāpannā*; she who is not corrupted is *avyāpannā*.
Regarding *avī*: he whose gait (*gati*) is unhindered (*avihatā*), that is, unimpeded due to the force of the wind (*vāyuvaśāt*).
"Unimpeded movement.
Regarding "dṛśi" in the sense of "seeing": is it the action [expressed] as "you will see" (drakṣyasi) in the eighth lakāra, the suffix syap? No.
Regarding "bhrātṛ": the wife of a brother is *bhrātṛjāyā*; [he approached] that *bhrātṛjāyā*.
Having heard your thunder, which is auspicious to the ear and capable of making the earth fertile with sprouts of *śilīndhra* mushrooms, those cranes, longing for Lake Mānasa,
carry provisions of lotus-stalk shoots from Mount Kailāsa.
Your royal swans, your companions, will find their way through the sky to the fruitful *ucchilīndhra* flowers.
With its parasol-like canopy of spreading branches, with its shoots like slender arrows—
Vallī.
Having heard this intimation of your intent, your royal swans, your followers,
will proceed as far as Mount Kailāsa;
for they are longing for Lake Mānasa and their minds are fixed upon it, especially during the rainy season when they seek refuge there.
They go there. What is that thundering? He says:
it is that which [shakes] the earth, the ground, covered with *ucchilindhra* flowers—flowers known by the name *ucchilindra*—that have sprouted forth.
It is capable of, that is, able to, bring about [those results]. For those [results] arise from the thundering of clouds; therefore, it is not barren, but fruitful.
"Delightful to hear," meaning causing pleasure to the ears—this consists of four words.
What kind of swans? They are described as such because they possess as their provisions for the journey (pātheya)— that is, their food on the way— the cutting or fragments of lotus stalks (bisāni).
The analysis of the compound is: "possessing provisions for the journey" (*pātheyavantaḥ*) by means of the cutting of fresh sprouts (*kisalaya*).
The term "up to Kailāsa" (*ā kailāsāt*) is an optional *avyayībhāva* compound. 12.
! *Dakṣiṇāvarta* 11.
He says "to do" [in the verse] because companions will arise for you on the path.

The word *cakāraḥ* (the letter *ca*) is connected with the term *sahāyāḥ* (companions). *Utsilindhram* means one from which *kandalikā* (young shoots) have emerged; for this very reason, it is *avandhyam* (not barren). By this word, it should be understood that the thundering is described as belonging to the rainy season (*vārṣikatvam*).
"Delightful to the ear" means pleasant to the hearing of royal swans;
it is well known that the thundering of clouds is harsh. And he will say later: "In whose water they have made their dwelling," and so forth. Therefore, how [can it be said] of the swans...?
It was said that [the lake] is pleasant to hear; this is true.

Yet, while it is somewhat harsh due to the abandonment of the tanks and other sites they had occupied, it is exceedingly dear because it is the cause for their departure to Mānasa-taṭāka, which has become their own place of residence.

And it is said: "In some places, [the lakes] are dear to the birds who frequent Lake Mānasa" (Raghuvamśa 13.55). Now, if the swans are indeed fond of Lake Mānasa, for what reason have they abandoned it to go to another region?

They wander about. It is said that because the waters and other elements of Lake Mānasa, situated in a certain region of the Himālaya, become unfit for enjoyment due to being corrupted by frost, they then travel to other regions. However, during the rainy season, because the frost is dispersed by the rainwater, [the lake becomes fit for use].
It possesses the fitness to be a dwelling place for swans; because it is eternally serene,
it does not become turbid like the lakes of other regions— this is what the northerners teach, so it should be understood.
"Longing for Lake Mānasa," "eager for Lake Mānasa"— this is a sign of a beloved person's longing for Lake Mānasa.
It should be understood that by this word, the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of calling upon a companion for a man about to depart for the world is intended.
"Carrying provisions consisting of cuttings of fresh lotus stalks. *Pātheya* refers to food fit for a journey;
the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied according to the rule *pathyatithivasatisvapater ḍhañ*.
Although one could have simply said "carrying cuttings of fresh lotus stalks as provisions," the intended meaning is nonetheless established [by the use of the compound].
Nevertheless, it should be understood that the possessive suffix *matup* has been employed for the sake of clarity:
"The path must be traversed by this [person] accompanied by helpers."
It was indicated [by the word *rājahaṃsa*]. *Rājahaṃsas* are those swans whose beaks and feet are red;
"the *rājahaṃsas*, however, are white with red beaks and feet," according to Amara. (11) — Mallinātha.
He says "to act" (kartum) to show that he also possesses the excellence of having assistants at this time.
That which roars makes the earth covered in mushrooms (*ucchilindhra*) and sprouting *kandalī* shoots;

for it is stated in the *Śabdārṇava* that "in the word *kandalī*, there may be *śilīndhra*. Therefore, it is able—that is, capable—to make [the earth] fruitful, meaning not barren. Of the mushrooms...
The meaning is that it indicates the future abundance of crops. As it has been said in the *Nimittanidāna*:
"Mushrooms that have arisen through the conjunction with seasonal clouds announce that the earth is rich with ripened grain."

That is pleasant to the ear; "of the world" is the ellipsis. Having heard your roar, they become *mānasotsukāḥ*—that is, longing for Lake Mānasa, their minds turned toward it. "Longing" (*utsuka*) is the intended meaning.
The forms *utkaḥ* and *unmanāḥ* are correct by virtue of being established as irregular (*nipāta*). This is because at other times, Lake Mānasa is afflicted by frost.
It is well known that because cold weather causes disease to swans, they depart elsewhere, only to return to Lake Mānasa again during the rainy season.
[This refers to] the fragments or pieces resulting from the cutting of *bisakisalaya*, which are the tips of lotus stalks (*mṛṇāla*).
"Pātheyavantaḥ" means those possessing provisions for a journey; "pātheya" refers to food suitable for the road.
[The suffix] ḍhañ [is applied] after the words *pathin*, *atithi*, *vasati*, and *svapati*. Thus, they possess that [provisions].
The meaning is that they possess connections with fragments of lotus-stalk tips.
*Rājahaṃsas* are a specific kind of swan; according to Amara, "the *rājahaṃsa* is white with red beak and feet.

In the sky (*nabhasi*), that is, in the atmosphere (*vyomni*), from Kailāsa up to the edge of Kailāsa—these two words form a compound (*dvandva*). *Sahāyas* means those who have set out on a journey (*sayātras*); *sahāya* is synonymous with *sayātra*.
"May it be so," [it is said] in the *Śabdārṇava*. "They will be accomplished" means they will come into being.
—12— This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.
O Lord, as you proceed from one Kailāsa to another Kailāsa mountain, royal swans shall become your companions and friends.
Where? In the sky, or in the month of Śrāvaṇa. Having done what? Having heard that thundering roar of yours.

Of what nature were the royal swans? They possessed provisions for their journey consisting of cuttings of young *viśa* sprouts, and they were equipped with bundles of lotus-fiber threads as their travel gear.
Of what nature was the thundering? It was pleasant to hear, providing delight to the ears. And furthermore—
The grammatical construction (*anvaya*) is as follows: that thunder which is capable— that is, has the power— to make the vast earth such that its royal umbrellas are uprooted.

"Viśakiśalayacchedapātheyāntaḥ" refers to those for whom the lotus stalks, sprouts, and buds— their very fragments— constitute the provisions for the journey (pātheya) or the travel-baggage (śambala).

"Ucchilamdhrātapatrām": *ucchilamdhrāṇi* means those things which have their openings turned upwards, namely, small earthen pots used as umbrellas; that [city] in which these very pots serve as sunshades (*ātapatra*) is *ucchilamdhrātapatrā*; [the word refers to] that [city], *ucchilamdhrātapatrām*. || 12 ||
O cloud, first hear from me as I describe the primary route favorable for your journey; thereafter you shall hear my message, which is a draught for the ears.
When you are weary, you shall rest your feet upon the mountain peaks and proceed;
when exhausted, you shall drink the very light water of the flowing streams. (13) 11 Su;
Ma, Su, Da; *anurūpam* Ma, Su, Da; *śrāvyabandham* Da; *upabhujya* Ma, Su, Da;
VALL:
O cloud, listen for a moment to me as I speak of the path suitable for your journey.
Immediately thereafter, you shall hear—that is, you shall listen to—a message that is to be drunk by the ears and that brings delight to the ears.
To explain the suitability of the path, he says: "weary for the weary."

Exhausted as you are on that path, where you will go by placing one foot after another upon the mountains; and having consumed—that is, drunk—the light water of the rivers, which is now nearly exhausted, you will proceed quickly. For drinking and rest are of the utmost importance on a journey.
These two are employed [as examples].
Expressions such as *tadanu* and *tadupari* are considered correct because they are seen in the usage of ancient poets;
for indeed, a genitive compound with an indeclinable is prohibited.

In the rule *śtotrapeyam iti kṛtyair adhikārthavacane*, it is stated that when there is an expression of excess (*ādhikya*), reduplication (*dvitva*) occurs— as in *khinnaḥ khinnaḥ* and so forth— and because this functions like a *karmadhāraya* compound,
there is no elision of the case-ending (*sub-luk*). Furthermore, the fact that reduplication occurs to express excess is indicated by the use of the technical term *āmreḍita*.
"Gantāsi" is the periphrastic future (luṭ).
"Parilaghu" is an adverbial modifier (kriyāviśeṣaṇa) of the action. || 13 ||
"The path that turns to the right."
Regarding the reading "mārgaṃ mattaḥ śṛṇu kathayata," the word *mattaḥ* is in the ablative case.
In the reading "mārgaṃ tāvat kathayata," one should note that there is no qualifying noun (*viśeṣyapada*) for the word *kathayata*.

The "message" (sandeśa) is that which will be described by the verse beginning with "śyāmāṅgīm" and so forth. "Śrāvyabandha" means a composition that must necessarily be heard; the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *śru* according to the rule "orāvaśyake."

The meaning is: whenever you become weary, whenever you are exhausted, then at that very time you shall proceed by placing your foot upon the mountain peaks. And "weariness" here refers to physical exhaustion;
"where" means on whichever path.

"Exhausted, exhausted" (*kṣīṇaḥ kṣīṇaḥ*) is not a compound; rather, "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) is intended here as internal. "Extremely light" (*parilaghu*) means devoid of heaviness. The phrase "of streams arising from mountains" is the ellipsis required [to complete the sense]. The mention of "extremely light" and the mention of "streams" refer to the drinking water.

For the sake of wholesomeness: here Vāhaṭa says, "Waters originating from the Himavat and Malaya mountains, whose flow has been agitated, tossed, and interrupted by striking against rocks, are wholesome. (13) Ma!
"O Cloud, tell me now— the word 'from me' being understood— the path, the road, which is suitable and favorable for your journey," says Mallinātha.

"Mārga" refers to the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a gentle asterism (nakṣatra), or a path; according to Yādava, it also means "in search" or "on a journey. Listen: following that—that is, after hearing [the name]—it is "fit to be drunk" (peya) by the two ears.
The meaning is that it should be heard with great eagerness. By the mention of "drink," the message is understood to be equal to nectar (*amṛta*).
"My *sandeśam*" means my verbal message; according to Amarasimha, "the verbal message is called *vācika*."
You will hear [it] at that path where, being repeatedly exhausted and having your strength diminished, you shall set down—

having placed— your foot upon the peaks, that is, the mountains, in order to regain your strength again. (The doubling of the word *nityam* is for the sake of expressing frequency, according to Pāṇini 8.1.4.)
The meaning is "resting at times.
Being repeatedly diminished (*kṣīṇaḥ kṣīṇaḥ*), that is, having become thin-limbed; here too, because it is a *kṛt*-derived form, there is reduplication as before. Lightly [flowing] with its currents.

It is free from the defect of heaviness; the meaning is that it is wholesome because it has been agitated by striking against stones. Likewise, Vāgbhaṭa says: "These rivers originating from the Himavat and Malaya mountains, whose waters have been agitated by striking, throwing, and breaking against stones, become wholesome. Da!

Having consumed milk and water, and having taken them internally for the sake of nourishing the body, you will go; you shall depart. [This is from] the root *gam* in the *luṭ* (periphrastic future) tense. 13.
The commentary on this is as follows:
O cloud (*jalada*), first of all, upon which path you shall go; where—meaning, in whichever direction—you will travel.

Listen—pay close attention—to that path which you have traveled; while I am speaking and telling it to you. Of what nature is that path? It is one that corresponds to your departure, being suitable for your journey.
O Cloud, thereafter you shall hear my message—my news—which is "fit to be drunk by the ears," meaning it brings delight to the sense of hearing.
Having done what? Having repeatedly set foot upon the mountain peaks whenever you were weary.
Having placed and set down his foot;
and furthermore, having done what? Being exhausted and parched with thirst, his limbs dried up due to the meagerness of the water, [he drank] the water of the flowing rivers.
"Having used" means having drunk the water.
Of what nature was the water? It was "extremely light," meaning endowed with lightness due to its purity. This is the grammatical construction.
In this passage, the poetic figures are *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *svabhāvokti* (description of nature).
Regarding the phrase *tvatprayāṇānurūpam*: it means "suitable for your departure," that is, appropriate for your setting out (*prasthāna*).
"He who gives water is *jalada*; [the vocative] *he jalada* is the address.
(Verse 13)—compare with verse 17a:
"By women looking upwards, wondering, 'Does the wind perhaps carry away the mountain peak?'"
Having witnessed your prowess, take flight from this place of lush *nicula* trees toward the sky facing north, while being watched with great trepidation by the innocent wives of the Siddhas;
on your path, avoid the lashing of the thick trunks of the elephants of the quarters.
A little [is said] by Su; [it is] by Dignāga’s Su; [it is] by Avaḷe’s Ma,Da;
[it is] by VAḶ [who] states the beginning of the path.

From this place, rise up into the sky facing north, [to where] there are lakes and *nicula* and *vetasa* reeds—such is the description of the rainy season. What kind of person are you? One who rises with faces turned upward, trembling with great fear.

Having seen such enthusiasm and such effort from the wives of the simple-minded Siddhas, he asks, "How so? [The answer follows: Does the wind (pavana) perhaps carry away (harati)—that is, remove—the peak of the mountain?
And for this reason, there is a state of agitation due to the fear of falling; from this very cause arises his bewilderment.
What is he doing? He is avoiding the seizing of his great trunk—the grasping of his massive hand—by the elephants of the quarters (the elephants of the directions) as they lick it on their path.
For those elephants, mistaking him for a rival elephant, desire to seize him.
And the elephants of the quarters [emerge] starting from the netherworld;
as it is said:
"The remaining water of the Mandākinī is turbid with the rut of the elephants of the directions. (Ku. 2.44)
Likewise:
"The stream of the celestial Gaṅgā resounded as the wild elephants of the quarters [roared]. The doubling [of the suffix] occurs in the sense of "frightened-frightened" (*cakitacakita*). 14.
"From the mountain that spirals to the right."
The word *kiṃsvit* expresses conjecture. In this context, the following should be considered:
it is well known that Śrīparvata, Rāmagiri, and other such places are the abodes of the *siddhas*.
For this very reason, there is the longing of the *siddha* women residing on Rāmagiri.
It is possible because of his power of moving through the air (*khecaratva*). He will say later:
"The path was abandoned by lute-players who feared even a drop of water.
By this, a place other than the [usual] location is intended; [it is] from the marshy *nicula* grove.

From Ārdavānīrava. Regarding the phrase "from Sarasanicula," it is intended that by the word *nicula* there is a certain poet named Nicula who is meant, whose elegant verses (*sūkti*) are heard among the wise sayings (*subhāṣita*).
The claim that virtues and faults arise from association is false, since even the *nicula* tree, though situated in water,
protects itself by remaining still against the current while the river flows past.
Thus;
by this description of the *nicula* tree, it should be understood that the poet bore the name *Nicula*.
That poet Nicula, however, being present at the assembly, honors the eloquent verses of Kālidāsa;

therefore, he praises that poet with a word full of aesthetic flavor (*sarasapada*). Furthermore, by the phrase "flying up into the sky," he intends to express the expansion of his own poem into a lofty position.
The intended meaning is this: "What use are these other envious people?

That very *nicula* tree, standing in the assembly, increases your height"—thus, through the pretext of the cloud, he consoles his own composition titled *Meghasandeśa*, which was composed out of fear of the threats of wicked men.
Keeping in mind the inquiry, "Who indeed would disparage your poetry?", he says [the following] regarding the *diṅnāgas*, the elephants of the quarters. By this, the teacher Diṅnāga is intended.
By the word *pathin* (path), both the opportunity for expansion and the path of ascent are intended.
Avoiding and shunning the thick hand-pastes, one perceives a rising cloud and,
through a confusion with something of a similar nature, imagines blows from thick hands. By this,
it is intended that at the time of critiquing the composition, there are also gestures of thick hands.

The intention here is as follows: a certain teacher named Dignāga, elsewhere stating that this point [is found] in the compositions of Kālidāsa, refutes it with broad gestures of the hand. That teacher, regarding his own composition—
Relying on the principle that [the Veda] expresses a previously unknown meaning, the poet reproaches [the opponent] under the guise of the instruction of the clouds. || 14 ||

"Is the wind, the breeze, perhaps carrying away a peak of Mount Citrakūṭa?"—with such a doubt, by those women with upturned faces and uplifted countenances, [they gazed] even from their own limbs... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available text.)
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *upasarjanād asaṃyogopadhāt*.

"Mugdhabhiḥ" means by those who are bewildered; according to Amara, "mugdha" refers to both the beautiful and the foolish. "Siddhānām" refers to the women (*aṅganābhiḥ*) of the Siddhas, a specific class of divine beings. "Cakitacakitam" [denotes a state of being repeatedly startled].
"In whatever manner it was startled" (*cakitaprakāram*); there is reduplication [of the suffix] in the sense of "manner" (*prakāre*) as in *guṇavantaḥ*.
Being one whose energy (*utsāha*) or exertion (*udyoga*) has been observed;
from that place where the *nicula* trees—i.e., the marshy reeds (*sthalavetasa*)—are lush and moist; [the word] *vānīra*.

According to the *Śabdārṇava*, the *nicula* tree is the *sthala-vetasa* (the marshy reed) found in different poetic traditions. From this place, from the hermitage, along the path in the sky— the route of the *diṅnāgas*, the elephants of the quarters—
he avoids the insults and provocations of their massive trunks.

The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *hasta* may refer to a specific lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), as well as to a hand or an elephant's trunk; *avalepa*, however, refers to pride, as well as to casting away or defilement. The intention [of the author] is that Alakā is situated in the north.
"O sky, fly up, go!
Here, the great poet named Nicula— a connoisseur and a fellow student of Kālidāsa— also suggests this further meaning regarding those things brought about by others.

He who is the refuter of the criticisms against the compositions of Kālidāsa, from that place facing north— his face uplifted because of his faultlessness— on the path of Sarasvatī, [he addresses] the Diṅnāgas; the plural is used for honor.

Avoiding the "hand-anointings"—that is, the refutations preceded by the placement of hands—of the teacher Diṅnāga, who was a rival to Kālidāsa; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *avalepa* may mean pride, an ointment, or a refutation. [He composed this] of the mountain, which was like a mountain.
The "peak" (śṛṅga) of the teacher Diṅnāga refers to his preeminence; according to Amarasimha, "śṛṅga" denotes both preeminence and a mountain peak. By what cause does he captivate?
It is by means of the perfected ones (siddhas)—the accomplished masters of Sarasvatī who are great poets—and by women.
"Having seen the effort, he flew up high and cried out 'Bava'— this is the poet's statement directed either toward his own composition or toward himself.
That 'faults and virtues arise from association' is false, since even in a body of water [there are both]."
Standing still, the *nicula* tree protects itself from the surging current of the river by moving along with it;
they say that because of this composition of a verse, the poet was named Nicula. 14.
% NB An explicit statement that the poet was named after an expression in a verse of his own!!!
Sumativijaya’s commentary on this:
O cloud, fly up from this place, from the mountain named Rāmagiri;
toward what? Toward the sky, the atmosphere.
From what kind of place? From one possessed of marshy *nicula* reeds and *vetasa* canes. Of what nature were you? Facing north, with your face turned toward the north.
Furthermore, of what nature were you? By means of charming *siddha* women.

"Having seen his enthusiasm—that is, having observed his effort to fly—in such a manner that the women of the Vidyādharas were utterly startled (*cakitacakita*), [he wondered] as follows. The word *iti* indicates a reflection; what is this? Is the wind (*pavana*) carrying away, or shaking, the peak (*śṛṅga*)—the summit—of the mountain (*adri*)?"
By what kind of charming Siddha women? By those with their faces turned upward (*unmukhībhiḥ*), having raised their countenances.
What were you doing? On the path, on the road, [you were looking at] the elephants of the quarters (*dignāgānām*), the world-elephants (*diggajānām*).
The grammatical construction is as follows: "avoiding," that is, abandoning, of elephants; what? "the arrogance of their thick trunks," meaning the touch of their stout trunk-staffs.
"Mugdha" means charming; those who are charming *siddhāṅganās*—that is, *siddha*-women—are "charming *siddhāṅganās*.
By those charming *siddhāṅganās*, meaning by the celestial nymphs (*devavadhūs*), [the place is] "full of sap" (*sarasa*).
Where there are *sarasā niculāḥ*—that is, *vetasāḥ*, reed trees—that is where it is.
Therefore, from that place abounding in *sara* and *nicula* reeds;
[the word] "patet" is derived from the root *pat* (to fall) with the suffix *āśiṣi* (in the sense of a benediction), preceded by the prefix *ut*;
[the word] "diś" refers to the elephants of the directions (*diggaja*), for they are indeed the elephants of the quarters (*dignāga*). These, indeed...
"Because the elephants of the quarters will strike you under the delusion that you are rival elephants"—this is the figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt). 14.
Before you, emerging from the top of an anthill, appears a fragment of Indra’s bow, as if mingled with the radiance of jewels; by this,
your dark body will attain an exceeding beauty.
Like a peacock feather of shimmering luster upon Viṣṇu in his cowherd guise. ||15||

A fragment of a bow (Ma, Su); with a peacock feather (Su); of the dress (Da, Ma, Su); VALL: "In front of this," that is, from the edge of a mound of earth excavated by ants from the top of an anthill.
A fragment of the bow of Ākhaṇḍala— Indra’s bow— is produced, that is, it appears;
for it is said that an anthill containing a serpent is the source of the rainbow during the rainy season.
It is scripture.
Of what nature is it?
Because it consists of many syllables, it is like the intermingling of the lusters of jewels.
It is beautiful and lovely to behold, possessing the contact of the luster of many kinds of jewels,
by which your body, O Kṛṣṇa, will attain exceeding splendor—
just as the body of Hari in the form of a cowherd attained beauty through the peacock feather with its spreading luster.
Like one who has reached his destination; for cowherds generally wear peacock feathers like the Śabaras.
Furthermore, since the poet also provides a description of the rainy season in this context, there is no lack of occasion for this verse to serve as an instruction on the poetic path (mārga).
*Vyatikara* means a mixture or blending.
In the term *dhanuṣkhaṇḍa*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs because it is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*). ||15||
The "right-turning jewel" (dakṣiṇāvarta-ratna).

The reading is *ratnacchāyāvyatikara*. The meaning is that from the tip of the anthill emerges a fragment of a bow, beautiful to behold, like the intermingling of the reflections of the jewels on the heads of serpents residing within it.
The appearance of Indra’s bow from the top of an anthill is described in the *Saṃhitā*:
"If it appears in the midst of water, there will be drought; if on the ground, the destruction of crops; if rising from a tree, disease;
if from an anthill, fear of weapons; and if at night, it portends the death of the minister."
By this meaning as well, the omen is indicated. Thus it is said in the *Mahāyātrā*:
"A bow belonging to Indra (the rainbow) that is favorable, unbroken, intensely radiant, thick, and long, is desired."
Mallinātha says: "Ratna... [and so forth].
The mingling, or mixture, of the shadows of gems— such as the radiance of rubies and other jewels—
is beautiful to behold, worthy of being seen. "This is a fragment of the bow of Ākhaṇḍala," [he says], pointing with his hand.
The intended explanation is as follows:

"In front," that is, at the very top of an anthill (*valmīka*), specifically from the opening of an ant-hollow (*vāmalūra*). According to Amara, *vāmalūra*, *nāku*, and *valmīka* are synonyms for an anthill, used in both masculine and neuter genders. From there, it originates.
It becomes manifest by that fragment of a bow, with which your dark body [is adorned] by a feather— by a plume of radiant,
shimmering luster. "Piccha and barha are neuter," according to Amara.
Like the dark body of Viṣṇu, the cowherd Kṛṣṇa, it will attain an exceedingly lovely luster and beauty. || 15 ||
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
This visible fragment of the bow of Ākhaṇḍala— the rainbow of Indra— is appearing, manifesting itself in the east, in the direction before him, amidst the clouds.
Why? From the top of an anthill—an anthill being a mound of earth accumulated by ants and other insects—from that [top].
Of what nature was the fragment of the bow? It was beautiful to behold, as if it were the intermingling of the luster of jewels.
It is to be beheld like a mass of jewel-lustre. What is this? Because it is incomplete.
By which fragment of Indra’s bow your body is darkened.
It will surpass [all others] by an exceeding degree.
In relation to what? In relation to *kānti*, that is, beauty. By means of what? Like Viṣṇu’s—that is, Kṛṣṇa’s—by means of his *barha*, the peacock feather.

Of what nature was Viṣṇu? He was one wearing the dress of a cowherd (*gopaveśa*), assuming the guise of a cowherd boy. Of what nature was the peacock feather (*barha*)? It was one whose luster was shimmering with radiant brilliance, illuminating five colors; just as Kṛṣṇa was [adorned] by the feather, so too...
The grammatical connection is: "You are a cloud by means of a fragment of Indra’s bow."
"In the eastern direction" means "in front. A "termite mound" (*valmīka*) is a heap of earth; "from its peak" means from the top of that termite mound.
Regarding "jewel": the luster or beauty of jewels is "jewel-luster" (*ratnacchāyā*); its "intermingling" (*vyatikara*) [is what follows].
The collection [of feathers] is an intermingling of the luster of jewels.
Because Kṛṣṇa wears the dress of a cowherd, it is said that he bears peacock feathers;
for cowherds generally fashion ornaments from peacock feathers.
Herein lies the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile). 15.
Drunk in by the eyes of the village women— eyes moist with affection and ignorant of the play of the eyebrows, for they believe the fruit of agriculture depends entirely upon you—
you shall ascend the Māla field, fragrant from the recent turning of the plow.
Having turned slightly to the west, proceed once more toward the north.
With a movement of the eyebrows... go with a light gait. Having ascended slightly onto the field of Mālamuḍḍāra, afterwards...
Immediately thereafter, turn your course further northward toward the northern direction;
for you must avoid the southern quarter and proceed instead toward the north.
The movement of the gait;
the ascending of the garland with rain for the sake of the bride's pleasure— for by means of the garland,
the sky situated above her is indicated.
What kind of person are you? Because the fruit of agriculture depends upon you through the granting of rain,
for that reason you are being drunk in— meaning beheld with longing— by the eyes of the women of the countryside.
By what kind [of people]? By those who, due to their rusticity, were unacquainted with the play of the eyebrows; for that very reason, they were affectionate and not harsh, out of the power of love.
Of what kind was the garland? That which, at that very moment (sadyas), had been [woven] by a plowman with a plow (sīra).
*Utkarṣaṇa* means plowing; by that, it becomes *surabhi*, meaning fragrant.
For the earth, when plowed by a plow, becomes fragrant due to its contact with droplets of water from the clouds.
*Pravalana* means expanding.
With the verse beginning "To the north," they [go] with the *enavant* verses. ||16||
"O Dākṣiṇāvarta,
[the matter] depends on you."

In this regard, the following should be considered: to the north of Rāmagiri there are certain districts inhabited by Devamātṛkas; the women there are rustic (pāmara). Therefore, it is said that those women are ignorant of the playfulness of the eyebrows.
"Sadyaḥsīrotkaṣaṇasurabhi" is an adverbial compound (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) meaning "fragrant with the plowing of the furrows immediately [after the rains]";
that is to say, it possesses a fragrant scent from the turning of the plowshare right after the monsoon.
"Mālam" refers to a high plateau consisting mostly of mountains. Likewise, in the case of the *utpalamālā* (lotus-garland).
"Among *megha*, *manmatha*, and *māra*, *māra* is desired as death;
*mālā* occurs in the sense of binding flowers and so forth; *māla* refers to elevated ground. Thus, from the connection with *mālā*, the region known as Mālava became famous.

By the word "having ascended" (*āruhya*), its height is also implied. "Moving with light speed" means that because he released rain upon the field of Māla, he moved with light speed. Moving behind Māla and then moving to the north of it [occurs] at the place called Āmrakūṭa.
It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of providing rest on the mountain. || 16 ||
Mallinātha says: "In you... [etc.].

The fruit of *kṛṣi*—the act of plowing—is the crop; the locative case is used here because the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended. "Dependent" (*āyatta*) means subject to or under the control of. Amara states: "In the sense of being dependent, the words *nighna*, *āyatta*, and so forth.
"For this reason" (*itiha*) means for that cause. "With affection" (*prītyā*) means with those who are tender; the meaning is: moistened by unfeigned love.

Being drunk in— meaning gazed upon with reverence— by the eyes of the village women, those rustic folk who are ignorant of the movements of the eyebrows and the playfulness of the brows, [he proceeds]. (The word "because of their vulgarity" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.)
*Māla* is the field known as Mālā, a high-lying place consisting mostly of mountains;
*māla* means a high-lying place, as stated in the *Utpalamālā*.
O King! Immediately at that very moment, by the plowing and tilling with ploughs, it became fragrant.
"Having ascended so as to gratify the sense of smell"—the meaning is that he rained down there. According to Amara, *surabhigandha* means "that which gratifies the sense of smell.
O! Moving somewhat slowly from behind, he proceeded quickly because he had already rained down [his gifts] there.
"San" means light, very swift, or quick—so says Amara.
"Bhūyaḥ" means again; go, proceed, by the very same path as the previous one, namely the northern route.
The instrumental case is used here according to the rule: "There is an extension [of the usage] for words such as *prakṛti* when forming an instrument."

Just as a certain husband who has many beloveds, having sported secretly with his wife in a certain field— wherein *kṣetra* refers to the body and *kedāra* to a field, according to the *Viśva* lexicon: "the word *kṣetra* denotes the body, a field, a place of accomplishment (*siddhasthāna*), and a wife"— [he remains hidden].

The implied meaning is that, just as [the breath] exits through a low path out of fear of breaking its courtesy and then returns again to circulate as the universal supervisor (sarvādhyakṣa), so it is here. || 16 ||
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
Go again, once more, toward the north, indeed in the northern direction itself.
Having done what? Having ascended slightly—that is, having stayed upon it—over the Māla region, known as Māla, in the eastern direction behind you. At that moment, there was rain.
The meaning is "having done. Of what nature was the field?
Fragrant from the immediate plowing—that is, sweet-smelling from the recent drawing of the plow. Of what nature were you? Of light gait—that is, swift-moving.
Furthermore, of what nature are you? You are being drunk in—meaning gazed upon with reverence—by the eyes of the village women.
Of what nature are those eyes of the village women? They are ignorant of the play of the eyebrows.

By the eyes of the village women, which were clever in the playful movements of their eyebrows; and again, by what kind of eyes? By those affectionately moist with joy, for the reason that the fruit of agriculture—the success of cultivation—was dependent upon you.
The grammatical construction is "with the unctuous and the dry. "Immediately" means at that very moment; "by the plowing" refers to the scraping or tilling by means of a plow.
That [place] in which the fields are fragrant and sweet-smelling is "surabhi-mālam," meaning it is fragrant from the recent turning up of the furrows.
The word *māla* is said to refer to a region, a forest, the outskirts of a village, a wilderness, and the province of Mālava; it also denotes an upper story of a dwelling.
From the statement, "What is the source? there is the figure of speech known as *svabhāvokti* (description of inherent nature). 16.
The mountain Āmrakūṭa will properly bear you upon its peak with its head— you who have been overcome by the fatigue of the journey and whose forest calamities were quelled by its showers—
just as even a lowly person, out of regard for past favors, provides shelter.
If one turns away even when a friend has arrived, how much more so when that friend is so exalted? 17.
The mountain peak,
with its peaks, [seemed to] embrace you who were overcome by the fatigue of the journey.
Āmrakūṭa will properly and correctly explain and uphold [this] with his head as its peak;

for by you, through your downpour, the calamity of the forest has been pacified. Indeed, by you— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]
The forest fire was extinguished by a torrential downpour.
To the question, "Why then carry it on one's head? he says, "Even a lowly person," and so forth;
for when a friend arrives seeking shelter—that is, a place to stay—even a lowly person, even a wicked man [acts thus].
He does not even turn away;
how much less so he who is thus highly exalted by that manner? Why? Because of his prior good deed: "In the beginning, he rendered me a great service."
Thinking, "Now I shall repay this person," one does not turn away due to reflecting on a previous favor;
such a person is indeed mean, base, and small-minded.
"High," "tall," and "great-minded"—these are forms of the root *vah* (to carry/bear). "The mountain possesses peaks"; this is an example of inference (*anumāna*).
By the word "tathā" (thus), he declares the well-known status of its loftiness. ||17||
Dakṣiṇāvarta says that she [the Goddess] rests upon you alone, as expressed by the word "āsāre."
By this, the first benefit is indicated. "Āsāra" means a downpour of rain.
It is implied that [the mountain] receives it with its crest, its peak, and even its head;
the poet will later state that this is a form of the root *vah*.
They explain that "overcome by the fatigue of the journey" means that his progress was exhausted by the weariness of the road.
Anticipating the question, "What is the reason for my carrying him?", he says, "Not even a lowly one.
"For shelter" means for a dwelling place.
Likewise, the word "tathā" (thus) is employed because of the contemplation of that [friend's] majesty as it resides in the heart;
even one who is insignificant, when a friend arrives for refuge in him, [is uplifted].
He does not turn away even with respect to his first good deed; how much less, then, with respect to one that is superior—this is the meaning. || 17 ||
"O Mallinātha, you... [Thus ends the commentary.]

The mountain named Āmrakuṭa is a lofty peak upon whose summits (kūṭeṣu) there are mango trees (cūtāḥ). Regarding this, Amarasimha states: "Āmra, cūta, and rasāla are synonyms for the mango; and kūṭa, which is not feminine, means summit (śikhara) or peak (śṛṅga)."
A *āsāra* is a torrential downpour; according to Amara, "the falling of a stream of water is *āsāra*.

He by whom the forest calamity—the wild fire—has been quelled by that [rain]; the meaning is "one who has rendered assistance. You, who are overcome—that is, pervaded—by the fatigue of the journey, [he will refresh] properly and well.
The bearer will speak with his head; this is the *lṛṭ* (future) tense of the root *vah*.

For instance, even one who is base and wretched—Yādava states that "base" (*kṣudra*) refers to a pauper, a miser, or a cruel person—he [will speak] for the sake of seeking refuge, that is, for the purpose of taking shelter, in a friend, a well-wisher. Now, "friend" (*mitra*), "companion" (*sakhi*), and "well-wisher" (*suhṛd*) are synonyms.
Thus says Amara. When [the guest] has arrived—that is, upon his arrival—he does not turn away out of regard for previous good deeds, that is, by reflecting upon former favors.
How much less, then, would he turn away from that very high and lofty Āmrakūṭa? He does not turn away.

The meaning is: "What need is there to say more? By this, it is indicated that because you have obtained happiness in your first dwelling, your purpose will be accomplished. As it is said in the *Nimittanidāna*:
"For one who has happiness in the first dwelling, there will be auspiciousness throughout the entire journey; otherwise, misfortune is certain. Thus [says] Sumativijaya. || 17 ||
The explanation of this [is as follows].

The mountain named Jaladāmrakūṭa will, with its head—that is, its summit—properly support you, holding you as is fitting. Of what nature is Āmrakūṭa? It is *sānumat*, meaning it is possessed of peaks.

In what state were you? You were one whose forest afflictions had been quelled by a downpour of rain. Furthermore, in what state were you? You were overcome by the fatigue of the journey, yet had cast off the exhaustion of the road.

For this reason, even one who is insignificant or lowly does not turn away or become averse— out of regard for a previous good deed or by performing a first service— when a friend has been obtained or when a friend has arrived, for the sake of seeking refuge. In that same manner...
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: what more need be said of one who, by his very nature, is like Mount Āmrakūṭa and is furthermore a knower of lofty virtues?

He by whom the forest calamity— characterized by the blazing of a forest fire and the affliction of the woodland groves— has been quelled and dispelled by the *āsāra*, that is, by a torrential downpour; him, [the one] by whom the forest calamity has been quelled by the *āsāra*.

"Overcome by the fatigue of the journey"—that is, accompanied by the exhaustion of the road; "overcome by the fatigue of the journey" refers to him who has undergone the weariness of the way. "First meritorious deed"—that which is both first and meritorious is a "first meritorious deed"; [it refers] to that.
"Expectation" means courtesy; "expectation of former merit" means by that expectation of former merit. This is an *arthāntaranyāsa* based on inference. || 17 ||
O cloud, the mountain Āmrakūṭa, filled with longing, will greet you as you approach from the direction of your journey, honoring you with his lofty crest;
and you, in turn, shall quench his summer heat with your downpour.
A service rendered to the great, when moistened with sincere respect, bears fruit before long.
Vallabha: This verse also exists somewhere as an imitation of that.
When you have grown weary on the path, the mountain named Āmrakūṭa, coming to meet you with its lofty peak, will greet you with praise;
and you, in turn, shall extinguish its forest fire with a torrent of rain, for:
Whatever service is rendered to great beings, moistened by respect and moistened by worship, will bear fruit before long.
In this case, the greatness belongs to the cloud; in the previous case, however, it belonged to the mountain, even though it was the highest of all.
"The cloud rests here"—this is praise for the mountain. (17a)
The commentary on this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
That mountain Āmrakūṭa, possessing peaks like a water-bearing cloud, will certainly—without a doubt—bear you upon its head;
how so? You who are weary from the road, exhausted by the journey.
Furthermore, of what nature were you? You were standing face-to-face, having come before him.
With what kind of head? With one that was lofty, exceedingly high.
O you, you too [saw] the fire, the flame, of that mountain named Āmrakūṭa.
You should pacify it; you would attain peace.
By what means? By a downpour, that is, by a torrential rain.
Of what nature is the fire? That which belongs to the summer season, the *naidāgha*.
For this reason: the assistance rendered toward those who are great and preeminent in virtue does not bear fruit after a long time or from afar, but rather bears fruit at that very moment.
Of what nature is that assistance? It is moist with sincerity—that is, accompanied by the essence of perfect affection.
Such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
Regarding "jala": one who gives water (*jala*) is a cloud (*jalada*); [the term] is used in the vocative as "O cloud" (*he jalada*).
Regarding "adhva": one who is weary from the road is "road-weary" (*adhvaklānta*); [the term refers to] that road-weary person.
"The swift one pours forth [rain]," according to the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*. "Naidāgham" means that which occurs in the summer or the heat of the season.
"By way of true being" (*sadbhāvena*) means moistened—that is, filled with passion—by way of a virtuous disposition or intention.
Moist with the presence of reality;
the figure of speech is *arthāntaranyāsa*. 18 || -17a- With its outskirts concealed by forest mango trees shining with ripened fruit...
When you, whose color is like that of a glossy braid of hair, have ascended its peak,
the mountain will surely attain a state worthy of being gazed upon by celestial couples—
dark in the middle like the breast of the Earth, pale with the remainder of its expanse. (18) 19 Su.
O serpent,
when your horn has risen up, the mountain Āmrakūṭa will certainly be destroyed.
He will attain a delightful state worthy of being beheld by a pair of celestial damsels;
for its borders are covered by forest mango trees that shine with ripened fruit and possess the beauty of mature mangoes.

You too, with a dark mass of hair as lustrous as a glossy braid and not coarse, and with black nipples, are like the entire earth with its yellow garment; thus there is a comparison [to the Earth], and for this very reason, there is the sight of a pair of deities. 18.
"O you who are covered by a clockwise-turning [shell]!"
"With its borders covered" means its periphery is concealed.
"By those shining with ripened fruits" means by those radiant with the pale-white color of ripened fruit;
and this pale-white color is the same as the color of a deer, not whiteness.
Because mango fruits possess many colors;

for it is seen in the words of the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* (4.28.19): "The ripe mango fruit, shaken by the wind, falls to the ground with its many colors. By this [it is indicated] that during the rainy season...
It is indicated that the mango trees in the forest bear fruit.
"Sarpaveṇīsavarṇe" [means]: *veṇī* is a braid of hair; *sarpaveṇī* is the coiling of a serpent. Thus, it is similar to a serpent's coil in both color and configuration.
The word *artha* refers to dark tresses of hair, a mass of clouds, the nipples on the breasts, and the circle of black serpents; it is also said to denote a serpent-like braid of hair. (Divākara)
Elsewhere than from the middle of the remaining white expanse, it is the color of a deer; for Amara states: "hariṇa, pāṇḍura, and pāṇḍu [all mean] pale-white. 18.
Mallinātha says: "Channa" means covered.
They are so described because they shine with fruits that have ripened and reached full maturity through the clouds.
The intention is that in the month of Āṣāḍha, the wild mango trees bear fruit and ripen due to the wind from the clouds.

The mountain Āmrakūṭa has its edges covered with wild mangoes and forest *cūta* trees, and its sides are enveloped [by them]. It possesses the luster of smooth hair-tresses (*masṛṇakeśabandha*), which have the color of glossy braids (*snigdhaveṇī*).
The meaning is that it is dark-complexioned (*śyāmavarṇa*). Regarding the word *veṇī*, it refers to a braid of hair or a stream of water.

O Yādava! When you have ascended to the peak—that is, the summit—the locative case is used here according to the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). We shall remain in the middle; that is, elsewhere than the remainder [the peak].
In its expanse, it is entirely pale-white like a deer; for Amara states that *hariṇa*, *pāṇḍura*, and *pāṇḍu* all mean "pale-white.
It is like a breast of the earth—that is, of the goddess Earth—belonging to the pairs of immortals, meaning those who move through the sky.
He will surely reach a state that is worthy of being beheld and beautiful to look upon.
The mention of "couples" is made because such a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*)—regarding [the breasts] as the very essence of lovers—is possible only for those who possess desire.
It is just as when a certain lover, exhausted, [rests] upon the jar-like breasts of his beloveds.
Just as one who is rested sleeps, so too do you; this is the suggested meaning (*dhvani*) that you are the breast of the heroine of the earth. || 18 ||
The commentary on this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O Cloud, that mountain named Āmrakūṭa will surely— certainly—
attain, that is, maintain, a state worthy of being beheld by immortal couples, a condition pleasing to the divine pair.
When what? When you have ascended—that is, when you have taken refuge upon—the peak, the summit, of the mountain.
Of what nature is the mountain? Its slopes are covered by forest mango trees.
Its borders were covered by wild mango trees;
of what kind were these forest mangoes? They were shining with ripened fruits, beautiful with their fully matured fruit.

Of what nature is he in relation to you? He is compared to one who has the color of a glossy braid and is equal to a beautiful, staff-like braid. That mountain named Āmrakūṭa is imagined to be like what for whom?
It is like a breast, a nipple, of the Earth (Bhū).

In what manner is the breast? In the middle it is dark, and at the nipple (*cūcuka*) it is black in color. Furthermore, in what manner is the breast? With the remainder of its expanse it is pale, [save for] the nipple.
The grammatical construction is: "having abandoned [them] from all sides, the fair one.
Regarding the word *pariṇata*: those which are *pariṇatāni* are fully ripened fruits.
By those luminous [fruits], which are like ripe fruits; by those with ripe luminosity.
Regarding "snigdha": *snigdhā* means radiant; *veṇī* is a braid; *snigdhā veṇī* is a radiant braid;
*savarṇaḥ* means similar or resembling it; *śyāmaḥ* is dark; *snigdhaveṇīsavarṇaḥ* refers to that which is dark and resembles a radiant braid; *tasmin* (in that).
"Of the color of a glossy braid of hair.
Regarding the word "śeṣa": on the remaining part, that is, the outer portion of the breast, the expansion is pale all over; thus it is "pale in its remaining expansion" (śeṣavistārapāṇḍu).
Here, the mountain Āmrakūṭa is compared to breasts, and the *cūcaka* (the nipple) is compared to a cloud;
this is the figure of speech known as *mukhyopamā* (primary simile). 19.
Having stayed for a moment in that bower enjoyed by the wives of the forest-dwellers... 18.
Having crossed that path with a speed even swifter than the discharge of water from a toy,
you will see the Revā river scattered at the rocky foot of the Vindhya mountains like the decorative patterns painted on the body of an elephant.
There, in that forest thicket frequented by the beloveds of the forest-dwellers such as Aśvamukha and others, after the offering of water for the libation (toyotsargāt).
Having stood on Adrauṣaṇa, you will immediately thereafter descend onto the path, the road, and behold the Revā, the Narmadā.
Of what sort? She who is shattered at the foot—the lower part—of the Vindhya mountain, which is uneven with rocks.
"Scattered"—
and thus, the simile is that the ash applied to the elephant's body with decorative patterns and artistic divisions is like nectar (*sudhā*).
The reason for crossing the path is that his gait is exceedingly swift and clever due to the shedding of water—that is, the casting off of the spray.
[In the compound *vanacara-śabde*,] the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending is by virtue of a general rule (*bāhulaka*). 19.
"Having remained in a clockwise direction," it is said.
A *kuñja* is a mountain-cave whose interior is concealed by creepers and the like; by this, it is meant that you shall behold the enjoyment of forest-dwelling women.
Because of this momentary sight of the enjoyment of forest-dwelling women, there will be a delay in your time.
It was intended that this should not be the case.

In the verse, "With its exceedingly swift course due to the discharge of water, it extinguished the calamity of forest fires by means of its showers," it is this "discharge of water" (*toyotsarga*) that is intended here.
"Beyond that mountain": having crossed over or passed beyond it.
He says this with the intention: "Let there be no despondency in you from seeing the excessive enjoyment of the forest-dwelling pair;
you shall see another couple eager for sexual union."
"You shall see the Revā"— that is, the Narmadā— at the foot of the Vindhya,

on the mountain that forms its boundary. By the phrase "fallen at the foot of the Vindhya," there is implied (dhvani) the falling of a certain woman at the feet of her beloved due to the excess of her passion.

The ash (bhūti)—that is, the smeared ashes—was fashioned and offered with various types of patterns (bhakti), consisting of many kinds of lines (rekhā) in the form of divisions (cheda). And it is said:
"It was offered with many kinds of patterns."
"It shines like the rut-fluid of a maddened elephant. Thus [ends verse 19].
Mallinātha comments on "sthitvā" (having stood) as follows:

O Cloud! Those who roam in the forest are "forest-dwellers" (*vanacara*). By virtue of the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, the elision (*luk*) occurs due to the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*). In that place where the bowers (*kuñja*), meaning vine-arbors (*latāgṛha*), have been enjoyed by their wives; for the words *nikuñja* and *kuñja* are used in the neuter gender.
"Latādipihitodara" is defined by Amara as "one whose interior is covered with creepers and the like. The meaning is that there you will find diversion for your eyes.
On that Āmrakūṭa, stay for a *muhūrta*—that is, for a short time and not for long—because of the conflict with your own duties.
This is the intended meaning. According to the *Śabdārṇava*, "muhūrta" may refer to a short duration or even to two *ghaṭikās*. "Having stayed" means having rested.
"By the discharge of water" refers to the heavy rain described as "āsāra"; by this, [the cloud's] speed becomes exceedingly swift.
On account of his lightness, moving with extreme speed, he crossed— that is, traversed— the path beyond that Āmrakūṭa mountain;
[he did so] at the foot of the Vindhya range, on its rugged outlying spur, which was uneven with stones and rocks.

"Feet" refers to the foothills (*pratyantaparvata*), according to Amara. "Scattered on all sides" means spreading everywhere. By this, the falling of the feet of a certain amorous woman upon her beloved is also suggested (*dhvanyate*).

The Revā is the Narmadā; for the *Amara-kośa* states: "The Revā is the Narmadā, born from the Moon, the daughter of Mekala. The term *bhakti* refers to the divisions, arrangements, or lines upon the body or limbs of the elephant;
for the *Śabdārṇava* states: "*Bhakti* [is used] in the sense of service, a portion, and arrangement. Of those...

You shall behold prosperity fashioned by cuts, breaks, and luster—like an ornament (*śṛṅgāra*) or like ashes (*bhasita*). According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *bhūti* occurs in the senses of an elephant's ornament, ashes, and wealth. You shall behold it.
The sense is that this too is a great gain for you, a source of visual curiosity.
This verse is seen as having been interpolated somewhere between the two [original] verses:
"Mount Āmrakūṭa, with its peaks, [beheld] him who was weary from the road as he approached."

O cloud, he will address you with his lofty head, praising you; you too, moistened by your true nature, shall quench his summer heat with your downpour. A service rendered to the great bears fruit before long.
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O cloud, you shall behold the river named Revā, the Narmadā.
Having done what? Having stayed for a mere moment on that mountain Āmrakūṭa and having sent down rain there.
Of what nature are you? You who are *tatpara*, meaning beyond that mountain Āmrakūṭa.
Having crossed—that is, traversed—the path that lies on the opposite side; in what kind of state was that path? It was one where the bowers had been enjoyed by the wives of forest-dwellers.
Furthermore, of what nature was it? It had a very swift motion, a rapid course.
Why? Because of the discharge of water, that is, from the raining down of water.
Of what nature was the Revā? At the foot of the Vindhya, at the base of the Vindhya mountain range.
Shattered and spread out;
on what kind of foot of the Vindhya? On one uneven with stones, difficult to traverse because of rocks.
He imagines the Revā to be like what? Like a [garland] fashioned upon the body of an elephant.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: [He was adorned] with prosperity, as if with protection, by means of various kinds of decorative patterns (*bhakticcheda*).

"In that place where the bowers or thickets— places covered with creepers— which had been enjoyed and frequented at the time of amorous dalliance by the wives, that is, the women, of the forest-dwellers, namely the Kinnaras and Bhillas, [are found], it is 'vanacaravadhūbhuktakuñja'."
By this, the place of enjoyment (*sambhogasthāna*) has been described.

"From the discharge of water" (*toyotsargāt*): *toya* means water; its discharge (*utsarga*), falling, or raining is the "discharge of water. From that discharge of water—due to the shedding of water—one proceeds with rapid gait.

"Druta" means swift; one whose gait is even swifter than that is "drutatara-gati. "Tat-param" means the distance beyond that Āmrakūṭa mountain. "Upalaviṣama" refers to a place made uneven and difficult to cross by stones; in such a place.
"On the uneven ground of the Uplava mountain; at the foot of the Vindhya—meaning at the base of the famous Vindhya peak;
that is to say, on a peripheral mountain."
Herein lies the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). 20.
Having shed your rain, you should proceed to take water from that river, which is perfumed by the bitter ichor of wild elephants and whose current is checked by groves of rose-apple trees (*jambū*).
The wind will not be able to weigh you, O cloud, for it possesses no inner substance; indeed,
everything that is empty is light, while fullness leads to weightiness.
Taking— that is, having taken— the water of that Revā river, you should go,
because its rain has been vomited forth and its waters have been released.
What kind of water? It is perfumed—made fragrant—by the bitter and pungent ichor of wild elephants;
for the Vindhya is indeed a dwelling place for elephants.

Likewise, the phrase "its speed checked by the grove of rose-apple trees growing on the bank" (jambūṣaṇḍena jambūvanena pratihatarayam) is said to mean that its velocity has been rendered sluggish; for the Revā is indeed swift-flowing. By this, he expresses her excellence.

The wind will not be able to weigh you— that is, to measure your full internal essence— once you have become completely filled by drinking in the dense clouds; for anyone who is empty, void, devoid of substance, is light.

One becomes an object of contempt; however, fullness leads to respect, for the wealthy are honored by everyone. Therefore, since you possess weight through your water, you shall not suffer humiliation from the wind.
"Her [hair] curls to the right."
In this context, by the word "tikta" (bitter), both a fragrant odor and a bitter taste are intended;
for Haladhara states: "Bitter, pungent, and astringent [qualities] are proclaimed to be [included] within fragrance."
By this [word], being perfumed with the ichor of wild elephants— that is, the ichor of elephants from the Vindhya forest— and being stained by the mixture of scents is intended.
By this [word], the discharge of rain— that is, the letting fall of rain— and vomiting are intended.
By this [word] *jambūkuñja* (the rose-apple grove), the obstruction of its speed and its lightness, as well as the cultivation of astringency (*kaṣāya*), are intended;

by this [word] *antaḥsāra* (having internal essence), the state of having water within and the state of having strength within are intended; and by this [word] *ghana* (dense/cloud), both a cloud and a firm body are intended.
By this [term], the external wind and the bodily air are intended;
by "empty" (rikta), emaciation and the purification achieved through vomiting are intended;
and by "fullness" (pūrṇatā), nourishment through the pouring of water and the sequential administration of liquid gruels and so forth is intended.
This is the analogy here: a person who has performed purification through emesis drinks light water scented with bitter and astringent substances in order to dry up the remaining morbid humors;
subsequently, even his powerful *vāyu* (wind) will not become provoked. On this point, Vāhaṭa says:
"Astringent decoctions that are not cold are beneficial for the purification of his phlegm;
how much more so those that are bitter or astringent, which by their very nature remove kapha. Thus it is stated regarding the tone of voice as well.

"For one who has undergone purification and gradually consumes a wholesome diet such as thin gruel and so forth, there shall be no affliction by wind and the other humors, just as a yogin is not afflicted by the sense organs. (20)
Mallinātha says: "Of her..."
The cloud, having emitted rain— that is, having disgorged its water—
is revealed as one that has vomited; it is [described] by means of words possessing a bitter taste and fragrant odors, for "tikta" applies both to a bitter taste and to a fragrant scent.
Thus says the *Viśva* lexicon. "Perfumed" (*vāsita*) means made fragrant or infused by the rut-fluid of wild elephants.

The sense is that the Himavat, Vindhya, and Malaya mountains are the sources of elephants, because the Vindhya is the origin of elephants. [The wind] has its velocity checked by groves of *jambū* trees.
"With its momentum checked" means it is easy to drink; by this, its lightness and the state of being a decoction (kaṣāya) are suggested.
Taking the water of that Revā river, you should go—proceed.

The wind— the air of the atmosphere, as well as the breath residing within the body— will not be able to equal you, that one whose strength is the essence within the heart of dense clouds; it will not be capable of doing so.
For indeed, everything that is empty—that is, devoid of internal essence—is light;
the meaning is that it becomes easily shaken.
Fullness and substantiality lead to weightiness and to being unshakable; such is the meaning.

The suggested meaning (*dhvani*) here is as follows: first, for a person whose body has been purified by emetics, and subsequently, having gained strength from drinking light, bitter, and astringent water to dry up the phlegm, the agitation caused by wind (*vāta*) does not occur.
Thus said Vāgbhaṭa:
"Astringents that are not cold are beneficial for the purification of that [person's] phlegm."
How much more so those that are bitter or astringent, which by their very nature remove phlegm?

"For one whose purification has been accomplished through the sequential stages of drinking thin gruel and so forth, and who eats wholesome food, there shall be no affliction by the humors such as wind (vāta), just as a yogin is not afflicted by the sense organs. (20)
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O Meghāgra, you should go to Vraja;
having done what? Having taken—that is, having seized—the water, the liquid, of that river named Narmadā.
In what state were you? You had discharged your rain, having made your downpour upon the mountain named Āmrakūṭa.
In what state was the water? It was perfumed, made fragrant by the ichor of wild elephants produced in the forest.
By what kind of forest-elephant rut? Bitter and pungent.
Of what nature was the water? Its current checked by rose-apple thickets, its velocity impeded by the dense groves of jambū trees.
The wind of the dense clouds will not be able—that is, it will not be capable—of weighing you down or bringing about your defeat.
How are you? You are one whose inner essence consists of water within your central part.
For when the stomach is empty and the body is pure, the vital wind (marudvāyu) prevails. The poet confirms this very point:
because everyone who is empty—devoid of wealth—is light and disregarded.
It comes to be;
fullness and prosperity serve for the sake of honor and respect—
this is the logical connection.

"Vanaja" means the elephants of the forest; "vanagaja-mada" refers to the rut of those forest elephants. [The compound] "jambū-pratihata-raya" refers to that whose speed or momentum was checked by the grove of Jambu trees.
Its speed was checked by the groves of *jambū* trees.

"End" (*anta*) means the limit; "essence within" (*antaḥsāram*) refers to the water within. The word *sāra* has multiple meanings—such as logic, water, and density—and here, by the word *sāra*, water is meant.
"Gaura" refers to the state of being heavy (guru-bhāva), which is "gaurava" (gravity/respect); it is for that gravity.
Here, the poetic figure *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) is employed. 21.
Having seen the *nīpa* tree, greenish-brown with its half-grown filaments... 20.
And along the marshy banks, the *kandalī* plants with their first buds appearing,
and having smelled the fragrance of the earth— more intensely sweet in the burnt forests—
those deer will indicate the path as you shed drops of water. (21–22)
In the burnt forests,
O cloud that releases drops of water and rains down tiny droplets, the deer and peacocks [follow] your path.
They will indicate [his presence] by signs and will proclaim: "Surely our friend Jīmūta has come by this path. For they must drink drops of water from the cloud;
thus is their pursuit of him.
"Because his mind was captivated by the taste [of the food] and so forth, he was not noticed by them as he departed"— this is the "ascertaining of the path.
Having asked, "By doing what will they indicate [his departure]?", he states the signs.

Having seen the *nīpa* flower— half-ripened and half-unripe, with filaments that are greenish-brown and dark-tawny— one knows that this indeed does not arise during the rainy season without the falling of fresh rain.
Having seen along the marshy banks the *kandalī* plants with their first buds just beginning to emerge— since they indeed flower during the rainy season—
and likewise [the fragrance] exceedingly sweet in the burnt forests where the woods have been scorched by the summer heat;

"Having smelled the fragrance of the earth" means having sniffed it; for it is indeed from the falling of drops of water that the fragrance manifests there. "Releasing droplets of water" is an epithet of the cloud (*megha*), and not of the wind (*jasa*). 21.
"A *nīpa* tree that curls to the right."

*Nīpa* is the *kadamba*. It is of two kinds: the water-*kadamba* and the land-*kadamba*. The water-*kadamba* is generally a tree; the land-*kadamba* is a specific type of herb that grows to the height of a span (*prādeśa*). Here, the land-*kadamba* is intended. Of that [tree], during the rainy season...
Because it appears in this very way, the *kadamba* tree is designated as "belonging to the rainy season" (*prāvṛṣeṇya*).
Yādava states: "The *kadamba* is *pulakī*, *śrīmān*, *prāvṛṣeṇya*, and *halipriya*.
As for *nīpa*, it is greenish-brown; "green" (*harita*) refers to the color of *pālāśa* leaves, while "brown" (*kapiśa*) has the luster of gold.

By the phrase "half-climbed" (*ardharūḍhaiḥ*) and "grown in one part" (*ekadeśaprarūḍhaiḥ*), its recent manifestation is indicated. By the phrase "having first buds manifested" (*āvirbhūtaprathamamukulāḥ*),
the novelty of the emergence of the *kandalī* buds is also expressed.
"A region abounding in marshes and water" (anukacchamanujalaprāyadeśam). According to Amara: "Anūpa is a region abounding in water; kaccha is likewise defined as such.
Regarding the word *jagdhvā*: it means "having eaten. From the root *ad*, meaning "to eat."
When the suffix *ktvā* is added to this verbal root, the substitution of *jagdhi* for *ada* occurs by the rule *ado jagdhir lyapi kitī* (Pāṇini 2.4.36).
Now, since the fragrance of the *urvī* grass will be mentioned later, the reading should be *dagdhāraṇyeṣu*.
[The opponent argues: "It is thus [i.e., it must be so]. That is not correct; for the scent of the earth can exist even without burning. Furthermore, he will state later:
"O you who are delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth, which has been revived by its natural outflow (*niḥṣyanda*)," in the context of the forests.
This applies to all remaining cases. The word "exceedingly" (*adhika*) is employed in reference to the earth's natural state of being fragrant, in comparison to its mere possession of scent.
*Sāraṅga* refers to deer.
According to the *Abhidhānasaṃgraha*, "saraṅga" refers to the cātaka bird and the male deer, while "śabala" means variegated in the three genders.
By this [term], the capacity of the water-drops to produce the fragrance of the *nīpa* flower, the *kandalī* plant, and the earth is expressed. In the forests devoid of humans, the deer [are yours].

Seeing the *nīpa* trees brought forth by the fall of fresh rain, as well as the *kandalī* plants along the marshy banks, and having smelled the exceedingly fragrant scent of the earth from which they have been grazed,
they will indicate your path to the travelers who are longing for your arrival.
This is the meaning.

As for those who explain that by the word *sāraṅga* the cātaka bird, the deer, and the elephant are intended, their opinion is to be disregarded, given that the word *sāraṅga*— [The remainder of the sentence would follow here.]

Because no usage of the word *gaja* [in that sense] is observed; for Yādava states: "Sāraṅga means variegated color, a cātaka bird, a bee, or a deer. Furthermore, it is cumbersome for a single word to have multiple meanings simultaneously and to be construed with different actions.
And because a conjunction [of meanings] is untenable in the phrase "and the *kandalī* flowers," enough with this over-elaboration. || 21 ||
Mallinātha [comments] on the word "nīpa": "nīpam iti."
"Sāraṅga" refers to a peacock, an elephant, or a deer;
"bhṛṅga" refers to a bee, a cātaka bird, or a deer; and "mataṅgaja" refers to an elephant—so says the Viśvakośa.
It was green with filaments (kesara), that is, stamens, which were half-ripened and emerged from only one side.

"Pālāśa-varṇa" means tawny, blackish-yellow, or greenish-black. According to the *Amara-kośa*: "pālāśa" means green (*harita*); "hariṇ" is another term for it; "kapiśa" means brown or smoke-colored (*dhūmra-dhūmala*); and "kṛṣṇa-lohita" means blackish-red. This refers to a dark or dusky complexion (*śyāma-varṇa*). The compound is formed according to the rule "varṇo varṇena" (a color [is compounded] with a color).
*Nīpa* refers to the *sthalakadamba* flower. Now, regarding the *sthalakadamba*: according to the *Śabdārṇava*, "nīpa" may mean "pulaka. "Having seen" means having perceived or understood.

Likewise, "in the marshes" (*kaccheṣu*) means in the low-lying lands (*anūpeṣu*). [The word *kaccheṣu* is used] with the indeclinable particle *vibhakti* (by the rule beginning with *avyayam vibhakti...*) to indicate the case-ending.
An *avayavībhāva* compound: according to Amarasimha, "anūpa" means a place abounding in water, while "kaccha" likewise refers to a marshy bank; it is also an "avadhi" (limit).
Those [creepers] whose buds have appeared—that is, those that have first emerged or first arisen.
*Kandalī* refers to the *bhūmikadalī*. According to the *Śabdārṇava*: "The *droṇaparṇī*, which has a smooth bulb, is called both *kandalī* and *bhūkadala*.
*Jagdhvā* means having eaten; the substitution of *jadhi* for *ada* occurs according to the rule *ado jagdhir lyap-ti*.

"In the forests, exceedingly fragrant" refers to the gratification of the sense of smell. In the reading "in the burnt forests," the word "burnt" (*dagdha*) is an additional qualifier. Due to the force of the context, the syntactical connection should be understood as "having seen the kandalī plants [there]."
Having smelled the fragrance of the vast earth, those clouds shedding drops of water will indicate— will lead you to infer— your path; for wherever the effects of rain,
such as the budding of the *kandalī* lily and the blossoming of the *nīpa* tree, are seen, there it can be inferred that you have rained.
The meaning is that it is inferred. || 21 ||
The commentary on this is the Sumativijaya.
Those clouds, variegated with rainbows, will indicate and announce your path.
