Having done what? Having seen the *nīpa* flower of the *kadamba* tree, and furthermore, having seen the *kadamba* trees, which are a particular species of forest tree.
Of what nature was the *nīpa* tree? It was greenish-brown (*haritakapiśa*) with filaments (*kesara*) of blue and yellow color.
Of what nature were those filaments? They were half-grown, meaning half-blossomed.
Of what nature were the *kandalī* plants? Their first buds had appeared at the arrival of the clouds.

Where? Along the marshy banks (anukaccham), that is, taking the marshy banks as their mark. Of what kind are they? Of those that shed drops of water—that is, whose nature it is to rain down streams of water—and which have produced fresh buds.
Furthermore, having done what? Having smelled—that is, having inhaled—the fragrance, the scent, of the earth, of the ground; in what places? In the burnt forests, in forest lands consumed by fire.
Of what nature was the fragrance? It was *adhikasurabhi*, meaning extremely fragrant;
such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
For the fragrance of the earth is indeed natural, yet it becomes even more abundant when sprinkled with drops of water.
*Sāraṅga* means "those who sing of the essence" (*sāram gāyanti*); thus, *sāraṅga*s are bees (*bhramara*s). *Nipam*.

"Having seen [the lotuses]," refers to the *sāraṅga* deer; "having seen the *kandalī* plants," refers to the *saraṅga* elephants, so called because they go toward the *sāra*, which is water. "In the water" means that which releases drops of water; thus, it refers to those who discharge droplets of water (*jalalavamuktasya jalalavamucaḥ*).
Herein lies the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference). 22.
-21- Beholding the cātakas, who are clever at catching drops of water, and pointing out the cranes as they stand in rows by counting them one by one;
Having encountered you at the time of thundering, the Siddhas will honor those trembling embraces of their beloved companions, offered in a state of agitation.
°rabhasān Su; sotkaṇṭhāni Su;
Mallinātha explains that although [the reading] was rejected, it is interpreted as "water" (ambhaḥ).

Regarding the seizing of drops of water—that is, raindrops—the scripture states that water fallen upon the "all-enduring" earth is not beneficial for the cātaka bird; because such ground-contacted water causes them disease, they are clever enough to accept it only while it is still in mid-air. Thus, [the verse refers to] the cātaka birds.
Looking on with curiosity, they beheld rows of cranes— lines of *balākās*— standing in formation,
pointing them out with their hands by counting them as "one, two, three," and so forth.
Manifesting themselves at the time of your thundering, O perfected ones, they receive the embraces of their beloved companions, who are trembling with agitation at the moment of your roar.

The meaning is: having experienced the pleasure of embracing you by taking hold of you yourself. The underlying sense is that they will honor you because the attainment of happiness is due to you. || 22 ||
-21a- This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.
The *megha-siddhas*, a specific class of deities, will—with longing or with enthusiasm—honor and experience [these things].
What are they? Embraces, performed with agitation by their beloved companions, with both arms and with their hearts.
[He performs] embraces, kisses, and so forth, along with [the touch of] the heart.
Having done what? Having approached and reached you, O cloud. Where? At the time of thundering, on the occasion of roaring.
Of what nature were the Siddhas? They were gazing—that is, looking—at the cātakas, the birds that live on rainwater; the word "in the sky" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Of what nature were those cātakas? They were eager to seize the drops of water, being impetuous in their desire to grasp the water released by the clouds.

Furthermore, of what nature are the perfected ones (*siddhas*)? They point out the female cranes—the wives or consorts of the cranes—by using their fingers to indicate them. By what means? By mere counting, such as "one, two," and so forth.
In what state were the cranes, the female birds? They had become "arrayed in rows," meaning they had attained a state of unification by forming a line;
such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).

"Sotkaṇṭhāni" means accompanied by longing (*utkaṇṭhā*). "Priya" refers to those embraces (*āliṅgitāni*) performed with agitation (*sambhrama*) by beloved female companions (*priyasahacarīṇām*), who were embraced against their hard breasts and hearts.

I foresee, my friend, that although you wish to travel swiftly for the sake of my beloved, there will be delay for you on every mountain fragrant with *kakubha* flowers, embraced by bees wandering in confusion among their mates. || 23 || -21a-
Having welcomed you with cries of joy from their white-cornered eyes filled with tears,
the peacocks will come forth to meet you; therefore, you should somehow resolve to depart quickly.
Welcomed with eyes full of tears by Dāma and Sumanas, and by Śuci,
O VALLI,
though you desire to depart quickly for the sake of our welfare, [the breeze] fragrant with *kakubha* flowers [waits for you].
On every mountain, I perceive and imagine you to be wearing a black snake-garland (*kālahāra*).
Why? He says: because the beloved friends—the peacocks with white-cornered eyes—have offered a welcome with their cries (*kekā*) accompanied by tears from their eyes.
Having offered a welcome and engaged in a series of greetings and responses, time has been wasted; therefore, I entreat you:
for our sake, you should somehow resolve to go and exert yourself.
The sense is: "I am distressed and you are exalted.
Here, the presence of tears in the eyes is due to seeing a friend after a long time. 22.
"I see it turning to the right."
"I perceive," "I imagine," or "I contemplate"—this is the meaning.
By the phrase "fragrant with *kakubha* flowers," it is stated that the abundance of blossoms [on the trees] is naturally established for the purpose of welcoming [the guests].
"With peacocks having white outer corners of their eyes. A peacock is called *barhin* or *barhī*.
"Śikhāvala means a peacock," according to Yādava.
"With eyes full of water" means with eyes containing tears due to the joy of seeing the clouds;
by this, the water for washing the feet (pādya) contained in a white vessel is indicated.
By the word *kekāḥ* (peacock cries), a greeting of welcome is intended;
by *pratyudyātaḥ*, "gone forth to meet," the act of going out to receive a guest through hospitable rites is intended here. || 22 ||
Mallinātha says: "I perceive."

O friend cloud, for the sake of my beloved, quickly— swiftly, most rapidly, or fleetly (as Amara states: *laghu*, *kṣiprataraṃ*, *drutam*)— even though you desire to go (*yiyāsoḥ*), that is, though you wish to depart (from the desiderative form of the root *yā* with the suffix *u*), [you must proceed] by means of your *kakubha* flowers, the *kuṭaja* blossoms.

*Surabhau* means fragrant. According to the *Śabdārṇava*, *kakubhaḥ* refers to the *kuṭa* tree or the *arjuna* tree. *Pratiparvatam* means on every mountain; the double usage is for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
*Kālakṣepam* means a delay of time. The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *kṣepa* is used in the sense of delay and censure. *Utpaśyāmi*.
I imagine that, showing the cause for his delay, he prays for a swift departure with the words "O Śuklā!"—
by those white-winged ones whose eyes were filled with tears of joy and water.

"By peacocks. Regarding the peacock: *mayūra*, *barhiṇa*, *barhī*, *śuklāpāṅga*, and *śikhāvala*—thus says Yādava. "Keke" refers to its own cries; "the cry (*kakā*) of the peacock is its voice (*vāṇī*)"—thus says Amara.

"Having offered a welcome" means having greeted with words of welcome; "having gone forth to meet" means having gone out to receive [the guest], that is, having performed hospitality consisting of the cries of peacocks. "May you somehow" means in any way whatsoever; "you should quickly resolve to go" means you should exert yourself. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of a request (*prārthana*).

"According to the rule *śeṣe prathamaḥ*, the first person [is used]; and this word *bhavat* is considered 'residual' (*śeṣa*) because it is distinct from the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. In the phrase *svāgatīkṛtya kekāḥ*, that which is superimposed upon the *kekā* [sounds]..."
Because the words of welcome are employed for the purpose of the actual act of rising to greet, this is the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).
As it is stated in the *Alaṃkārasarvasva*: "When that which is being superimposed serves the purpose of the subject at hand, it is *pariṇāma*. || 23 ||
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.

O friend, O companion, O cloud! On every mountain, on every peak, I perceive, I anticipate your delay, your wasting of time—even though you are desirous of going, even though you wish to depart swiftly. In what state are you? You who are eager to travel quickly.
Or for one desiring to go—why? For the sake of my beloved, that is, to deliver my message to my wife. For this reason, O cloud, you must go quickly by some means or other.
One should resolve to go quickly. What is the point? It means that one should act in such a way that, having gone there, one may return here again as soon as possible.
On what kind of mountain? On one rendered auspiciously fragrant by the flowers produced from *arjuna* trees, which possess the scent of *kakubha* blossoms.
Furthermore, on what kind of mountain? On one that had risen up to meet him, having come forward to face him.
Having done what? Having made the cries of the peacocks—with their white-cornered eyes—into a welcome, treating them with respect.
Of what kind were those white-cornered ones? With eyes full of tears.
Such is the grammatical connection (anvaya).
In the word *kekā*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental;
in *matpriya*, the meaning is "for the sake of my beloved wife" (*mama priyāyā bhāryāyā eva arthaḥ*), which is "for the purpose of procreating offspring for my beloved" (*matpriyārtham*).
"Yiyāsuḥ" means one who desires to go; "of him who desires to go" (yiyāsoḥ).
"Kakubha-surabhau" means in that [place] fragrant with *kakubha* trees—the *kakubha* being a tree named *arjuna*—possessing an abundance of sweet scent.
With eyes that were tearful, having become moist with tears;
When you have arrived, the Daśārṇa country will have its village shrines crowded with the nest-building of house-crows, its rose-apple groves darkened by the ripening of fruit at their edges,
and its swans remaining for only a few days. (23)
Su;
[the fruit of] ripening, Da?, Ma, Su;
VALL (creeper)
While you are nearby, the regions known as Daśārṇa will become, that is, will exist, in such a state.
Of what kind? Having a pale-white luster, or white splendor, due to *ketaka* flowers.

Those whose garden fences border the pleasure groves; because the *ketaka* flowers are white, they are pierced— that is, split open— by the needle-like thorns within their calyxes, for it is from within them that the needle emerges after piercing through.

Likewise, the village shrines (*caityas*) were crowded with and pervaded by the nest-building activities and nesting sequences of crows that feed on household offerings; for due to the fear of rain, birds do not go elsewhere during the monsoon. A *caitya* is a temple of the Buddha; or alternatively—
It was a great tree, most renowned for its vast abundance, serving as a sacred shrine (*caitya*).
Thus, due to the ripening and maturation of its fruits, the edge of the Jambu forest became dark;
for the Jambu fruits, like *kapittha* fruits, turn dark through the process of ripening.
And those lakes in which the swans remain for only a few days, because they depart for Lake Mānasa upon the appearance of clouds.
"O white one with a clockwise curl," he said.
Those whose surrounding groves have a pale-green hue— where the enclosures of the nearby gardens possess a pale-green luster, the color of a deer;
[and] with *ketaka* flowers, that is, *ketakī* blossoms, which are "pierced by needles," meaning at the tips of their buds shaped like needles.
By the opening and expanding nests— the construction of bird nests—
of the house-crows and other scavengers who eat the offerings in houses and consume the sacrificial food.
This is the meaning.
"A village caitya in a crowded place. A *caitya* is a tree situated at a crossroads.
Yādava states: "A *caitya* is [found] on a funeral pyre, on a Buddha-egg (an icon), on a tree at a designated spot, or for the sake of the gods (*suralāya*)."
The Daśārṇas are certain regions situated to the north of the Vindhya mountains. According to Yādava, the Daśārṇas are the Vaidikas, while the Mālavas are the Avantyas.
Now, by the rule *poṭāyuvatī* etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.65), in a compound, the word *katipaya*— [is placed first].

Because it is prescribed as a compound with the latter member being predominant (*uttarapada*), it should be stated that [the state of being a lord] lasts for only a few days; furthermore, this is merely the general rule.
For there is the saying of Bhartṛhari: "What kind of fever of pride is this among men who are lords of only a few towns? (Bhartṛhari Subhāṣita 3.57). || 23 ||
Mallinātha says: "O Pāṇḍu..."

O cloud, when you have approached—that is, when you are near—the country known as Daśārṇa [is filled] with *ketaka* flowers that have blossomed, being pierced by "needles," that is, opened at the tips of their buds.
For it is stated in the *Śabdārṇava*: "The word *sūci* may refer to the tip of a *ketaka* bud. With these *ketaka* flowers...

The enclosures of the groves, having the pale hue of *ketakī* flowers and being green in color, were such that their fences consisted of thorny branches; for Amara states: "A fence (*varaṇa*) is a wall (*prākāra*), a *sāla* tree, a rampart (*prācīra*), or a hedge (*vṛti*) at the edge. And likewise:
By the building of nests—the construction of bird-souls—by village birds such as crows and others that eat household offerings; for Amara states: "Kulāya and nīḍa mean a nest, and are not feminine.
And by these *caityas*, which are trees standing at crossroads; for Amara states: "*Caitya* refers to a sanctuary (*āyatana*)."
The *Viśva* lexicon states that "uddeśa" refers to a tree worthy of being saluted by Buddhas.

Those [forests] are so described because they contain shrines (*caityas*) within their villages that are crowded or intermingled. Likewise, they are delightful at their extremities because of the rose-apple groves (*jambūvana*) that are dark with ripe, mature fruits. In death...

In the *Śabdārṇava*, it is stated that the word *avasita* means "delightful" (*ramya*) and "at the end" (*samāptau anta*). Thus, those [lakes] in which swans remain for a few days will become such as these;
they will come to be so.

By the rule *poṭāyuvatistokakatipayetyādinā* (Pāṇini 2.1.65), although the word *katipaya* functions as the final member (*uttarapada*) [of a compound], the word *tat* does not follow it; this is because that rule is merely conventional within the system of grammar. || 24 || -23-
The commentary on this is the *Sumativijaya*.
O Megha, those regions known as the Daśārṇas will become such; that is, they will come to exist in this manner.
Under what condition? When you, O Megha, are near—that is, when you are present nearby.
Of what nature were the regions? Their garden enclosures possessed a pale-white luster along with *ketaka* flowers—that is, *ketaka* blossoms.

Of what nature were those *ketakas*? They were "pierced by needles," meaning half-opened. Furthermore, of what nature were the Daśārṇas? [They were characterized] by the building of nests by the house-crows.

The villages and shrines of Daśārṇa were agitated by the *vakas* and others, who, through the concealment of their own limbs or by means of *śalaka* weapons, had thrown the village trees into disorder.
Furthermore, of what nature were the Daśārṇas?

The construction is as follows: the Daśārṇas have the edges of their rose-apple groves dark with ripened fruit; furthermore, how are they characterized? They are places where swans remain for only a few days.
"Pāṇḍu" means white; thus, "pāṇḍucchāyopavanavṛtayaḥ" refers to those whose garden enclosures have white radiance.
"Gṛha" means house or wife; thus, they are consuming the offering brought by their wives.
Crows are called *gṛhavalibhuj* (house-feeding birds), or alternatively, sparrows.
"In a state of agitation" (*ākula*) means that the village shrines (*grāmacaitya*), that is, the trees belonging to the village, have become agitated or thrown into confusion where [the birds] are.

"Pariṇata" means fully ripened or matured fruits; "pariṇataphala-śyāma-jambūvana-anta" refers to those [regions] whose borders consist of groves of rose-apple trees (*jambūvana*) that have become dark green due to the presence of those ripe fruits upon the upper parts of the *jambū* trees.
The word *anta* denotes intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Indeed, during the rainy season, the groves of *jambū* trees appear exceedingly dark.

"For how many days" means for only a few days, for a very short duration; [this refers to] swans that remain for only a few days—swans staying for a limited number of days. For indeed, during the rainy season, there is a turbidity of the waters.
It happens; for swans drink from water that is free of impurities—this is the intended meaning.
Here, the figure of speech is inference (anumānālaṅkāra). 25 || 23 || Their capital city, renowned in all directions by the name Vidishā—
Having gone there, you shall immediately obtain the full fruit of your amorous longing;
you will drink the sweet water of the Vetravatī, its waves rippling like a face graced with a frown, made melodious by the thundering near its banks.
26. O auspicious one! O fair-browed one! (Su yasmāt Ma; subhrū° Su; VALL)
Having gone to their capital city named Vidiśā,
you will at that very moment obtain the complete and perfect fruit of your lustful desires.
He asks "Why? and says: because you shall drink such water as this from the river Vetravatī.
Of what kind? [Water] that is faltering due to the thundering or the warbling of birds near the edge of the bank.

It is fortunate, beautiful, sweet, and pleasing; with its moving waves, it causes the ripples to falter. For this very reason, it is comparable to a face with arched eyebrows. Precisely for this reason, there is the attainment of the fruit of desire;
for a lover indeed drinks the sweet nectar from the face of his beloved, with its curved brows.
The waves are the point of comparison for the eyebrows. "Yat" (that which) is the word expressing the reason; "tat" (that) is the designation of the water.
The word *vidiśā* belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
*Lakṣaṇam* means a name;
[the form] *labdhā* ends in the suffix *tṛn*. || 24 ||
"Among them, they turn to the right."

Among those Daśārṇas, there was a city named Vidiśā, renowned in all directions for its characteristic feature— the name "Vidiśā" being well-known; for Yādava states that *lakṣaṇa* refers to a mark, a sign, a name, or the excellence of a seal and its parts.
In the *Kathāsāra*, it is said, "on the banks of the Vetravatī. There is also a certain river called the Vidiśā;
in its warbling cuckoos, you take delight and lead Spring to the gardens on the banks of the Vidiśā, like the embodied god of love himself.
This is because of the statement in *Mālavikāgnimitra* 5.1; however, it should be understood that she is mentioned as enjoying the Vetravatī river in another region.

"Rājadhānīm" means the principal city; the grammatical construction is "their capital city. The reading is "labdhā"; it means "she will obtain. This form is the periphrastic future (*luṅ*) in the passive voice. Having reached the capital city, she will obtain the fruit of your lustful conduct.
The meaning [of the verse] is as follows. In response to the expectation "from where will [the pleasure] be obtained?", he says: "made beautiful by thundering at the edge of the bank.
By this, the intention is to express that which is made beautiful by the sound of *sītkāra* (panting) thundering at the edge of the lower lip.

"Yad" means "because"; "tat" means "therefore. By the word "tat," that which is well-known is referred to, according to the rule that the word "tat" situated near the word "yat" refers to what is well-established. "Sabhrūbhaṅgam" means accompanied by the knitting of the eyebrows.
The reading is *vetravatyāścalormī* (of the Vetravatī with moving waves). *Calormi* means "with moving ripples.
This adjective stands in the place of the qualification "with a knitting of the eyebrows" (*sabhrūbhaṅga*).
Just as the face of a passionate woman [is described] as being with hissing sounds and a knitting of the eyebrows, so too is the Vetravatī.
The meaning is: "Because you will drink that sweet water, pleasant with its sound echoing near the banks and rippling with moving waves, therefore you shall obtain the fruit of your lustful nature.
To understand the following verse, this point should be kept in mind.
The courtesans residing in the city of Vidiśā are beautiful in every limb,
highly skilled in all graceful arts, and adept at winning over all men; moreover,
the city-dwelling men there are even more handsome than they.
They possess fortunate youth and are skilled in the enjoyment of women. Desiring those city-dwellers because of their extraordinary beauty, courtesans—
unable to enjoy them in their own homes due to fear of their mothers and others— [flee] from that city.

Having departed, they repeatedly enjoyed amorous dalliances without restraint in stone chambers located on the nearby mountain called Nīcais— which served as their secret meeting place— and then, according to tradition, they would secretly re-enter Vidiśā. || 24 ||
Mallinātha [comments] on the word "teṣām" (of them): ||
May she have the name Vidiśā, a designation well-known and celebrated throughout the quarters; for the *Viśva* lexicon states that *lakṣaṇa* means "name" and "mark.
May she be the *dhānī*, that is, the capital city belonging to those Daśārṇas—so called because [the people] are supported (*dhīyante*) therein.

The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the rule "in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*"). Thus, the seat of kings is the "royal capital" (*rājadhānī*). Since it is stated that a genitive case governed by a verbal derivative (*kṛt*) may form a compound, this is a compound. That [city] is the principal city; for the principal city of kings is the royal capital.
"It is said" [is found] in the *Śabdārṇava*: "Having gone to, that is, having attained, immediately the state of being playful (*vilāsitā*) of the lover (*kāmuka*).

Regarding the word *vilāsī*: "A *vilāsī*, a *kāmuka*, a *kāmī*, one devoted to women, and one greedy for sexual pleasure," according to the *Śabdārṇava*. "He will obtain"—that is, he shall receive—the "entire," meaning complete, "fruit," which is the purpose.
The word "by you" (*tvayā*) is to be supplied as the agent. The suffix *luṭ* denotes the object.
Why? Because for that reason, the water of the river named Vetravatī—which is sweet and pleasant, and which possesses moving waves—is [treated] with a frown (*sabhrūbhaṅgam*).

"Joined with a frown" means with the intent of biting the lip. "Like the face" means like the lower lip. "In a manner beautiful with thundering upon the edge of the bank" means on the extremity of the shore.

Even the word *bhaṇita* is designated by the term *stanita*; for according to the definition, *huṅkṛta* is that which rises from the throat and nose, while *stanita* is like a low sound. [The form] *pāsyasi* is the future tense (*ḷṭ*) of the root *pā* (to drink). It refers to the tasting of the lips of amorous women.
The meaning is that it excels even the *suratā* (erotic union).
25 || -24- This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.
That Megha will immediately and swiftly obtain—the word *lapsyate* being used in the sense of *labdhā*, "having obtained"—the unimpaired, that is, the full fruit of his amorous desire.
Having done what? Having gone to the capital city of those Daśārṇas.
Of what nature was the royal city? It was characterized by the fame of Vidiśā throughout the quarters—that is, its renown was established in all directions.
O cloud, [this occurred] so that there might be a beautiful frown, a beautiful hissing sound, or a beautiful noise.
Likewise, you shall drink—that is, you will take as a draught—the sweet and delicious water of the river named Vetravatī.
Of what nature is that water? It is made beautiful by the sound [of your voice] echoing near its banks.
Furthermore, of what nature is the water? It has moving waves, with flickering ripples.
It is compared as follows: what is the water of the Vetravatī like? It is like the face of a lovely woman.
Just as a lover drinks from the face of a lovely woman, characterized by the knitting of beautiful brows and soft sighs, so too do you.
Thus ends the positive concomitance (anvaya).
"Prathitā" means that which has become famous or attained renown; "vidiśālakṣaṇā" refers to her whose characteristic mark is Vidiśā—that is, she who is characterized by the famous Vidiśā.
"Kāmukatva" is the state of being a lover; [the phrase] "tasya kāmukatvasya" refers to that state of being a lover.

"Subhagam" means beautiful due to the thundering near the banks—that is, sounding in the vicinity of the shore; for water splashing against the edge of a riverbank becomes noisy. "Calormi" refers to that which possesses moving, that is, flickering waves.
Herein lies the figure of speech *upamā* (simile).
26 || 24 || You shall dwell upon the mountain named Nīcais for the sake of rest;
it will seem as if its hair stands on end through contact with you, owing to its *kadamba* trees in full bloom.
He who proclaims the unrestrained youthfulness of the city-dwellers through stone mansions that emit the fragrances of the dalliance of courtesans.
There, at Vidisha, you should dwell upon the mountain named Nīca for the sake of rest; that is, you should occupy or take shelter there.

Of what sort? By means of the *kadamba* trees with their full-blown flowers—flowers in full bloom—it is as if it has become "pulakita," or possessed of horripilation, due to its embrace with your friend;
for when a *kadamba* flower blooms, it acquires the beauty of hair.
Some, however, read "aprauḍha" (immature/unblossomed), and they say that because of its budding state, it assumes the form of horripilation;
and that mountain which [is the source] of the unrestrained and fierce [songs] of the clever citizens...
It proclaims its youthful vigor through stone dwellings;
for the word "rest" among poets is born of negligence, since [these palaces] emit the fragrance of the amorous dalliances of courtesans and release the scent of the pleasure of harlots. 25.
"Turning to the right, downwards."
The mountain is designated as "low" (nīcais) because it possesses the nature of a house for love-making (*suratagṛha*). There, on that mountain,

for the sake of rest— and not for the sake of noble instruction (*udāttopadeśa*)— the term *viśramahetoḥ* must be stated, because of the prohibition [of the suffix *ma*] by the rule *māntasyānācamer* (Pāṇini 7.3.34).
The grammatical derivation of the term *viśrāmahetoḥ* should be investigated according to the *Cāndravyākaraṇa*.

Although it is stated "with *kadamba*s possessing full-blown flowers" (*prauḍhapuṣpaiḥ pariṇatapuṣpaiḥ kadambaiḥ*), the meaning "with *kadamba* flowers" (*kadambakusumaiḥ*) is understood; for [the fragrance] of *kadamba* flowers—
There is the presence of *pulaka* (buds/horripilation). Yādava states: "The glorious *kadamba* tree, blooming in the rainy season, is called *pulakī* and *halipriya*.
[The breeze was] wafting the fragrance of the amorous dalliance of courtesans—that is, wafting the scent of the passion of the women of the brothel—[of the city-dwellers].
Of the inhabitants of the city of Vidiśā;
"uddāmāni" means unrestrained or unbridled.
This is the intended meaning: whose stone dwellings emit the fragrance of the amorous dalliance of courtesans.
Seeing this, the people there were struck with wonder, saying, "Oh, what youthfulness these city-dwellers possess! For even courtesans, without the payment of a fee,
have been won over by their own good fortune and now enjoy themselves at will in these stone houses."
Mallinātha: O cloud, there—in the vicinity of Vidiśā—resting (*viśrāmaḥ*) means the removal of fatigue; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāvārthe*).

The reason for this is as follows: the meaning is "for the sake of rest. The genitive case is used here according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* ("the genitive is used when there is an expression of a cause").
Regarding the term *viśrāma*, although Pāṇini’s rule *na udāttopadeśasya māntasyānācamer* prohibits *vṛddhi* [substitution], the form *viśrāmaḥ* is nonetheless valid.

The formation of the word [prauḍha] is established by the optional rule for *vṛddhi* in the *Candravyākaraṇa*. By the *kadambas*, that is, the *nīpa* trees with full-blown flowers— meaning blossomed flowers—
[the world is filled] through contact with you, that is, from association with you.
"His hair has stood on end; it remains as if 'pulakita,' that is, as if horripilation has arisen [in him].
The suffix *itac* is applied according to the rule beginning with *tārakā*.
You should dwell upon the mountain named Nīcaiḥ, whose name is Nīcais. [On the] mountain.
The meaning is "he dwelt. [The status of] the object is established by the rule *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ*.
That which is a low mountain. "Merchandise women" (*paṇyastriyaḥ*) means women who are for sale;
that is, courtesans. As it is said: "A woman of the *vāra*, a *gaṇikā*, a *veśyā*, a *paṇyastrī*, and a *rūpajīvinī* [are synonyms]."
In the *Śabdārṇava*: "The *parimala* among their amorous delights is a particular kind of fragrance.
Amara states: "*Parimala* refers to a fragrance arising from crushing [of flowers], which is captivating to the people. They are so described because they "emit" or manifest that [fragrance].

Through its stone dwellings and caves, it proclaims and manifests the unrestrained, intense youthfulness of the city-dwellers; here, women of the courtesans' quarter, possessed of such intense youth, are sometimes infatuated and longing for confidential diversions.
Out of fear of their mothers and others, they take pleasure at midnight by resorting to some secluded place; and this is well known to be common in this regard.
Here, the word "eructation" (udgāra), being used in a figurative sense, does not cause disgust; on the contrary—
It is indeed that which brings about the supreme beauty of poetry. As Daṇḍin has stated:

"Expressions such as *niḥṣṭhyūta* (spat out), *udgīrṇa* (vomited), and *vānta* (ejected), when based on metaphorical usage (*gauṇavṛtti*), are exceedingly beautiful; otherwise, they fall into the category of vulgarity. (26) —25—
The commentary on this is the Sumativijaya.
O Cloud, you should dwell upon that mountain there in the capital city called Nīcais, the peak named Kharva, for the sake of rest— that is, for the purpose of taking repose.
Which one? That mountain named Nīcairākhyā which spreads—that is, extends—the unrestrained, intense youthfulness of the city-dwellers, the people of Nāgara.
By what means? By stone dwellings, that is, cave-houses.
Of what nature are those stone dwellings? They are those from which wafts the fragrance of the dalliance of courtesans.
It is imagined: the mountain named Nīcais—like what? As if thrilled, as if its hair stood on end (pulakita) because of the *kadamba* flowers;
why? Because of contact with you, that is, through union with the cloud.
By what kind of kadamba trees? By those with full-blown flowers, that is, by those that have blossomed excessively; such is the grammatical construction.
"Nāgara" means those who exist in the city; of them, [it is said] "of the nāgaras.
"Viśrāma" means the cause of rest; of that, [it is said] "for the cause of rest.
"Tvatsama" means your contact or meeting; from that, [it is said] "from your contact."
"From contact with you. Regarding the word *paṇya*: it refers to courtesans (*veśyāṅganā*), for they emit that "fragrance of dalliance"—the charming scent arising from the friction of sexual union.
"Exuding the fragrance of courtesans' perfumes"—by those [trees] exuding the fragrance of the dalliance of courtesans.
This is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). 27.
Being rested, proceed while sprinkling the trees growing on the banks of the forest river.
The clusters of *yūthikā* flowers in the gardens, moistened by fresh droplets of water,

have become momentarily acquainted with the faces of the flower-gathering women— faces whose ear-lotuses were weary from the pain of wiping away perspiration from their cheeks— as they provide them shade.
28. Su; nada° (Ma); naga° Su; °jānām niṣiñcan Da; °rujā klānta° Su; VALL.
Having rested there, you should proceed immediately thereafter.
Doing what? [You should go] to the clusters of jasmine creepers and thickets of *hariṇī* shrubs belonging to the groves situated on the banks of that particular forest river or mountain stream.
Sprinkling fresh drops of water,
he became a friend for a mere moment through the granting of shade to the faces of the flower-gathering women— the wives of the florists— by removing their heat.

Of what kind of faces? Of those whose ear-lotuses (karṇotpala)— that is, their blue water-lilies at the ears— were withered by the affliction, the distress, and the crushing pressure caused by the removal and wiping away of the sweat and perspiration upon their cheeks.
The suffix *aṅ* is applied after the root *lū* (to cut) when preceded by *rujā*, *atra*, or *utpala*, due to its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group.
Thus, *puṣpalāvyaḥ* means "those who cut flowers"; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. 26. {Pāṇini 3.2.1} — Dākṣiṇāvarta.
"Rested" means:
Because those growing on the banks of forest rivers are natural, the term "riverbank" is used [to describe them].
Of the gardens—that is, the flower groves—the *yūthikā* clusters are the fresh blossoms of the *māgadhī* jasmine. Indeed, [is it not so?]
"Having placed him on his lap, [he seemed] to drench him with nectar upon the skin through the pleasures born of bodily contact. (Raghuvamśa 3.26).
In this passage, the substance *amṛta* (nectar), being liquid in nature, becomes the object (*karman*) of the verbal root *siñcati* (to sprinkle/drench).

How is it that here, setting aside the drops of water, the nets are stated to be the object (*karman*) of the verb *siñcati*? In the case of verbs such as *kirati* and *siñcati*, flowers, water, and so forth, sometimes become the object.
Of those whose ear-lotuses were withered by the pain of removing sweat from their cheeks;
of those whose ear-lotuses were withered by the sensation of touch from the hand that was wiping away the sweat from their cheeks.
"Flower-gatherers" (puṣpalāvyaḥ) refers to those who pluck flowers.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *karman* by [Pāṇini 4.1.84]. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15], beginning with the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
Mallinātha says: "Viśrānta" (rested).

Having rested there on the low mountain, his fatigue from the journey dispelled, he then—immediately after that rest—[beheld] the clusters of *yūthikā* flowers belonging to those gardens and groves growing spontaneously upon the banks of the rivers and streams in the forest; that is to say, they were naturally produced, not artificial. (In the reading *nadanadī*, the formation of a singular remainder according to the rule *pumān striyā* would be unavoidable. These were the *yūthikā* blossoms associated with those pleasure-gardens and parks.

The buds of the *māgadhī* flower. Now, regarding *māgadhī*: according to Amara, it is a *gaṇikā* or *yūthikā*. Halāyudha states that *koraka*, *jālaka*, *kalikā*, *kuḍmala*, and *mukula* are synonyms. "Sprinkling" means moistening with fresh drops of water; here, the root *sic* [is used].

Because its purpose is to cause moistening, a liquid substance functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, where the purpose is flowing, there the liquid substance functions as the object (*karman*), as in such examples as "having emitted semen upon virgins" (*kumārīṣu retaḥ siktvā*) and "pouring nectar with blisses upon the skin" (*sukhair niṣiñcantam amṛtaṃ tvaci*). Thus...

In cases such as "kirati" (he scatters) and others, as well as in examples like "The wind scatters dust" (rajaḥ kirati mārutaḥ) and "The elderly women of the city scattered parched grain over him" (avākiran vayovṛddhāstaṃ lājaiḥ paurayoṣitaḥ),

one must understand that the status of being either the object (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) for words such as *rajas* (dust) and *lāja* (parched grain) is to be inferred by resorting to a distinction in their meanings.

Likewise, there was the pain (*rujā*)— the word being formed with the suffix *aṅ* according to the rule for the *bhidādi* group— caused by the wiping away or removal of sweat from the cheeks (*gaṇḍau*, i.e.,
the temples); likewise, those whose ear-lotuses (*karṇotpalāni*) were exhausted or withered.

Regarding those mentioned: "flower-gatherers" (*puṣpalāvyaḥ*) refers to women who pluck flowers (*puṣpāvacāyikāḥ*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the verbal root [meaning] "to pluck" (*lū*) when it denotes the object; [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by the rule beginning with *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*.
Their faces, because they grant shade—that is, freedom from heat—and their granting of beauty is also suggested.
"Chāyā" means the sun's beloved, radiance, reflection, or non-heat—according to Amara.
The sense is that upon seeing a lover, the faces of loving women bloom.
"Kṣaṇaparicitaḥ" means having been met for a moment, being in contact for a brief time and not for long. Go!
Go! 27 || -26- [This is the commentary on Sumativijaya.]
O cloud, having rested and being weary, you should proceed; you should go.
What are you doing? You are sprinkling the clusters of jasmine buds—the *yūthikā* blossoms—of the gardens with fresh drops of water, that is, new droplets of rainwater.
Of what nature are the *yūthikā* buds? They are born on the banks of mountain rivers, having arisen upon the slopes of mountain streams.
Of what nature are you? [They are] of those whose faces are like flower-gatherers.

By providing shade through the act of gathering flowers and by creating a cloud-like shadow, he granted pleasure for a moment to those led by the flower-gatherers—those whose ear-lotuses were weary—even though he had been acquainted with them for only an instant.
How were those led by the flower-gatherers? Their ear-lotuses were fatigued.
Of those whose lotus-ears have become withered;
by what? By the pain arising from the removal of sweat on the cheeks—that is, the affliction produced by the wiping away of perspiration generated upon the surface of the temples.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).
"Naga" means mountain; "nadinī" means river; thus, "naganadī" is a mountain river. Those trees grown on its bank are "naganadītīrajātāni.
"Nava" means new or fresh; those drops of water are "navajalakaṇāni."
By those fresh drops of water;

"on the cheeks" (gaṇḍa) means on the two temples or the sides of the face; "gaṇḍasveda" is the perspiration on the cheeks; by its removal—that is, by wiping it away repeatedly—a pain or disease was produced.

The meaning is that their radiance has become faded due to the repeated touch of hands occupied with wiping away perspiration from their cheeks— [the phrase] "gaṇḍasvedāpanayanaruktena" being an analysis of "gaṇḍasvedāpanayanarujā," meaning by the act of removing sweat from the cheeks.
"Klānta" means those whose ear-lotuses are withered; thus, it refers to those "of withered ear-lotuses.
"Chāyādāna" means the taking of shade; therefore, it is "from the taking of shade."

"Of those with flower-gathering faces" (*puṣpalāvīmukhānām*): "flower-gathering faces" (*puṣpalāvīmukhāni*) refers to the faces of women who gather flowers; the sense is that in those gardens, there are many such flower-gatherers present.

The figure of speech is Inference (anumānālaṅkāra). 28 || 26 || Even though the path is circuitous for you as you set out toward the northern quarter, do not be averse to the embrace of the balconies of Ujjayinī.
If you do not delight in the tremulous glances of the city women there, which are startled by the flashing of streaks of lightning, you have been cheated.
May it be yours, O Dā; may you not be deceived, O Dā;
for although the path to Kauveryāmāśā (the northern quarter) leading toward Ujjayinī is crooked for you who desire to go there, [may you still reach your goal]. Dā; VALL.

The path is winding and the road is long; nevertheless, do not be one who turns away from the embrace of Ujjayinī’s palatial towers, nor be one who is devoid of desire for the enjoyment of her courtyards.
The meaning is: you must certainly go.
For if you do not delight in nor sport with the playful glances of the city women there, then you are being deceived by not seeing what ought to be seen.
With what kind of glances? With those startled by the flashing of streaks of lightning, and terrified by the quivering of the cords of the thunderbolt.
Likewise, with their tremulous outer corners of the eyes flickering. || 27 ||
The right-turning conch.

The word *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The intention is this: although the path for you who have set out toward the northern direction may be crooked, it must nevertheless be endured because of the gravity of the task.
In this regard, the following should be considered: [the rivers] originating from the Vindhya and other mountains, having pierced through the Vindhya range...

There is a certain northward-flowing river called the Nirvindhyā; indeed, Ujjayinī is situated after one has traveled some distance along its eastern bank. Therefore, for one traveling northward by way of the western bank of the Nirvindhyā—
The path for the cloud’s journey to Ujjayinī would be circuitous;
thus, [the reading] "mā ca bhūrujjayinyāḥ" (do not be averse to Ujjayinī) implies that one should not turn away from intimacy with the lap of the palace.
*Praṇaya* means familiarity. *Praṇaya* may signify familiarity, a request, or friendship.
According to Yādava, "api ca" means "and also.

The particle *ca* serves to connect another sentence. The meaning is that even by this consideration of the crookedness of the path, one should not turn away from the experience of the embrace of the upper stories of the new Ujjayinī palaces.
"If I do not let you experience that pleasure, then you would be deceived by me"—this is the meaning. Or rather, "you would be deceived" means that your birth would become fruitless. || 27 ||
"O Mallinātha, you are crooked! [Thus ends the verse.]
Although the path for you, setting out toward the northern direction— the region of Uttara—
is circuitous and distant,
meaning it lies some distance to the east of the Nirvindhyā river, which flows northward from the Vindhya range.
Ujjayinī is situated at a distance; however, the Northern Route lies to the west of the Nirvindhyā river, which accounts for its curvature.
Nevertheless, Viśālānagara is equal to Ujjayinī; Viśālā and Ujjayinī are the same.

Thus says Utpala. "Praṇaya" means intimacy or familiarity in the context of "saudhānām utsaṅgeṣu" (in the laps or upper parts of the palaces). Yādava states: "Praṇaya may mean familiarity, a request, or even friendship. Do not be "vimukha"—that is, do not be turned away or averse toward that. Do not become so.

This is the meaning. In the case of *smottare laṅ* ("the *laṅ* suffix occurs after the root *smṛ* when followed by a word ending in *u*"), the particle *ca* (in the rule) implies that the *luṅ* suffix is used in the sense of benediction (*āśīḥ*). By the rule *na māṅyoge*, there is a prohibition of the augment *aṅ*.
In that context, from the flashes of the lightning-vines (*vidyuddāman*) in Ujjayinī—
If you do not take delight in the eyes of the city women—with their tremulous outer corners and flickering side-glances that are startled by your radiance—then you have been cheated;
the meaning is that your birth would be rendered fruitless. (28) —27—
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O Cloud,

although the path leading toward your northern direction— the north— be winding for you as you set forth, nevertheless, do not turn away from the embrace of the palace terraces of the city of Ujjayinī.
O Earth, do not become [the cause of my distress]; do not abandon that city and depart.
O Cloud, if you do not take delight there in Ujjayinī in mutual glances with the eyes of the city's women.
If you do not experience the pleasure of mutual gazing, then you are deceived and your birth is fruitless.
With what kind of eyes? With those having tremulous corners—that is, with the flickering edges of the eyes.

Furthermore, by what kind of eyes? By those "trembling at the flashing of streaks of lightning," meaning they looked again and again with wonder as they were dazzled by the flickering garlands of lightning; such is the grammatical construction.
"Uttareti" means the northern direction; that is the north, the *uttarāśā*.
"Saudheti" means the lap of the palaces—that is, the region of the windows (*gavākṣa*);
there he was averse, turning his face away from affection (*praṇaya*).
Averse to the affection of the palace lap;

"vidyuddāma" refers to streaks of lightning—those flashes of lightning garlands—and by those flashes of lightning garlands, he was startled. Thus, by those flashes of lightning garlands, he was startled.
"Paura" refers to women belonging to the city; thus, "pauraṅganāḥ" means city women.
Of those city women—"lole" means those side-glances (apāṅga), that is, the corners of the eyes, which are restless and flickering.
With those tremulous side-glances, their eyes possessing flickering outer corners;
this is the poetic figure *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state). 29. -27.
Of her whose girdle-string is the row of birds warbling amidst the agitation of the ripples...
On the road to the Nirvindhyā river, which flows with charming faltering steps and reveals its whirling eddies, become one who tastes her essence;
for among beloved ones, the first expression of affection from women is indeed a playful coquetry.
Ma; 30 Su; °abhyantaram Su; VALL
Now he states the instruction on the path to Ujjayinī.

There is a river named Nirvindhyā. Having fallen into its course on the way and having merged with it, become "rasābhyantara"—that is, have water within you (the meaning being derived from the root *ap*, "to drink"). Furthermore, it also means that you should become "rasābhyantara," permeated by the aesthetic flavor of love (*śṛṅgāra*).
It is *vakrokti* (indirect speech). The meaning is: "you should desire her. He states her similarity to a beloved woman (*kāminī*). Of what sort is she?

She is one whose rows of birds (*vihagaśreṇī*) are cooing (*kokūyamānā*)—that is, crying out—as they are made to tremble by the agitation of the waves (*vīcikṣobheṇa*), which is the shaking of the ripples (*kallola*).
She whose girdle-string and jeweled waistband were that very garland of birds;
likewise, she who moved with grace and beauty, stumbling and rolling as she traversed over stones and other uneven ground.
Her navel was shown to have such a whorl that,

even in the absence of an actual invitation, how could my state of passion not be justified? For it is the very coquetry and playful charm of women that constitutes their words of endearment toward their lovers.
It refers to words of entreaty or words of affection.
Since the graceful gestures (*vibhrama*) of women proceed by the power of his very sight, he would be requested by those [gestures] alone; however, their direct entreaty is [what follows].
It produces lightness;
and here, the graceful movement (*vilāsa*) consisting of the turning of the navel and so forth has indeed commenced. || 28 ||
"The wave that turns to the right."
By the phrase "gracefully stumbling as she glides along," her playful gait (*vilāsagamanam*) is also suggested.
By this word *rasa*, both water and the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) are intended. *Sannipatya* means having come together or having met. Thus, she manifests such playful charm.
The meaning is: "Experience delight with the Nirvindhyā.
Anticipating the objection, "How can I experience it without a request?", he says:
"For in the case of beloveds, the first word of affection from women is indeed a playful gesture (vibhrama)."

A "word of entreaty" (*praṇayavacana*) is a statement of request. The sense is that this was indeed her first such statement of request toward those she holds dear; it was a moment of *vibhrama* (confusion or agitation) that had arisen within her.
Thus, setting aside the intended journey to Ujjayinī, she arrived at the Nirvindhyā river by way of the road.
It should be understood that this has already been stated. || 28 ||
Now, Mallinātha describes the connection with the Nirvindhyā river while he was traveling toward Ujjayinī along the way: "The waves... and so forth.

O friend, on the road to Ujjayinī, [be mindful] of her whose girdle-string is a row— a line— of birds, that is, swans, made resonant by the agitation of the waves, the movement of the ripples; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent.

By her stumbling, her tripping, and her faltering through intoxication, she was made so beautiful that it was as if the very whirlpool of the waters— the circular eddy itself— had been revealed and manifested as her navel by her as she crawled, flowed, and walked. May she be so.
"Āvarta" means the whirling of waters; thus says Amara.

The river named Nirvindhyā has emerged from the Vindhya mountains. This is a compound formed according to the rule "nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā," meaning that words beginning with "nir" are compounded with a word in the ablative case when they convey the sense of "having gone out from" or similar meanings. [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied] by the rule "dviguprāptāpannalaṃ... [to form the feminine].

By these words, the rule regarding the adoption of the gender of the preceding word is prohibited. Having come together with—that is, having joined with—that river; he whose interior is filled with *rasa*, meaning water—elsewhere, become one whose inner self is filled with *rasa*, that is, with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

The meaning is: "Experience its flavor (rasa) in every way. Regarding the word *rasa*, the *Śabdārṇava* states: "They call *rasa* [that which is found] in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, in water, in semen, in gold, in poison and semen, in the bitter and other tastes, in nectar, in exudation, in mercury, and in aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*)."
Now, one might ask: "How can experience in that regard be possible without a prior longing for it?
To this he says: "Of women," etc. In the case of women, with respect to their beloveds, *vibhrama*—that is, mere playful coquetry (*vilāsa*)—is the primary [cause].

A "word of affection" (*praṇayavacana*) is indeed a statement of entreaty. The point is that this is the nature of women: that they manifest their passion through graceful gestures (*vilāsa*) alone, rather than through direct speech. Furthermore, "bewilderment" (*vibhrama*) in this context refers precisely to such acts as exposing the navel and so forth. || 22 || -28-
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O cloud, be on the path— that is, travel by way— of the river named Nirvindhyā.
This is the meaning.
Having done what? Having entered within the water—that is, having become situated in the midst of the liquid. Of what kind of Nirvindhyā river?
One for whom the girdle-string consists of rows of birds warbling amidst the agitation of the waves.
Furthermore, of what nature was the Nirvindhyā?
She was gliding—that is, moving—toward places that were uneven due to depressions and elevations, which made her gait charmingly faltering.
Furthermore, of what nature was the Nirvindhyā? She displayed a navel-like depression on her banks.
The form of the whirling water seen by Avalokita was indeed that of the region of her navel;
he spoke these words of acceptance in order to dispel the suspicion of clouds.
For, because of this reason, among women who are full of desire, [there is no such thing] regarding their beloveds, their husbands.
The construction is as follows: "bewilderment" (vibhrama) is "coquetry" (vilāsa), and that very thing is the "first word of affection," the initial statement of entreaty.

Without knowing her intention, how can the place for the insertion of the organ be prepared? For women reveal their desire for sexual enjoyment only through their gestures and not by speaking with words alone; this is the meaning.
"Rasa" refers to water by the word "rasa"; "rasābhyantara" means the interior or middle of that water.
"Vīci" refers to those birds which have become noisy—that is, accompanied by sound—due to the agitation of the waves.
Of her whose girdle-string was the row of birds— that is, the line of birds—
whose sound was the agitation of the waves; just as it is with women.
The meaning is that just as there is a waist-belt at the waist, so too is there a row of birds for the river;
"revealed" means she whose navel is revealed as a mere whirlpool.

She displays the appearance of a whirling navel; for another woman as well, when she is enamored with a man, she displays her waist or a girdle at the waist. Likewise, the word *praṇaya* is used in the senses of affection and entreaty.
O fortunate one, as you cross the Sindhu, whose thin waters have become like braided hair and whose pale banks are covered with withered leaves falling from the trees growing upon them,
she reveals her beauty through the state of separation.
That method by which he may abandon his emaciation must be provided by you alone. [The river] there was the Sindhu of the deceased, flowing with its waters.
The river Sindhu, with its waters, reveals that [beauty] which has passed away, as if through its shadows and leaves. (VALL)

O fortunate one, that method or means by which that Nirvindhyā river—which is the cause of your emaciation—returns to its natural state must be accomplished by you alone. This refers to the rainy season; for in this way, through the arrival of the floodwaters, the river ceases to be thin.
He says, "Why do I rain there for the sake of abandoning emaciation?
because you [the cloud] reveal— that is, speak of— the good fortune and loveliness [of the mountain] through its state of separation in the past.
For thus, due to separation from you, her water has become like a single braid (veṇī) because of its thinness;
"veṇī" here meaning a mass of hair.
Likewise, it is [strewn] with [leaves] fallen from the trees growing on her banks.
Withered by withered leaves and shriveled sprouts, it has turned pale;
for in separation from her beloved, a woman’s body indeed becomes pale. (29)
The reading is "daksināvarta-veṇībhūta-pratana-salilā. By the word *veṇī*, both a stream and a braid of hair are intended.

The reading is *sā tv atītasya*. The word "of the past" (*atītasya*) means "of that which has passed," with "of the future" (*bhaviṣyataḥ*) as the understood complement. *Sindhuḥ* means a river. By the phrase "pale-hued" (*pāṇḍucchāyā*), the paleness caused by separation (*viraha-pāṇḍutvam*) is intended to be expressed. The reading is *virahāvasthayā*.
"By the rite of the release of rain" means by you alone, who remained having experienced it yourself;
[it refers to] the river whose thin waters have become like a single braid due to your state of separation from that fortunate one of the past.

The meaning is this: that river, its pale waters revealing its beauty through the withered leaves falling from the trees growing on its banks, will abandon its emaciation through the release of water by you alone, who have become its beloved; therefore, it is for you to perform that act of release.
Some, adopting the reading *tāmatītasya* (or *āśṛtya*), claim that *sindhuḥ* refers to another river; however, in that case, the meaning is insufficient,
for there is no river called *Sindhu* in this region, namely Kashmir.
It should be understood that the Sindhu flows forth. || 29 ||
Describing the state of separation of Mallinātha’s wife, Nirvindhyā, he prays for her restoration with the verse beginning "veṇī".

She is so described because her water—which was once not a braid (*aveṇī*)—has become a braid (*veṇībhūta*), taking the form of a braid (*venyākāra*), being thin and meager; elsewhere, it is also suggested that she possesses a mass of hair that has become a braid (*veṇībhūtakeśapāśa*).
[The word] *ruhāḥ* means "growing"; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*. [This refers to] the two banks.
[The forest] has a pale luster, being pale-colored due to withered leaves— so called because they fall from the trees (ruha)— which are dry leaves;
therefore, O fortunate one, by means of that previously described state of separation, her...
The meaning is: having passed over the Nirvindhyā river, having gone beyond for such a long time, that is, having been away on a journey;
*te* means "your"; *saubhāgyam* means "good fortune" or "the state of being fortunate. [This is according to the rule: *hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca*.
Thus, there is vowel strengthening (vṛddhi) in both syllables. "Vyañcantī" means manifesting or revealing. The sense is that he is indeed fortunate, for women desire him.
"Asau" refers to the aforementioned river Sindhu, the Nirvindhyā; [here] "sindhu" is used for a female river.
According to the *Vaijayantī*, "born from the mass of ocean waters" refers to rain in different regions.
The meaning is that you yourself must devise—that is, perform—the specific method or operation by which [the earth] abandons its emaciation; and that method consists, in one place, of rain.
The meaning is that enjoyment occurs elsewhere, because emaciation is caused by the absence of that [enjoyment].
This is the fifth stage of love (madanāvasthā); as it is said in the *Ratirahasya*:
"First is the delight of the eyes, then attachment of the mind, and then volition."
"Loss of sleep, emaciation, withdrawal from sense objects, loss of shame,
madness, fainting, and death— these are the ten stages of love.
Thus it is said.

Relying on the reading *tām atītasya*, it was explained that [the region] is named Sindhu because it is another river; however, some say that this should be disregarded, as there is a certain river named Sindhu in the land of Kaśmīra, but no such river exists anywhere else. || 30 ||
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
For him who has crossed—that is, traversed—the river Nirvindhyā, there lies ahead the Sindhu, a river named Sindhu.
Of what nature is the Sindhu? Its waters have become thin and reduced to mere streaks.
Furthermore, of what nature was the river? It was pale-hued, possessing a whitish luster, caused by withered leaves—that is, ancient foliage.
Of what kind were those withered leaves? They were those falling from the trees growing on its banks.

What is the Sindhu river doing with those [waves] prone to falling from the trees growing on its banks? She is manifesting—making evident—your good fortune (*saubhāgya*) by means of what? By means of the state of separation (*virahāvasthā*), that is, by the distress of being separated [from you].
When her husband is far away, a woman’s single braid remains unknotted and she becomes pale in complexion due to the separation from her lord.
O fortunate one, by what method or manner does that beloved woman, who is like the river named Sindhu—
The grammatical construction is as follows: "That very method, that very manner, by which he abandons emaciation and weakness, must be brought about and performed by you, O cloud."
"Veṇī" means that whose thin water has become a stream (veṇībhūta), having flowed with an exceedingly narrow and constricted current; thus it is "veṇībhūtapratanusalilā.
"Taṭa" refers to those falling from the trees growing on the banks—that is, from the trees associated with the riverbanks.
By those [birds] whose nature it is to fall—that is, those that cause trees growing on the banks to fall—[the women's hair] has become like the matted tresses of the state of separation.
"Viraha" refers to the condition of separation; thus, their braided locks have become entwined with the state of separation.
And she, possessing a pale complexion due to that state of separation—
the state of being emaciated (*kārśyam*) meaning weakness—
this description by way of the path indicated that the cloud possesses an extreme degree of desolation caused by its separation from the river.
There is a figure of speech consisting of a combination (*saṅkara*) of the *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) and the *dīpaka* (lamp/illustrative metaphor).
Having reached Avanti, where the village elders are experts in the tales of Udayana, proceed toward the city of Viśālā, previously mentioned, which is vast in its splendor.

When the fruit of their good conduct had become very small for those celestial beings who had descended to earth, it was as if a single radiant fragment of heaven had been carried away by their remaining merits.
31 Monday; 32 Sunday;
Upasara Monday;
VALL.
Then, having reached the country named Avanti, proceed toward—go to—the city of Ujjayinī previously mentioned and indicated.

Of what sort are they? They are those village elders who are long-established and proficient (kovidāḥ) in the story of Udayana, the Bṛhatkathā, and the history of King Vatsarāja, for that [history] is to be described there.
What kind of city? Vast and immense due to its splendor and prosperity, possessing various halls;
and which we imagine to be like a single, radiant fragment of heaven.
He states what the source for that portion of heaven is:

when the fruit of good conduct— the fruit of meritorious deeds— has been enjoyed by the inhabitants of heaven, those possessing merit, and has become diminished with only a small remainder left, they have "gone to the earth," meaning they have reached the ground.
The meaning is that it was brought to earth by the residue of merit, like a portion of heaven personified. Why this meaning? [Because] the country inhabited by the Avantīs is called "Avantī. (30)
"Having obtained [the conch] turning to the right," it says.
"Village elders who are experts in the stories of Udayana"— that is, village elders who are proficient in the tales of Udayana, the King of Vatsa,
whose great and wondrous deeds exist;
[do not be] like those previously mentioned.
"Of Ujjayinī" refers to that which was previously mentioned. [27] "Viśālā" is also a name for Ujjayinī; as Amarasimha states: "Viśālā and Ujjayinī are synonyms."

Intending to convey that Ujjayinī is equal to heaven and its citizens are like gods, he says, "having become small. Regarding the fruit of good conduct—that is, the fruit of good conduct known as heaven—he says "the earth" (gām).
This is the intended meaning: for those who dwell in heaven, their own merit constitutes the fruit.

When almost all of the enjoyment of heaven has been experienced and only a small remnant remains, their merits are exhausted by that enjoyment of the fruit; realizing that even the full enjoyment of heaven is difficult to attain,
they [descend] to earth with their remaining merits, in accordance with those merits of their own.
The meaning is that they would make it shine like heaven itself, as if it were a single, unified realm of heaven.

Now, if one asks: "Is there not supreme and immeasurable happiness for all castes (*varṇas*) in the performance of their own duties (*svadharma*), and from that, upon returning [to earth], do they not obtain birth, form, caste, and strength by means of the remainder of the fruits of their karma? [The answer follows:]...

From the statement of Āpastamba— "one acquires intelligence, wisdom, material goods, and the performance of dharma"— it is understood that living beings are born already endowed with the remnants of their past actions (karmaśeṣa). Therefore, this is the meaning [of the passage].
"Why was it overlooked? [The answer is: If this position were adopted, there would be no elevation of the *viśālā* [cow] through its connection with the remainder of the ritual act (*karmaśeṣa*).
Because it is common to all living beings; enough with this elaboration. || 30 ||
Mallinātha says: "Having reached... (prāpya).

Those who know are "vidāḥ. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in short *i* or *u*. Those who know the *okas*, that is, the place of the altar (*vedisthāna*), are "kovidāḥ" (experts). The form is grammatically correct because the vowel *o* is elided according to the *pṛṣodarādi* group of words. Those elders who dwell in the villages and are experts—that is, knowers of the truth—of the stories of Udayana, the King of Vatsa, such as the wondrous accounts beginning with the abduction of Vāsavadattā; [he went] to those [villages] where they reside.
Having reached the Avantīs, the people of that region;
do not be averse to the affection of the terrace of the palace at Ujjayinī, which was previously mentioned by you—
thus was she described— as the illustrious Viśālā, possessed of great wealth, for the word *śrī* denotes both beauty and prosperity.
"Lakṣmī is seen like Śrī," says the Śāśvata lexicon. Proceed toward the vast city of Ujjayinī.
How do they stand there? In the fruit of good conduct—that is, the fruit of merit characterized by enjoyment in heaven.

The meaning is: "when it has become very small," that is, when only a tiny remnant remains. "Of those who have gone to Gā" means of those who have gone to the earth (*gā*); according to Amara, *gaur*, *ilā*, *kumbhinī*, and *kṣamā* are synonyms for the earth. The meaning is: "of those once again returned to the world of mortals. "Of the denizens of heaven" means of people possessing heaven.

The meaning is that it has been brought or drawn forth by the remaining merits and good deeds that were left over after being consumed; for there is an inevitable necessity for those who have performed actions for the sake of heaven to attain heaven through the remnants of those deeds.
"Kāntimat" means possessing luster; "ujjvala" means radiant or essential.
"Eka" means other than what has been enjoyed [or distinct]. According to Amara, "eke" means faces or exclusive.
The phrase "situated like a fragment of the sky" (divaḥ khaṇḍam iva) is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). By this—
The fact that Ujjayinī surpasses the excellence and essence of all cities in the world of mortals is manifested [here];
this is the explanation of Sumativijaya.
O Megha, follow and go to another city named Ujjayinī. Of what nature is that vast city? It is the one previously indicated, mentioned before.
Furthermore, of what nature was Viśālā? It was Śrīviśālā, extensive in its splendor.
Having done what? Having reached the Avanti countries, that is, the Mālava regions.
Of what nature were those Avantis? They were village elders well-versed in the stories of Udayana.
It is imagined: what is this vast city like? It is like a single, peerless fragment of heaven (divaḥ).
Of what nature is that fragment? It is one left over (śeṣaiḥ) from the gods (svargiṇām), those who dwell in heaven.
By merits, [the city] was brought—that is, led away—endowed with splendor and prosperity.
Of what kind of celestial beings? Of those who had gone to the earth, that is, those who had reached the ground.
Under what condition? When the fruit of their good conduct, characterized by well-performed deeds, had become diminished, that is, had become trivial.
The grammatical connection is as follows: "when there is."

"Udaya" refers to the story or life of King Udayana; those who are "skilled" (*kovidāḥ*)— meaning clever— in that "Udayana-story" (*udayanakathā*), namely the village elders (*grāmavṛdhāḥ*), those aged men who reside in the villages, [he addressed] those village elders skilled in the story of Udayana.
The poetic figure is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). 32.
Prolonging the sharp, sweetly warbling cries of the cranes at dawn, [the breeze] is rendered turbid by its intimacy with the fragrance of blooming lotuses.

There, the breeze from the Siprā river, which is so agreeable to the limbs, removes the exhaustion of women after lovemaking, like a beloved husband who utters flattering words of entreaty. (31) 32 Ma;
35 Su;
Where, in Ujjayinī, the breeze from the Siprā river removes the fatigue of amorous women caused by sexual union.
It removes and casts away the distress of delusion.
Of what sort is it? It lengthens and extends the sweet and distinct warbling of cranes (*sārasa*) and *lakṣmaṇa* birds, which is produced by their passion.
Likewise, "kaṣāya" means that which has been infused with the fragrance— the scent— of those lotuses (*kamala*) that have burst open and blossomed at dawn;
the meaning is that it is endowed with an astringent flavor.

It is favorable to the limbs and brings comfort to the body because it is cool and fragrant. To what is it like? He says: it is like a lover who, through his entreaties and flatteries, does what is pleasing and is beloved by a passionate woman.
It removes bodily ailments;
it is the river named Siprā in Ujjayinī. 31.
"Making it long, turning to the right."
The cry of the cranes is prolonged by their running against the wind;
it is rendered pungent by its friendship with the fragrance of blooming lotuses,
made sweet by contact with the scent of blossoming rice stalks.
Regarding the word *kaṣāya*: Yādava states that it is not feminine when referring to a substance of passion (*rāga-dravya*), while it means "exudation" (*niryāsa*) or "flavor" (*saurabha-rasa*).
A "flatterer" (*prārthanā-cāṭukāra*) is one who utters endearing words through entreaty. This is the resolution here:
the beloved, having committed an offense, arrives in the morning.
Without even waiting for the opportunity to speak his beloved's words, he— his own voice clever and honeyed with intoxication,
his body fragrant from the enjoyment of another woman's form, and acting as a flatterer— begged his beloved, "Forgive my offense."
Just as the falling at her feet, being favorable to her limbs, removes the exhaustion born of not obtaining sexual union, so too did the breeze from the *sīpra* river [remove it]. || 31 ||
Mallinātha says: "prolonging."

In that city of Viśālā, at the break of dawn—the term *aharmukha* being synonymous with *pratyūṣa* and *kalya* according to Amara—there arose a clear (*paṭu*) and distinct sound, sweet and indistinct due to intoxication (*madakala*). Regarding the word *dhvani*: [the commentary continues].
*Madhura-asphuṭe* means "sweet and indistinct. *Kala* is defined by Amara as such.
Regarding *sārasānām*, it refers to a specific kind of bird.
Yādava states: "The *sārasa* is a bird of passion, a lover; it is also called *gonarda* and *puṣkara*."
Of the cranes and swans;
for the *Śabdārṇava* states: "The *cakrāṅga*, the crane (*sārasa*), and the swan (*haṃsa*) [are synonymous].
"Making the cooing—that is, the cry—prolonged" means extending it as long as the wind [carries it].

The meaning is that [the sound] is a repetition of words. By this, it is also understood that the beloved lover does not interrupt the warbling of the play-birds that follows his own flattering speech.
Together with the fragrance—the perfume—of the blossomed, i.e., fully opened, lotuses...

Through association with that [jasmine], the *kaṣāya* becomes fragrant. Regarding the word *kaṣāya*, Yādava states: "In the context of coloring substances (*rāgadravya*), *kaṣāya* is not feminine; it refers to a resinous exudate (*niryāsa*) or a fragrance (*saurabha*). Elsewhere, the meaning is "having the scent of being crushed" (*vimardagandhin*). That fragrance arising from crushing, which is pleasing to the people's hearts, is called *āmoda*.
*Atinirhārī* is defined by Amara [as one who removes fatigue].
*Aṅgānukūla* means a pleasant touch to the limbs; elsewhere, it means massaging the body through a firm embrace. And by Bhavabhūti:
It has been said that they provide massages with firm embraces;
and young women, exhausted by sexual union, are massaged by their lovers.
The poet himself will say this later: "At the conclusion of our lovemaking, it is appropriate for me..."
Regarding the phrase "of hand-massages": there is a certain river there named Śiprā;

the wind from that river is "Śiprāvāta. The mention of Śiprā is for the purpose of indicating its coolness. He is so described because he performs endearments (*cāṭu*) during the solicitation—that is, the request—for sexual union.
Furthermore, it means one who employs endearing words for the sake of sexual pleasure (*surata*). The suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Like a most beloved husband (*priyatama*), he [removes] the exhaustion of sexual pleasure (*surataglāni*), that is, the fatigue from copulation, for women.
"He takes away" means he drives away. The sense is that women, having forgotten the fatigue of previous lovemaking through his flattering words, make their beloved's request fruitful.
Regarding the phrase "one who performs flatteries at the time of request," this refers to one who has conciliated a woman whose lover has been unfaithful (*khaṇḍitā*).
It is impossible for there to be a removal of exhaustion from sexual union during the act of explanation itself; since she had no prior sexual union,

The explanation of this is as follows:

O Cloud, in that city, at dawn— every day at the break of day— the breeze from the Śiprā, the wind associated with the river named Śiprā, removes, dispels, and drives away the exhaustion born of sexual union, the fatigue arising from enjoyment.
Of whom? Of women. Of what nature is the wind from the Śiprā? The wind from the Śiprā is favorable to the limbs, providing comfort to the body.

Doing what? Lengthening—that is, increasing—the warbling, the sound, of the *sārasa* cranes, those birds of the lake. Of what nature was that warbling? Skillful and sweet with passion; endowed with proficiency and intoxication.

With an excess of joy, it was sweet and melodious; that is to say, its sound was exceedingly sweet. Furthermore, of what nature was the Śiprā breeze? It was "scented by friendship with the fragrance of blooming lotuses. How is this imagined? Like what? Like a beloved husband.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "How is the beloved? He is one who utters flattering words of entreaty."
Just as even a most beloved lover, though acting with flattering entreaties and conforming to one's limbs, yet—
uttering clever coos filled with passion, blended and united with the intoxicating fragrance of various unguents and ointments— [becomes unbearable].
The meaning is that just as [the breeze] generates languor during lovemaking and a desire for sexual union, so too does the wind from the Śiprā;
because it belongs to the morning and is contained within lotuses, the three qualities of coolness, gentleness, and fragrance are indicated of this wind.
"Sphuṭita" means blossomed or opened; "sphuṭitakamalāni" refers to those blossomed lotuses.
Their "āmodaḥ" is their fragrance or scent. "Maitrī" means friendship or association. "Kaṣāyaḥ" means mixed with or joined with.
Thus, "sasphuṭitakamalāmodamaitrīkaṣāyaḥ" means mixed with or joined with the friendship—that is, the association—of the fragrance of the blossomed lotuses.
The wind from the Śiprā is the Śiprāvāta.

Of what sort [are the palaces]? They are those from which [the moonlight] is emitted through the lattices, having issued forth from the openings of the windows.

Among those who were marked: "What kind of person are you? [He replied: "I am one gazed upon with affection by the Gaṇas;

"He is called 'Śamī' by the virtuous heroes, and he is regarded as 'Sāhasī' (the daring one). Thus it is said. O Teacher of the Three Worlds! In Ujjayinī there is a certain temple of the deity known as Mahākāla;

In this regard, the following should be considered: in the first half [of the verse], it is stated that the sanctity of the abode of the Teacher of the Three Worlds consists in its being meritorious; in the second half, however, it is stated that this very abode serves as a locus for aesthetic delight by virtue of possessing gardens and other such features.

Now, one might object: since the quality of being fragrant has already been stated by the phrase "scented with the pollen of blue lotuses," how can the quality of being fragrant be stated again by the phrase "by breezes pungent from the bathing of young women delighting in water-sports"?

It is said that the quality of fragrance exists in two ways: through flowers and the like which serve as the cause for the bodily adornment of playful women, and through the friction of sexual union with women; it is by means of this [fragrance] that the winds are also described as being characterized [by scent]. || 33 ||
"mallinātha explains: 'emitted from the lattice-work' (jālodgirṇaiḥ)."

By means of the smoke from hair-adorning incense—incense made of fragrant substances intended for perfuming the hair of women—the smoke was emitted through the lattice-work, having passed out through the openings of the windows. In those things fragrant with flowers...

"You shall obtain the full fruit of your non-gentle thunders."

It comes within the range of the eye, that is, it becomes visible to the eye;
the meaning is "until the time of the morning twilight.
To the question "For what purpose? he says:

By serving as a drum for the twilight offering to Śūlin Mahākāla, you shall attain the full fruit of your deep and entirely sweet roars, which bring praise. For this is the time of the offering for the gods.

It should be accompanied by musical instruments such as the *ḍhakkā* and *paṭaha*; however, since it is your own voices that will become those very drums, that is their fulfillment. "They should stand" (*sthātavyam taiḥ*)—this is according to Pāṇini 3.4.71, which prescribes the suffix *kṛtya* (gerundive) in the sense of the agent.
"Even the *dakṣiṇāvarta*," it says.

This Mahākāla is the abode of the Lord (Īśvara) in Ujjayinī. "You must stay" means you must remain there. "As far as is visible by the eye" refers to that extent of land which can be seen.
The range of vision; the meaning is that it extends as far as the range of vision.

*Sandhyābalipaṭaha* refers to the drum used for the offering of oblations (*bali*) at the time of twilight.
