"Profound" (gambhīra) is defined thus by Amara. || 34 ||
"mallinātha apīti || yugmam | O Cloud, [go to] the place of Caṇḍīśvara previously mentioned, named Mahākāla."

The meaning is that even at another time besides the twilight (saṃdhyā), having reached or attained it, you must remain; "you must remain" is the sense. The genitive case is used according to the rule: "the genitive is optionally used for the agent of gerundives (kṛtya)."

"As long as" (*yāvat*) means for as long as the sun (*bhānuḥ sūryaḥ*), the eye, does not pass beyond or transcend the range of vision—the meaning is that one should remain until the time of sunset. The word *yāvat* here serves the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Both *yāvat* and *tāvat* are used in the sense of totality (*sākalya*) and limitation (*avadhi*).
Regarding the word *māne*, Amara states that it means "certainty" (*avadhāraṇa*).

To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "performing. That is, performing the role of a drum (*paṭaha*) at the twilight worship (*sandhyā-bali*)—the praiseworthy and commendable offering—to the Trident-bearer, Śiva.

By performing this, you will obtain—that is, attain—the complete and unimpaired fruit of your thundering, which is neither dull nor excessively deep. The verb *labh* is used here in the active voice with the future suffix (*lṛṭ*).
Through its employment as the sacrificial drum for the Lord Mahākāla, your thundering shall become fruitful.
This is the meaning. 37 || -34- Sumativijaya’s commentary on this.

"One should remain; one should stay.

By those [palms] which possess handles (*daṇḍa*) inlaid with the luster of jewels, whose folds (*vali*) are variegated;
as it is said: "The word *vali* has many meanings: in a chowrie-handle, in a house, in wood, and in a portion. In this poem, the attainment of both seen and unseen fruits is described.

"Subsequently, [the breath] turns to the right."

Afterwards: "uccairbhujataruvanam" is a single compound word. While it could have been expressed simply as "bhujavana," the use of the word "taru" (tree) indicates its suitability for the descent of clouds. "Pratinavajapāpuṣparaktaṃ" means red like a freshly blossomed *japā* flower.

"Afterwards" means after the evening *sandhyā-bali* offering, at the commencement of the dance of Paśupati Śiva— that is, at the beginning of the *tāṇḍava*— [the sky] was as red as a fresh *japā* flower.
Bearing at twilight the evening radiance of Śiva, which is as crimson as a freshly blossomed Japā flower,

Being "abhilīnaḥ," meaning pervaded, in the shape of a mandala—the *kta* suffix here having an active sense—with Bhavānī, the wife of Bhava (Śiva). [This follows the rule:
"In the case of Indra, Varuṇa, Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Mṛḍa, Himavat, Araṇya, Yavana, Mātula, and Ācārya..."
The suffix *ānuk* is added, along with the augment *ṅīp*.

"Śāntodvega" refers to those two [eyes] whose agitation (*udvega*)—the fear caused by the sight of the elephant hide—has been stilled; for this very reason, their eyes are "stimite," meaning motionless. Regarding the term *udvega*, the *Śabdārṇava* states: "Agitation occurs in haste, in distress, and in fear, while one moves slowly."

Devotion (*bhakti*) is affection for those worthy of worship; the suffix *ktin* is used here in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāva*). Being one whose devotion has been witnessed (*dṛṣṭabhaktiḥ*), he [beheld] the elephant-hide (*nāgājina*)—that is, the hide of an elephant (*gajacarma*)—which was wet with blood (*ārdram*, meaning moistened by blood). According to Amara: "Hide (*ajina*), skin (*carma*), and leather (*kṛtti*) are feminine."
In this matter, remove [your] desire; that is to say, you yourself should take his place.
After subduing the demon Gajāsura, Lord Mahādeva performed the tāṇḍava dance while bearing his wet antelope skin upon the circle of his arms.

It is well-known. How is the formation of the word *dṛṣṭabhakti* established? Since the application of the masculine form (*pumvadbhāva*) to the word *dṛṣṭa*—by means of the rule beginning with *striyāḥ pumvat*—is difficult to justify here because [the feminine noun] does not belong to the group beginning with *apūraṇīpriyādiṣu*.

Because of this prohibition, and because the word *bhakti* is listed among [the words] beginning with *priya* [in Pāṇini’s Gaṇapāṭha]. This objection has been answered by relying on the term *dṛḍhabhakti* in the commentary on that list: "He whose devotion (*bhakti*) is firm (*dṛḍha*); thus, the first member of the compound is neuter."

The lack of firmness regarding the intent toward cessation [is indicated] by the word "dṛḍha" (firm); since a specific gender would be of no service, the feminine gender is not intended to be significant. Bhojarāja, however, [explains it] by the rule *bhaktaśca karmasādhanāyām* as "that which is worshipped or served."

When [the suffix] has the sense of an action (*karmārthatva*), forms such as *bhavānībhaktiḥ* (devotion to Bhavānī) arise; when it is a derivation based on state (*bhāvasādhana*), forms such as *sthirabhaktir bhavānyām* (firm devotion toward Bhavānī) arise—so he says. All of this has been correctly analyzed in the *Raghuvaṃśasañjīvanī* [commentary] under the term *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ*.

Regarding the word *jyeṣṭha* here, it is established that even in the case of *dṛṣṭabhakti*, the formation of the form of the first member as either feminine or neuter occurs according to different grammatical opinions. || 39 || -36-
The commentary on this is the Sumativijaya.

O Cloud, you should take from that previous poem the desire for the wet elephant-hide— the desire for the blood-drenched elephant skin— of Mahādeva, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), located there in the temple of Mahākāla; you must remove it.

Where? At the commencement of the dance, at the opening of the drama; for Mahādeva, in order to delude the mind of Pārvatī, being himself infatuated by Kandarpa, took the hide of an elephant wet with blood upon his own arm and, beneath that elephant-hide, he indeed dances himself.
This is the intended meaning. Therefore, it was said that the dance begins.

What are you doing? You are bearing—that is, wearing—the twilight radiance, which belongs to the time of twilight and is equal to a blood-drenched elephant hide, resembling the glow of the evening sky.
Of what nature is that twilight radiance? It is as red as a blooming hibiscus flower.
Furthermore, of what nature are you? Having left the range of vision behind, you are at the rear, with your arms raised high behind you like a forest of trees, forming a circle.
"Abhilīna" means resting or supported in the form of a circle; that is to say, you are situated upon the arm of Rudra in the form of a circle.
Furthermore, of what nature are you? [One] such that the eyes are motionless due to the cessation of agitation.
In the same way, the construction is: "having seen such devotion in Bhavānī Pārvatī toward Hara."
"Ārdra" means moist with blood; "ārdranāgājinecchā" refers to the desire for the moist hide (*ajina*) of a *nāga*, that is, an elephant.
"Vikasita" means like a blooming *japā* flower, a *jāsūna* blossom.
"Red" means as red as a blooming *japā* flower.
"Behind" (*paścāt*) refers to the rear part; the trees themselves are the high-reaching arms, and their forest is the "forest of high-reaching arm-trees" behind.

"Peaceful" (*śānta*) means that agitation has subsided and departed; thus, "with eyes peaceful, free from agitation, and steady" (*śāntodvegastimitanayana*) refers to her state when, at the time of beginning her dance every day upon beholding the elephant hide wet with blood, her eyes are motionless and unmoving. In this regard— [regarding] her... upon beholding the elephant hide moist with blood, at the time of commencing the dance daily... [the text continues].

Pārvatī was distressed. That Rudra, however, became pacified when you attained the state of being equal to an elephant hide. "Dṛṣṭabhakti" means one by whom devotion has been witnessed; he is so called according to the rule *puṃvadeti sūtreṇa*.
Herein lies the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). 40.

of what sort was she?
Be neither too smooth nor too rough, like gold being rubbed on a touchstone of refined gold;

"Of those going clockwise."

There, in Ujjayinī, on the royal road—the path of the lord of men—[the sky was covered] by [clouds] so dense that they were capable of being pierced by needles; the meaning is that they could be split even by the point of a needle.
The particle *ca* (and) indicates that this action should not occur, serving as a conjunction with the verb to express a prohibition.
Having thus described the manner of service to Mahākālanātha, Mallinātha further describes the manner of moving about the city with the verse beginning "gacchantīnām."
There, in Ujjayinī, at night—meaning during the evening—for the women going toward the dwelling of their lover, that is to say, the house of their beloved;
[the air was] with needles, meaning exceedingly dense and capable of being pierced by needles; [and it was like] the streak of gold on a touchstone.

By the etymological derivation *nikaṣyate* ("it is rubbed"), *nikaṣa* refers to a streak on a touchstone; [the goddess] is one whose luster is as smooth (*snigdha*) as that streak. According to the *Śabdārṇava*: "The word *snigdha* denotes what is smooth, dense, beautiful, and also, in the neuter, luster."

*Saudāmanī* is lightning, so called because it is in the same direction (*ekadik*) as Mount Sudāman; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.112, meaning "in the same direction as that. Likewise, show me the path to the broad earth (*urvī*). Furthermore, [protect me] by means of the discharge of water and thunder.
Do not be noisy—that is, do not make a sound—by means of rain and thunder.
Why? Because those women are distressed and timid; therefore, the meaning is that rain and thunder should not be produced.

The analysis of the compound here is not "thunder accompanied by the discharge of water," because mere thunder alone, just like thunder characterized [by rain], is undesirable. Nor does the alternative view of it being a *dvandva* compound contradict the rule regarding the prior placement of the word with fewer syllables (*alpāctara-pūrvanipāta*), because of the rule: "In the case of [words denoting] a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*) of an action... [the order may be reversed].
Thus, because the very Sūtra, by means of an inverted explanation, makes known the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the grammatical rule regarding prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). — 37—

The explanation of this is as follows:
O Cloud, there in the city of Ujjayinī, you should show the ground— the earth— to the women at night by means of the lightning flash.
Under what circumstances? When the royal road—the king's highway—had its light obstructed by darkness, such that the path could no longer be seen.
Of what kind of women? Of those going to their lover’s dwelling, the place of enjoyment with their husbands.
O cloud, as you do for the earth, so too should you be; do not be one who merely roars with loud thundering in the absence of water.
Why? Because the beautiful women going toward the dwelling of their lovers will become distressed, overwhelmed by fear—this is the intended meaning.
Of what nature were the darknesses? They were "pierceable by needles," meaning they were so extremely dense that they could not be pierced even by the tip of a needle.
Of what nature was the lightning? It was "smooth like a streak of gold on a touchstone," like a line of refined gold.
The grammatical construction is: "with one that is equal."

"Toyotsarga" means the discharge or raining of water, or its cessation; "toyotsargāt" refers to the state of being emptied of water. Therefore, "toyotsargastanitamukharaḥ" refers to one who is vocal—that is, habitually speaking—by means of thundering, which is the roar [of clouds] following the discharge of rain. [This is due to] both the rain and the thunder.
One must not obstruct the movement of women;
the sense is that, generally, women are overwhelmed by fear.
By the word *kanaka-nikaṣa*, a touchstone—a dark stone—is meant for testing gold. Of the gold...
By that [lightning], which is as smooth as a streak on a touchstone for gold— smooth like a streak of gold rubbed upon a touchstone—
the cloud also appears dark like a touchstone, possessing a yellowish hue just like the color of gold when it has been rubbed upon a touchstone.
The sense is "like lightning.

Having spent that aforementioned night on some palace turret— the upper story of the house— you should then, at sunrise, proceed further and traverse the remaining portion of the path.
For those by whom a service for their friends has been undertaken, accepted, embraced with the head, and consented to, they certainly do not falter; indeed, they do not become indolent.
On what kind of roof? One where pigeons—a specific type of bird—have fallen asleep; for these are kept by city-dwellers in their houses so that they may hear the sound of their throat-voices.

This "purpose" (*artha*) is a duty (*kṛtya*), hence "purpose-action" (*arthakṛtya*). "Purpose" (*artha*) means an objective;

"In a certain state where the pigeons are asleep. By this qualification it is stated that, because it is the rainy season, the citizens have left Valabhī and are sleeping in inner chambers; there, only the pigeons remain, and even when they are asleep, [the place] becomes silent.
By the word *vilasana* (shining), both *sphuraṇa* (throbbing) and *vilāsa* (graceful play) are intended.

"O Mallinātha, her— " so [it says].
He whose wife is lightning itself, weary from long shimmering and flashing—you, O Lord—in that secluded place where the pigeons (pārāvata) are silent;

The sense is that the movement of people there is simply impossible.

Having passed that night, when the sun is seen— that is, when it has risen—
he should again travel the remainder of the journey;
for such is the duty toward friends who have undertaken or accepted one's purpose.

"By those through whom the purpose is accomplished by means of ritual action (kṛtyā). "The welfare of a friend who has approached [for help]" is the meaning. Although there is a state of mutual dependence, a compound is formed because the sense is clearly understood. Regarding the word *kṛtyā*, Yādava states: "In the sense of ritual action (*kriyā*) or a deity, it is feminine; when meaning 'work,' it is used in all three genders. "They do not falter" (*na mandāyante*) indeed means they do not become slow; that is to say, they do not delay. The suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *lohitādi-ḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.13). [The form *mandāyante* is derived] by the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90).
The term *ātmanepada* [is used] in Pāṇini 1.3.90. Why so many meanings?
This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.
O Cloud, you should once again traverse—that is, cross over—the remainder of the path that has been left;
when? When the sun is seen, that is, when the sun has come into view at sunrise.
This is the meaning.
Having done what? Having spent—that is, having passed—that night on a certain wall atop the house, which is the beloved of the dwelling.
In what state are you? You are one whose wife, Vidyut (Lightning), has become exhausted—that is, whose spouse in the form of Lightning has grown weary.
Why? Because of her long flashing and the enjoyment of frequent rain-showers.

In what state was the palace? It was one where the pigeons were asleep. He now describes the act of repeatedly crossing the threshold: "Khalu" means certainly; O cloud, [this is] by the affection—that is, by the friendship—of friends, as is understood from the context.
Virtuous persons, having fulfilled their obligations once they have accepted a task and having made a firm vow to accomplish the affairs of others, do not falter nor do they succumb to indolence.
Such is the grammatical connection (anvaya).
The sense is that it has been accepted by me that "I must perform my friend's task," and thus he indeed does not delay nor does he show indolence.
"Bhavana" refers to the *valabhī* (pinnacle) of the house, or the *kuṭṭi* (terrace), or the *varaṇḍī* (roof-ledge) atop the dwelling.
On that palace roof;
"suptā" means that on which pigeons have fallen asleep— on that [roof] where the pigeons are sleeping.

Out of friendship and affection,
the tears of women who have been slighted should at that time be brought to peace by their lovers; therefore, abandon the path of the sun immediately.

The meaning is that you must not be deceptive.
For at that time known as dawn, the tears— the water of the eyes— of those separated lovers whose limbs have been broken by the pangs of longing must be stilled by their beloveds upon their arrival.
If you become like a cloth for him, then, due to the lack of clarity in his vision, he might not come because of the suspicion that it is night; therefore, leave the path of the sun.
Moreover, even that sun is [the cause of the grief] of his beloved, the lotus-plant, who has been abandoned by him.
[The moon] has returned— that is, come back— from the face of Kamalādevī to remove and soothe the frost-like tears; by this, it is meant that he must also fulfill the request of Padminī.
Therefore, one who obstructs your hand—the hand that holds back [the enemy]—would feel no small amount of envy;
he would harbor great wrath toward you. For when someone seeks the beloved of another and that other person should seize his hand, anger arises in him toward that person.
"Closed by the impurity of sleep," and so forth. (Su) "In that [which is] right-turning (*dakṣiṇāvarta*)," [it means] quickly.

A *khaṇḍitā* is one who is jealous upon seeing her husband’s attachment to another woman; as stated in the *Daśarūpaka*: "When the husband's altered state due to attachment to another is known, she is a *khaṇḍitā*, stained by the impurity of jealousy" (2.25). (Ma)

Peace and cessation must be brought about; this must be achieved. The path of rising and the path of returning—when you have blocked the eastern direction, lovers who are deceived even at dawn by the suspicion that it is night will not grant their favor.

Therefore, the intention is: "Abandon the path of the rising sun. That sun, too, belongs to the *khaṇḍitā* type of woman—that is, to the lotus-plant. Her status as a *khaṇḍitā* arises from the sun's departure to another region. "Pratyāvṛttaḥ" means returned or turned back.
And by the obstruction of the throat, the obstruction of the hands is also understood. || 39 ||

At that aforementioned time, at the hour of sunrise, for those women who have been abandoned by their beloveds—their lovers having been discovered to be altered by attachment to others; as defined in the *Daśarūpaka*: "A 'khaṇḍitā' is one whose jealousy is inflamed by the discovery of her lover's infidelity."
The tears from your eyes must be brought to a state of peace; the root *nī* takes two objects. For this reason, quickly abandon the path of the sun—that which obstructs it.
The meaning is "bhūḥ. He too, the Sun, declares an undesirable consequence in the opposing case:

she is a *nalini*, a lotus-pond, because it possesses *nalināni*, which are water-born lotuses. According to the *Śabdārṇava*: "The word *nala* [is used] for grass and a lotus; the masculine form *nā* [is used] for a king; but *nāla* is not feminine [and means] a stalk. Of her—
The lotus is the very flower of his own beloved, and her face is likewise; therefore, he has returned—having come back—to remove and soothe the frost, that is, the tears.
And because the sun, the lover of the lotus, has gone to another region by traveling to another lotus pond.
The intention is that she has been violated.
Therefore, regarding you: *kararuṭ* means "one who obstructs rays" (from *kara* [rays] + *ruṇaddhi* [he obstructs]), with the suffix *kvip*.
This implies "while he is obstructing rays," which is understood as "while he is obstructing the hand. *Vali*, *hasta*, and *aṃśu* all mean "rays."
"Karāḥ" [means hands], according to Amara. "Analpābhyasūyaḥ" means one with excessive malice or hatred.
The sense is that, for the most part, among those possessed by desire, hatred and specific outbursts of anger arise from the frustration of particular wishes. Furthermore:

Any person who hates the Self, or Arka, or Īśāna, or Viṣṇu—his prospects of welfare perish, and he will certainly become wretched (*raukha*). By the word *raukha*, the implied meaning is that due to such prohibition, there will be a failure in his undertakings. 42. (39) ????
The explanation of this is *Sumativijaya*.

O Cloud, at that time, when the sun has risen, the tears from the eyes— the weeping from the eyes— of women who have been abandoned by their lovers; these lovers having lain elsewhere during the night and returned only at sunrise with such affectionate husbands.
Peace should be brought [to you] by means of a cloth or a hand; the tears from your eyes must not be wiped away.
Therefore, for the reason that will be stated, at the time of sunrise, O cloud, you must quickly and swiftly abandon the path of Bhānu—the way of the sun—and remain above the sun.
Do not act under the guise of a cloud by means of concealment; otherwise, while you, a cloud,
stand as an obstruction to the sun, blocking its rays with your hands, the sun would feel no small amount of malice— that is, he would become intensely envious— toward you, the cloud.

He too— the sun, who acts like a husband toward a woman whose lover has been unfaithful— returned to remove, that is, to distance, the frost-like tears of weeping from the lotus-eyed, unfaithful lotus plant, which were like the water from the eyes of a woman whose husband has been unfaithful.
The grammatical connection is as follows: "Having turned back later, he has returned like a man whose mistress has been unfaithful at sunrise."
"Nayana" refers to the water of the eye; "nayanasalila" means the water of the eyes, that is to say, tears.
"Prāleya" refers to frost or dew-water; "prāleyāśru" means tears that are like frost.
"Kamala" refers to a lotus; "kamalanayana" means an eye that is like a lotus, from which [the tears fall].
From Kamalanayana.
"Analpa" means not small, that is, very great; he who possesses such great envy (abhyasūyā) is called "analpābhyasūyaḥ."
This is the characteristic of a *khaṇḍitā*:

she whose husband returns home at dawn from somewhere or other, his eyes copper-red and heavy with sleep as if closed in a bud, and his body marked by the distinct scratches of a woman’s nails; she is called a *khaṇḍitā*.
It has been told by ancient poets.
The sun serves as a comparison for the husband of a *khaṇḍitā* woman; the lotus plant serves as a comparison for the *khaṇḍitā* herself;

the lotus flower serves as a comparison for her eye; and the dew serves as a comparison for her tear. By this, it is indicated that she should cultivate friendship with the sun. This is the figure of speech known as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).

43 || -39- Where have all the *kimbhūtas* gone? At what time? After the sense of "do not be" (*mā bhava naḥ*), first the sense of "thus" (*iti*). In the water of the deep river, as if in a serene mind.
Even the reflection of your form, naturally beautiful, shall find entrance there;
therefore, you ought not, out of stubborn pride, to render fruitless her glances, as pure as white water-lilies, which are like the darting leaps of restless fish. (40)
In the clear waters of the river named Gambhīrā, your self—
naturally beautiful even in its shadow-form— enters [the water] as a reflected image, just as it enters the mind.
He will obtain [them].
For that reason, the dwellings of this river— [like those of the kumuda lily]—
are characterized by the glances of darting minnows leaping up and the sightings of trembling fish quivering about.
Out of steadfastness and profundity, you ought not to render them fruitless—that is, to make them vain. Therefore, do not depart; for by going, those [feelings] would become ineffective.
Moreover, a gallant man delays when his beloved gazes upon him with passion.
For he had entered her heart. "White as the water-lily," [referring to] the deep river Dākṣiṇāvarta.
By the word "gambhīra" (deep), the noble heroine (*udāttanāyikā*) is understood.
[The term] *chāyātmā* means one whose nature is a reflection (*pratibimbātmā*).
Regarding this, Yādava states: "The word *chāyā* refers to shade, luster, and the reflection of the sun and the moon."
By this distinction, the reflection of the Supreme Self is also suggested.

"Naturally beautiful" (*prakṛtisubhaga*) means beautiful by nature; the meaning may also be understood as beautiful through union with the principle known as *Prakṛti*. [He is] naturally beautiful in his mind.

It should be understood that the meaning "the reflection of the Supreme Self is reflected" is also suggested (dhvani). Even if you do not wish to enter that deep [water] by your own essential nature (*svarūpa*), nevertheless, your shadow-self (*chāyātman*) will certainly enter it.
Therefore, having summoned your fortitude, you ought not to disregard even the glances of the darting fish; for then there will be a delay in my mission—this is the intended meaning. || 40 ||
Mallinātha [comments] on the word "gambhīrāyāḥ": |||

The river named Gambhīrā is suggested as a noble heroine (*udāttanāyikā*). In her water—which is exceedingly pure and clear, like a mind that is serene and free from defects due to being bright and affectionate—he is naturally and by his very essence (*prakṛtyā*) fortunate and handsome; for "handsome" implies one who possesses great good fortune.
And on a day other than an ill-fated one; "in the fourth part" and "the glorious and fortunate one"—thus it is said in the *Śabdārṇava*.
That which is your shadow and that which is your self—that too is either a reflected image or a body.
She will obtain entry; by the use of the word "api" (even), the sense is that she will enter even if she does not desire it.
Therefore, because her entry is inevitable even through the medium of her shadow, the words of this deep-mouthed woman are as clear, white, clever, and swift as white water-lilies.
The "glances" are the very leaping and tossing about of the *śaphara* fish; according to the *Viśva* lexicon, the word *tvaritam* (in the compound *triṣu syāttvaritaṃ śīghram*) means "swift."
This alone is the sign of deep affection:
that you ought not to render it fruitless through fortitude, audacity, or impudence—the meaning being that one who is truly in love should not be deceived. As for the characteristics of a rogue:
"The handsome man constantly torments the woman he has already won; the rogue approaches with effort the one who is not yet enamored, and abandons the one who is already in love. (43)
The commentary on this is the Sumativijaya.
"He megha api" means "even he, O cloud," used here in the sense of possibility. Your own manifest form—
even its shadow-self, that is, the body which is the nature of the reflected shadow— will obtain entry into this [image].
Where? In the water of the river named Gambhīrā;
in whose [water], as in what? It is imagined to be as if in the mind of a woman possessing the quality of depth (gambhīrya). Just as...
A person who is naturally handsome and clever by birth— even his shadow-self,
or even a form painted in a picture, enters the heart of a woman of profound nature; likewise, she becomes impassioned toward that painted form even when it is out of her sight.
In your deep mind, there is even the state of joy, like the reflection of a self; in what kind of mind? In one that is serene and clear.
O cloud, for that reason, [you are the cause] of this deep river.
You ought not—indeed, you are not fit—to render fruitless, to make useless, these eyes of yours which are like shimmering, restless minnows darting about.
Why? Because of *dhairya*, the quality of manhood characterized by fortitude.
And of what nature are these glances, resembling the darting of restless minnows? They are "white as white lotuses," meaning they are as pale as the *kumuda* lily;
such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
"Caṭulā" refers to glances that are like the leaping of darting fish; thus, "caṭulaśapharodvartanāni eva prekṣitāni netrāṇi" means eyes whose glances are like the leaping of darting fish.
Because the surface of the belly is seen to be exceedingly white due to the leaping of the fish, the term "udvartana" (leaping) is used.
By this, the fulfillment of the cloud’s journey through its contact with the body of the river is described.
Here, there is the poetic figure of *saṅkara* (commingling), consisting of both *upamā* (simile) and *rūpaka* (metaphor).
—40— *maccha* is a Prakrit form for *matsya* (fish), though it is used here with an incorrect gender.

O friend, having stolen her dark garment of water— which has slipped from its hips of the riverbanks and clings to the reed-branches as if held by her hand— your departure will somehow be possible even as you linger there.
Who, having tasted its flavor, would be able to abandon a river whose hips are her sandy banks? (41)
The deep blue water itself is the garment and the sky of that river;
having taken it off under the influence of drinking, it hangs down because of its sluggishness due to the weight of the water.
While remaining right there, a departure will somehow occur; a journey will somehow come to pass—
for he who has known its taste and experienced its flavor [will not leave] that riverbank which is like a woman’s hips.
Who is capable of abandoning a young woman whose broad hips are the riverbanks? And you have experienced its flavor from drinking the water;
she too has "sandy banks for her hips" (pulinajaghanā).

Of what kind was the water-garment? It reached, or as if had obtained, the branches of the *vānīra* reeds—that is, it clung to the branches of the *vetasa* creepers. This is the meaning: "clinging to the branches of the *vānīra*. [This is an example of] the rule "prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā" (Pāṇini 2.1.24).
Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "by whom the branch of the cane (*vānīra*) has been reached.
And from this, he offers a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): as if held by the hand, that is, grasped by the hand.
For when lovers steal away her garment—

whether blue or green, as it is scanty in the summer— the women block them with both hands; thus, because of that stealing, the very bank (rodhas) which was abandoned and left behind becomes her hip (nitamba).
By which [means]. Even that garment which is being carried away becomes one from which the hips are released.
"Bhāvi" means that which will come to be. 41. Friend, something... she too, etc. [This portion is not provided].
"Will it be necessary?
"It will be, O Daksināvarta; it is for her."

"Having abandoned the obstructed hips": "having abandoned the obstruction," meaning the region of the waist; "hips" (*nitamba*) refers to the posterior part of the pelvis and the slope of the buttocks, according to Yādava, who states: "The word *nitamba* is used for the back of the hip and for a mountain ridge. "One who has known the taste" means one who has experienced the flavor of sexual union with women.
"With her hips exposed" means with the region of her waist exposed; Yādava states: "The word *jaghana* refers to the waist, the front part of the hip, and the hindquarters. (41)
Mallinātha says: "Of her..."
O friend, it has reached the branches of the *vānīra* reeds; therefore, it is as described, standing as if slightly supported by the hand.
It is that by which the bank—the slope—is released, that is, abandoned, acting as its very hip.
It has been said: "The term *nitamba* refers to the western part of the hips, the ridge of a mountain, or the waist" (Yādava).
Her garment is the very water of that deep [river], which is blue, meaning black in color.

"Having taken and brought. It is well known that at the time of departure, the lover's garment is seized for the purpose of dispelling the heat of separation. "Of one hanging down" means hanging down due to the weight of the water it has drunk. Elsewhere...

For you who have mounted [upon her] hips, your departure—your journey—will somehow occur with great difficulty. He states the reason for this difficulty by saying "jñāta-": one who has known the taste, that is, one who has experienced the flavor [of pleasure].

"Whose?"—referring to her whose *jaghana* (the hips or the region of the buttocks) was *vivṛtam*, meaning made manifest or revealed. Yādava states: "The word *jaghana* may refer to the hips, or to the front and back portions of the buttocks. [He wishes] to *vihātum*, that is, to abandon or leave her.
"Capable": the meaning is that no one at all [is so]. 44.
—41— This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.
O friend, O companion, by some means or other, with great difficulty, your departure—your journey—will come to pass.
Of what sort are you? You who are hanging down, unable to go because of being made sluggish by the weight of water.
Thus he was filled with doubt.
Having done what? Having taken—that is, having seized—the dark blue garment of water, which is the very water itself appearing as a cloth, from that deep river.
Of what nature was the water-garment? It had abandoned its banks and slopes.
Again, of what nature was the water-garment? It had reached the branches of the *vānīra* reeds.
What is the water-garment of that deep river like? It is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as something [specific].

"Like something held in the hand" means as if grasped by the hand; just as something held in the hand by someone is difficult to let go of, he confirms this very point: "a person who has known the taste," that is, a man who possesses aesthetic sensitivity (*rasika*).
The grammatical construction is as follows: who is capable of abandoning—that is, of giving up—her who has broad hips and a beautiful region of the hips? No one at all is capable of abandoning her.
"Salilavasana" means that the water itself is the garment; the sense is that, just as a woman has clothing, so too does this deep river have water as its garment.
"Mukta-nitamba" means that by which the banks (rodhas) themselves, being released [from the water], constitute the hips (nitamba).
"Where the obstruction has been abandoned" means it is free from hindrance.
"Where the branches of the *vānīra* trees have been reached" means that place where the branches of the *vānīra* trees have been attained.
"Jñātāsvādaḥ" means one by whom the taste of a beloved woman has been known.
"Vipulajaghanām" refers to her whose hips are broad.
Here, the poetic figure (alaṅkāra) is *rūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a metaphorical identification). 45 || -41-
After the phrase "no one is able to abandon it," should the meaning be as follows:

"Being sanctified by contact with the fragrance of the earth, which is revived by the outpouring of your [river's] flow, and being drunk by elephants whose pleasure is enhanced by the sound echoing from their ear-holes..."
As you approach the mountain that precedes the gods,
a cool breeze will blow from below, ripening the *udumbara* fruits of the forest.
°nisyando° Su; ramyas Da,Ma.Su;
VALL Then, as you desired to go toward the Mountain of the Gods, wishing to depart, a wind carrying snow [arose].
It will sound low and move slowly;
of what nature? By contact with the fragrance of that earth—the ground which has been uplifted, blossomed, and thrilled by your outpouring, that is, the release of water.
It was holy and charming due to its pervasive fragrance;
likewise, it was being drunk by elephants out of pleasure.
How so? By means of the sound of "śūtkāra" (the hissing sound) from the openings of their trunks, which are like the apertures of channels.

"Subhagam" means delightful; it implies being accompanied by a whistling sound (*saśūtkṛtam*). For in a hollow object, a louder resonance arises due to the entry of wind. "Srotaḥkaraḥ" refers to the trunk of an elephant, as in Māgha’s verse: "by the internal wound from the stream [of blood] pierced by a spear" (*śiśupālavadha* 18.49).
Likewise, in the forest grove, he is the ripener and the cooker of the udumbara fruits, because the production of their ripening occurs through his power. 42.
"O clockwise-whirling wind, you are delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth, which is revived by your outpouring;
[or rather,] you are delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth, augmented by your fresh waters. By this, [the nature] of the wind [is described].
The state of being fragrant has been described. "Srotorandhra" refers to the opening of a stream; the term *srotorandhra*—meaning the aperture of a stream—is intended here to signify a water conduit.
The meaning is that it is beautiful with the sound of water swirling within the openings of the channels.
The air being drunk in by elephants through their trunks with their openings makes a sound like a stream issuing from a water-pipe; this is the meaning. By this—
Slowness has been mentioned.
Because it is being drunk up from below by elephants, your slow-moving wind will blow only from below;
thus, for you who travel long distances, there will be exhaustion caused by the propulsion of that wind.

The intention is that it will not exist. "Preceded by the word *deva*" means preceded by the word *deva*; "the mountain" means the word *giri*. These two words, *deva* and *giri*, because they do not themselves denote clouds, [denote] that which is approached by clouds—that is, what is expressed by their own aggregate.
It should be understood that "devagirim" is being perceived;
[it refers to] the *udumbara* fruits of the forest *udumbara* trees. The genitive case is used here due to its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛt*). 42.
Mallinātha says: "tvad" [etc.].
It is delightful due to contact with the fragrance of the earth—the ground—which has been revived and nourished by your outpouring, that is, by your rain.
The meaning is "fragrant.
By the word *srotaḥ* (stream), which denotes a sense organ in general, its specific instance, the nose, is indicated through metonymy (*lakṣaṇā*).

According to Amara, the word *srotas* refers to both a stream of water and a sense organ. Thus, it was being drunk by elephants— that is, being inhaled— by those beasts out of greed for the fragrance of the earth, in such a way as to be rendered beautiful by the sound produced within the nostrils, the cavities at the tips of their trunks.

This is the meaning. By this, sluggishness is expressed. In the *kānanas*, that is, in the forests, [there are] *udumbaras*, which have "living beings" (*jantu*) as their fruit. According to Amara: "The *udumbara* has 'living beings' as its fruit; it is a constituent of sacrifice and is called *hemadugdhaka*. [He is] the one who causes them to ripen, the one who brings them to maturity. Of measured... [mitāṃ]... [the root √mā].
"Short" means short. "Śita" means cold wind. "Devapūrva" means preceded by the word "deva";
that is to say, the mountain Devagiri. "Upajigamiṣoḥ" means desiring to approach;
the suffix *u* is added to the root *gam* after it has taken the desiderative suffix (*san*). "Te" means for you; "nīcaiḥ" means slowly or softly. It will blow.
The meaning is "she will fan you.
When there is an intention to express mere relationship (*sambandha-mātra*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used.
In the expression *devapūrvaṃ girim*, the quality of being preceded by "deva" (*devapūrvatva*) belongs to the word *giri* (mountain), and not [to the mountain itself].

The Alamkārikas state that it is a fault of "speaking the unspeakable" (*avācyavacana*) because the designator (*sañjñā*) lacks the status of being the designated (*sañjñitva*), as expressed by the phrase "of the designatum [which is] its referent. As it is said in the *Ekāvalī*:
"That which is the speaking of the unspeakable is indeed the fault of 'speaking the unspeakable' (*avācyavacana*). However, the resolution [is as follows]:

It must somehow be established that by the word *giri* (mountain), which is qualified by the word *deva* (god) and is primarily intended as a sound, the "Divine Mountain" (*Devagiri*)—which is suitable for being approached by clouds—is indicated. 45. —42. [End of final part?]
The commentary on this is the Sumativijaya.
O friend, O cloud, the wind—that very breeze of yours—will blow low, gently, and ever so slowly.
Of what nature is that wind? It is cool, exceedingly refreshing.
O Cloud, what do you wish to do? You desire to go toward, and intend to approach, the mountain named Devagiri.
Of what nature is that mountain? It is preceded by the word "deva" (divine), meaning the word "deva" [is applied] to the mountain.
[Previously] it means "from Devagiri.
Furthermore, of what nature is the wind?
It is delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth, which has been revived by the flow of your [tears].

Furthermore, of what nature is the wind? It is that which causes the *udumbara* trees of the forest to ripen—that is, to reach full maturity. By these two adjectives, the fragrance of the wind is expressed.
Furthermore, of what nature is the wind? It is such that it is as pleasant as the sound resonating within the cavities of the ears.
It is thus that [the water] is drunk by the tuskers, the elephants; such is the grammatical connection.

*Upeti* means desiring to go near (*upa-samīpe gantum-icchuḥ*), one who is about to approach (*upagamiṣuḥ*). For that one who is about to approach, *devapūrvam* means a mountain preceded by the word "Deva"— that is to say, the mountain named Devagiri.

"Dependent on you" (*tvanniṣyam*) means: delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth, which has been revived and made to blossom by the sprinkling of the water of existence (*bhava-jala*) that is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) from you;
thus it is "delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth revived by the outflow from you. By this—

Fragrance. "Srota" means the sense organ, the opening of the trunk, or the trunk itself; its resonance is "srotorandhradhvanita," and that which is beautiful by virtue of this resonance is "srotorandhradhvanitasubhaga. [This refers to] the fear of the elephant.
Since elephants drink [the water] with a hissing sound (*saphūtkāram*), therefore the wind possesses the quality of slowness (*mandatva*).
Regarding the term *kānana*: "forests of *udumbara* trees" are *kānanodumbarāṇi*; [it refers to] those *kānanodumbarāṇi*.
Because of the wind among the trees, there is a quality of coolness here.

On the side of the Devagiri mountain, there are many *udumbara* trees; indeed, they ripen only upon the arrival of the clouds. Therefore, O Cloud, if you are here in this poem, a cool wind shall blow for you.

Therefore, you are distinguished as being delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth revived by your outpouring; otherwise, this would be a qualification of the wind rather than the cloud.
Here, the poetic figure is *anumāna* (inference). 46. —42—
There, making yourself a cloud of flowers, may you bathe Skanda— who has made his dwelling permanent there— with showers of blossoms drenched by the waters of the celestial Ganges;
for the sake of protecting Indra’s armies against the wielder of the new moon.
For that splendor, surpassing the sun, was indeed concentrated within the mouth of the consumer of oblations (Agni).

There, on Mount Devagiri, you should bathe and worship the Youth (Kumāra), who is ever-present, with showers of excellent flowers whose essence is the water of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), since you have become like a cloud of flowers;
for the sake of protecting the armies of Vāsava, the forces of Indra.
The bearer of the new moon, the Moon-crested Lord, has concentrated and projected that splendor and vigor which is more intense than even the sun;
for Kārttikeya was begotten by Hara upon Gaurī for the sake of protecting the gods who were oppressed by the asuras.
Such is the traditional teaching (āgama). Furthermore, that semen, having moved from its own place, was swallowed by the fire;
thus, the application [of the suffix] *vāsavīnām* is difficult to justify, because the suffix *cha* after a word ending in *vṛddhi* is superseded [by other rules].
That which has transcended the sun is "beyond the sun" (*atyāditya*). [The phrase] "in the mouth of the sacrificial fire" refers to that which is clockwise (*dakṣiṇāvarta*) there.

Regarding that, it is said that in ancient times, after Skanda had slain the asuras for the sake of the gods and rested there, he was entreated by the gods to remain; he then promised, "I shall dwell here eternally together with Śiva and Śivā, who have come to see me. Thus, his residence on Mount Devagiri is constant.
He has made this vow; therefore, one should consider the traditional account that it was stated there that Skanda’s residence is fixed.
Because he can assume any form at will (*kāmarūpatva*), it is said that this [transformation] is possible for a cloud, as he has become a flower-cloud (*puṣpameghīkṛtātman*).

He explains a certain traditional account (*aitihya*). [The phrase] "for the sake of protection" (*rakṣāhetoh*) uses the genitive case; this is a genitive used in the sense of a causal instrument (*hetu-prayoga*).
[The term] *atyādityam* means "beyond the sun" (*atikrāntādityam*).
For it has been stated that "that energy was indeed concentrated in the mouth of the fire," explaining Skanda's emergence from the mouth of Agni. || 43 ||
Mallinātha says: "In that [regard]..."

In that regard, "one whose residence is on Devagiri" means one who is eternally present; the sense is that he is constantly manifest there. It is said that in ancient times, the Lord Skanda, the son of Bhavānī, being pleased by his victory over the asura named Tāraka and impelled by the prayers of the gods, [remained] eternally...
Having said, "I dwell here together with Śiva and Śivā," he became renowned as one who dwells there. Skanda is the youthful Lord Kumāra.
A cloud of flowers is a *puṣpamegha*. One who has made himself into a cloud of flowers is *puṣpameghīkṛtātmā*.

Being able to assume any form at will, you have transformed your body into a cloud raining flowers; with showers of flowers— *āsāra* being defined by Amara as a "downpour of rain"— moistened by the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā, may you yourself bathe [him].
"Let him consecrate [himself]. The intention is that one's own worship is the most excellent. And so it is said in the *Śambhurahasya*:
"If one worships the God oneself, that is the best; [otherwise, it is done] by sons of the same womb."
That which is performed by servants is middling; that which is performed by officiating priests is the lowest form of sacrificial action.
Thus, by establishing Skanda’s worthiness of worship, he introduces a different point with the word "rakṣā" (protection).

The meaning is that the Blessed One is Skanda. The neuter gender is used because the predicate is predominant. "Vāsavya" means belonging to Vāsava; [the suffix -ya] is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to him").

*Aṇ*. For the sake of protecting those armies—the hosts belonging to Vāsava and Indra—for the purpose of their protection; this is the meaning. The genitive case is used here according to the rule "the genitive is employed when a word expressing a cause is used."
By the Blessed One who bears the new moon, the moon-crested one (*candraśekhara*).

"Vaha" means that which carries; it is derived from the root *vah* with the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādyac* class). "Hutavaha" is the fire, so called because it carries the oblation (*huta*); "collected in the mouth of that [fire]" means accumulated within its opening. "Exceeding the sun" (*atyādityam*) means surpassing the sun.

The compound is formed according to the rule "atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā" (Pāṇini 2.2.18). The meaning is that splendor (*tejas*) is indeed another form of the Lord Hara himself; therefore, the sense is that it is worthy of worship. The mention of the "mouth," however, is for the purpose of indicating its purity. That...
It is stated in the *Śambhurahasya*:
"One should know that the hindquarters of cows, the feet of a twice-born, the heart of yogis, the speech of a poet, the face of women, fire, and horses are supremely pure. (46)
-43- *Sumativijaya’s Commentary on This* ||

O Cloud, having transformed yourself into a flower-cloud on that mountain Devagiri and having assumed the form of a cloud that creates a rain of blossoms, may you, being thus, bathe— that is, wash— Skanda Kārttikeya, the son of Mahādeva.
By what? By showers of flowers (*puṣpāsāraiḥ*), meaning either by flowers acting as showers or by showers of flowers characterized by rapid rain;
the sense is that even in the absence of [actual] flowers, it is by means of showers of flowers, that is, by the most excellent flowers themselves.
Of what nature was Skanda? He was one whose dwelling was fixed on Devagiri, remaining there without interruption.
Of what nature were the showers of flowers? They were moistened by the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā, purified by the waters of the heavenly Ganges.

He speaks of its majesty: for indeed, O Cloud, that splendor which is his own power was gathered— that is, preserved— by Mahādeva, the bearer of the new moon, within the mouth of the fire, in the midst of the flames.

For what reason? For what purpose? For the sake of protecting the Vāsavī armies—the hosts belonging to Indra—from the Daityas, that is, for the purpose of providing protection against them. This is that splendor (tejas). By this mention of splendor, [the greatness] of Skanda [is established].
It has been stated that he is the son of Rudra.
Of what nature is that splendor? It is a splendor exceeding even the sun (atyāditya).
This is the grammatical connection.
"Flower": he by whom his own self—the body—has been turned into a flower-cloud is "one who has turned his self into a flower-cloud.
"Fixed": he by whom his dwelling—his stay or station—has been made fixed and immovable is "one of fixed dwelling."

"Pushpaih" means with flowers; "pushpasaraih" means with showers of flowers. According to the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*, "āsāraḥ" refers to a heavy downpour of rain. "Vasoh" refers to Indra; "vāsavīnām" means belonging to those [clouds] of Indra. By this, [the nature of] the cloud is indicated.
The worship of Skanda with showers of flowers has been described;
here, the poetic figure is *jāti* (natural description). || 47 || —43— [Note:
The explanation of *puṣpāsāraiḥ* appears confused and contradictory.]

May that peacock of Pāvaka protect you— he whose fallen plumage, encircled by streaks of light, Bhavānī places upon her ear out of affection for her son, reaching as far as her blue-lotus-like ear, its outer corner washed by the radiance of Hara’s moon.
Afterwards, you should make [the mountain] dance with thunderclaps heavy from seizing the peaks.
Immediately after that, you should cause Skanda’s vehicle, the peacock,
to dance with its cries— that is, you should make it perform a dance— by listening to the thundering of the clouds.
Indeed, peacocks dance;
that has been stated. To the question "Which one?", he says:
that from whose tail-feather (*varha*)—the plumage—has fallen or dropped, Gaurī, out of affection for her son, [placed] upon her ear.
He makes it his crest-ornament; and that [ornament] reaches the position of a *kuvalaya* lotus, having ascended to the place of a blue water-lily (*utpala*).
It is thus characterized by a circle of streaks of light—a halo consisting of a mass of radiance.
It has been said:
[her] outer corners of the eyes were washed and the edges of her eyes cleansed by the moonlight of the moon on Śiva’s head— the radiance of Hara’s lunar crest.

With what kind of roars? With those heavy with the seizing of mountains—that is, as massive as the grasping of a mountain. In the compound *adrigrahaṇa*, the word *śabda* (sound) is the agent; it is not a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound.
[Regarding the imperative] *nartayethāḥ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not apply by virtue of the rule beginning with *na pādami* (Pāṇini 1.3.89). 44. !Beisp!
"The light that turns to the right."

The reading is *kuvalayadalakṣepī*; the meaning is "casting [glances] that mock the petals of the blue lotus. *Dhautāpāṅgam* means "with the corners of the eyes cleansed"; this cleansing consists in making the corners of the eyes radiant with whiteness. By this, the refinement of the dancer’s facial adornment is indicated.
And it is understood [from the context]:
"of Skanda by Pavaki. By this, the explanation has been provided that "for that splendor was indeed concentrated in the mouth of the fire-eater (Agni). {43}
After the bathing with flowers;
"adrigrahaṇa" (mountain-grasping) refers to the grasping of the cave.
You should cause [the deity] to dance; by that, the dance intended here is his worship.

Since the consecration has already been described and because it will be stated later that "having propitiated him," it should be understood that by this verse the presence of the two Śivas (Śiva and Śivā) is declared. || 44 ||
"Jyotir Mallinātha."

"Jyotiṣastejasaḥ" means streaks or lines of light; "valayam" refers to a circle or ring. That [peacock] is so described because it possesses such a circle. "Galitam" means fallen or dropped, but the sense is that it was not cut off by itself out of fickleness. This refers to the "barham," the tail-feather of the peacock (piccha-barha).

"A neuter [term]," says Amara. Bhavānī (Gaurī), out of affection for her son—that is, through love for her child—places upon her ear something reaching as far as a petal of a blue lotus (*kuvalaya*); that is, she wears it together with its petal. Or alternatively:

"In the ear, which possesses petals and is worthy of petals, [the bee] acts as one reaching for the petal of the blue water-lily (kuvalaya). This is the locative case derived from a word ending in the *kvip* suffix. The meaning is that, having discarded its own petal, it places a feather (*barha*) in its stead.
However, Nātha, following the reading "one who casts away the petal of the blue water-lily" (*kuvalayadalakṣepī*), interprets *kṣepa* [as casting away].
Or [it may mean] "the removal of blame," as he has explained.

"With the moonlight on Hara’s head" (*haraśaśirucā*) means with the moonlight upon the head of Śiva; "with the corners of the eyes washed" (*dhautāpāṅgam*) means that the outer corners of the eyes are made exceedingly white, even more so than their natural whiteness. "Apāṅgau" refers to the outer ends of the eyes.

*Amara* [is the lexicon]. *Pāvaki* is Skanda, the offspring of *pāvaka*, the fire; [the suffix] *iñ* is applied here. His—that aforementioned peacock of his—[he saw] behind the mountain, after the flower-bath (*puṣpābhiṣecana*).
By means of the thundering roars of Devagiri— the maker of caves—
resonant with deep echoes, you should cause him to dance; that is,
you should attend upon the Lord Kumāra by acting as his drummer.
[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used].
In the case of *nartayethāḥ*, the suffix *ātmanepada* is set aside by the rule *aṇāvakarmakāccittavatkartṛkāt*; however, the suffix *parasmaipada* is applied by the rule *nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca*.
It does not occur [in that case], because of the prohibition: "na pādamyāḍyamāḍyasaparimuharucinṛtivadavasaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.5). — Sumativijaya.
The explanation of this is as follows:
O Cloud, after Skanda has been worshipped with flowers, you should afterwards cause that peacock— the vehicle of Kārttikeya, the offspring of Agni— to dance.
By what means? By means of roars, that is, by the sounds of thundering.
Which one? That peacock whose plumage—its tail feathers—Bhavānī, Pārvatī, places upon her ear, making it an ear-ornament.
By what? By love for his son; [he carried] Kārttikeya, out of affection for that [child’s] vehicle.
Of what nature was the peacock feather? Encircled by streaks of light.
Furthermore, of what nature was the feather? Slipped off, but not plucked.
Furthermore, of what nature was the plumage? It was "reaching the petals of the blue lotus," having the quality of extending to the petals of the blue lotus.
Of what nature was the peacock? Its body was white, with its corners of the eyes washed clean.
By what? By the luster of Hara’s moon—the radiance of Rudra’s crescent moon.
Of what nature were the roars? Heavy with the seizing of mountains, vying with the echoes of the divine mountain.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).
Regarding the term *pāvaki*: the offspring (*apatyam*) of Pāvaka—that is, Agni—is *pāvaki*.
This is derived by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*, for Skanda was indeed born from Agni. How so? For the sake of protecting the divine army (*devasenā*) from the Daityas.
Śiva cast his own semen into the fire; from that semen Skanda was born.
The sense is that the Daityas were slain by Skanda.
"Putreṇa" means "by the son's love," that is, by the affection for a son (*putraprema*).
"Jyotirlekha-valayi" means that which possesses a circle (valaya), a wreath (lekhā), of lights (jyotis), that is, of splendors (kānti).
"Kuvalayadala-anukāri" means it attains the likeness of a petal (dala) of a blue water-lily (kuvalaya).
Such is his character, which reaches even the petals of the blue water-lily. "Dhauta" means washed;

he whose outer corners of the eyes (*apāṅga*) have been washed—that is, made white—is "dhautāpāṅga. [He gazes at] the peacock that has become white through contact with the moonlight upon Śiva’s head.
This is the meaning.
"Hareti" means by the moonlight of Hara (Śiva), that is, by the radiance of the moon on Śiva's head. By this, the worship of Skanda on the path of the cloud is expressed.

The figure of speech is *jāti* (natural description). [Verse 48] — Having thus propitiated the god born of the Śara-reed forest, he traversed the path with his body white from the oil used for carrying that [deity], and with his peacock rendered pure white.
The path was cleared by pairs of perfected beings (siddhas) who, carrying lutes, had abandoned it out of fear of the water droplets.

You should descend [to earth], honoring the fame of Rantideva— which was born from the sacrifice of his own daughter Surabhi’s offspring— and which has now been transformed on the ground into the form of a river.
In this manner, [the gods] bathed the youth born in the Śara forest with showers of flower-essence and other such rites.
Having propitiated [him] and traveled some distance, you should resort to— that is, take refuge in and go toward— the fame of King Rantideva, known as the Carmaṇvatī, in order to honor it.
Of what kind was she? She was born from the *alambhana*—the sprinkling or consecration—of cows, the daughters of Surabhi;
she was born upon the earth and had undergone a transformation of form by becoming a river in the guise of a flowing stream. Indeed, by that king, during his sacrifices...
According to tradition, the exceedingly numerous cows were slaughtered there, and from their blood and hides the Carmaṇvatī river was formed.
What kind of person are you? One whose path has been cleared by pairs of perfected beings out of fear of the drops of water [falling upon them].
He whose path was avoided by lute-players with *vallakī* lutes in their hands— because the strings become discordant when wet with water—
and by the Gaṅgā, who, unable to endure the power of Agni upon reaching it, fled into the reed-thicket (*śaravaṇa*).
Because he has abandoned [the world], Skanda is known as Śaraja;
the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs according to the rule beginning with "pra-nir-antar-śara-ikṣu-plakṣa. || 45 ||
"Having propitiated Dakṣiṇāvarta..."
The sense is that [the gods] came with groups of Siddhas to play the lute for Skanda;
"vīṇibhiḥ" means those possessing lutes (vīṇāvat). The suffix *ini* is applied here according to the rule for the *vrīhy-ādi* class.

*vrīhi*, *śikhā*, *aṣṭakā*, *mālā*, *patākā*, *varma*, *karman*, *mekhalā*, *baḍavā*, *vīṇā*, *sañjñā*, *carman*, and *valākā*— this is the *vrīhy-ādi* group. A lute (*vīṇā*) whose strings have been moistened with water does not sound.
The abandonment of the path of the clouds by the Siddhas.
To fully understand the matter about to be described, the following should be connected here:
there was a certain Rantideva of virtuous fame, the sovereign of the city named Daśapura.

Thus it was with the king. Among his cows, certain celestial beings, descending daily with their hooves, horns, and other limbs made of gold, would wander at will and then depart. Such was their form.
Having seen them, Rantideva’s cows asked, "From where has such a form as this arisen for you?
They replied in turn, "In former times, we were consecrated in sacrifices; it is from that that we have become like this."
And those cows, having approached their master Rantideva, said:
"O King, for all this time we have served you;
therefore, you should sacrifice us in the ritual offerings so that we may attain divine forms."
He too, having slaughtered them at sacrifices, carried their hides away somewhere like a mountain.
From that mountain of hides, dripping with blood, a river flows forth which, because it originates from hides (*carman*), they call the Carmaṇvatī; such is the narrative from the *Bhārata*.

Keeping that river in his heart, he describes it by way of its fame, saying: "vyālambethāḥ. This means you should descend, bending down; "surabhitanayālambhajāṃ" refers to the slaughter (*ālambha*) of the daughters of Surabhi, who are the cows.
The slaughter [was performed] by means of the form of the Sotru [river] and the form of the waters of the Carmaṇvatī river. (45) [Is "gaṇa" an addition?
— Mallinātha.
"Having propitiated," it says.

"Śara" refers to arrows and *bāṇatṛṇa* (reed-grass); according to the *Śabdārṇava*, "śara" means both an arrow and *bāṇatṛṇa*. A forest (*vana*) of these is a *śaravaṇa*; the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs here by the rule *pra-nir-antar-śara-* etc. (*Pāṇini* 8.4.5). He whose birth (*janma*) occurred there is [described as] *tadbhava*.

Born in a forest of reeds (*śaravaṇabhava*). Vāmana states that a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) *bahuvrīhi* compound is not to be avoided when "birth" (*janman*) is the final member. This means it must be resorted to because there is no other way. "The god Skanda. According to Amarasimha, "He whose birth is in reeds" (*śarajanmā*) is the six-faced one (*ṣaḍānana*).
Having propitiated and worshipped [him];

by those possessing lutes (*vīṇibhiḥ*), i.e., those possessing lutes—the suffix *ini* being applied according to the rule for the *vrihy-ādi* group; by pairs of perfected ones (*siddha-dvandvaiḥ*), i.e., by couples of perfected ones who had come to play the lute for the Blessed Lord Skanda.

The meaning is: "out of fear of water-drops. The reason is that the sprinkling of water would obstruct the resonance of the lute; this is the sense. "Having left the path" (*muktamārgaḥ*) means having abandoned the way or having traversed the road.
The meaning is: "how far has he gone? [This refers to] the cows, the daughters of Surabhi.
She was so called because she was born through being touched and pacified; on earth, in the world,
she had transformed into the form of a stream— a flowing current— and attained a specific physical form as the river named Carmaṇvatī, the fame of the great king Rantideva, lord of Daśapura.
The meaning is "to the river. "Mānayiṣyan" means intending to honor or show respect. "Vyālambheyithāḥ" means you would have descended after having grasped [the branch].
It is said that formerly, at the immolation of cows by King Rantideva, [this occurred] from a place where [the branches] were gathered together.
From the flow of blood from that heap of skins, a certain river surged forth; it is known by the name Carmaṇvatī. || 48 || —45— Sumativijaya.
The explanation of this is as follows.
O cloud, having traversed the path, how much further have you traveled when you are met by pairs of *siddhas* and *kinnaras* holding lutes in their hands; for this very reason,
out of fear that the lutes will be damaged by the water droplets— fearing they will perish upon contact with the water— [they remain] with their lutes fixed in the water.

Having abandoned the path and being one who has left the path behind, you should take hold—that is, you should provide support—by propitiating this god Kārttikeya, the son of Śaravaṇa. What having done? Having propitiated him.
Having propitiated and worshipped [the deity] at Devagiri,
O Cloud, what will you do? You will honor the fame of King Rantideva— named Rantideva— and listen to it with great reverence.
Of what nature was that fame? It was born from the embrace of the daughter of Surabhi.
Furthermore, of what nature was that fame? It was spread abroad upon the earth;
by what means? By way of a stream, in the form of a river.
Such is the grammatical connection (anvaya).
The meaning is that on the way, from the mouth of a *kiṃnara* who has come face-to-face, you should abandon the path and hear the fame of Rantideva.
Regarding the word *ullam*: one by whom the *adhvan*—the path—has been *ullaṅghita* (traversed) is *ullaṅghitādhvā*.
"Siddha-dvandvaiḥ" means by pairs of Siddhas or by pairs of specific classes of deities or Kinnaras.
"Jalakaṇa-bhayāt" means from the fear of water droplets, that is, from the fear arising due to the falling of drops of water.
The meaning is that out of fear of water droplets, the *siddhas* will not sing when the lute (*vīṇā*) has become wet with water.
"By those possessing lutes" (*vīṇibhiḥ*) means by those who hold lutes in their hands.
"Surabhi" refers to the cows, the daughters of Surabhi; "tanyālambha" is their slaughter.

Therefore, it is called *surabhitanyālambhajam*, meaning born from the slaughter of those cows. For indeed, at the Gomedha sacrifice performed by Rantideva, hundreds of excellent cows were summoned for the sacrifice.

It is well known that the Carmaṇvatī river was born from the flow of the stream of his blood; by this, the hearing of King Rantideva’s fame by the cloud is expressed. This is the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor). 49. -45-

The phrase *adhvani san* and so forth appears strange and contradicts the first explanation, namely that *siddha* refers to a *kinnara* or a specific class of deity (*devaviśeṣaṇa*). There are two identical explanations regarding the *vīṇibhiḥ*. The word *yajñe* is unnecessary. This is because of the phrase *yato hi*.
When you, the thief of the peacock’s plumage, bend down to take water from her,
the sky-dwellers will gaze upon that river’s current— which, though broad, appears slender due to its distance— by turning their eyes far upward.
Like a single string of pearls from the earth, with a large sapphire in its center. (46) 49 Ma;
50 Su;
nūnam Da?, Ma;
O Vallabha, while you were bent down to take water from her,
the sky-dwelling Siddhas called the river Carmaṇvatī by the name Sindhu and fixed their eyes upon its flowing current.
Turning their gaze very far away and casting it out of curiosity, they will behold [the mountain],
for the earth possesses a single large central sapphire, just as a string of pearls consists of a single strand of pearls;
and because the stream resembles a string of pearls, the cloud possesses a quality equal to that of a great sapphire.
Of what kind is the stream? Though broad, it is thin; though extensive, it is very small.
Why? Because of its distance, that is, due to remoteness; for even a large object appears small when seen from afar. Because it contains water, it is dark blue, a thief of color. By this—
The resemblance to sapphire has been stated. || 46 ||
In response to the inquiry, "O Dākṣiṇāvarta, what honor should be shown to her by me?", he says: "In you... and so forth.
The grammatical connection is: "even though it is broad, it appears thin from a distance; [it is] a stream.

The "sky-goers" (gaganagatayaḥ) are the Siddhas and others who move through the air. The word "one" (eka) in the phrase "a single string of pearls" (ekamuktāguṇam) is used here with the same intention as the term "single-string necklace" (ekāvalī). || 46 ||
Mallinātha says: "In you... [etc.].
O thief of the complexion and beauty of Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow— the meaning is that you possess a complexion equal to His— when you bend down to take water,
her [the Yamunā’s] broad [form], though appearing thin due to its distance, is perceived as subtle.
The stream of the river named Carmaṇvatī from the Sindhu;

"those whose movement is in the sky" are the sky-dwellers, such as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and others. This is also a bahuvrīhi compound, with the elision of the middle member (*madhyamapadalopa*) as before.
This should be understood as applying to the subsequent words: "Surely, having turned toward the truth and restrained his views,
he is like the earth (bhuvaḥ), which possesses a great, thick [mountain] with a single central pillar, wherein a massive sapphire serves as the central gem."
They will behold it like a string of pearls, a pearl necklace;
here, because the stream joined with the intensely dark cloud is imagined as a string of pearls released from the neck of the earth, this is indeed a figure of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

The word *iva* indicates this [metaphor]. However, the author of the *Nirukta*, seeing the word *iva* here and there where it occurs in similes, was deluded into thinking that because the word *iva* is seen here as well, this too must be a simile. || 49 || -46-
The explanation of this is the *Sumativijaya*.

O Cloud, the Vidyadhara gods dwelling in the sky, having turned their gaze toward and extended it very far, [behold] the flow of that river Sindhu— from the middle of which, though broad and vast, it appears distant due to its great extent.
They will behold from afar your body—subtle, solitary, and like a string of pearls released from the earth—as if it were a garland of pearls.
When? While you, the cloud, have bent down to take up water.
When you were present—of what nature? You who steal the complexion of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, dark-hued like Kṛṣṇa.
Of what nature was the string of pearls? It had a large sapphire in its center.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).

"Śārṅgin" means one who possesses the Śārṅga bow; [the term] "of him" refers to Śārṅgin, that is, Kṛṣṇa. "Varṇacaura" means a thief of color—one who steals the dark hue (śyāmarūpa). In that thief of color...
"Gaganā" means those whose movement is in the sky (gagana), that is, in space (ākāśa); they are the "sky-goers" (gaganagatayaḥ), meaning the gods and the Vidyādharas.
"Sthūla" refers to a large, medium-sized sapphire (indranīla), a specific type of gemstone belonging to the class of jewels.
Or rather, that which belongs to him is a "thick-middle sapphire" (sthūlamadhya-indranīla).
For there is a comparison with the very extensive pearl necklace of the Indus River;
and within that [necklace], there is a comparison for the cloud with the thick-middle sapphire, just as [one might compare] a woman.
Just as there might be a string of pearls, so too is this "string of pearls" (mauktikamālā) on the earth; the sense is that the gods will cast their eyes [upon it] and behold it.
Here, the poetic figure is *upamā* (simile). || 50 || -46-

*madhyāt uttaram* (superior to the average? appears to be in the wrong place in only three manuscripts if it qualifies *pravāham*. *devās vidyādharās* is explained twice. *prasārayitvā* is a gerund (*prasārya*).
Having crossed that river, proceed toward those women whose playful movements of their creeper-like brows are well-known,
whose dark and dappled luster shines above as they lift their eyelashes,
and who steal the beauty of bees following the scattering of *kunda* flowers— show them your own reflection.
Making himself the object of the curiosity of the eyes of the women of Daśapura. || 47 || 50 Mall; 51 Su;
°sāra° Su; VALL
Having crossed that river Carmaṇvatī, you should proceed toward the city named Daśapura,
making yourself an object of curiosity for the eyes of young women and bringing yourself within the range of their vision; and by whatever path leads near to Daśapura...
The meaning is that the city-dwellers should behold you. Of what sort?
Those whose playful movements of the eyebrow-branches are familiar and practiced due to their urbanity;
likewise, those who, by virtue of beholding you, flash and quiver above with the raising of their eyelashes.
Those whose luster is like that of black-spotted deer; and therefore, those which steal the beauty— the splendor— of the bees that follow after the scattering or projection of the *kunda* flowers,
because the *kunda* flowers are white and the bees are dark.
Because of the nature of time. Although these are qualifiers of curiosity, nevertheless, by the force of the facts, these qualities belong specifically to the eyes that possess them. || 47 ||
"O you who turn to the right! Thus [he says].
"Of those possessing a variegated luster (*śāraprabhā*) shining above, [the color] is variegated (*śāra*)— black, red,
and white. Although Yādavaprakāśa states that the word *śāra* denotes a mixture of the three colors, here the word *kṛṣṇa* occurs separately from the word *śāra*.
When there is a mixture of white and red colors, the function [of the term] is restricted; likewise, there is the usage in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*: "eyes like a black antelope" (*kṛṣṇaśāre vilocane*).
And in the *Saptaśatī*, it says: "one body with a black antelope as its essence" (*eko hi kālasāreṇa dehaḥ*).

[The wind] steals the beauty of the bees following the scattering of the *kunda* flowers. "Scattering of the *kunda*" refers to the impelling of the *kunda* by the wind. "The beauty of the bees" refers to the splendor of the bees; because the bees enter into the interiors of the red blossoms for the sake of drinking nectar, the bees become pale-red due to that pollen.
It should be understood that [the word] "exists" (vidyate) is to be supplied.

"The reflection of the self" (ātmabimba) refers to the orb of one's own body. Regarding the term *bimba*: "The word *bimba*—which is not feminine—is used for an orb, a likeness, a face, and a mark; whereas *pratibimba* refers to its original form (*tatprakṛti*)."
The Yādava [is the object] of the curiosity of the eyes of the women of Daśapura. "Vadhū" means a woman.
"Netrakautūhalāni" refers to the opening of the eyes and other such actions that have arisen from the curiosity of the eyes;
therefore, it refers to the curiosity of the eyes, namely the opening of the eyes and so forth.
The state of possessing the graceful play of well-cultivated, creeper-like eyebrows, and the quality of having a dark, variegated luster shimmering above, is possible. || 47 ||
"O Mallinātha, her— " so [it says].

Having crossed that Carmaṇvatī river, [he beheld] those whose playful charms (*vibhrama*)—the graceful movements (*vilāsa*)—are fashioned through familiarity with those whose creeper-like eyebrows (*bhrūlatā*) are like creepers (*latā*); this is a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison). Of such persons...?

"Palakṣma" refers to the eyelashes; according to the Viśvakośa, "palakṣma" denotes a thread, a minute part, a filament, and the eyelashes. "On account of their upward tossing" means due to their being raised or lifted up. "Kṛṣṇaśārāḥ" means those that are both black and variegated—dark-spotted.

The compound is *varṇo varṇena* (color by color). Yādava states that "black, red, and white" constitute *śāra*. Consequently, since the quality of blackness (*kārṣṇya*) is already established by the word *śāra* alone, the further inclusion of the word *kṛṣṇa* is for the purpose of emphasizing the predominance of blackness. However, redness (*raktatva*) is not [emphasized].

What is intended [as the object of comparison] follows from the analogy; for that which is natural [to the eyes] is contradicted by the *sāmudrika* (physiognomic) rules regarding women's eyes, and thus another [quality] is not applicable here. However, the mention of a particular state (*bhāva*) in some instances is within the scope of logical justification. Those whose splendors are black-spotted (*kṛṣṇaśāra*) and shimmering above.

Of those [trees], *kundas* are the *mādhyaka* flowers; according to Amara, "the *kunda* is the *mādhyaka*. Those which follow—that is, which move along with—the scattering (*kṣepa*) of them, which is their tossing here and there.

"Madhukaras" refers to those who steal the beauty of others; thus, it means the bees that imitate the scattered *kunda* flowers. "Daśapura" is the city of Rantideva; its "vadhvas" are the women. *Vadhūḥ*.
"Jāyā and snuṣā," according to Amara. Of those "curiosities of the eyes"—meaning their longing glances—make your own form the object, making it the focus of their desire; go, proceed. 50.
The explanation of this [is] *Sumatīvijaya*.
O cloud, having crossed and caused others to cross that river Sindhu, proceed; go!
What are you doing? You are making your own form—the reflection of yourself—the vessel, that is, the recipient.
Of whom? Of the curious glances of the women of Daśapura—of those visual observations produced by curiosity.
Of what kind were the curious glances of the women of Daśapura?
Of those whose playful movements of the creeper-like eyebrows were well-cultivated, whose graceful dalliances of the creeper-like eyebrows were constantly practiced;
furthermore, of what nature? Of the eyes of the women of Daśapura, which possessed the luster of black antelopes shimmering above [their brows].
Why? Because of the raising of the eyelashes, because of looking with half-closed eyes, and because of looking with a sidelong glance.
Furthermore, of what kind were they? Of those who were objects of curiosity for the eyes of the women of Daśapura.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Because of the very lifting of the eyelashes, [the glances] possess the beauty of stealing the splendor of bees that follow the scattering of *kunda* flowers; they imitate the charm of the bees that pursue the tossing of *kunda* blossoms."

The curiosities of the eyes— the curious glances consisting of restless gazes— of the women of Daśapura, those very curiosities of the eyes of the women of Daśapura; by means of familiarity, that is, through repeated practice.
The playful movements of the creeper-like eyebrows; for those whose playful movements of the creeper-like eyebrows are well-practiced.
"Above" means sporting above; "black antelopes" refers to those that are black, i.e., of a dark color.
Those whose essence consists of black and white luster— referring to those upon whom the black luster of the *kṛṣṇasāra* deer shines above;
"with jasmine" means by one following the scattering of jasmine, brought forth by the impulse of the fragrance of the *mucukunda* flower.
They are "stealers of the beauty of the bees" (*madhukara-śrī-muṣaḥ*), meaning they rob the splendor or the likeness of such bees as rest upon *kunda* flowers;
thus, they are those who steal the beauty of the bees that have descended upon the scattered *kunda* blossoms.

[O you] who steal the beauty of the bees following the smoke from the sacrificial pits; by this [path], you must travel having gone above the city of Daśapura. There is a figure of speech (alaṃkāra) called *upamā* here. 51.
Piercing the land of Brahmāvarta with your shadow from below, you should resort to that Kuru field which betokens the great battle of the kṣatriyas,
