where the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow [will strike] the kings with hundreds of sharp arrows.
With showers of falling rain, they sprinkled their faces like lotuses, just as you do. 48 || 51 Ma; 52 Su; now with shade Da, Ma; below with shade Su; raining Da?, Ma, Su.
Then, touching with its lower shadow— the reflection— of the region known as Brahmāvarta, it went toward Kurukṣetra, which portends a great battle among the Kṣatriyas.
It indicates the battle of the princes; even now, from the sight of the fragments of arrows.
And there, with hundreds of sharp arrows, Arjuna sprinkled, inflamed, and filled the faces of the kṣatriyas, just as you do.
"By showers of water [he makes] lotuses"—this is a statement regarding the abundance of *śara* grass. || 48 ||
"Brahman is that which spirals to the right."
"Brahmāvarta" is a certain meritorious region in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa). Regarding this, [Manu says]:
"That region created by the gods which lies between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, they call Brahmāvarta. (2.17)

Immediately thereafter: by the phrase "penetrating with his shadow," it is indicated that because this is a sacred place (*puṇyadeśa*), it is not appropriate for him to approach in his own physical form.
[The term] *kṣatrapradhanapiśunam* refers to the fact that even now [the site] possesses skull-bones and other such remains that testify to the great battle of the Kṣatriyas.
It was indicative of war for the Pāṇḍavas, the Kṣatriyas; it belonged to the Kauravas, the descendants of Kuru;
and it pertained to the Rājanyas, those consecrated as kings.
Arjuna is the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow; [in the formation of this compound], the word *dhanus* undergoes the substitution of *anaṅ*.
The inclusion of the term *mukha* (mouth/face) is employed because it serves as the locus for multiple actions. 48.
Mallinātha says: "Brahmāvarta."
Immediately thereafter [he went] to the country and region named Brahmāvarta. Regarding this, it is said:
"That region which lies between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī—Manu calls that god-created land Brahmāvarta. (2.17)
He should enter by means of his shadow—that is, by the circle of light—and not with his own physical form;
for there is a scriptural injunction stating that one should circumambulate seats, sacred fields, hermitages, and so forth, and then proceed elsewhere.
Even today, [the land] betokens its former sovereignty over the realm through the presence of skulls and other such remains.
The meaning is that it indicates the war between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas. According to Amara, *yuddha*, *āyodhana*, *janya*, *pradhana*, and *pravidāraṇa* are synonyms for battle.
You should resort to that well-known field belonging to the Kurus, known as Kaurava-kṣetra.

The meaning is "go to Kurukṣetra. In that Kurukṣetra, there is the Gāṇḍīva, a specific bow belonging to one who possesses a *gāṇḍī* (mark on the cheek). The suffix *matup* (expressing possession) is applied here according to the rule *gāṇḍyajagātsañjñāyām*.

The suffix *vapra* [is applied after the word *gāṇḍīva*] according to Pāṇini 5.2.110. According to Amara, *gāṇḍīva* and *gāṇḍīva* refer to the bow of Kapi-dhvaja (Arjuna) and are used in both masculine and neuter genders. He whose bow is that [Gāṇḍīva] is Gāṇḍīvadhanvā, namely Arjuna.
By the rule *vā saṃjñāyām*, the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs. [He is pierced] by hundreds of sharp arrows.
With thousands of sharpened arrows, he showered the faces of the kṣatriya kings as you would shower lotuses with falls of water-streams;
that is to say, he severed their heads with a rain of shafts. || 51 ||
The explanation of this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O Megha, you should resort to—that is, you should serve—that Kaurava field, Kurukṣetra, which has become a sacred site (tīrtha).
Of what nature is that Kaurava field? It is one that betokens the great battle of the kṣatriyas.
O Cloud, what are you doing? You are plunging into, that is, entering the country known as Brahmāvarta, which is situated below Kurukṣetra, on its western side.
By what? By the shadow, that is, by his own reflection.

What is that? The king named Dhanañjaya, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, [is present] there at Kurukṣetra, where the faces—the countenances—of the rājanyas, the assembly of kings, [are gathered]. You...
Like a rain-cloud that has been rained upon, he showered with hundreds of sharp arrows—countless hundreds of keen shafts. With what kind of hundreds of sharp arrows? With showers of falling torrents.
O cloud,
just as you cause rain to fall upon the lotuses by means of hundreds of sharp torrents of water, so too does the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).
*Kṣatrapradhanapiśunam* means "indicating the battle, that is, the great conflict, of the *kṣatras*, the kings.
*Rājanyānām* refers to those who belong to the group of kings (*rājagaṇāḥ*), namely the *rājanyas*.
"Śitaiḥ" means sharp; those hundreds of arrows numbering in the hundreds at the edge are "śitaśaraśatāni. By means of those hundreds of sharp arrows, the cloud's beholding of Kurukṣetra is described.
Herein lies the figure of speech *upamā* (simile).
[Verse 52] —48— Regarding the phrase *adhaḥ*, the expression *yathā tvam* etc. lacks the particle *iti*; furthermore, *kṛtvā* and *vṛṣṭiṃ karoṣi* appear to be secondary glosses.

O gentle friend, having abandoned the waters of the Revatī river— whose taste is so pleasing and which are marked by the eyes of the goddesses— and turning away from battle out of affection for his kin, the horse Lāṅgulī served those waters of the Sarasvatī; go now to them.
You too shall become pure within, though black only in outward color.
Vallī:

O dear one, you who are worthy of being seen, having prescribed the approach to— that is, the service of— those waters connected with the Sarasvatī, you yourself have become inwardly pure, though devoid of consciousness.

"You shall become internally pure; you will be so. You are called 'Kṛṣṇa' (the Black One) or 'Kāla' (Time) merely by way of color, which is a statement of your great merit. Furthermore, this blackness of the clouds is simply due to their very nature, resulting from their having drunk water."

Regarding those [women] mentioned, he asks "of which ones? and says: those waters which Haladhara (Balarāma), having abandoned *hālā*—that is, wine (*surā*)—resorted to and enjoyed out of affection for his kinsmen, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, and out of a desire to avoid hostility; for he was indeed about to fight with them.
Solicited [by both sides], he reflected, "Both groups are my kinsmen; where, then, shall I go?

Having thus deliberated, he abandoned his home and undertook a pilgrimage to the Sarasvatī river. By the renunciation of *hālā* (liquor), he demonstrates the undertaking of religious observances (*niyama*) for the purpose of serving sacred sites (*tīrtha*).
Of what kind was the liquor? It possessed a desirable flavor, a pleasing taste;
for he (Śiva) is fond of wine. Revatī is his wife; she whose mark—the reflection—was upon her eye. The word "bhavitā" ends in the suffix -tṛ. For he...
In the sense of "similarity of time":
*somya* (like Soma). [The suffix] *yat* is applied after words such as *śākhā*. [Note: The form] *tṛjanta* [is used].
*Dakṣiṇāvarta*.

Although Kurukṣetra is meritorious by its very nature, one might still wonder: "How shall I become pure after reaching that region which was defiled by human skulls and other such things due to the battle that took place there?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having abandoned... and so forth.
The meaning is: having attained the state of being a desired object of taste for Revatī’s eyes— reflected therein—

and because he behaves with equality toward Dharmaputra and others as well as Duryodhana and others due to his affection for his kinsmen, [he is] "lāṅgulī," one who has turned away from battle and abandoned the fight.
Balabhadra: From this it is understood that even though he was equipped with weapons, he turned away from battle out of affection for his kinsmen.
"Those which he served" means that having consumed water, he performed penance.
*Abhimukha* means going toward [something] with direct orientation.

"You shall become one who is internally pure" (*antaḥśuddhas tvam asi bhavitā*). Here, *asi* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that corresponds in form to the middle person. Likewise, in the *Māghakāvya*:
"O son of Śantanu, you yourself have declared this group to be worthy of honor.
This [form] ends in the suffix *tṛ*. "You will be pure within" (*antaḥśuddho bhavitāsi*) means "you shall be pure within" (*antaḥśuddho bhaviṣyasi*). Compare verse 12.
Anticipating the objection that—since the word *śuddha* (pure) is heard in the sense of being freed from blackness (*pāpakārṣṇya*)—the loss of your black color should not be suspected, he says:
"Black by color alone" (*varṇamātreṇa kṛṣṇaḥ*), meaning by color alone, by the color itself. [This refers to] you.
The intention is that there is no reversal of the black color for the sake of beauty; [this is Mallinātha’s explanation of the word] "having abandoned."

Out of affection for his kinsmen and love for the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, and not out of fear; turning away from battle and having no desire for combat— the wielder of the plow (Haladhara), so called because he has a tail (lāṅgula)—
[offered] that which possessed a desirable flavor, a beloved taste, to Revatī, his own dear wife.

She was drinking *hālā*—that is, wine—for which the *Amara-kośa* states, "wine is called *hālā*, as it is dear to the goddess Surā. In this context, the word *hālā* is also considered a regional term (*deśabhāṣāpada*), according to the rule stating that such words may be employed. She was one whose very eyes bore the mark of her reflection. *Locana evāṅkaḥ pratibimbitatvacihnaṃ yasyāstāṃ hālāṃ surām | surāhalipriyā hāletyamaras | abhiprayuktaṃ deśabhāṣāpadamityatra sūtre hāleti deśabhāṣāpadamapi ||*

Vāmana declared that [the usage] is excellent because it conforms to the practice of great poets (*kaviprayoga*). "Having abandoned" means having cast aside; the sense is that even though they were difficult to relinquish.
O gentle and fortunate one, those waters of Sarasvatī which you have resorted to—of those...

By performing the approach and service of these waters of the Sarasvatī river, you will become pure, stainless, and faultless within your inner self. By the rule *ṇvultṛcau*, the suffix *tṛc* is used; moreover, you shall become purified even immediately.

This is the meaning. The present tense suffix is used according to the rule *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat* (Pāṇini 3.3.131), which allows for the use of a present tense form when there is proximity to the present time.
He is dark-complexioned (*śyāma*) by his very complexion (*varṇamātreṇa*), that is, by his physical color alone, and not because of sin.

The meaning is this: internal purity alone must be accomplished, not external purity. Even one who is pure externally, such as the venerable Lord Balabhadra, who resorted to the waters of the Sarasvatī for the sake of expiation for the killing of Sūta, serves as an illustration in that regard. Therefore, you too must by all means [resort to] the Sarasvatī.
The sense is that [he] should be served. 52.
-49- This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.
O cloud, although you are pure within and free from sin due to the clarity of your water, you,
as a cloud, will be black or dark only by outward appearance,
but not within.

Having done what? Having performed an approach to, that is, a confluence with, those waters belonging to the Sarasvatī—that is, the waters connected to the river Sarasvatī. Of which waters? Those waters which King Lāṅgulī, whose name is Balabhadra, [drank].
He served; that is, he attended upon [him].
With what? With affection for his kinsman, not out of fear of the sin of killing a relative in battle.
Of what nature was Lāṅgulī? One who had turned away from the fight, having his back toward the conflict.
Having abandoned the battle; furthermore, having done what? Having left behind—that is, having abandoned—*hālā*, wine.
Of what nature was that *hālā*? One whose flavor is desired, meaning it has a delightful taste.
Furthermore, of what nature was the liquor? "Marked by the eyes of Revatī"—this is the grammatical construction.

The sense is that, having abandoned Queen Revatī and wine because he beheld the face of the woman Revatī in the wine-cup, Balabhadra— being fearful of the sin of killing his kinsmen in battle— resorted to the Sarasvatī-tīrtha.
"Sārasvatī" means those [waters] belonging to Sarasvatī; "of those Sārasvatīs.
"Abhi" means that which possesses a desired, sweet, and delicious flavor. Thus, [it refers to] her who has such [a flavor].
"Of desired flavor. By this, it is stated that the cloud has reached a perfected sacred ford (*siddhatīrtha*).
Herein lies the poetic figure of inference (*anumānālaṅkāra*).
[Regarding the phrase] "thus the state of being," is it well-known from worldly experience (*bhāva*) or from scripture (*āgama*)?
Therefore, you should go to the daughter of Jahnu, who descended from the king of mountains near Anukanakhala; she is a flight of stairs to heaven for the sons of Sagara,
and she seems to mock with her foam the knitting of the eyebrows on Gauri’s face.
With her hand-like waves clinging to the moon, she seized Śambhu by the hair. (50) [Mallinātha 53; Sūktimuktāvalī 54; Daṇḍin’s *Daśakumāracarita* vaktrebhru°]
Therefore, from the land of Sarasvatī, you should go toward Anukanakhala, to the Jāhnavī as it flows forth from the Himavat near the sacred site known as Kanakhala.
Of what kind? A flight of stairs, a series of steps, for the sixty thousand sons of Sagara, serving as the means for their attainment of heaven.
For they, having been consumed by Kapila in Pātāla out of wrath, attained the third heaven once their ashes were washed away by the Bhāgīrathī brought down by Bhagīratha;
and that Goddess, while descending to earth, [assumed] the knitting of the eyebrows on Gaurī’s face.
As if mocking [the moon] with its foam, she seized him by the hair like a co-wife of Śambhu;
this is the superimposition of the characteristics of a young woman.
She is one whose hands are indeed the waves clinging to the moon. For, by the hand...

The pulling of hair is performed. Gaurī’s knitting of the brows signifies, "These hairs are being seized by her right in my presence. Because she was held by the hair, Gaṅgā is said to be "hair-seizing"; for she, as she fell from heaven, was held by Hara at the tip of his matted locks.
Such is the traditional teaching (āgama).
Since the word *bhrukuṭi* exists as well as the form *bhṛkuṭi* beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is no violation of the meter. || 50 ||
"Therefore, O Dākṣiṇāvarta."
Near Kanakhala, at Gaṅgādvāra, there is a certain mountain called Kanakhala; likewise,
in the Mahābhārata, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [it is mentioned as] Gaṅgādvāra.
O King, that merit is renowned as being frequented by hosts of brahmin seers.
"Sanatkumāra, O descendant of Kuru, as well as the holy Kanakhala, and the mountain named Puru, where Purūravas was born. Thus [it is said].
[She is] descended from the king of mountains, originating from Himavat, and born of Himavat.
The story of Sagara’s sons is well known as a flight of stairs leading to heaven for the sons of Sagara;
[the Goddess] Gaurī has a knitting of the brows upon her face—this is the reading "vaktrebhrukuṭiracanām.
She is so described because she possesses a knitting of the brows (*bhṛkuṭiracanā*) upon her face (*vaktra*). [This compound follows the rule: *amūrdhamastakāt*.
Thus, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending. *Bhrukuṭi* means the knitting of the eyebrows;

the sense is "one whose eyebrows are arched, flashing with anger. By the mention of "seizing the hair" (*keśagrahaṇa*), both the natural state of the hair and the forcible seizing of the hair are intended to be expressed.
By this [phrase], the grasping of the waves with his hands is implied,

as well as the state of having hands fixed upon the crest-ornaments made of *mālatī* and other flowers; the underlying intention is that while both of us share the common origin of being born from the King of Mountains (*śailarāja*), you belong to Śambhu.

"You are the Half-seizer (Ardhaharā). The meaning is that she appears as if laughing under the guise of foam at Gaurī, who is angry at seeing her hair seized, because she herself had taken her position upon his head. || 50 ||?
Mallinātha [comments]: "Therefore" (tasmāt).

From that Kurukṣetra, near the mountain Kanakhala, lies Anukanakhala— formed as an *avyayībhāva* compound with the indeclinable *anu* meaning "near" (Pāṇini 2.1.15)— where she descended from Himavat, the king of mountains,
like a flight of stairs to heaven for the sons of Sagara.

The meaning is: "that which serves as the means for attaining heaven. You should go to Jāhnavī, the daughter of the king named Jahnu. The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*). That Jāhnavī is the knitting of the eyebrows by Gaurī on her face, performed out of anger at being supplanted by a co-wife.
She seems to laugh and mock with her froths; this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) identifying the froths as laughter because of their whiteness.
She is one whose waves alone serve as hands, clinging to the moon which has become the crest-jewel (*śiromāṇikya*).
Having her hand submerged in the waves, she seized the hair of Śambhu;
just as a certain mature heroine, unable to endure a co-wife and displaying her own favorability,
pulls her husband by the hair along with his crest-jewel.
The sense is "in the same way.
This refers to the story that in former times, at the request of Bhagīratha, Gaṅgādhara (Śiva) caught with his mass of matted hair the goddess Gaṅgā as she was falling from the path of the sky.
This was stated by Upajīvya. [Verse 53] –50–.
Herein lies the commentary by Sumativijaya.
O Cloud, therefore, after crossing from Kurukṣetra the sacred ford named Kanakhala, you should go to that river named Gaṅgā, the daughter of King Jahnu.

Of what nature was that daughter of Jahnu? She had descended from the king of mountains, having come down from the mountain named Himavat. Furthermore, of what nature was that daughter of Jahnu? She was a flight of stairs leading to heaven for the sons of Sagara.
Furthermore, of what nature was that daughter of Jahnu? She who fashioned the frown upon the face of Gaurī.
Who was she? That daughter of Jahnu, Gaṅgā, who, as if laughing with her froth, seemed to seize the hair of Śambhu, the Great God.
Of what nature was she? She was the daughter of Jahnu, whose hands were the waves clinging to the moon;
such is the grammatical construction.
"Anu" means "having aimed at," as in "anukakhalam," meaning toward the Kanakhala-tīrtha;
the sense is that the tīrtha is behind (paścāt) Kanakhala.
"Śaila" refers to Himavat, the king of mountains; she descended from that mountain.
That [river] which descended from the king of mountains— [the phrase] "descended from the king of mountains" being repeated for emphasis—
is a flight of stairs, a succession of steps leading to heaven, for the sons of Sagara, the children of the king named Sagara.
The row of steps to heaven for the sons of Sagara;
for indeed, the sons of Sagara were reduced to ashes by the fire of the wrath of the sage Kapila,
and they too, from that...
The sense is that those who had set out on the path of the illustrious Bhagīratha, being flooded by the mass of waters flowing off-course, ascended to heaven.
"Gaurī" refers to the knitting of the eyebrows upon the face of Gaurī, like the fashioning of a frown.
The knitting of the eyebrows on Gaurī’s face: the knitting of the brows is compared [to the Gaṅgā] because of its movement toward the mouth and because of its wrathful nature.
Regarding "hair" (*keśa*): the act of seizing the hair is "seizing by the hair. [The phrase] "with the hand, having seized the hair... [is thus explained].
Such is the meaning.

"Indulagnormihastā" means she whose hands are the very waves (ūrmi) that have descended (lagna) upon the moon (indu). For she, having fallen from heaven, was placed by Mahādeva within the mass of his own matted locks (jaṭājūṭa).
"Is held" (*dhṛtā*) is a conventional designation (*prasiddhi*).

This is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). [End of verse 54]. Is it "thus the state of being" (*iti bhāvaḥ*) or "thus the meaning" (*iti arthaḥ*)? It is "thus the state of being. "Thus the conventional designation. Gaurī—[two explanations]: as an adjective and as a noun.
If you, hanging by your forequarters like a celestial elephant in the sky, should look askance at her water, which is as clear as pure crystal, while drinking from it;
then she, by your shadow suddenly gliding upon the current, [will be transformed].
It may be delightful like the confluence of the Yamunā river, which has arrived at an unexpected place,
as it flows along.
If you should desire to drink the water of that Ganges, white as pure crystal,
you would see it flowing in its current with the beauty of your own reflection.
Instantly, at that very moment, she would become as delightful even elsewhere than at Prayāga— as beautiful as the confluence of the Yamunā reached at Gaṅgāsthāna—
since her own reflection would take on the form of the Yamunā.
What kind of person are you? Like the celestial elephant Airāvaṇa, you hang from the sky with your forepart—the upper portion—thus you are "one who hangs by the forepart. Look askance! Look!
"Her [hair] curls to the right."
"Hanging in the sky" means suspended by the hind part in the atmosphere;

for in common usage, the words "paścāt" (behind) and "uttara" (upper/latter) are synonyms. Here, why is the word "paścārdha" (hind-part) not intended to mean "uttarārdha" (upper-part)? And it has been said: "With his upper body bent down from the vehicle..."

Thus [it is said in] Raghuvamśa IX.65. This is because the word *paścārdha* is observed to be used in reference to the hindquarters alone in cases such as deer; likewise, in the Śākuntala: "He entered with his hindquarters, with the greater part of his body toward the front out of fear of the arrow's fall" (I.7).

"You should conjecture" means you should think: "If you were to conjecture that she would drink that water while hanging sideways from the sky with the hind part of her body," then [the water] was [drunk] by her as she moved along and plunged in. The grammatical connection is: "by her who was moving along at once."

Through her shadow—that is, her reflection—Gaṅgā’s confluence with the Yamunā occurs at the very sacred ford (tīrtha) called Prayāga, even though [the reflection] has reached a place other than [the actual river]; everything else is an improper location. Here, the meditative absorption (samādhi) of the union of two distinguished entities is suggested (dhvanyate). || 51 ||
Mallinātha [comments] on "tasyā" as follows:
Like a celestial elephant, like some world-elephant (diggaja) in the sky; "paścārdham" means the western half. It is grammatically correct by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* class.
Hanging by that [half], being one who hangs from the western half (*paścārdhalambī*), [he remained] in the sky with his western portion.
Having stood with the upper half [of your body] facing upward— that is,
looking up— you should, I think, drink the water of that Gaṅgā, which is as clear as pure crystal, in such a way that it flows crosswise or obliquely.

If you were to reflect upon it: by your shadow— your reflection— which is gliding along, moving swiftly in the current or stream, that [river] has reached a confluence with the Yamunā at a place other than Prayāga, which is the usual location for the Gaṅgā.
Or rather, it would be delightful even when such [a state] has occurred.
|| 54 || -51- This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.
O Cloud, if you should suddenly desire to drink the water of that Gaṅgā— its flow slanting across the sky like the celestial elephant Airāvata— then that Gaṅgā...
She would be delightful and enchanting, like the Yamunā at its confluence with the Ganges when it has reached its place of meeting, by means of your shadow—that dark luster of yours.
Of what [Ganges] is she like? Of the Ganges as it flows into the stream or current of you, the cloud.
Of her who was crawling and spreading forth;
of what nature was the celestial elephant? It was one whose forepart was hanging down—that is, having the habit of hanging by its front body.
What kind of cloud are you? Hanging by its foremost part, suspended from the upper half.
Of what nature is the water, flowing sideways? It is as clear and transparent as pure crystal.
The grammatical construction is: "It is stainless."
"Asthāna" means not having reached its proper place; "asthānopagatayamunā" refers to the Yamunā that has reached the Yamunā-sthāna;
"asthānopagatayamunāsaṅgamā" is that which possesses a confluence (*saṅgama*), a meeting, with such a Yamunā.
The sense is that it will maintain its confluence with the Yamunā at a place other than a sacred ford (tīrtha). "Accha" means pure, auspicious, and as clear and brilliant as crystal.

It is as clear as pure crystal. Because the cloud possesses a dark luster, the Ganges is compared to the Yamunā; the sense is that a sacred ford (tīrtha) is produced by the confluence of the Ganges and the Yamunā in one place.
Here, there is the *guḍhopamā* (sugar-candy) simile. [55] —51— Is *prakṛtiḥ* intended as *melāpaka*?
Does the second sentence not make sense? Should the first *iti bhāvaḥ* be *iti arthaḥ*? Is the comparison of the Yamunā with the Gaṅgā incorrect? [End of last line]

Having reached that very mountain, the source of that [river], whose rocks are perfumed by the musk-scented navels of deer sitting upon them and which is white with snow; is this a sentence misplaced?
Seated upon its peak to dispel the fatigue of the journey,
you shall possess a lovely splendor comparable to the mud scraped away from the eye of the Three-eyed One.

...to the Discipliner (Śiva); [the mountain] Himavat, the source and progenitor of that very river, possessing a white splendor, O Ma, Su; [the mountain] Himavat, possessing a white splendor and three [peaks], O Da;
Vallī [says]: ...the mountain Himavat, the origin and father of that very river.
Having reached its peak and standing there,
you will possess and display a captivating splendor resembling the mud torn up by the head of Śiva’s bull; for the bull is white, while you are dark like mire.

Of what sort is this mountain? Its rocks are made fragrant by the musk-odors of seated deer—specifically kastūrikā antelopes—and it is white and bright due to the frost and snow; and because the peak is cooled by the ice, [it is thus described].
It is that which removes the fatigue of the path.
It is called "prabhava" because it originates from this. || 52 ||
"Turning to the right for those who are seated."
"With the scents of the navel [of musk deer] and the scents of mṛgamada. According to Amara, *mṛganābhi* means *mṛgamada*.
Since it has been stated that these belong to "deer" (*mṛga*), the phrase "with the scents of *mṛganābhi*" is redundant.
"Of that very [Ganges]"; its source means the place of origin of the Gaṅgā itself. "You shall speak": you will become a bearer (voḍhā) of this form of fire. "Bright" (śubhrām) means radiant;
as Amara states: "The word *śubhra* may mean radiant or white."

The white-colored one, who was previously disregarded as being like mud, [now] bestows an indescribable splendor comparable to the mud uprooted by the bull of the Three-eyed One (Śiva). [This refers to him] who, having left behind a certain bride, dispels her fatigue with perfumes and other offerings in the very house of her birth.
The splendor of the son-in-law is suggested here. || 52 ||
Mallinātha says: "Of those who were seated..."

Of the deer that were sitting—that is, seated—namely, the musk deer; for otherwise, the presence of the scent of the navel would be inexplicable. By "the scents of the navel," it means the musk scents, because those [deer] originate from them. For this very reason...

And there is the designation *mṛganābhi*. According to Amara, *mṛgandha*, *mṛgamada*, and *kastūrī* [are synonyms]. Alternatively, *nābhayaḥ* refers to musks. According to Viśva, *nābhi* is said in some instances to mean "the principal" (*pradhāna*) and "musk" (*kastūrīmada*).
He whose rocks are made fragrant—rendered sweet-smelling—by their scents; [this refers to] that very Gaṅgā. "Source" (*prabhava*) means the cause, as it originates from this.
"White with frost" (*tuṣāragaura*) means bright white; according to Amara, "white, bright, and fair" are synonyms for *avadāta*.

Having reached Acala; "vinayanam" means that by which one is disciplined (*vinīyate*), derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the instrumental sense. While seated upon a peak of that Snowy Mountain, which serves to discipline—that is, to dispel—the fatigue of the journey.

The white bull of the three-eyed god—*vṛṣabha* means "bull" or "excellent one" (*vṛṣa*) for one who performs good deeds, according to Amara; with the mud dug up and torn apart by that [bull], you shall bear—that is, carry—the beauty that is worthy of being compared to that of the object of comparison. This is from the root *vah* (to carry), in the *lṛt* (future) tense.

In the word *trinayana*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur due to the rule "in a compound name, after a preceding word ending in *a*, there is no *ṇ*" (Pāṇini 8.4.3), because of the prohibition [contained] in the list beginning with *kṣubhna*.
By the rule "its origin" (*tasyāḥ prabhavaḥ*), etc., the term *vāvāhika* refers to the cloud on Mount Himavat.
The dwelling in a house is implied. || 55 ||
The commentary on this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O cloud, you shall attain and bear a beauty comparable to the mud dug up by the white bull of the three-eyed Śiva, resembling the mire scraped from the horns of the great god’s white bull.
Having done what? Having reached Himācala, the mountain that is the source of that very river, the celestial Gaṅgā.
In what state were you? Seated upon a peak, a summit, of that Himācala.
He sat down. For whom? To dispel the fatigue of the journey, for the sake of removing the exhaustion produced by the road.
Of what nature was the mountain? White with frost.
Furthermore, of what nature was that immovable mountain? Its rocky interior was made fragrant—its stone surfaces scented—with the musk-glands (*nābhigandha*) of deer.
Of what kind of deer? Of those that were seated, that is, sitting down.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).

"Śubhra" means white or bright; that which belongs to the three-eyed Rudra is "śubhra-trinayana. By his bull—that is, the ox—the mud was uprooted; the state of being comparable to, or resembling, that mud is "śubhra-trinayana-vṛṣotkhāta-paṅkopameyatā"; [the word] refers to that.
To him who is accustomed to removing the fatigue and weariness of the journey— [fatigue] comparable to the mud dug up by the bull of the bright three-eyed Lord (Śiva).
"Surabhita-śilam" means that the rocks were made fragrant or scented; it refers to that [place] where the middle portion of the rock was thus perfumed.
Because of the whiteness of the mountain, there is a comparison of the immovable mountain to a bull (vṛṣabha), and because of the blackness of the cloud.

Therefore, it is like mud; here, the figure of speech is *upamā* (simile). [56] —52— [Regarding] "similarity" (*sādṛśyatā*): for one who has dispelled the fatigue of the journey... [diff. explanations? ...white, etc.
If that [fire], born from the friction of the trunks of *sarala* trees as the wind blows, [should arise...]
The forest fire, having scorched the bushy tails of the yaks with its flames, is now threatening [you];
you ought to extinguish it with thousands of streams of water,
for the wealth of the noble is intended to have the fruit of alleviating the suffering of those in distress.

He carries; he flows. He protects. He covers. He causes to grow. He brings forth. He is beautiful. He is auspicious. He is the one who leads. He is the one who bestows. He is the one who is praised. He is the one who is victorious. He is the one who is exalted. He is the one who is pure. He is the one who is radiant. He is the one who is firm. He is the one who is steadfast. He is the one who is true. He is the one who is eternal. He is the one who is all-pervading. He is the one who is the source of all. He is the one who is the refuge of all. He is the one who is the goal of all. He is the one who is the beginning and the end of all. He is the one who is beyond all. He is the one who is the witness of all. He is the one who is the knower of all. He is the one who is the ruler of all. He is the one who is the creator of all. He is the one who is the sustainer of all. He is the one who is the destroyer of all. He is the one who is the one without a second. He is the one who is without a peer. He is the one who is without a compare. He is the one who is without a rival. He is the one who is without a match. He is the one who is without a limit. He is the one who is without a boundary. He is the one who is without a shore. He is the one who is without a center. He is the one who is without a periphery. He is the one who is without a beginning. He is the one who is without an end. He is the one who is without a middle. He is the one who is without a name. He is the one who is without a form. He is the one who is without a mark. He is the one who is without a sign. He is the one who is without a symbol. He is the one who is without a definition. He is the one who is without a description. He is the one who is without a characterization. He is the one who is without a distinction. He is the one who is without a difference. He is the one who is without a variety. He is the one who is without a manifoldness. He is the one who is without a duality. He is the one who is without a plurality. He is the one who is without a division. He is the one who is without a separation. He is the one who is without a disjunction. He is the one who is without a dissociation. He is the one who is without a detachment. He is the one who is without a liberation. He is the one who is without a release. He is the one who is without a freedom. He is the one who is without a cessation. He is the one who is without a destruction. He is the one who is without a disappearance. He is the one who is without a vanishing. He is the one who is without a fading away. He is the one who is without a passing away. He is the one who is without a departure. He is the one who is without a going. He is the one who is without a coming. He is the one who is without a staying. He is the one who is without a resting. He is the one who is without a sitting. He is the one who is without a lying down. He is the one who is without a sleeping. He is the one who is without a waking. He is the one who is without a dreaming. He is the one who is without a seeing. He is the one who is without a hearing. He is the one who is without a smelling. He is the one who is without a tasting. He is the one who is without a touching. He is the one who is without a thinking. He is the one who is without a knowing. He is the one who is without a perceiving. He is the one who is without a cognizing. He is the one who is without a conceiving. He is the one who is without a imagining. He is the one who is without a conceptualizing. He is the one who is without a mental construction. He is the one who is without a mental fabrication. He is the one who is without a mental projection. He is the one who is without a mental attribution. He is the one who is without a mental superimposition. He is the one who is without a mental misapprehension. He is the one who is without a mental error. He is the one who is without a mental delusion. He is the one who is without a mental confusion. He is the one who is without a mental distraction. He is the one who is without a mental agitation

If a forest fire should afflict that mountain, you ought to extinguish that fire with a torrential downpour of swift rain; for the supernatural powers of the great have as their fruit the alleviation of the suffering of those in distress. For if [you do not act] when the distressed are in calamity...
Since it is being destroyed, what is the use of prosperity?

What kind of forest fire is this? It is one born from the friction of the trunks of *sarala* trees and arisen from contact with the branches of *devadāru* trees, while the wind is blowing; for it is by the force of the clashing of trees that [the fire spreads].
A forest fire breaks out; likewise, the bushy tail of the yak is scorched by meteors and flames. Enough with thousands [of other things], O Daksināvarta!
"Regarding that [it is said]: 'tam'."
Born from the friction of the trunks of *sarala* trees— the *sarala* being a specific species of tree— and since the word "trunk" (*skandha*) here refers to the branches of the trunk,
how could there be any calamity for the Himalaya, which is essentially composed of snow-water, due to fire?
Or rather, is it like the mass of yak-tail hair scorched by a firebrand?
"Dāvāgni" refers to a forest fire; when the wind blows, a forest fire is produced by the friction against the trunks of the *sarala* trees.
The meaning is: "if he were to afflict him after becoming one who has destroyed the mass of yak-tail hair with a meteor.

[This refers to] "with thousands of streams of water from clouds," that is, from clouds numbering in the thousands. Here, although the word *sahasra* denotes a number, it lacks the capacity for syntactic connection with the action [and thus functions as a multiplier].
It should be understood that it concludes at the end of the *saṅkhyeya* [kalpa]; the meaning is "by means of streams of water. || 53 ||
Mallinātha says: "tam iti" (regarding the word "tam").

When the forest wind blows— that is, when the wind is blowing— the trunks (skandha), meaning the specific portions of the trees extending from the root to the branches— according to Amara, "the term *skandha* is not feminine and refers to that part of a tree starting from the root up to the branches"— [are shaken] by their mutual friction.

He whose birth was from Saṅkarṣaṇa is described as such; for it has been stated that when a word meaning "birth" (janman) occurs as the final member of a compound, a locative-based *bahuvrīhi* is also valid. By means of firebrands—that is, sparks—the masses of hair of the yak-cows were consumed, meaning they were scorched.

By whom [the mass of hair is gathered]. *Dava* itself is fire; thus *davāgni* is forest-fire. Regarding the words *vana*, *vanavahni*, *dava*, and *dāva*, Yādava states that they are intended to mean "forest" and "forest-fire.
If he were to afflict—that is, if he were to torment—that Himālaya mountain, [then] this *davāgni* (forest-fire).
"You ought to pacify [this] with thousands of streams of water.
And he said that this was appropriate: "The prosperity and abundance of the great and noble serve to pacify the suffering of those who have fallen into distress."
Those [actions] whose fruit and purpose is precisely the warding off of calamities are so described.
Therefore, the sense is that you must extinguish the forest fire of the Himālaya mountain. — Sumativijaya.
The explanation of this is as follows:

O Cloud, if a forest fire, a conflagration, were to afflict— that is, to torment— this mountain named Himācala, then you ought to, that is, you are capable of, thoroughly extinguishing— that is, putting out— that very forest fire.
By what means? By thousands of streams of water, numbering in the thousands of torrents.
Of what nature was the forest fire? Born from the friction of the trunks of *sarala* trees.
Furthermore, of what nature was the forest fire? One that destroyed the masses of yak-tail hair with its sparks.
Under what condition? When the wind, the air, is blowing—that is, when it is wafting.
He speaks of the performance of assistance in quelling that forest fire: for indeed, from this [reason], the prosperity of clouds such as yourself—consisting of rain—is a form of true wealth.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having taken on the form of that forest fire, they become the means for pacifying the suffering of those who have fallen into distress.
"Saralā" refers to a specific species of pine tree; their "skandhas" are their trunks or branches;
their "saṅghaṭṭa" is their friction against one another; that which has its birth from this is "saralaskandhasaṅghaṭṭajanmā. [This occurs] due to the mutual rubbing of the trees.
The sense is that the fire has arisen.

"Ulka" refers to a meteor or flame; by those [flames], the mass of hair—the collection of locks—of the *camarī* cows, the yak-cows, has been consumed, that is, brought to destruction. He by whom this was done is [the one described].
The mass of her tail-hair was scorched by meteors;
"vārī" refers to thousands of streams of water— that is, thousands of torrents of water— and [the phrase] "by those thousands of streams of water."

"Āpanna-ārti-praśamana-phalāḥ" means those in which the fruit is the pacification of the suffering of those who have fallen into distress. The poetic figure (alaṅkāra) is Arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration by a general principle). || 57 ||
O you whose sound is released! Those śarabhas, unable to endure it, will out of arrogant pride attempt to leap over you— who are otherwise unassailable— in order to break their own bodies.
You should make them scattered by the laughter of a shower of tumultuous hand-claps;
for who indeed would not become an object of contempt when their efforts at undertaking an enterprise are fruitless? (54)
If those śarabhas, impetuous in their leaping and onset, were suddenly to leap at you upon that path— only to break their own limbs—
then you would have escaped unharmed.
And those creatures called *śarabhas* who were on that mountain there while you were roaring— [they fell] by your fall; [the fruit of their actions].
VALL:
...you, while roaring on that mountain... [those beings known as *śarabhas*...]

Out of arrogance and excessive pride, being unable to endure it, they will attempt to leap over even that which is unassailable; you shall seize them as they are scattered by the laughter of a tumultuous shower of stones.
"You should cover them with a rain of jagged stones and strike them with lightning"—
this is the meaning. It is not surprising that they perish, for their undertaking and effort are fruitless."
Who among those of such a kind would not be a fit object or vessel for contempt?
The meaning is that they are inevitably humiliated. Your desire to attack the śarabhas is fruitless, because you are unable to seize them. (54)
Is it not the case that "for the destruction of the upper body" refers to lightning?
[No,] it means "that which turns to the right."

"Saṃrambhotpatanarabhasāḥ" means those characterized by the impetuosity of rising up in agitation; "saṃrambhaḥ" signifies anger, and thus the meaning is "possessing the force of rising up in anger. "Svāṅgabhaṅgāya" means for the breaking of one's own body.
Having abandoned the path of the *śarabhas*, which is a long-reaching track left behind by them;
the intention is that because their tracks have been cleared, leaping over them is impossible for those [monkeys], and there will only be a breaking of their bodies.
"A shower of tumultuous hailstones" (*tumula-karaka-vṛṣṭi-pāta*); "hailstone" (*karaka*) means a solid mass of water from the clouds (*ghanopala*). A solid mass of water from the clouds.
According to Yādava, *karaka* means hail; thus, there was a falling of rain on all sides (*samantāt*) consisting of hailstones.

Those whose fruit is humiliation (*paribhava*) are those for whom the result is contempt. Furthermore, their efforts at undertaking tasks are fruitless (*niṣphala-ārambha-yatnāḥ*), meaning both the undertakings and the exertions are without result.

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It refers to the fruitlessness of efforts and exertions due to the impossibility of leaping over the clouds; or alternatively, there is a word-division as "niṣphalāḥ. Thus, "niṣphalāḥ" means fruitless, and "rambhayatnāḥ" means efforts of exertion (*saṃrambha*). In this context, *rambhā* refers to exertion, though it is [also] a name for a woman.
"Of Moca and Apsaras," says Keśava. The meaning is: "What efforts made with zeal would be fruitless, or what [efforts] would have humiliation as their result?"—Mallinātha.
"Ya" means "who."

On that Himalaya mountain, *saṃrambhaḥ* means anger; according to the *Śabdārṇava*, "saṃrambhaḥ" denotes agitation or anger. By that [anger], they are so described as having *rabhasaḥ*—that is, speed or impetuosity—in their leaping or springing up. According to Amara, "rabhasaḥ" refers to both speed and joy.

Those *śarabhas* are a specific kind of eight-legged deer; the *Viśva* lexicon states that *śarabha*, *śalabha*, and *aṣṭāpada* refer to a particular type of animal. [He saw] you, by whom the path—the route of the *śarabha’s* leap—had been cleared, instantly.

They might leap for the sake of breaking their own limbs; the *liṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhavanā*). The meaning is that because you are so far away, there is no result from leaping other than the breaking of one's own limbs.
Those śarabhas were tumultuous, that is, crowded, like hailstones.

According to Amara, *varṣopala* means hailstone (*karakā*). You should scatter—that is, disperse—those [hailstones] by the falling of their rain. The *liṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*). Even a lowly opponent who insults [one] must be refuted immediately.
This is the intended meaning.
For instance: "undertakings" (*ārambhāḥ*) are those things which are begun, namely actions; "effort" (*yatna*) is exertion;
those for whom that [effort] is fruitless are so described. Thus, they are "those whose commencement of action is fruitless."
The meaning is as follows: therefore, who indeed would not become an object of humiliation or an object of contempt?
The sense is that everyone indeed becomes so.
In this context, according to the statement of Yādava, "ghanopala" (a hailstone) is "karaka," the word *karaka* [is used].
The explanation offered by some, namely that "the non-falling of hailstones" (*karakāṇām avṛṣṭiḥ*) is intended to establish a fixed masculine gender, is not accepted by others;
for Kṣīrasvāmin, in his commentary on the *Amara-kośa* under the entry "hailstone is a *kāraka*," [states as follows].

Regarding the statement that "karaka" refers to a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and "vināyaka" refers to the Sugata (Buddha), the author intends to demonstrate that both terms possess dual genders by stating that he will describe them as masculine even when they have various meanings.
However, the intention of Yādava lies in prescribing their masculine gender, and not otherwise.

Since there is a prohibition against the feminine gender [for this word], there is no contradiction therein either. However, in the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon, which states: "The word *karakas* may refer to a skull, a pomegranate, a water-pot, a species of bird, and also to the hand; and *karakā* refers to hailstones," its dual gender (masculine and feminine) is clearly evident.
There is no report of contradiction anywhere; for this very reason, it is seen that *rudra*, *varṣopala*, *karakā*, and *karaka* are synonyms. || 57 || —54— Sumativijaya.
The explanation of this [is as follows].
O Cloud, those śarabhas and lions on that Himācala mountain who might suddenly, at that very moment, leap over you— O Cloud—
you [should scatter] those śarabhas and lions with a laugh consisting of a tumultuous rain of hailstones.
You would make yourself an object of derision under the pretext of a laugh at your own shower of hailstones— making you, O cloud, what kind of being? One who has released his roar, that is,
one who has uttered the sound of thundering.
In what state were the śarabhas? They were impetuous in their leaping due to agitation;
that is, they were hastening to leap up because of anger upon hearing the roar.
For what purpose? To break their own limbs by falling from the mountain in order to overtake the cloud.

How could there be the breaking of one's own limb by bowing before such a lion? He demonstrates this very point through the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle). The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Who would not become a target of contempt— that is, a locus of defeat— being virtuous yet possessing efforts toward fruitless undertakings, meaning being one whose exertion in performing tasks has become fruitless?
By the use of the word "vā" (or), it is implied that all such people, even if they possess efforts toward fruitless undertakings, [would become so].
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).

"Tumuleti" means those who were scattered—that is, impelled—by laughter in the form of a shower of hailstones, which was white due to its laughter-like quality; thus, "tumulakarakāvṛṣṭihāsāvakīrṇān. "Tumula" refers to a tumultuous battle.
*Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*: *Karako* refers to hail; it is of three genders: *karako*, *karakā*, and *karaṇkam*.
Regarding *saṃrambha*: the leaping or jumping up that occurs through *saṃrambha*, which is a great intensity.

In that regard, "rabhasāḥ" means those who are impetuous; "samrambhotpatanarabhasāḥ" refers to those whose impetuosity consists in their forceful leaping. "Svāṅgabhaṅgāya" means for the purpose of breaking one's own limb;
"svāṅgasyaiva bhaṅgaḥ" is the breaking of one's very own limb. || 58 || -54-

The explanation of *vā* is [as follows]; the explanation of *svāṅgabhaṅgāya* is obscure. Because it is white due to laughter, the footprint of the Lord whose crest is the half-moon is clearly visible there upon the rock.
Bowing with devotion, you should circumambulate him to whom offerings are constantly presented by the Siddhas;
upon seeing him, those who possess faith, their sins shaken off, become fit for the attainment of his eternal state as a member of his retinue after the dissolution of the senses.
59. *Su*; *upacita* Ma; *upahuta* Su; *kalpiṣyante* Da, Ma; *saṅkalpante* Su; VALL.
There, on that snowy rock in the Himalayas, you should devoutly bow down and circumambulate the clearly manifest footprint of Śiva, whose crest is the crescent moon.
Because, when he is beheld, those who have destroyed their sins, being full of faith and devotion,

become fit for the attainment of the stable rank of his attendants after the departure of the senses— that is, immediately upon the falling away of the body; they become imperishable *pramatha* spirits.

For this very reason, he is called *Ardhamauli* (Half-Crested), for the crescent moon (*ardhendu*) is offered as a sacrificial oblation by the Siddhas at all times upon his crest (*mauli*). Although it consists of only a single digit (*kalā*), its designation as "half" (*ardha*) is relative to its shape.
The form *parīyāḥ* is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by *pari*, used with the suffix *sip* of the optative (*liṅ*).
That body is called *karaṇa* because the instruments—the sense organs—exist therein; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *arśa-ādibhyo 'c*. 55.
"In that regard, it turns to the right."
It is well known that the footprint of Rudra exists upon a certain rock of the Himavat;
it is one where offerings are always presented by the Siddhas, like those made for a hare.
According to Yādava, *bali* refers to an offering for worship, a type of demon, and also a tax. By this, the means of knowledge (*jñānopāya*) is indicated.
*Parīyāḥ* means you should go around; that is to say, you should perform circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).
"From the departure of the instruments"—the instrument (*karaṇa*) here refers to the body (*śarīra*).
Yādava states that "instrument" may also refer to the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), as well as to fields, limbs, and sense organs.
The meaning is: after the abandonment of the body.
"They will be deemed fit for the attainment of the rank of a permanent Gaṇa"— in this sense, according to the rule *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alam*,
since the word *alam* is taken there as signifying "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*),
the dative case is employed in the expression "for the attainment of the rank of a permanent Gaṇa" in connection with the verbal root *kḷp*.
Mallinātha says "tatra" (therein).
There, on a certain rock on the Himalaya mountain, it is manifest— clearly visible—
eternally and always by the *siddhas*, the yogis; for the *Viśva* lexicon states that *siddha* refers to both accomplishment and yoga.

To that Lord whose crest bears the crescent moon (*ardhendu*)—wherein *bali* refers to both an offering and a sacrifice according to Yādava, and *ardhendu* is a compound of *ardha* (half) and *indu* (moon)—*ardha* meaning "a part" or "a portion" according to the Viśva lexicon; and who has prepared various forms of worship with accumulated offerings. (Note: The term *ardhendu* is explained as the crescent moon worn on the head of Śiva; *bali* here denotes sacrificial offerings; and the verse describes the Lord adorned with these.)

Place your feet—that is, set down your steps—and being bowed down with devotion—an affection for those worthy of worship—perform a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*). The suffix *liṅ* is used here after the root *iṇ* preceded by *pari*. Upon seeing that placement of your feet, people shall have their sins shaken off and their impurities cast away.
The men are peaceful, full of faith, and trusting. "Faith" (śraddhā) means trust;

that is to say, it is the conviction of the existence of the afterlife (āstikyabuddhi). According to the rule that "the function of the prefixes *śrad* and *antar* should be stated as being like [that of other] prefixes," the suffix *śānac* is applied to the root *dhā* preceded by *śrat*.

"Upon the departure of the instruments," that is, after the abandonment of the body; "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is defined by Amara as "the most effective means" (*sādhakatama*), referring to the field, the limbs, and the senses. "Steadfast" means eternal; "the first place among the hosts" refers to the primary station.
The *vaijayantī* states that "groups" (*gaṇāḥ*) are "the first mass of numbers. They will be fit for its attainment;

they will become capable. Since the root *kḷp-* expresses sufficiency and has the sense of "being enough," the dative case is used in connection with it according to the rule *namas-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alam-vaṣaṭ-yogācca* (Pāṇini 2.3.16).
The author of the Bhāṣya states that the word *alam* is used here in the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*). Śiva manifested his two glorious feet, which were previously unmanifest,
on the Himālaya mountain for the sake of accomplishing all rites for the followers of Śambhu and others.
Having beheld the placement of the feet of Śrī, the practitioner prepares his body for stability;
indeed, with a body subject to his own will, he may wander through the three worlds.
Thus, in the *Śambhurahasya*. [58] — 55—
This is the commentary by Sumativijaya.

O Cloud, there on that rocky surface, the stone slab of Himācala, you, bowing with devotion, should circumambulate— that is, go around from all sides and perform the ritual of circumambulation for— the footprint-mark of Rudra, who wears the crescent moon upon his crest.
Which one? That upon which, when the placement of Mahādeva’s feet is seen,
faithful persons— endowed with faith— resolve to attain the upward path, for the sake of reaching the stable state of the Gaṇas, that is, for the sake of liberation, for the attainment of liberation.
They become capable. Why? Because of the cessation of the instruments [of action] and the destruction of the body accompanied by impurities and urine.
Of what nature is the placement of the feet? Manifest, that is, clearly evident.

Furthermore, of what nature was that placement of the feet? It was one where offerings (*bali*) and ritual services (*pūjopacāra*) were constantly and incessantly presented by the *siddhas*, a specific class of deities. Of what nature were the faithful people? They were those whose sins had been shaken off (*uddhūtapāpa*).
The grammatical construction is: "those by whom sins have been cast far away."
"Of him whose crest is the half-moon": he whose *mauli*—that is, his head (*mastaka*)—is adorned with a half-moon (*ardhendu*), meaning the half-moon; [this refers to] Mahādeva.
"Bowing in devotion": one who is habituated to bowing (*namana-śīla*) through devotion (*bhakti*), that is, by means of devotion (*bhakti-yuktyā*).
The dissolution of the instrument, that is, the body, is the destruction of the instrument; from that dissolution of the instrument.
Those by whom sin has been shaken off—that is, those by whom sin has been dispelled or destroyed—are "those who have shaken off their sins."
"Sthira" refers to the attainment of the state of the Stable Host (Sthiragaṇa), which is liberation; "for the attainment of the state of the Stable Host" means for that purpose.
Here, the figure of speech is *hetu* (cause). —59—55—
The word "ūrdhvam" (above/afterwards) should be construed with "karaṇavigamāt" (from the cessation of the senses).
Being filled by the winds, the hollow bamboos (*kīcakas*) resound sweetly;
and the victory over Tripura is sung by the *kinnarīs* with impassioned voices.
If your sound, resonant like a drum, should arise within the mountain caves,
then indeed the entire purpose of the musical performance for Paśupati will be fulfilled there.
*saṃrakta* (Ma, Su); *saṃsakta* (Da, Ma); *nirhrādas* (Ma);
*murave* (Da); *muraje* (Ma); *kandareṣu* (Da, Ma, Su);
*tatra bhāvī samastaḥ* (Da); *tatra bhāvī samagraḥ* (Da, Ma, Su).
As you dance, O Pūrṇa,
your resounding voice echoes through the mountain clefts and caves, swirling like a large drum.
If that were the case, then the entire purpose of Hara’s musical practice and its constituent elements would remain unfulfilled; for other necessary materials are present there.
To wit, the hollow bamboos, stirred by the winds, produce sweet sounds.
They resound and echo; and by the Kimpuruṣa women, who have been inspired [by you], the poem titled "The Burning of Tripura" is being sung.
And if your reflection in sound were to resemble the sound of a drum, then—
There, the entire meaning of the Saṅgīta of Paśupati will come to pass; they make sound and cause sound to be made. The resonance is deep and cavernous. 56.
Is it not the case that the term *ghūrṇamāna-gambhīra* has a twofold explanation?
[The answer is: "By the word *dakṣiṇāvarta*."
The suffix *kyan* is applied after the words *śabda*, *vaira*, *kalaha*, *abhra*, *kaṇva*, and *megha* when they function as instruments (Pāṇini 3.1.17).

The present-tense designation in the phrase "they sound" (*śabdāyante*) is employed because it is possible at all times [to describe them as such]. They [the clouds] are accompanied by those who are devoted.
"If your roar were to exist in the caves like it is in your mouth...
According to Yādava: "Nirhrāda, ravaṇa, nāda, kveḍa, dhvāna, and dhvani are synonyms for 'sound' (kala).
Although they circulate as synonyms, here [the intended meaning] is an echo (anunāda).
It is intended as being resonant (*nirhrāda*). "In the mouth" (*mukhe*) is in the locative case. The meaning is: if your sound were to resound within the caves like a resonant sound in the mouth;
it is the cause of musical performance (*saṅgīta*).
What is called *saṅgīta* consists of the triad of performance (*prekṣaṇīya*), dance (*nṛtta*), song (*gīta*), and instrumental music (*vādya*).

Now, it may be argued that the word *saṅgīta* does not denote this triad of dance and so forth, since we observe the usage in plays such as "I shall perform a *saṅgītaka*. However, the word *saṅgīta*— [The text provided ends abruptly here.]

It is employed in the sense of singing alone; thus, in the *Kumārasambhava*, he will say, "He made the female companions of the forest-singing weep" (5.56), and also, "those whose mouths were struck for the sake of song" (2.1). How, then, can the word *saṅgīta* here have the meaning of the triad beginning with dance?
Regarding the phrase "it is explained": it is said that Yādava stated that the word *saṅgīta* itself denotes the triad beginning with dance (*nṛtta*), namely:
"Dance, song, and instrumental music—this triad is called *nāṭya*, *tauryatrika*, and *saṅgīta* in this context for the purpose of performance."
The reading is "pūrṇa" [referring] to that dancing Paśupati.

However, if the reading were "samagra" [referring] to Paśupati there, the meaning of the musical performance (*saṅgīta*) would not be complete, because the dancing would not have been mentioned. Others, however, say: "Surely the meaning of the musical performance is [complete] there for Paśupati."

Some read "bhāvī samasta" [instead of *bhāvyasamasta*]. It is well known that Paśupati dwells there even in his own essential form (*svarūpa*), apart from his manifestation as the placement of feet (*pādanyāsa*). || 56 ||
"Malinātha says: 'They make sounds.'"
The *kīcakas*—a specific type of bamboo—are being filled by the clouds and winds.

According to Amara: "Those bamboos which resound when agitated by the wind are *kīcakas*. And according to Viśva: "*Kīcaka* may refer to a particular demon, or to a dry bamboo, or another kind of tree."

They "sound" (śabdāyante), meaning they produce sound or resonate in a manner that is sweet and pleasant to the ear; this is according to the rule *śabdavairakalahābhrakaṇvameghebhyaḥ karaṇe* (Pāṇini 3.1.17), which prescribes the suffix *kyaṅ*. By this, the excellence of the bamboo wind-instrument is described.

By the *kinnarīs*—that is, by the women of the *kinnaras*—who are either closely joined, united, or accompanied by the playing of flutes; or, according to the reading *saṃraktābhiḥ*, it means those with impassioned throats. [The compound] *trayāṇāṃ purāṇāṃ samāhāraḥ* refers to the collection of the three cities.

*Tripura*: this is a compound formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.51 (*taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*), meaning "the city of the three. It is neuter because it belongs to the *pātra*-class (Vārttika). Its victory is sung of in the *kandaras*, that is, in the caves; for *darī* and *kandara* are synonyms, with *kandara* being feminine as well.

Thus says Amara. "Te" means yours; "nirhrada" refers to the sound of a specific type of drum (muraja), meaning like the sound of a drum. If that were so, then there [would be] the music of Śiva—who is eternally present near that place—in the vicinity of his feet. As for the *Tāra-yatrika*:

The term *saṅgīta* is well-known at the commencement of a formal undertaking; it is also defined as "the cessation of musical instruments" (*tūryāṇāṃ triyate*) according to the *Śabdārṇava*. Its meaning is thus the subject matter of the performance, the substance of the *saṅgīta*. According to Amarasimha, the word *artha* is used in the senses of "that which is expressed," "wealth," "substance," "purpose," and "accomplishment. *Samagra* means complete or entire.

"Bhāvī" indeed means "it will surely come to be. The suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of the future according to Pāṇini 3.3.3, as in the rule stating that *gamyā* and other such words take this suffix.
— Sumativijaya.
The explanation of this is as follows.
O cloud, the hollow bamboos resound with a sweet and melodious sound;
Mahādeva is being sung of and praised by the Kinnarīs for his victory over Tripura. Your resonance in the caves and mountain recesses is like the sound produced by a *muraja* drum.
If, indeed, there should be such a resounding noise, then surely on that mountain Himācala,
the entire performance of the dance— the ritual of the spectacle— for the purpose of celebrating the placement of the feet of Paśupati Rudra, will come to pass.
Of what nature were the *kīcakas*? They were being filled—that is, being made full—by the winds or breezes.
Of what nature were the *kinnarīs*? They were deeply impassioned and possessed sweet voices.
Such is the syntactical connection (anvaya).

The meaning of *saṅgīta* is "the purpose of the assembly" (*saṅgītārtha*). According to Hemacandra, *saṅgīta* means "that in which there is a spectacle. According to the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*, [he is] the Lord of the Pāśupatas, the Pramathas, and the Bhūtas. By this much, one attains the rank of a Gaṇa upon seeing him.
The sense is that this is because singing and instrumental music before him are the cause of infinite merit. || 60 ||
Regarding the placement of the feet— if Mahādeva is not in his proper place— [this is] the final sentence,
an explanation for the sake of the musical meaning:
"Having traversed those various particular features on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain..."
Through that Krauñca-cleft, the path of the glory of Bhṛgupati known as Haṃsadvāra, you should proceed toward the northern direction— you,
dark-hued and beautiful with your horizontal stretch, like the foot of Viṣṇu when he was intent upon subduing Bali.
Ma; 61 Su; anusares Da, Ma, Su; vali° Su; °vimathana° Da; VALL

Having traversed— that is, having passed beyond— the various wonderful features on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain Himavat, such as the footprints [of Śiva] and others, you [should pass] through that opening in Mount Krauñca which serves as a gateway for the swans.
One should go toward the direction of Kubera (the north).
It is beautiful with its horizontal extent—that is, its width—and thus there is a simile:
it is like the dark foot of Viṣṇu, which rose up after the deception of Bali.

What kind of fissure? It is the path—the route of expansion—of the glory of Bhṛgupati, that is, Paraśurāma, because by means of it the Krauñca mountain was being shattered. "Prāleya" means snow. [The form] "atikramya" is derived from the rule *parāvarayoge ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.20), which prescribes the suffix *ktvā*.
"O clockwise-whorled one, O dewy one!"
"Go from there to those various specific places, including Anukanakhala"—thus were the specific places mentioned. Haṃsadvāra is the gate through which the swans depart for the lake named Mānasa.
Bhṛgupatiyaśovartma [is another]. Here, this should be considered by one with reference to Skanda:
Rivaling the enemy of Krauñca (Śiva), Paraśurāma made Mount Krauñca perforated with an arrow;
by that act, his fame became great.
Therefore, it is said that [this path] is "the track of the glory of the Lord of Bhṛgu. As Murāri has said:
Because of the path of the wounds made by his arrows, fragments of the bones of Mount Krauñca still fall today under the guise of swans; yet that sage Bhārgava remains enraged.
Thus:
"One should go having aimed at the anus.
It is stated that it is beautiful when extended horizontally because the anus is horizontal and upward-facing.
"Like Viṣṇu intent upon crushing Bali" means one intent upon breaking the power of Bali;
this is an epithet appropriate for that occasion because it expresses pervasiveness. (57)
Mallinātha says: "prāleya... and so forth.

"Near the slopes of the Prāleyādri," that is, near the slopes of the Himādri (Himalaya). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of proximity, according to the rule "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a word ending in a case-suffix," etc. "Those various"—the repetition indicates distributive frequency (*vīpsā*). "Particulars" refers to objects worthy of being seen. "Particular" (*viśeṣa*) [also denotes] a limb or a substance.
"In the ocean of words [it is said]: 'the two bright objects are to be seen.

The connection with the future tense is: 'having passed over, one should go following [the path]. 'The gate of the swans' (haṃsadvāram) means the gate for swans; the swans are those who set out for Lake Mānasa."

"They move through the Krauñca-cleft"—such is the traditional teaching (āgama). It is the path of the glory of Bhṛgupati, the son of Jamadagni; that is to say, it is the cause for the manifestation of his fame.
By means of that cleft in the mountain Krauñca—the "Krauñca-hole"—[the arrows of] Bali...
As Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Trivikrama, exerted himself in the subduing and binding of the Daitya, his dark,
black-colored foot shone with its transverse length for the sake of swift entry.
Thus being, you should proceed toward the northern direction, the *udīcī*.

It is said that in ancient times, the son of Bhṛgu, while studying the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the bow from the blessed Lord Dhūrjaṭi, [pierced] the Krauñca mountain out of rivalry with Skanda.

The story goes that, having effortlessly shattered a mound of clay with the tip of an exceedingly cold arrow, he immediately caused a certain ocean of fame to swell forth from the very heart of the Krauñca mountain,
thereby flooding the entire web of the world.
It is heard [in scripture]. 60.
-57- This is the commentary on *Sumativijaya*.

O Megha, for this reason, you should follow the northern direction— that is, proceed toward the north— by means of the Krauñca-cavity, a mountain named Krauñca-cavity, which serves as the gateway to that mountain.

Having done what? Having passed by— that is, having traversed— those various particularities of Paśupati, such as his footprints and so forth, in the vicinity of the Prāleyādri, the Himācala mountain.
Of what nature was the Krauñca-cleft? It was the gateway for swans, the path of the swans.
Furthermore, of what nature was the Krauñca-cleft? It was the track of Bhṛgupati’s fame, the path created by Paraśurāma.
In what state are you? You are beautiful with your horizontal extension. You are compared to a cloud; like what? Like the dark foot—the dark-colored foot—of Viṣṇu, that is, Kṛṣṇa.
Of what nature was Viṣṇu? He was "exerting himself to subdue Bali"—this is the grammatical connection.
"Haṃsa" means the gate of the swans; thus, it is called Haṃsadvāra. It is said that in ancient times, Krauñca Mountain was split asunder by Paraśurāma with blows from his axe;
hence it bears the name Haṃsadvāra. By this [gate], the swans come to and depart from Lake Mānasa.
Such is the meaning.
"Prāleyādri" means the mountain (adri) of snow (prāleya), that is, the snowy mountain; [the term refers to] that snowy mountain.

"Bhṛgu" refers to the path of the glory of the Lord of the Bhṛgus (Bhṛgupati-yaśas). "Tiryak" means that which is horizontal; "tiryagāyāmaśobhī" means one who is characterized by being beautiful due to that horizontal extension—the sense being that he is of a nature to spread out.

"Vali" refers to one who is intent upon the restraint of Vali, that is, intent upon the slaying of Vali; he who is vigilant toward such a person is "intent upon the restraint of Vali. Herein lies the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile). 61. -57-

Having gone near the Krauñca-cave on the slopes of Mount Krauñca, you should become a guest of Kailāsa— the mirror for the women of the gods— whose ridges and joints were once heaved up by the arms of the Ten-faced one.
With its peaks as white as water-lilies, it stands pervading the sky like the massed-up,
nightly loud laughter of the Three-eyed Lord.
May it be so: daily [may you go] to Da?ma; daily to Su;
having gone upwards immediately after VALL, may you become a guest of Mount Kailāsa; go there.
This is the meaning.
Of what sort [was he]?

One whose mountain ridges were puffed up by the arms of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), and whose slopes were crushed by the arms of Paulastya (Rāvaṇa). For he (the mountain) was indeed intended by him to be uprooted out of pride.
He became beloved,
just as [he was] to the celestial nymphs, because they beheld their own faces in him who resembled a mirror due to his crystalline nature.
And he who stands pervading the sky with lofty peaks white as water-lilies;
therefore, it is imagined:
he is like the exuberant smile, the loud laughter of Śiva, accumulated night after night. 58.
"Having gone to Daksinavarta..."
The meaning is: "having gone upwards through that opening.

[It refers to Mount Kailāsa,] whose joints of the plateaus were crushed by the uprooting of the arms of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), and which serves as a mirror for the women of the gods. Now, one might object: this epithet is inappropriate.
Because of contact with clouds and wind, a mirror becomes obscured; as it is said:
"By those pure in their conduct, I am [tainted] by a stain, just as a mirror is [stained] by clouds, wind, and so forth" (Raghuvamśa 14.37).
The resolution to this is that, due to the vastness of Kailāsa, its becoming darkened is impossible.
He demonstrates that very vastness with the words "by the heights of its peaks. "Vitastya" means having spread out or expanded;
the meaning is, having spread out as far as the sky. "Aṭṭahāsa" refers to a great laugh.
"Aṭṭahāsa" means "great laughter," according to Yādava. || 58 ||
"Having gone," says Mallinātha.

Having gone upward immediately after emerging from the Krauñca cave, [he reached] that mountain whose joints— the connections between its plateaus and ridges— had been expanded and separated by the arms of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa. By this...

The true nature of their delight in seeing [the Lord] has been stated. They are called "tridaśāḥ" because they possess thirty as their measure; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule *saṅkhyayāvyayā-* etc.
In this *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *ḍac* is applied as the final member of the compound according to the rule *bahuvrīhau saṅkhyeye ḍaj-* etc.

Kṣīrasvāmī [comments]: "Of the women of the thirty [gods], that is, the goddesses; of their mirror. Because Kailāsa is made of crystal or silver, it possesses the quality of reflecting images (bimbagrāhitva);
thus this was said. "May you be the guest of Kailāsa."
That Kailāsa, with the lofty heights of its peaks as pure and white as water-lilies,
stretches across and pervades the sky day after day,
appearing like the accumulated, immense laughter of the three-eyed Lord Śiva.

"Sthitah" (remained). According to Yādava, [the word] *aṭṭā* means "excessive agitation. Because of its whiteness, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding it being laughter; that laughter and the like possess whiteness is established by poetic convention. || 61 || -58-
The explanation of this is *Sumativijaya*.
Furthermore, O Cloud, having gone upward toward the northern peaks and higher still,
you shall become a guest— a visitor— at that mountain named Kailāsa.
Of what nature was Kailāsa? Its ridges and joints were heaved up by the arms of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa).
Again, of what nature was Kailāsa? It was a mirror for the women of the gods (the *tridaśavanitās*).
Of which [Kailāsa]? That mountain Kailāsa which, with the elevations of its peaks (*śṛṅga*)—that is, its summits—...
It stands having spread out and extended its lofty peaks as far as the sky, the atmosphere;
by what kind of peaks? By those as white as the *kumuda* lily—that is, as bright as the moon-blooming lotus.
Kailāsa is compared to what? It is like the loud laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*) of Tryambaka, the Great God (*mahādeva*).
Of what nature is that laughter? It has accumulated into a mass in every direction.
The grammatical connection is: "having become a mass" means "produced in one place."

"Daśa-mukha-bhuja-ucchvāsita-prastha-sandheḥ" means: *daśa* (ten) refers to Rāvaṇa, who has ten faces; *ucchvāsita* means raised or uplifted; *prastha* refers to mountain peaks; thus, *daśamukhabhujocchvāsitaprasthasandhiḥ* refers to one whose joints of the mountain peaks were raised by the arms of the ten-faced one.
"Tridaśa-vanitā-darpaṇasya" means: *tridaśa* refers to the gods; *vanitā* refers to beautiful women; *darpaṇa* means a mirror;
thus, *tridaśavanitādarpaṇaḥ* refers to the mirror of the celestial beauties. Of that [mirror].
Having made [the earth] high with peaks and summits— that is, with lofty elevations of the peaks—
this is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
Why is "having made" (*kṛtvā*) used at the end of the sentence?
I foresee that when you have reached its shore, appearing like smooth, moist collyrium,
you will behold that playful mountain— which is as white as the freshly severed tusk of an elephant—
and which shall be worthy of being gazed upon with steady eyes.
When the dark garment was placed upon his shoulder, it was like the dark-blue robe of the wielder of the plow (Balarāma).
While you are stationed upon its peak, I imagine the future splendor of that Kailāsa as it will be beheld by the unblinking eyes [of Śiva].
Of what is it like? It is like one upon whose shoulder is draped a dark blue garment.
Like that of Haladhara; because the cloud is dark.
"Resembling smooth, split collyrium" means it resembles non-dry powdered soot—this is an epithet of the cloud. But of that...
Even though he is fair-skinned, he is white like a fragment of an elephant's tusk severed at that very moment.
"Is it not a qualification of the cloud?
I see it as a right-turning spiral."
The connection is as follows: "I perceive her, who is to be gazed upon with steady eyes, resembling glossy, broken collyrium, and like a smooth slab of split collyrium;
[this applies] even to this plow-bearer (Balarāma), who wears blue garments."
The phrase beginning with "white as a freshly cut slice of an elephant's tusk" (*sadyaḥkṛttadviradaradanacchedagaura*) and so forth should be applied [here].
Regarding the word *mecaka*, it means dark blue, black, or deep black; as Amara states: "nīla, asita, śyāma, kāla, śyāmala, and mecaka" (1.5.15). || 59 ||
"Malinatha says:
'I perceive'."
When you had ascended the ridge of that mountain, the luster of that collyrium— which was smooth, soft, broken, and rubbed— became like the splendor of a freshly cut,
severed elephant tusk, white as its very fracture.
When a dark garment—
*mecaka*, meaning black, blue, dark, or deep black (according to Amarakośa 1.5.15)—
was placed upon his shoulder, he resembled Balabhadra, the wielder of the plow (*halabhṛt*).
With steady eyes, I foresee a beauty that is yet to be; I conjecture that such splendor will come to pass. This is the meaning.
The poetic figure is a full simile (*pūrṇopamā*) based on direct scriptural expression (*śrautī*). || 62 || -59-
The commentary on this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.
O cloud, I foresee the future human-like splendor and beauty of that mountain, Himācala; provided that you, the cloud, have reached its slopes— that is, when you have drawn near.
Of what nature was that mountain? White as the freshly severed tusks of an elephant.
Of what nature were you? Resembling smooth, split collyrium. Of what nature was the splendor? Capable of being gazed upon with steady eyes.
It is imagined: to whom is that Himācala like? It is like the splendor of Halabhṛt, Valabhadra;
just as the splendor of Valabhadra occurs when what? When a dark garment, a blue cloth (*mecake vāsasi nīlāmbare*), is placed upon his shoulder (*aṃsanyaste sati skandhe*).
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "when it has been established" and "when it has been maintained."

"Sadyaḥ" means immediately; "sadyaḥ-kṛtta" refers to that which has just been cut or split in two. Like a fragment from the severed tusk—that is, the broken portion of the tooth—of an elephant (*dvirada*), it is white or bright; thus, it is "white like a freshly severed tusk-fragment.
[The compound *sadyaḥ-kṛtta-radana-daśana-ccheda-gaura* means] "white like a freshly severed tusk-fragment."
