"Snigdha" means glossy and not rough; "bhinnamardita" refers to that which has been crushed and rubbed; that collyrium or lampblack (*añjana*) which possesses such a luster or beauty is "snigdhabhinnāñjanābha," and [the object] is in that state.
"Stimita-nayana-prekṣaṇīyām" means worthy of being gazed upon with steady eyes—that is, with motionless eyes.
Because of its whiteness, the Himālaya is comparable to Balabhadra; because of its dark-blue color, the cloud is comparable to a dark garment.
"Kṛṣṇa is black and dark," according to the *Abhidhānakośa* of Hemacandra.
Here, the poetic figure is *upamā* (simile). 63.
-59- Having abandoned her blue serpent-bracelet, she was given a hand by Śambhu.
And if Gaurī should wander on foot upon the pleasure-mountain, you,
whose body is formed by the art of your waves and who have solidified the waters within,
become her staircase— providing a pleasant touch for her feet during her ascents.
Having abandoned that [world] in Daśama, having abandoned that in Suka, one should wander in both Mañju and Suka; [crossing] the flood of waters in Daśama,
Mañju,
and Suka, you, O Daśama, are the leader for ascending the jeweled bank of the stairs.
And on that pleasure-mountain Kailāsa, if Pārvatī were to wander or stroll about on foot with her feet while Śiva supports her hand, then you—her... [would be... her.
You should serve as a staircase for those ascending,
for your body is fashioned with the artistry of waves, the grace of ripples, and the form of surging billows, by which the water within your belly is rendered motionless and stilled.

Otherwise, there would be the risk of stumbling; for precisely because it is terrifying, one must leave behind—that is, abandon—the blue snake-coil. "Pādacāra" means movement or going on foot with both feet. || 60 ||
"Having abandoned the clockwise-turning [conch]," etc.

The casting aside of the serpent-bracelets is for the sake of removing the Goddess’s fear. The word *ca* (and) in the phrase "yadi ca" (if [she]... is connected with the word *tvam* (you). She might "viharet"—meaning she might play, sport, or wander about.
*Bhaṅgī* means one who possesses breaks or divisions; Keśava states that *bhaṅgī*, *vibhaṅga*, and *śakala* are synonyms.
And it is said [in the *Raghuvamśa* 6.3]: "with the breaking apart of rocks. "With devotion" means with devotion to the Lord (*Īśvara*).
It was also stated previously: "one should circumambulate, bowed down by devotion" (verse 55). "Having fashioned its body":
"fashioning" (*viracana*) means arranging by repeatedly cutting [the rock]; the meaning is that it is a flight of stairs.
For the purpose of ascending the jeweled slope: the mention of "jewels" is intended to indicate that the cloud and the steps on the slope share the same color, since the cloud is blue.
[The Lord said: "If Gaurī were to roam upon the pleasure-mountain on foot, and you too, with devotion..."
The meaning is: "Having assumed a broken form, fashion your body into a staircase for ascending the jeweled slopes. (60)
Mallinātha says: "Having abandoned... (hitvā iti).
On that pleasure-mountain Kailāsa—[for it is said]:
"Kailāsa, Kanakādri, Mandara, and Gandhamādana were created by the gods for the sport of Śambhu; thus they became his pleasure-mountains."
In the *Śambhurahasya*:
"If Gaurī, out of timidity, were to walk on foot, leaving behind—that is, abandoning—the serpent-bracelet (valaya) given by Śambhu, that is, Śiva; and [if] Satī were to do likewise..."
Then, with its vanguard moving forward, it stood thus: having caused the flood— the current— of the inner water to become solidified and congealed,
its body was fashioned by the arrangement and division of its waves.

Being one whose body is fashioned from excellent jewels, become a staircase for the ascent to that jeweled shore (*maṇitaṭa*); that is to say, assume the state of a flight of steps. (63) — Sumativijaya.
This is its explanation.
O Cloud, if Gaurī Pārvatī should wander on foot— that is, by moving her feet— upon that pleasure-mountain Kailāsa, then you,
being the foremost traveler upon that mountain, [should go] to the jeweled slope for the sake of ascending the jeweled ridge.
"Act as a staircase for her ascent; construct a series of steps.
Having done what? Having cast off the serpent-bracelet—that is, having abandoned the garland of snakes.
Of what nature was Gaurī? Her hand was taken by Śambhu—by Mahādeva.
She has extended her hand as a support.
Of what nature are you? You are one whose body is fashioned with a graceful curvature (*bhaṅgī-bhaktyā*), resembling a surging wave (*kallola*). Your form is thus constructed.
Furthermore, of what nature are you? You are one whose internal flood of water has been solidified—that is, the mass of water within you has been made rigid.
This is the grammatical construction.
"Stambhitāntarjalaughaḥ" means one by whom the flood— the mass— of water within the interior has been solidified.
"Maṇitaṭarohanāya" means for the purpose of ascending or climbing onto the jeweled slope.
There is a figure of speech based on metaphor (*rūpaka*) here. (65)
— 60— There, the celestial maidens will surely lead you to the state of a fountain-house (*yantradhārāgṛha*) by making you enter within so that you emit sprays of water.
O friend, if you do not wish for their liberation from those [fetters] once they have been seized by the heat,
you should terrify them with roars harsh to the ear, as they are fond of play.
64 Ma; 64 Su;

water ejected by the striking of the vajra-ring; [the text reads] *kuliśavalayodghaṭṭanodgīrṇatoyaṃ* in Da, Ma, and *kuliśavalayodghaṭṭitodgīrṇatoyaṃ* in Su; [he] should cause [them] to fear (*bhāpayet*) in Su.

There on that mountain, because you were raining and emitting sprays of water, the celestial maidens— the young women of heaven— certainly regarded you as a fountain-house due to your entry within their dwellings.
They will lead; they will cause [you] to reach.
For if, indeed, by the force of the wind you are cast into the middle of a house and rain sparsely, then you yourself become a house consisting of a stream of mechanical water. For in the summer...
The wealthy construct fountain-houses to ward off the heat;

such being the case, if there were no release— that is, no escape— for you from those women who are addicted to pleasure once you have been caught in the summer heat, then they would surely drive you away with their thundering roars, harsh to the ear.
"Bhāyayeḥ" means you should frighten or terrify them; the intention is that they might abandon you out of fear.

"Udgāraḥ" means a spreading forth or emission. [Regarding the commentary on the verse beginning with] "O friend," [it explains] abandonment, liberation, and those who are intent on play. [End of] Dākṣiṇāvarta.
Regarding that: "therein."

"Valayakuliśodghaṭṭanodgīrṇatoya" means water ejected by the striking of the ring-thunderbolt (*valayakuliśa*). Here, "ring-thunderbolt" (*valayakuliśa*) refers to the thunderbolt that is the ring itself; by means of that ring-thunderbolt, there is the state of being pierced upward, which is the "striking with the ring-thunderbolt. By the mention of the "thunderbolt," its function as the instrument of the striking is indicated.
It has been said:
"The state of being an artificial fountain-house" means the state of being a man-made fountain-house. "Obtained during the heat" means obtained during the hot season.
"But surely it is the rainy season; how can there be the attainment of the summer season? [The answer is:
Because Kailāsa is a divine land, all six seasons exist there at all times. And he will say later:
"In his hand is a lotus for play" (2.2). Alternatively, by the word *gharma* (heat), "exertion" (*śrama*) is meant.
This is intended [to mean]: "of that which was obtained at the time of the pleasure-retreat. *Bhāyayeḥ* means "you should cause fear to arise. || 61 ||
Mallinātha says: "In that [regard]..."

In that Kailāsa, there are certainly, in every way, celestial maidens whose bracelets are like thunderbolts—the word *kuliśa* (thunderbolt), though meaning "one with a hundred edges," here indicates a mere "edge" or "point. By these [bracelets], they are struck; by those blows, it was emitted or cast forth.
They will lead you—the water by which you exist—to the state of being a house for fountain-streams (*yantradhārā*), that is, they will bring you to the state of artificial cascades.

O friend, O companion! [This refers to you] who have been obtained during the heat of the summer; and your state of being "obtained in the heat" is due to the fact that in celestial lands all seasons are present at all times, or because you are the very first cloud [of the season].
As it was said, "on the first [day] of Āṣāḍha," if at that time you had not been liberated from those celestial maidens— meaning those celestial maidens who were *krīḍālolāḥ*,
i.e., intent on play, or in other words, intoxicated by play— then [this would not have occurred]. Those celestial maidens...
You should cause [them] to tremble and terrify with roars that are harsh to the ears and instruments [of hearing];
here, because there is no cause for fear, the ātmanepada suffix and the augment *ṣuk* do not apply.
The commentary on this is the *Sumatīvijaya*.

O Cloud, there on Kailāsa, the celestial damsels—the wives of the gods—will certainly and surely lead you, that is, bring you, to the state of a fountain-house. To what sort of you? To one from whom water is being discharged by the striking of bracelets made of diamonds.
O friend, if there were no release— that is, no letting go— from those celestial women on your part, then you would have terrified the wives of the gods with your thunders,
making them filled with fear so that they might follow you.
The wives of the gods release [showers].
Of you, who are like what? Of you who have arrived during the summer season (*gharmalabdha*).
By what kind of thunders? By those harsh to the ears (*śravaṇaparuṣa*), that is, to both ears.
The meaning is as follows: "By means of harsh words" means by means of those that are painful to hear.
Of what nature were they? "[Restless in play]" means fickle because of their engagement in sport.
This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
The state of being a fountain-house is "fountain-houseness" (*yantradhārāgṛhatvam*).
By the word "thunderbolt" (*kuliśa*), diamonds are meant; the bracelets marked by them are "thunderbolt-bracelets.
From their striking, water is ejected.
"Surayuvati" refers to the young women of the gods (*surāṇāṃ yuvatayaḥ*). "Krīḍālolāḥ" means those who are eager for play, specifically for water-sports (*krīḍāsu jalakrīḍāsu lolāḥ*). (64)
The phrase *krīḍālolās* is missing; the explanation of *kuliśa* and so forth is incomplete; *muñcan* is the Jain-Sanskrit equivalent for *mocana*;
[he was] taking up the water of Lake Mānasa, which produces golden lotuses.
Providing for a moment the pleasure of a face-veil for the Ocean out of desire,
and shaking with its winds charged with water droplets the silken garments of the Kalpa-trees,
you should enter that mountain, which is as clear as crystal and distinguished by its shade. 62–65.
Ma; 66 Su; kāmam Ma,Su; airāvatasya Da,Ma,Su;
shaking with his breaths the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling trees as if they were silken garments.
One should enjoy that king of mountains with various playful activities,
like those of a cloud.
Separated by your shadow—that is, by your reflection—you have become twofold; thus, you may enter and enjoy that mountain, which is as pure as a white gem.
He describes the enjoyment: what kind of person are you?
Taking— that is, drawing from— the waters connected to Lake Mānasa, which produces (the word *prasūte* here being used figuratively) golden lotuses (*hemāmbhojāni*);
likewise,
for a moment, out of his own will (*kāmāt*), [he took] that of Airāvata.
Delighting in the face-cloth; for elephants are indeed delighted by a face-cloth.
Shaking—that is, moving—garments from the celestial tree with breezes accompanied by water droplets, that is, drops of water;
for the root *dhunoti* belonging to the *svādigaṇa* is accepted as ending in a short vowel, hence the form *dhunvan*.
Thus is form. || 62 ||
"Gold that spirals to the right."
*Prasava* means procreation or a flower; that which possesses this is *prasavin*.
Regarding *prasava*, Yādava states: "It refers to procreation, permission, a son, fruit, and flowers.
*Kāmāt* means according to one's desire. This applies as a supplement to everything [previously mentioned].
For a moment, there was the pleasure of the face-veil;

for a moment, the seizing [of the elephant] and the taking of water while desiring to speak. "Pleasure of the face-veil" means the pleasure of the veil that covers the face. Of Airāvata, who plunges into Lake Mānasa.
The meaning is: as you hang with your body suspended from the mouth of the emerging Airāvata, may you produce a sense of delight that conceals its face.
"Sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree" means those which have become like sprouts of the kalpavṛkṣa.
Those whose various activities consist of manifold gestures;
who, through graceful movements endowed with playfulness, enjoy [the scene].
Here, this should be considered: a certain friend, having gone to the house of his dear friend...
The implied meaning (dhvani) is that she enjoys his ponds, vehicles, gardens, and so forth at her own will. || 62 ||
Mallinātha says "hemeti."
He was a cloud that produced golden lotuses; by the rule beginning with *jidṛkṣi*, the suffix *ini* is applied. "Taking up the water of Lake Mānasa" means drinking it.

Likewise, regarding Airāvata, Indra’s elephant: the sense is that it has arrived either because it moves at will or because Indra has come for the purpose of serving Śiva. At that moment—the time for giving water—he displays the joy [the elephant feels] toward its face by means of the cloth.
Likewise, the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*) are like fine garments (*aṃśuka*), that is,
subtle cloths; for *aṃśuka* may denote a garment in general,
as well as an undergarment or an upper robe, and refers to a fine cloth that is not overly brilliant.

In the *Śabdārṇava*: "Shaking with winds—the winds of the clouds—by means of playful sports (*lalita*) consisting of various (*nānā*) and manifold (*bahuvidha*) activities such as drinking water; [the word] *lalita* is used in the sense of a particular emotion (*bhāva-bheda*), in female dance (*strī-nṛtya*), and as an adjective (*triṣu*) for 'beautiful'; it is not feminine when it refers to a pleasure-house (*pramadā-gāra*)."

In the ocean of sounds where [birds] cry out, "The shoots have sprouted! Play!"—you may enjoy that king of mountains, Kailāsa, as you wish, according to your pleasure. *Nirviś* means "to enjoy" or "to experience," according to Amara. Moving about as you desire in the houses of friends is the fruit of friendship.
The fruit is Kailāsa, which is his innate friend.
The meaning is that friendship exists naturally between clouds and mountains, the sun and the lotus, the ocean and the moon, fire and smoke, and wind and fire. (65) —62— Sumativijaya.
This is its explanation.
O Cloud, you should resort to and enjoy that king of mountains, the mountain [Kailāsa], by means of various activities—activities of diverse kinds—performed through your play as a cloud.
How are those various activities characterized? By your sport as a water-bearing cloud.
What were you doing with those heart-stealing [songs]? You were taking— that is, receiving— the water from Mānasa, the Mānasa lake.
Of what nature was the water? It produced golden lotuses—that is, it gave rise to gold-colored kamalas.
Furthermore, what were you doing? You were providing an intense, momentary pleasure for the face—a satisfaction for the countenance lasting but an instant.
Of whom? Of Airāvata, the elephant Airāvaṇa.
Furthermore, what were you doing? Shaking, as it were, the sprouts of the Kalpa-tree—those tender shoots of the celestial tree—with the winds, like garments.
The grammatical construction is "kampayan" (shaking). In some variant readings, it is also seen as "sajalapṛṣataiḥ" (with water droplets) in this same manner.
The ornament of form (rūpākālaṅkāraḥ).
[Verse 66] —62— Is the explanation of *hemāmbha* etc. impossible? Is the variant reading (*pāṭhāntara*) given incomplete? Where are the analyses (*vigrahas*)?
O wanderer at will, having seen Alakā upon his lap— where the Ganges flows like a slipping silken garment as if out of affection— you shall not fail to recognize it;
for she carries your celestial chariots aloft, emitting streams of water at the proper time.
The mass of clouds was like a passionate woman whose hair is bound with a net of pearls;
[it was adorned] with palanquins [and fine silken garments].
O Valli, having seen our city Alakā there on Kailāsa, you will not fail to recognize it; indeed, you will know it beyond doubt that "this is surely Alakā."
Whose silken garment is the Gaṅgā itself, slipped and fallen upon the lap of that mountain— for the Jāhnavī indeed flows there—
and which Alakā, at your time, that is, during the season known as the rains, [will see] a mass of clouds...
It carries. Of what kind? It emits water; thus it is "salilodgāram" (water-emitting), according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1).

He explains what [it is], how it is, and what it carries: just as a passionate woman bears a lock of hair adorned with a net of pearls, she too has her upper garment slipped off upon the lap of her beloved. In this case, the water is the object of comparison for the net of pearls.
The clouds are the hair on his forehead; the lofty celestial chariots are his high mansions. By the term "roaming at will," the dullness of the cloud is refuted. (63)
"His [hair] curls to the right."

"Utsaṅga" means on the upper surface or in the lap. "Of the lover, the husband": although one could have said "the beloved woman in the lap of the lover," the word "kāminī" (beloved woman) is not employed because it will be mentioned in the latter half of the verse.
"Srastagaṅgādukūlām"—Yādava states that *dukūla* refers to a white garment;
this term is to be applied to both [the city and the river].
"You will not fail to recognize Alakā upon seeing her again," as was previously stated.
Two negative particles (*nañ*) are employed to indicate that the cloud possesses the knowledge of *Alakā*.
By the term "one who acts according to desire" (*kāmacārin*), both his universal mobility and his state of being a lover are intended.
"At your time" means at the season for clouds such as you—the rainy season.

This is the meaning. *Salilodgāram*: that which emits water is *salilodgāraḥ*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule for the object (*karman*). *Uccaiḥ*: by means of lofty palaces (*vimāna*).
A palace consisting of seven stories is a *vimāna*. A *vimāna* is a celestial vehicle (and is not feminine).

And regarding the phrase "in the dwelling on the seventh floor," Yādava [states that it means] "strung with a network of pearls," that is, bound by a thread of pearls. Here, this should be considered:
noble men who have been away from home, having returned during the rainy season, are free from pride.

The intended meaning is that, having become women, they seize the long, hanging tresses on the cheeks of [the enemies] and bind them with nets of pearls. By the second half of the verse as well, a means for recognizing the tresses (or the women) has been stated. 63.
The First Message is completed.
Mallinātha [comments] on the word "tasya" (of him): |||
On the lap—the upper part and the slope—of that Kailāsa, which is like a beloved lover;

for the *Mālatīmālā* states: "The word *utsaṅga* refers to a place where contact has been released, as well as the upper surface of the thigh. [He is] like the Gaṅgā, a white garment (*dukūla*), upon it.

This is a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison). According to the *Śabdārṇava*, "dukūla" refers to fine cloth, an upper garment, or white silk; however, in this context, the Ganges itself is the *dukūla*.
[He went to] that Alakā, the city of Kubera, which is described as such because its [Ganges-dukūla] had slipped away.
"Having seen"—the word "like a woman full of desire" (*kāminīmiva*) is to be supplied.

O you who act according to your own will (*kāmacārin*), it is not that you will not know [this] again; rather, the meaning is that you will certainly know it. For you, who act according to your own will, [this has happened] many times before as well.

The employment of two negative particles (*nañ*) is for the purpose of establishing the certainty that ignorance is indeed impossible because perception is possible. As it has been said: "The employment of two negatives is for the sake of establishing a certainty regarding recollection."
That [city] in which there are lofty, elevated palaces (*vimāna*), that is, seven-storied mansions.
According to Yādava, "the word *vimāna* is not feminine; it refers to a celestial vehicle (*devayāna*) and a seven-storied dwelling.
This epithet is intended to indicate the location of the chariot drawn by clouds (*meghasaṃvāhana*). Elsewhere, [it refers to] palaces.
"Niṣkopā" means free from agitation.
"Yālakā" refers to your time, meaning the rainy season; the plural "vo" is used because that time is common to all clouds.

"Salilodgāram" means "emitting water"; that is to say, with streams of water flowing forth. "Abhravṛndam" refers to a mass of clouds; "kāminī" refers to a woman. "Grathitam" means strung together or inlaid with "muktājālaiḥ," that is, with nets of pearls. According to lexicographers, the word "muktā" may denote both a prostitute and a pearl.
Thus says Yādava. *Alakam* means "like curls" (*cūrṇakuntalāni*); the singular number is used to denote a class (*jātāvekavacanam*).
"Curls are *alakāḥ*"—so says Amara. *Vahati* means "it bears" or "possesses.
Here, Kailāsa is the favorable hero (*anukūlanāyaka*), while Alakā is [the heroine].

The status of the heroine known as *svādhīnapatikā* (one who has her husband under her control) is suggested. They define her thus: "She who is constantly cherished by her beloved, thinking that he is favorable toward her alone, is considered *svādhīnapatikā*.
And they cite an example: "Caressing the tips of her curls and arranging clusters of blossoms..."
Entertaining his beloved alone, he follows her like a shadow.
"Whence is this source? NB: This is cited as an example for *svādhīnapatikā* in the *Rasakalikā* (with improved readings!).
Thus ends [the section] accompanied by the commentary titled *Saṃjīvanī*, composed by the illustrious Mahāmahopādhyāya Mallinātha Sūri.
The first cloud in the poem *Meghadūta*, composed by the great poet Śrī Kālidāsa,
is completed.
The explanation of this [is] *Sumatīvijaya*.
O cloud who acts according to your own will, having seen the city named Tāmalakāmalakā, you will not fail to recognize it again; indeed, you will recognize it.
To what might Tāmalakā be compared? It is like the beloved of that mountain-form [cloud].
Whom [do you not see], like the Ganges-garment slipped from her husband’s lap? She whom, at the proper time— the rainy season— your children carry upon clouds, that is,
masses of water-bearing vapors, by means of lofty palaces and mansions.
He bears [it]. Like what? Like locks of hair; like a loving woman, just as a loving woman bears—that is, wears—locks of hair, which is to say, her hair.
What kind of ornament? "Woven with a network of pearls," meaning strung together with a multitude of pearl drops.
What kind of mass of clouds? "Emitting water.
This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).

"Srasta" means fallen; she whose *dukūla*—the garment in the form of the Gaṅgā—is fallen is "srastagaṅgādukūlā. Just as another beloved woman, while clinging to the lap of a lustful man, has her garment fall away, so too is she.
The sense is: "This is Alakā as well. Here, Alakā is [conceived of as] a beloved woman, and the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) is [conceived of as] her head.
(67) —63— Does *iva* refer to *srasta* and so forth? [It refers to] the final sentence.
The women with graceful wives [long for] the cloud accompanied by lightning, and the paintings [long for] it together with Indra’s bow.

Where palaces— whose floors are made of jewels, which possess water within, whose lofty peaks touch the clouds, and where drums are struck to the accompaniment of song— suffice to equal you through various such distinctive qualities, with their smooth and deep resonance.
1 Da, Ma;
*saṅgītārtha* Da; *°muravās* Da; *°parjanya* Da; 68 Su; Vall.
In that city of Alakā, the palaces and houses are capable of equalling and emulating you through various qualities they possess;
for even they, with their charming women, resemble you as you are possessed of lightning and accompanied by flashes of thunder.

They too have women full of grace; they too possess rainbows and celestial weapons, and are thus variegated like paintings. They too have voices that are smooth and deep, with sweet and steady resonance, just like you.
Where the drums are struck for musical performance and the mṛdaṅgas are played;
where the ground is made of jewels and the courtyards are of crystal— even those [palaces] call out to you from within their waters,
while those with peaks touching the sky and summits scraping the clouds call out to you as you soar high above.
Thus there is similarity in all respects. *Abhraṃliha* means that which reaches or pervades the sky (*kha*);
those whose tops are *abhraṃliha*. [The suffix] *lih* occurs after *vaha* and *abhra*; furthermore, *tuli* is also [a word ending in] a short vowel. 64.
O Dākṣiṇāvarta, hereafter, in seven verses, he describes Alakā by means of some manner of connection with the clouds, beginning with the words "vidyudvantam."

"Variegated" (*sacitrāḥ*) means accompanied by paintings. Regarding the reading *saṅgītārthaprahatamuravāḥ*: "concert" (*saṅgīta*) refers to the triad of dance, instrumental music, and song. The word "purpose" (*artha*) here signifies "cause. Thus, it refers to those for whom drums (*murava*) have been struck for the purpose of concert.
"Snigdhaparjanyaghoṣam" means having a sound like that of a pleasant rain-cloud; "parjanya" refers to the thundering of a cloud.
Yādava states: "Parjanya [is used] for a roaring cloud, the thundering of a cloud, Indra, and a mechanical weapon.
The meaning here is "having a sound of pleasant thundering. In this context, it refers to that which denotes the thundering of a cloud.

Although the intended meaning is established by the use of the word *parjanya* alone, the use of the word *ghoṣa* must be tolerated— just as in the phrase "peacocks with their *kekā* cries"— as being like the inclusion of the word *kekārava*.
The suffix *khaś* [is applied] by the rule *vahābhre lihaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.32), resulting in the form *abhraṃliha*, meaning "that which licks the clouds.
*Tulayitum* means "to make a balance" or "to weigh. There is also a word *tulā* that signifies "similarity"; thus, the meaning is "to make you similar."
Now, one might object: since the verbal root *tula* meaning "to weigh" belongs to the curādigaṇa, how is the form *tulā* derived? [The answer is:
because the suffix *ṇic* is not invariably applied, the form *tulā* also occurs. It means "sufficient" or "adequate."

"By those various particularities"—that is, by those various particularities such as charming women and so forth. Since the previously mentioned particularities were obscured by their being compounded [in the previous verse], the phrase "by those various particularities" is stated for the sake of clarity. Here, there is a connection with the cloud.
This is clear. —64— Mallinātha [comments]:
"vidyudvantam" (possessing lightning).
In that city of Alakā, there are women who are graceful and beautiful; those [houses] in which they dwell are "sacitrāḥ" (accompanied by paintings).

According to Amara, *citra* means both "painting" (*ālekhya*) and "wonder" (*āścarya*). The compound *sacitra* is a *bahuvrīhi*, formed according to the rule *tena saheti tulyayoge* ("with that, in the sense of association"). Alternatively, it may be interpreted as "possessing wonders."

The compound is formed with the word *saha* as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). "For the sake of music" (*saṅgītāya*) means for the sake of the triple symphony (*tauryatrika*). "With beaten drums" (*prahatamurajāḥ*) means with struck clay drums (*mṛdaṅga*).
According to the *Śabdārṇava*, the word *muraja* may refer to a *mṛdaṅga*, a *ḍhakkā*, or even a *muraja*.

Those [palaces] on the earth which consist of jewels—that is, are made of jewel-products—are "cloud-licking" (*abhraṃliha*), meaning they reach up to the clouds. The suffix *khaś* is applied according to the rule *vahābhre lihaḥ*; the augment *mum* is added by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*.
Those whose tops are peaks are so described; the meaning is "extremely lofty.
Prāsādas are temples for the gods; as Amarasimha states: "Prāsāda refers to the dwellings of gods and kings."

"Vidyudvantam" means possessing lightning; "sendracāpam" means possessing Indra’s bow (the rainbow); "snigdhaḥ śrāvyaḥ gambhīraḥ ghoṣaḥ garjitam yasya tam" means that from which there is a smooth, resonant, and deep roar;
"antaḥ antargatam toyam yasya tam" means that within which water is contained; and "tuṅgam unnatam tvām taiḥ taiḥ" refers to You, who are lofty and exalted by those various [qualities].
They are "alaṃ" (capable/sufficient) to "tulayituṃ" (weigh/compare), that is, to equalize, by means of "viśeṣaiḥ" (distinctions), namely the qualities such as playful womanhood and so forth.
According to Amara, "alam" denotes ornament, sufficiency, ability, and prohibition.

Here, because the attributes of the cloud and the palace— which serve as the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya)— such as lightning and the woman, are mutually similar according to their respective order,
the similarity between the cloud and the palace is established. This [simile] exists by way of the relationship between the original image (bimba) and its reflection (pratibimba).

The *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile). Due to the mutual resemblance between two things that are distinct in reality, yet appear non-distinct as the attributes of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), there exists the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*). [Example:
"In her hand, a play-lotus; in her hair, young *kunda* flowers intertwined..."
Where the beauty of the women's faces was turned pale by the pollen of *rodhra* blossoms;
where fresh *kuravaka* flowers were placed in their braided hair, lovely *śirīṣa* in their ears, and *nīpa* flowers— born of your arrival— at the parting of their hair.
Su;
curly locks Da,Ma; °creator Da; *lodhra*° Da,Ma; on the face Śrī Da,Ma; *kurabaka* Ma;
And where this collection of six seasons serves as the refined ornament for women—what does he say? "What? What? [he asks].
In her hand she holds a play-lotus, a graceful lotus;
her locks of hair are interwoven with young jasmine blossoms;
and even the beauty of her face has attained a pale whiteness through the pollen of the *rodhra* flower.
She has been brought [to this state]: a fresh, juicy *kuravaka* flower at her tresses;
a lovely *śirīṣa* flower at her ears;
and at her parting, a *nīpa* flower born of the rainy season through your arrival—for that indeed...
It blooms during the rainy season; thus, by this very rejection of golden ornaments, the urbanity of the women is expressed. || 65 ||
"The hand is turned to the right."

By this verse, it is stated that in Alakā, the six seasons— autumn, winter, the cool season, spring, summer, and the rainy season— occur simultaneously, as evidenced by their respective, unique, and characteristic flowers.
For example, in the phrase "a play-lotus in the hand," the proximity of the autumn season is expressed by means of the lotus, which is a characteristic mark of autumn.
Furthermore, the reading "tresses interwoven with young *kunda* flowers" (*alakam bālakundānuviddham*) is a corruption; for the word *alaka*— [The remainder of the sentence would follow here.]
Because of its masculine gender. According to Amara, *alakāḥ* means "curly locks of hair.
There is a variant reading: *alake bālakundānuvedhaḥ*. In this reading, there is no violation of the poetic style (*rīti*).
By means of the *kunda* flower, the proximity of the winter season is indicated.

An objection is raised: "In the verse 'nanu niṣiñcan mādhavīvṛttiṃ kundaśeṣaṃ ca vardhayan,' the kunda flower is perceived as a characteristic (liṅga) of the cold season (śiśira), which precedes spring;
how then can it be said to be a characteristic of winter (hemanta)? It is replied: [This is because] of the connection between winter and the cold season...

The *liṅga* for both is the *kunda* flower; the distinction is that it appears in the *hemanta* season and reaches full maturity in the *śiśira* season. For this very reason, the word "young" (*bāla*) is employed in the expression "pierced by young *kunda* flowers" (*bālakundānuvedha*).
The reading "śrīḥ" (glory) ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) is as follows: "The beauty on her face has been led to paleness by the pollen of the *lodhra* flower.
This means that the luster on her face has been rendered pale by the pollen of the *lodhra* flower.
Indeed, the *lodhra* blossom is a sign of the cold season. Thus, it is stated in the *Māghakāvya*: [text omitted].

In the description of the cool season: "The mass of *lodhra* pollen, which desires to conquer the worlds like the God of Love... and so forth (6.64). "In the *cūḍāpāśa*"—that is, in the mass of hair on the crest; *śikhā* means the tuft of hair.
According to Amara, *cūḍā* means "a mass of hair. Indeed, the new *kuravaka* flower is a sign of spring;
as it has been said:
"The *kuravaka* is as pale-red as a woman's fingernail."

A beautiful *śirīṣa* flower [was placed] on her ear, for the *śirīṣa* is indeed the emblem of summer. And it has been said: "The *śirīṣa* flower, though its filaments were mostly bitten off upon the cheek marked by moist nail-scratches drenched in perspiration, did not suddenly fall even from the ear of the passionate women."
Thus [ends verse 12.48]. By the phrase "born from your arrival," it is understood that the *nīpa* tree is a characteristic sign of the rainy season.
Regarding the word *vadhū*: it refers to women; according to Amara, *vadhū* means both a wife and a daughter-in-law.
In the phrase "where the *nīpa* tree arises from your arrival," the connection with the cloud has been stated. [Now,
Mallinātha] says "hasta" etc., to describe the abundance of all seasons at all times.

In that city of Alakā, there is a play-lotus (*līlākamala*) in the hands of the young women for the sake of sport; this is a characteristic sign of autumn, as it is said: "Autumn is characterized by lotuses. [The word] *alake* refers to the hair; it is used in the singular to denote the class (*jātāvekavacana*). [Thus, it means] "in the locks of hair" (*alakeṣu*).

This is the meaning. "Anuviddha" means interwoven with fresh spring flowers (*bālakunda*). *Anuvedha* signifies the act of stringing together; here the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter sense of an abstract state.
Although the *kunda* flower is cool in nature, according to the lexicon which states "the *kunda* is of the spring season," nevertheless—

The qualification "young girl" (*bālā*) is intended to convey that she possesses the nature of winter through the distinction of stages—namely, her manifestation in late autumn and her full maturity in early winter. If the reading were *alakaṃ* (with the accusative case ending), there would be a break in the sequence of the locative case. Nātha, however, [states...]
"That is true; however, there is another fault: the loss of its fixed masculine gender. [The opponent replies:
"Their eyebrows are naturally curved. [The author asks: "From what source?"

Because neuter gender is observed in such expressions as "the other earrings have been shaken off," "the chest has been torn open," and "the entire lower lip has been bitten," [the word *ānanam*] refers to the face (*mukhe*), [describing it as covered] with the blossoms of the *lodhra* tree— namely, the flowers of the *lodhra* that bloom in the cool season (*śaiśirāṇām*).

By the pollen of the *rajas* (dust); "procreation" (*prasava*) refers to the fruit or flower of trees, as the *Viśva* lexicon states it is the release of the embryo. "The splendor" (*śrī*)—meaning beauty—has been reduced to paleness.
In the "tress of the crest" (*cūḍāpāśe*), that is, in the mass of hair; the "fresh *kurabaka*" is a particular kind of spring flower.
A beautiful and delicate *śirīṣa* flower—a specific blossom of the summer season—is [placed] at your ear;

[it is placed] upon the parting of your hair (*sīmanta*), that line of hair on the crown of the head. As the *Śabdārṇava* states: "The word *sīmanta*, which is not feminine, refers to the line of hair on the crown of the head. Your approach [to me]...
The meaning is "the arrival of clouds. That which is born therein is "born from your arrival"; the meaning is "pertaining to the rainy season" (*vārṣika*).
"Nīpa" refers to the *kadamba* flower. The word "exists" (*asti*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis after every [term]. The verb "to be" (*asti*) [is understood].

Since the first-person verb ending *bhavanti* is employed [here], it follows by logical rule that the sense "there exists" (*asti*) is implied. Thus, by the expression of the collection of various effects such as the lotus and the kunda flower, the collection of all seasons is established by implication; for an effect cannot exist without its cause.
The sense is that [the reason] is unestablished (asiddhi).
|| 2 || -65- Where the trees are always in bloom and resonant with intoxicated bees, and where the lotus-pools always possess lotuses, their girdles formed by rows of swans;
The palace peacocks are ever-thrilled with longing, their plumage perpetually radiant; the nights are eternally moonlit, delightful as darkness is dispelled. (65a) [3 Ma;
77 Su]
declared *prakṣipta* (interpolated) by Ma;
[as stated by] Mallinātha: "yatreti" ||

In that city of Alakā, the trees have flowers that are eternal; the sense is that this is not due to the constraints of specific seasons. For this very reason, they are resonant with the humming of intoxicated bees.

The *nalinyas* are lotus-pools; those whose lotuses are eternal are so described. The meaning is that they are not devoid of [lotuses] even in winter. For this very reason, they have their girdles formed by rows of swans; the meaning is that they are constantly surrounded by swans.

They are the sporting peacocks of the palace-trees, whose plumage is ever radiant; they are so described because [their beauty] does not exist only during the rainy season. For this very reason, they have their necks outstretched in longing due to their cries (*kekā*).
Those [nights] whose nights are perpetually characterized by moonlight are "pradoṣā rātryo nityā jyotsnā yeṣām. They do not [occur] only during the bright fortnight.
For this very reason, they are described as "ramyāḥ" (delightful), being those in whom the activity—that is, the pervasion—of darkness has been obstructed. || 3 || -65a-
Where tears arise from joy and not from other causes; where there is no heat other than that produced by the flower-arrowed god [Kāma] which is to be remedied by union with the beloved;
nor is there the occurrence of separation from any other cause than a lover’s quarrel. Oṃ. Va, Da.
Indeed, for the lords of wealth, there is truly no age other than youth.
Mallinātha says: "Ānanda... [etc.]
In that city of Alakā, belonging to the lords of wealth—the Yakṣas—Kubera is the sovereign lord of wealth;

for the *Śabdārṇava* states, "The term *vittādhipa* applies to Kubera, as well as to a wealthy man and a Yakṣa. The tears arising from joy are produced solely by joy, and not by other causes such as grief and the like.

The meaning is that [the fever] is to be warded off from the undesirable by means of union with the beloved, but not from that which is incurable; for there is no other heat born of the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) than that arising from love-quarrels, and there is no occurrence of separation caused by any reason other than this.
Nor is there even the attainment of separation.
Furthermore, there is no age other than youth, namely old age.
These two verses are interpolations. (4) -65b-
In that city, the Yakṣas, accompanied by their most excellent women, resort to palace terraces made of white jewels, which are adorned with the floral patterns of reflected stars;
there they enjoy the honey produced by the Kalpa-trees, which has pleasure as its fruit.
When your deep-sounding drums were slowly struck upon their skins.
Vallabha:

In that city of Āmalakā, the lords of the Guhyakas, accompanied by their excellent wives, constantly come to the terraces of their palaces and enjoy the honey produced by the wish-fulfilling trees— the fruit of which is pleasure, and not the generation of quarrels and the like.

What kind of places are they? They are made of white jewels and crystal; for this very reason, the shadows of the stars—the reflections of the rows of constellations—are themselves the floral arrangements, the clusters of blossoms, within them.
When do they serve [you]? At times when their resonance is as deep and resonant as yours.
When those lotuses, serving as the mouths of musical instruments, were struck and sounded—
by this, the constant state of happiness of the couples is expressed. (66) [Śanakaiḥ] (Gradually) [Dakṣiṇāvarta].
"In which" means: [in that which].
The "white jewel" is a crystal gem (*sphaṭikamaṇi*). One should understand that due to the translucence of crystal gems, an excellence of reflection occurs during the nights.
"They attend" means they serve with devotion.
By this resonance of your deep sound, a connection with the clouds is expressed.

"Puṣkaras" refers to the mouths of musical instruments. Bhaṭṭa Halāyudha has stated that the word *puṣkara* is designated for eight things: the tip of an elephant's trunk, a lotus, the blade of a sword, the sky, the mouth of a musical instrument, water, and a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*). "In the struck" means while they are being played. (3)
Mallinātha says:
"In which... (yasyām iti).

In that city of Āmalakā, there dwell Yakṣas— a particular class of divine beings— who are accompanied by excellent women and move in the company of graceful ladies; they possess [palaces] made of white gems, crystal,
or moonstone, and for this very reason, they bear the reflections of the luminous stars.

The flowers are merely reflections, and by them [the place] is fashioned and adorned. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "light" (*jyotis*) refers to the stars, fire, the moon, sight, a son, wealth, and sacrifice. By this, the unfading splendor of the drinking hall is expressed.

Having reached the palace grounds, they arrived at those *puṣkaras*—the mouths of musical instruments—which possess a resonance like your own deep sound; for *puṣkara* refers to the tip of an elephant’s trunk, the mouth of a sounding vessel, or water (Amara). [Regarding "karihastāgre"?]
When the surfaces of the musical instruments are struck slowly and gently; and this is also the characteristic of dance and song. [It is] produced from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).

Because it bestows the desired object, honey (*madhu*) is also produced there. That which has pleasure as its fruit is called "pleasure-fruit" (*ratiphalā*); they partake of—that is, drink—that honey-wine.
[It is made] from *tāla*, milk, sugar, *amṛtā*, pure jaggery, *unmatta*, *asthi*, *kāla*, *dāru*, *indradruma*, *morata*, sugarcane, *kadali*, and the flowers of *gulgulu*.

Thus, honey— accumulated by the grace of spring flowers, gathered at the roots of flowering trees, an aphrodisiac for the god of love, known as the fruit of passion, sweet and cool— is like nectar in the ocean of wine. (5) — 66—
Fanned by breezes cooled by the waters of the Mandākinī,
with their heat dispelled by the shade of mandāra trees growing along its banks,
they were refreshed as if by handfuls of golden sand hidden beneath the waves that must be sought out.
There, maidens sought after by the immortals sport with jewels.
"O Mallinātha, [regarding] the Mandākinī..."

In that Alakā, beautiful yakṣa maidens—meaning young women sought after by the immortals—[dwell]. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, the word *kanyā* refers to a maiden (*kumārikā*) or a noble woman (*nārī*).
[They are cooled] by the waters of the Mandākinī, the Gaṅgā, and by breezes cool with coldness.

Being served by the *satyas* (truths), they were likewise cooled from the heat by the shade—meaning the absence of sunlight—of those *manda-āra* trees, which grow along the slopes (*anu-taṭa*) and thus are called *anutaṭaruha*; [the suffix] *kvip* is used here. Their heat was dispelled by the shade of those *manda-āra* trees.

They truly play with jewels that are hidden by being buried in handfuls of golden sand—precious stones that must therefore be sought out and discovered. This is done through a regional game known as "the Hidden Jewels. Truly.
The meaning is "they play.
The middle voice (ātmanepada) is used according to the rule *krīḍo 'nusamparibhyaśca*.
[They play] with hidden objects such as jewels and the like, which are to be seen within the sand and so forth.
That which is performed by young maidens is known by the name Guptamaṇi.
Rāsakrīḍā is Gūḍhamaṇi, while Guptakeli is Lāyana.
Picchakanduka, Daṇḍādyaiḥ, and others are recorded as the regional games (daiśikakelayaḥ). Thus it is said.
In the Śabdārṇava (6.66a):
Where [there are] nets of threads suspended for women who, having been revived by the embrace of their beloveds' arms, [are resting] from the exhaustion of their limbs born of sexual union.
And now, moistened by the moonbeams that have become clear with the departure of your imprisonment,
the moonstones shed streams of clear water as they dissolve away.
In that city, at midnight, the exhaustion of the limbs produced by sexual union of longing women was dispelled by the rays of the moon as they were embraced and caressed by their arms.
Moonstones absorb and pacify [the heat].
Of what kind [of women]? Of those who have been revived by the embrace of their beloved’s arms—those oppressed by the binding of their husbands’ arms.

Of what nature are the moonstones? They are "suspended in webs of threads" (tantujālāvalambāḥ), meaning they hang within networks of fibers. Likewise, by the rays of the moon—the lunar beams—which have become clear through the removal of your obstruction, that is, purified by the cessation of your veiling.

They were massaged and rubbed; for that very reason, they were dripping with clear drops of water, shedding manifest droplets of moisture; and thus, they removed the exhaustion from the limbs. || 67 ||
"Where there is a clockwise whorl..."

"Ucchvāsita" means those who have been made to breathe again due to the forceful embrace by the arms of their beloveds; that is to say, those who were tightly embraced by the arms of their beloveds. "Hanging from webs of threads" [is said] for the purpose of warding off the falling of frost and water.
"Tantujālāvalambāḥ" refers to those hanging from the network of threads that serve as the place for pearl necklaces suspended from the canopy (vitāna) tied above; or alternatively,
it refers to the net-like covering made of thread (tantujāla) spread over the upper surfaces of the palaces to protect against frogs and other such creatures.

It is well known that they spread out a net to prevent descent; here, what is intended is a web of threads constructed from moonstone gems. By this, the connection with the clouds is expressed through their becoming clear upon the cessation of your obstruction.

"They plunder" means they carry away. The grammatical connection is: "those which, by the rays of the moon, drip with clear drops of water"—these are the *candrakāntas*, that is, moonstones (*candrakāntamaṇi*). — Mallinātha, verse 67.
"Wherein," etc.

In Alakā, at the hour of *niśītha*—that is, at midnight (*ardharātra*)—according to Amara’s lexicon which states that both *ardharātra* and *niśītha* denote the same time; by means of the moonbeams, which are clear and stainless due to the removal of your obstruction, namely the cloud-cover; "pādāḥ" refers to rays.
"Raśmi means a fourth part of a foot," according to Amara.
"Dripping clear drops of water" means shedding copious droplets of water;
"suspended from a network of threads" means supported by a mass of threads hanging from a canopy.

The meaning is that they are strung together with its [the moon's] qualities. "Moon-loved" refers to moonstones (*candrakānta-maṇi*) whose embraces by their beloveds' arms have become loosened due to exhaustion—either from sighing or for the purpose of sprinkling water. [This occurs] during embraces by the arms.

"Ucchvāsitānām" means those who have been relaxed or loosened; that is to say, those whose embraces have been slackened due to exhaustion or for the sake of sprinkling water—this is the reading. "Strīṇām" refers to the languor produced by sexual union, the fatigue of the body, or the weariness of the limbs.
This means: they plunder, that is, they carry away. [The phrase "iti yāvat" is provided by the editor in brackets; it serves as a gloss for both readings.]

There, in the grove known as Vaibhrāja, accompanied by the foremost courtesans of the celestial damsels and by Kinnaras with melodious throats who daily sing aloud the fame of the Lord of Wealth, there are inexhaustible treasures within the dwellings. Oṃ. Va, Da.
Engaging in conversation, lovers enter the outer garden.
After II.6, "yatra strīṇām," Mallinātha comments:
"akṣayyeti."

In that city of Alakā: "kṣayya" means capable of being destroyed; this is a nipātana (irregular formation) according to the rule "kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe. Then follows a negative compound (nañ-samāsa).
"Antarbhavana" means within the houses; it is an indeclinable according to the rule beginning with "avyayaṃ vibhakti... and so forth.

*Avyayībhāva*: Those for whom inexhaustible treasures (*akṣayya*) exist within their dwellings are described as such. This qualification is intended to suggest the possibility of enjoying whatever they desire. *Vibudhavanitāḥ* refers to the celestial nymphs (*apsarases*); they themselves are the *vāramukhyāḥ*, that is, the courtesans.

Those who have such companions are described as such. According to Amara, "vārastrī," "gaṇikā," "veśyā," and "rūpājīvā" are synonyms for a courtesan; furthermore, she who is honored is called a "vāramukhyā. Daily, the lovers—those possessed by desire—engage in conversation with her, their discourse being well-received.

Day after day; [this is] a compound formed by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* etc. By those possessing voices that were red and sweet—meaning those with beautiful vocal tones—they sang out the fame of Dhanapati, the glory of Kubera.
"By those whose habit is to sing loudly" means by those singing at a high pitch, because the *gāndhāra* scale (*grāma*) used for divine song is characterized by high notes.
"Together with the *kinnaras*" means in their company. "Vaibhrāja" is the name [of the city] belonging to Vibhrāja.
That [garden] is called Vaibhrāja; for it is stated in the *Śambhurahasya*: "It is called Vaibhrāja because it was protected by Vibhrāja, the lord of the Gaṇas. This is another name for Caitraratha.
They enjoy—that is, they experience—the outer grove, the external garden. 10. —67a—
I do not think it is Mallinātha; for the gods, led by Indra, having brought their aerial chariots to the upper floors [of the palace],
instantly produced a blemish upon the paintings with fresh drops of water.
Where clouds like you, as if touched by apprehension,
emerge through the lattices, shattered and skillfully imitating the emission of smoke. (68)
The fault of water droplets (salilakaṇikādoṣa), according to Da and Ma; the fault of one's own water droplets (svajalakaṇikādoṣa), according to Su;

"Thinking thus," according to Mallinātha.

The word *uttareṇa* ends in the suffix *enap* (Pāṇini 5.3.35). In connection with that, the word *gṛhān* takes the second case by the rule *enapā dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.31). A reading ending in the fifth case, however, is meaningless. 72.

The suffix *enaP* [is applied after a word ending in *a*] to form an adverbial instrument (avyayībhāva) [according to Pāṇini 5.3.35]. By the rule "with *enaP*, the second case" (Pāṇini 2.3.31), the second case ending is used.

"A son made by artifice" means an adopted son (*kṛtrimaputraka*). "A young coral tree" means a young wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*). [This is expressed] by the phrase "by the archway, beautiful with your divine bow."

what kind of tresses? Harsh and dry from being merely sprinkled with water after a pure bath.
For if she ever bathes for the sake of auspiciousness,
she does so with mere water, devoid of fragrant oils, *āmalaka* fruits, and the like.
"Hanging down to the cheeks" (*āgaṇḍalambam*) means fallen upon the cheeks.

Thus, that very night which was spent like a mere moment with me in amorous dalliances according to our desire, she now passes as if it were a month, weeping with hot tears upon her bed of separation. || 88 ||
"By the exhalation turning to the right."
"Vikṣipantīm" means moving or shaking.

The space [of her throat] was blocked by the pressure of tears from her eyes, and the opportunity for sleep was obstructed by a flood of weeping.
"By Mallinātha’s sigh," [it is said].

From bathing with pure water—meaning bathing devoid of oil and such—the hair on her cheeks became rough, that is, hard to the touch, and indeed hung down as far as the temples; this is a compound according to the rule *sup supā*.
"Alakam" refers to the curled locks of hair; the singular number is used here to denote the class.

By that which is so described—meaning by the heat, which "torments" (kliśayati) or "afflicts" (kliśnāti)—the lower lip-sprout; [this is formed] with the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action, from either the causative root *kliś* or the non-causative root *kliś*. She is one who "scatters" or "moves" [it] with her sighs.

Likewise, "even one born of a dream" means even that which is produced in the state of dreaming; the sense is that direct physical union is impossible. [The question is: "How might my union come about?"—that is, by what manner or means would it arrive? The word "excessively" (*atyāśayena*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the thought. Thus.

The Alaṅkārikas maintain that there is no failure to employ a word because its meaning has already been stated, nor is there tautology when it is employed; here, the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*). [She was] one whose space was obstructed by the pressure of tears from the flow of water from her eyes.

"Of those who have been overcome" means that sleep is difficult to obtain. The sense is that she longs for it because of her affection and devotion. Here, by the shedding of tears, the abandonment of shame is suggested. || 32 || -88-

Covering with her eyes— laden with tears and heavy lashes— the rays of the moon, cool as nectar, which had entered through the lattice-windows and turned back just as they had come out of former affection, she was overcome by exhaustion.

formerly Su; even then Da; from distress Su; with tears Da?, Ma, Su;

With her eyelashes and body hairs heavy with tears and difficult to bear, she was covering and shielding her eyes out of distress.
Of what sort? Like the rays of the moon—cool as nectar—which, having entered through the window, first went out toward him with affection and spread before him;
then, because they caused distress due to his separation from me, returned back in that very same way. Just so.
The meaning is that she had gone away in haste and returned in exactly the same manner;
therefore, because her eyes were closed, she was neither awake nor asleep—
due to the closing of the eyes there was an absence of waking, and due to the absence of sleep she was devoid of slumber.
And for this reason, the simile "like a land-lotus on a cloudy day" is employed; for that [lotus], due to the presence of clouds, is not blossomed, yet due to the power of the day, it is not asleep.
In these three sentences, the verb is the same as in the preceding one.
"With feet curling to the right."
"By former affection" means by the love of previous times. "Even though it had gone to the rays of the moon" means even though it had reached them.
The reading is "tataḥ sannivṛttaṃ tathaiva," meaning "returned from there [from the rays of the moon] in the same manner."

The meaning is that her eye, having turned back of its own accord— having turned away out of exhaustion from the suffering of separation— went toward the moonbeams due to affection from former times, and then returned the way it came because of the distress of separation from them.
With eyelashes— meaning the hairs of the eyes—
as on a cloudy day, a day overcast with clouds;
she was neither fully awake nor asleep, like a land-lotus touched by the rays of the sun.
She blooms when untouched by rays veiled by clouds, and she closes her eyes. —89— [Commentary:
"The feet of Mallinātha," etc.

The sense is that, by the thought that the moonbeams— cool as nectar, entering through the lattice-work and passing through the openings of the windows— will, as before, be a source of joy due to former affection, that is, former love.
Just as they had gone forward, so did they return; just as they had gone, so did they turn back. This is because, at that time, [the sight] was exceedingly difficult for them to bear.
[They cast] their gaze with eyes heavy with tears, burdened by water due to exhaustion.
Covering [her face] with her eyelashes;

for this very reason, on a cloudy, overcast day, she was neither awakened—meaning not blossomed due to the covering of clouds—nor asleep, but rather half-closed like a bud. This applies to both cases.

The compound *nañarthasya naśabdasya* is formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. "Standing like a lotus on dry land"—by this, the sixth stage, known as aversion toward sense objects (*viṣayadveṣa*), is indicated. (31) —89—
Then, by the rule *tatpuruṣaḥ samānādhikaraṇaḥ karmadhārayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.42),
I know that your heart holds affection for me; therefore, I infer her to be in such a state during this first separation.
It is not out of a sense of self-importance that I make you speak so much;
for everything that I have said, O brother, will soon be evident to you in its entirety.

"How did you perceive her to be in such an unwell state? he asked.
Because her heart has long been filled with affection for me and she is full of great love,
I therefore conjecture— that is, I imagine— that she has reached such a state as this due to our separation from the very beginning.

Nor is it appropriate to say that she has no affection for you at all; thus he says: "One who considers himself fortunate is called *subhagammanya*; the state of being such does not make me loquacious—that is, one who speaks whatever comes to mind. Therefore, as for what is yours..."
I have told you all of this; it will soon become manifest to you.
The meaning is that you will certainly see such a person within two or three days. 90.
"O brother!
O right-turning conch!
I do not know what the reason is for her having fallen into such a distressed state in your absence."
Anticipating this objection, he says: "knowing."

Thinking that you might have said this out of a sense of good fortune regarding such a previously described state of suffering, he says, "me, who am talkative. This refers to the state of considering oneself fortunate (*subhagammanyabhāva*), derived from the verbal root *man* with the word *subhaga* as its prefix.

By the rule *ātma-māne khaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.83), the suffix *khaś* is applied; by *arur-dviṣad-aja-antasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67), the augment *mum* is added after a word ending in *aja*, as in *subhaga-manyah*. The state of that is *subhaga-manyatā-bhāvaḥ*.
"All this has been said by me to you directly; all of this shall belong to you before long."
The meaning is that it will become directly perceptible. —90— Mallinātha:
But how was it determined by you that she had fallen into such a state? Therefore...
He said,
"I know."

O Cloud, I know that your friend’s heart is filled with affection for me and has accumulated deep passion for me. For this reason— namely, the knowledge of her affection— during our first separation (the word "first" is used to highlight the intensity of her suffering), [protect] that friend of yours.
I consider her to have reached this aforementioned state.

Indeed, it is the very nature of those who fancy themselves handsome that they manifest their passion for women toward themselves; regarding this, he says "vācālam" (talkative). [He considers himself] handsome.

"One who thinks himself fortunate" is *subhagammanyaḥ*. The suffix *khaś* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.83 (*ātma-māne khaś ca*). The augment *mum* is added according to Pāṇini 6.3.67 (*arur-dviṣad-ajantasya mum*). Its state is "the state of thinking oneself fortunate," that is, self-conceit. [He says this] to me, who am talkative and a much-speaker.
He indeed does not do it; the meaning is that he, being proud of his beauty, does not manifest it.
According to Amara, *jalpāka*, *vācāla*, and *vācāṭa* mean one who speaks much or whose speech is highly censurable.
The suffix *ālac* is applied to form *ālajāṭacau* in the sense of "one who speaks much. However, O brother!
That which I said, beginning with "that which is emaciated," all of it—
this is the ellipsis— will before long, that is, very quickly, become manifest to your direct perception.
That frail woman, having cast off her ornaments and wearing her body— repeatedly pained by grief— resting upon your lap on the couch,
will surely cause even you to shed tears consisting of fresh water.
Generally, everyone becomes one whose conduct is compassionate and whose inner self is moist with pity.
The *sābalā* creeper, possessing a slender body like this one, will surely cause you— who are insentient— to shed your flow of fresh water.
Of what nature was her body? It was delicate, emaciated, and tender;
for that very reason, she had cast off her ornaments and abandoned all decoration. Furthermore, although she was lying upon the surface of her bed, she bore herself with extreme suffering.
He says: "If she is of such a nature, why do I weep?
Because whoever has a moist inner self—that is, a tender heart—is for the most part characterized by compassion and disposed toward pity; and you, because of your being full of water...
"Ārdrāntaraḥ" means one whose internal state is moist with compassion. "Karuṇāvṛttiḥ" refers to one whose activity or function (*vṛtti*) is compassion itself (*karuṇā*).

Since the word *karuṇā*—which has the meaning of pity (*kṛpā*)—is not considered to have been previously used as a masculine term (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), [the rule for optional neuter gender does not apply].
There is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). In the phrase *duḥkhaduḥkhena*, the repetition [of the word] indicates intensity.
Since the root *muc* (to release), like the root *duh* (to milk), takes two objects, the construction is "he will cause you to be released from the sword" (*tvām asram mocayiṣyati*).
91 || Repeatedly,

Seeing her so distressed— having laid aside her ornaments and being forever deprived of them, and seeing that even you, though delicate and soft, will surely shed tears consisting of fresh water— you too will inevitably release your tears.
The meaning is as follows: "one whose mental state is compassion" means one whose internal disposition consists of compassion.
"One with a moist inner self" intends to express that the cloud's inner self is moistened by water. || 26 ||
Mallinātha says: "That."
The woman, weak and frail, having laid aside her ornaments because of her emaciation— having abandoned her jewelry—

[suffers] repeatedly, many times, with a sorrow that is sorrow upon sorrow (the reduplication occurs according to the rule *prakāre guṇavacanasya*). [She gazes at] the delicate [child] placed upon the lap of the bed.
Bearing and carrying a delicate body— by this, her state of extreme exhaustion and fainting is indicated—
that friend of yours [pours] even upon you tears consisting of fresh water, that is, tears in the form of new rainwater.

"He will certainly liberate [him] in every way. Regarding the roots beginning with *pac* (the second class), there is an extension of the rule for two objects (*dvikarma*); since *muc* belongs to the *pac*-class, it takes two objects.
Thus, "generally" (*prāyaḥ*) means that his inner self is moist, that is, he is soft-hearted; however, the cloud—

His body is liquid within; he is one whose internal mental state consists entirely of compassion, for he is indeed characterized by a compassionate disposition. At this moment, you must go quickly by all means to avoid the immediate calamity that follows.
Such is the intended meaning of the context.
Now, one might ask: why has the venerable poet here disregarded the initial stage of "delight of the eyes" (*cakṣuḥprīti*) and honored only the subsequent stages? It is said in reply:
The erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is said to be twofold: union (sambhoga) and separation (vipralambha).
Union occurs when the two are joined; separation occurs when they are apart.

In this context, *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) is fourfold, consisting of love born of prior attachment (*pūrvānurāga*), jealousy (*māna*), separation (*pravāsa*), and sorrow (*karuṇa*); among these, separation is further divided into three types.
In this poem, however, the [love] born of a curse arises from necessity, agitation, and a curse;
it occurs when there is prior affection between two youths who were previously unacquainted.
The ten stages, beginning with visual delight (*cakṣuḥprīti*), are as follows in their sequence:
sight, attachment of the mind, mental resolve, wakefulness, emaciation, and passion (*rati*).
Shame, longing, loss of appetite, intoxication, and fainting—these are the ten stages of love (anaṅgadaśā);
they occur specifically when two people who were previously acquainted are separated by travel.
In that case, a visual delight such as one never experienced before cannot arise;
rather, it is the non-interruption of that already established attachment which is increased here.
Otherwise, it must be stated as before; for such a conclusion being established, the first [alternative] is abandoned due to its futility, and likewise the last due to its lack of aesthetic appeal.

The established position here is that the poet has described eight [types of love], beginning with "union at the heart" (hṛtsaṅga). In this verse, "painting my likeness," it is set forth that "delight of the eyes" (cakṣuḥprīti) is that which leaves the face speechless with wonder.
Visual delight arises from seeing forms never before seen,
as in the case of one beholding the form of Mālavikā while Agnimitra is away;
and for husbands living abroad, it consists in seeing what was previously unseen.
Now, if there is still doubt even in that regard, let him ask his own wives:
"Is there recognition of their husbands, or is there only a sense of them being foreigners?"
"When he has returned from his journey, enough with these futile quarrels! (33)
With the movement of its outer corners obstructed by tears and devoid of the luster of collyrium, and having forgotten the play of its eyebrows due to its aversion even to honey,
I suspect that the deer-eyed girl’s eye is twitching upward as you draw near.
"It shall attain a beauty comparable to a blue lotus agitated by the movement of fish. (92) [Note on variants: *mīnakṣobhākulakuvalayaśrītulāmeṣyatīti* (Da);
*vāmam* (Da); *manye mīnoccala°* (Da); *mīnakṣobhāccala°* (Ma, Su).
When he stands nearby, the eye of that deer-eyed woman,
by its upward throbbing, will attain a resemblance to the beauty of a restless blue lotus that has blossomed without blinking.
"I suspect," that is, "I imagine"—this is an auspicious omen;
for the throbbing of the left eye in women announces approaching joy. Of what sort was her eye? Its outward movement toward the corner [of the eye] was obstructed by long, hanging locks of hair.

Her casting of side-long glances had ceased; due to grief, she was devoid of the application of collyrium; likewise, because of her abstinence from wine, the playful movement of her eyebrows had faltered. 92.

"Whose flow toward the outer corner of the eye is obstructed by its turning to the right"— *apāṅga* means the outer corner of the eye; "devoid of the gloss of collyrium"— *añjana-sneha-śūnya* refers to the lack of oily luster produced by collyrium.
It is devoid of the oiliness of collyrium;
that is to say, because of its rejection, its dismissal, and its prohibition. According to Amara, *pratyādeśa* means *nirākṛti* (rejection).
It is so called because of the prohibition of honey, that is, the drinking of honey.
The meaning is that the play of her eyebrows has been forgotten.
Now, one might object: the play of the eyebrows occurs naturally to playful women; as it has been said:
"The beauty of the two long lines of her eyebrows was such that it seemed as if they had been fashioned with a rod of collyrium."
Beholding her, who was so skillful in amorous play, the God of Love abandoned his pride in the beauty of his own bow.
Thus [it is asked]: "How is it stated here that the play of the eyebrows is dependent upon the drinking of wine? True.

Here, the poet's intention is that although the play of the eyebrows is established by nature, it is not manifested due to the absence of the drinking of wine, which serves as its excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).
For this very reason, the word "forgotten" (*vismṛta*) is employed in the phrase "having forgotten the play of her eyebrows.

He says that by the sight of you, there will be an omen for her in the form of a throbbing of her left eye, which indicates well-being; [this occurs] when you are near—that is, when you have arrived in close proximity.
"The throbbing of the left eye of the deer-eyed woman, I think, will attain a beauty comparable to a blue lotus tossed by a fish"— this is the reading.
In the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*, it is stated that this throbbing of the left eye of women is an omen of good fortune.
Her beautiful left eye was revealed, with its curved rows of lashes and its large black pupil surrounded by white.
"One of the fawn-eyed maiden's eyes throbbed, slightly reddened like a lotus struck by a fish. (28) —
Mallinātha.
He obstructs.
That whose expansion at the outer corners of the eyes is obstructed by the curls of hair is described as such;
it is devoid of moisture from collyrium, meaning it is free from glossy collyrium.
Furthermore, because of the rejection—that is, the renunciation—of honey, which here refers to wine.
The meaning is "due to abandonment. According to Amara, *pratyādeśa* means "rejection" or "refusal.

That [face] by which the play of the eyebrows—the knitting of the brows—has been forgotten; the sense is that the blocking of the outward flow of the eyes' outer corners (*apāṅga*) and so forth has arisen from separation (*viraha*).
"When you are near"—the ellipsis being "announcing news of one's own welfare.
It is "uparispandi" because it throbs or vibrates in the upper part; and so it is said in the *Nimittanidāna*:
"From a throbbing at the crown of the head, one should predict the acquisition of an umbrella; at the forehead, a silken turban;
above the eyes, the attainment of a desired object; and at the outer corner of the eye, loss.
Thus [it is said]. The eye of your deer-eyed friend—[the word] "left" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
For women, the left side is superior, whereas for men, the right side is best;
this is because, in the acts of giving, worshiping the gods and others, moving, and adorning oneself, the left side of women is considered more auspicious.

I suspect— that is, I reason— that it will attain a likeness, a similarity, with the beauty of a trembling blue lotus [caused] by the agitation and movement of fish. 35 || 92 || Or else, her left hand, being released from my nail-marks, [will become like that].

By the turn of fate, my thigh—long accustomed to a network of pearls and worthy of being massaged by my hands at the end of our lovemaking—pale as the trunk of a fresh plantain tree, shall now be made to tremble. 93.29 (Da; 36)
