When you are near, her left thigh will experience a state of trembling and throbbing;
the word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative in relation to the twitching of the eyes. Of what nature is it? It is being avoided by my nail-marks.

That pearl necklace, which he had worn constantly and had been accustomed to, was discarded due to a lapse in ritual propriety and neglected; for its use there was intended only for the sake of cooling him.
Likewise, at the conclusion of our lovemaking, it was fit to be pressed by my hand.
He is fair and white, like the trunk of a freshly harvested plantain tree. || 93 ||
The right-turning is the left.
By the marks of fingernails (*kararuha-pada*) means by nail-marks.
"Muktājāla" refers to the pearl-ornament of women, a waist-ornament made of pearls; it is called *muktājāla*. Kautilya, in his section on the various types of pearl necklaces (*hārayaṣṭi*), states:
There may be stairs with golden threads as the intervals, with jewels in the middle, or stairs made entirely of jewels.
By this, the various arrangements of head-ornaments, hand-ornaments, waist-bands, and lattices are explained.
"Long-composed" means fashioned over a long period of time. This is what should be understood here.
Indeed, women wear pearl nets personally fashioned by their most beloved lovers to soothe the nail-marks impressed upon the roots of their thighs; but she,
now that those nail-marks are absent, [seeks] the soothing of nail-marks...

The statement "she does not wear a net of pearls due to the turn of fate" is a word expressing grief. Regarding this matter, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the mention of the expiation for tooth-marks of that same kind; as in the *Kumārasambhava*:

"The lower lip, bitten and released, like a bimba fruit, with its sprout-like hand trembling from the sensation [of pain], was cooled for a moment by the cool crescent of the moon upon the head of the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva). Thus [it is said].
"Massaging" (*saṃvāhana*) refers to the pleasant rubbing with both hands. Massaging...
The *Amara* lexicon states that *mardana* means "massaging.

[Her thighs] are as pale as the trunk of a succulent plantain tree, white like the moist stem of a plantain; this whiteness of the thighs is due to their being kept in a sheltered place (*nivāta*), while their *calatva* (mobility) refers to their throbbing. || 29 || -93-
"Vāma" refers to Mallinātha.

By my nail-marks—*kararuhapada* meaning nail-prints; as Amara states: "The words *kararuha*, *nakha*, and *nakhara* (all masculine or neuter) mean a claw or nail"—by these being shed, that is, diminishing or becoming devoid of the growth of new nails, [upon] the thighs.
Regarding the locations for nail-marks, the *Ratirahasya* states: "They say the places for nail-marks are the throat, the belly, the breasts, the sides, the arms, the chest, the hips, and the thighs.
A long-familiar and long-practiced necklace of pearls—that is, one consisting of strings of pearls—[was worn].

The sense is that he was deprived of his waist-ornament by the movement of the Daityas through the power of fate; for now, due to the absence of the heat from [her] nail-marks, that cooling treatment has become useless.
The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*) after the causative form of the root *tyaj*. This applies to roots such as *pac* among the group of two-object verbs.

Since it is intended as a supplementary addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*), the state of having two objects (*vikarmatva*) arises by virtue of belonging to the *pacādi* group [of roots]. "At the end of our enjoyment" refers to the massaging of my hands—that is, the rubbing of them with the hand.
Amara states: "Massaging (*saṃvāhana*) is synonymous with rubbing (*mardana*)."
That which is appropriate, fit, full of essence, moist with rasa, fully ripened, and not withered—that alone is intended [as the subject], because it is in that very thing that paleness can occur.
And he is like a plantain trunk; he is fair, pale-white. [As it is said: "Fair is the *karīra*..."
In the *Mālatīmālā*, it is said that [omens] may be white, yellow, or even reddish when the goal is accomplished.

The left thigh of this beloved woman will undergo "movement," meaning it will experience a throbbing. One should know that from the throbbing of the thigh comes pleasure, and from the thighs, the acquisition of fine garments.
Thus ends the section on signs and causes (36).
-93- O Cloud, at that time, if your beloved should have fallen asleep,
sit beside her and endure for just one watch, refraining from thundering.
May she not suddenly loosen the firm embrace— the knot of her vine-like arms slipped from my neck— when I, her beloved, have somehow been found by her in a dream.
If she has obtained the pleasure of sleep (Da, Ma, Su); and if she is seated there (Su);
O cloud (Vall), if at that time—the hour of midnight—my beloved should be asleep, then...
Having attended upon her and ceased your thundering for even a moment, endure and wait; why? He says: "Because my beloved has somehow been reached in a dream by fate."
"May there not be a firm embrace— a tight hug— of her at that very moment, such that the knot of her vine-like arms slips from my neck, the coil of her creeper-like arms falls from my throat;
that is to say, may there be no interruption of the embrace."
"Surely she will see me embraced by her in a dream.
The word *upagūḍha* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).
*Anvāsana* means attendance or service; as in the expression, "she was attended upon by Arundhatī herself."
"Havirbhujam" (Raghu 1.56); "sthāṇum tapasyantam adhityakāyām" (Kumāra 3.17); and "anvāste" (Kumāra 3.17). || 94 ||
"In that [place] which turns to the right."
At that hour of midnight, look upon the virtuous woman so that she may be comforted by my messages;
for since it is said to be "midnight," she might have found the pleasure of sleep, yet she remains perpetually sleepless due to the agony of separation.

The meaning is: "If, by chance, she should fall asleep. Regarding the instruction "sit beside her for just one watch [yāma] and endure," one might object: "Indeed, those separated from their lovers do not sleep even for a single watch; and it has been said: 'And when three-quarters of the night remain, for a moment...'"

"He suddenly opened his eyes and woke up"—this is true. However, the expression "for only one watch" (*yāmamātra*) is not employed with reference to sleep, but rather with reference to sexual union (*sambhoga*).
For the maximum duration of sexual union is one watch, concluding at its end.

Those who know the science of love say that, in the play of passion, the supreme pleasure desired by young people is that which lasts for more than a watch (yāmāvasādhikī). The word division is: "sadyaḥ-kaṇṭha-cyuta-bhuja-latā-granthi."
"Gāḍhopagūḍham" means a firm embrace. —94— [Commentary by Mallinātha on the word "tasmin": In that [state].

O Cloud, at that time— namely, at the time of your approach— if my beloved were to have obtained the pleasure of sleep, then [you should] sit beside her while she is sleeping; that is to say, you should remain seated behind her.

The verb becomes transitive due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*). "Averse to thundering" means facing forward toward the roar; the sense is that if he were otherwise, there would be an interruption of sleep. "For only a watch" means for only one *prahara*; Amara states that "two *yāmas* and two *praharas* are equivalent."

"Endure; wait. [This is] the *loṭ* [imperative] mood used in the sense of a request. The intention is that since the two powers [of the couple] are limited to a single instance of sexual union per watch (*yāma*), it must likewise occur even in a dream. And so it is said in the *Ratisarvasva*: "A watch (*yāma*) is the limit for a single instance of sexual pleasure."
It is considered supreme that the two youths, possessing fierce power and moving with wondrous strides, [should act].
He states the purpose of his intolerance with the words "lest it be so": when I, her beloved, have somehow—with great difficulty—been obtained in a dream by this dear woman.

"Deep embrace" (*gāḍhopagūḍham*) means a firm hug; here the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter sense of an abstract state. "Let it not be" (*mā bhūt*) means let it not happen that the knot—the binding—of the two vine-like arms slips from the neck at that very moment (*sadyas*). [This refers to] an embrace obtained with great difficulty.
The meaning is: "May there be no immediate obstruction.

Nor does the mention of sleep here contradict what was stated previously—that she is "awake" (unnidrām)—because sleep may occur occasionally during the seventh and subsequent stages [of yoga]. And thus:

"Attachment, weeping, sleep, shamelessness, harmful speech, and delusion arise in the stages beginning from the seventh; thus says Vāsuki regarding the distinctions of the [ten] stages. (37) —94— [Contradiction: Sleep?]
Having raised her up and comforted her with a breeze cooled by his own spray of water, he led her—
her eyes fixed upon the window occupied by you— to a spot where *mālatī* buds were in full bloom, and where lightning was flickering within the clouds.
With words like the deep rumbling of thunder, you may proceed to speak to the proud woman.
Then, having awakened that high-minded woman as she slept with cool breezes and drops of his own water, he proceeded to speak with a voice like deep thunder.
Proceed!
In what state? She has been comforted by the touch of the cool breeze along with the clusters of *mālatī* flowers;
for she blossoms at dawn.

Likewise, because it was presided over by you, [he cast his eyes] through the window filled with lightning—like a cloud pregnant with lightning—with a desire to see. 95. *Abhinava-dakṣiṇāvarta* [commentary].
Regarding that: "tāmiti" (her).
"She who has been refreshed and awakened"—
that is, lifting up her who has returned to consciousness, just as the buds of *mālatī* flowers expand at night with a breeze cooled by droplets of rain from the clouds.

The meaning is this: by this, it is indicated that her delicacy (*saukumārya*) is even greater than that of *jātī* flowers. Indeed, *mālatī* flowers bloom during the rainy season and open at night. On this point, there is scriptural authority in the form of a statement from the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*.
"By the birds settling down, by the lotuses closing their petals,
and by the *mālatī* jasmine blooming, it is known that the sun has set. — *Rāmāyaṇa* (Uttarakāṇḍa).

"Vidyudgarbha" means one who has lightning suppressed within; this qualification is stated for the purpose of showing her pleasure at the sight of the cloud. "Stimitanayanām" means having motionless eyes.
"With you as her protector" means she is presided over by you or accompanied by you;
the intention is that, out of longing for someone to come from her husband's presence, she always keeps her gaze fixed upon the window. "Dhīraiḥ" means profound.
With words of thundering and words of roaring;

"māninīm" means one whose mind is elevated—that is, a high-spirited woman. According to Amara, "mānaḥ" is the loftiness of the mind. By this epithet, [the poet indicates] that she was standing before him.
It has been stated that one should speak only with composure; for if one speaks with timidity, she understands that [the statement] is false. —95— Mallinātha.
"Her," he said.

Having raised—that is, awakened—his beloved with cool breezes consisting of droplets of his own water, that is, drops of water; by this, her sovereignty is manifested through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the wind from a fan. As Bhojarāja has said regarding the feet: "With gentle massages..."
One should awaken the Lord from sleep with cool fans upon his body and with sweet songs to his ears;
[using] fresh, newly blossomed clusters of *mālatī* flowers along with buds of the *jāti*.
*Saha* means together; *sumanā*, *mālatī*, and *jāti* are synonyms for jasmine. According to the *Kṣāraka* lexicon: "The word *sākam* means together or simultaneously.
According to the *Amara-kośa*: "*Jālaka* (in the neuter) and *kalikā* (feminine) mean a bud; *koraka* is masculine.
*Pratyāśvastām* means well-composed or restored; she who has been revived once again through contact with the cool breeze.

This is the meaning. The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) for the root *śvas*. The prohibition of *iṭ* [augment] follows from the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *āditaśca*. By this, her extreme delicacy like a flower is understood.
"In your company" means accompanied by you; they say that *sanātha* refers to one who has a protector (*prabhu*), but it is also used in the sense of being accompanied (*sahite*).
"Cittatāpinī" is explained in the *Śabdārṇava* as follows:

[it refers to] a proud and high-minded woman (*māninī manasvinī*) who, at the window, has her eyes fixed in wonder, motionless, thinking "Who is this?", and is unable to endure being seen by people. This is the meaning.

"Vidyudgarbha" means that within which lightning is situated; the meaning is "one in whom lightning is hidden within. According to the *Śabdārṇava*, the word *garbha* refers to an inner chamber (*apavaraka*), the interior, fire, or a child in the womb. [This is used] because of the obstruction of vision.
The sense is that lightning must not flash, as it would obstruct the speaker’s looking at her face;
and he is "steadfast" (dhīra), meaning distinguished by fortitude, for otherwise, due to a lack of such character, there would be the risk of her losing confidence in him.

With words that are themselves thunders, you should begin to speak; that is, you should commence to speak. The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*). The *ātmanepada* ending is applied according to the rule *propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām*. 38. -95-
O lady whose husband lives, know me to be the dear friend of your lord, the cloud;
I have come to your side bearing his messages held within my heart.
I am he who hastens the crowds of weary travelers on their paths.
With deep and tender sounds, [the cuckoos] incite the women who are eager to loosen their braids,
by means of messages from him that are held in their hearts.
Vallabha says: "What shall I say? he asks.
O lady whose husband is living, know me to be your husband’s dear friend, the water-bearing cloud;
having taken his message to heart— that is, having held his message in your mind— [proceed].
It has reached your presence—
that cloud which, with its deep and tender sounds, [relieves] the multitudes of travelers who are weary and suffering from exhaustion on the road while away from home.
With sweet yet harsh thunders, he urges and impels [the women] toward their homes,
since the delicate beloveds are eager and longing to loosen their braided hair;
for in the sight of the clouds, separation is unbearable.
The use of the masculine gender and the first-person pronoun is in reference to the cloud, which "hurries"; however, in relation to me, O friend, this would be difficult to accomplish. (96)
"O right-turning one,
[this is] for the sake of the Lord."

By this, it was said that your husband lives as one who is not a widow (*avidhava*). One should not think that the word *avidhavā* is corrupted in poetic convention, for it is used in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*:
"They say of me, while in my father's house, that I am a mother of sons and not a widow."
"By his message" means by the act of delivering that message. The phrase "placed in the mind" is an indicator of this meaning.
It is not merely that I am a friend, but rather that I am the one who impels him toward union with you.
With the intention of saying "and I am," he says, "he who hastens the multitudes. This means for travelers weary on the road;
that is, for those who have gone abroad to other lands due to some business, leaving behind their wives and others.

The meaning is as follows: "With voices that are deep, tender, profound, and pleasant to hear"—this qualification is employed with the intention that, upon hearing the fierce thundering, there may be no destruction for those who are away from home. || 32 || -96-
Now Mallinātha teaches the messenger's skill in engaging the audience by saying,
"Of the master... and so forth.
"Avidhavā" means one who is not a widow—that is, one whose husband is living (*sabhartṛkā*). By this, he indicates that her husband is alive, thereby warding off any suspicion of misfortune.
"Mām" refers to me, the dear friend (*priyam mitram*) and beloved companion (*priyasuhṛdam*) of your husband. Furthermore—
"By those messages of her husband placed in her heart— that is, established in her mind—
know that she has come to you as a cloud (ambuvāha), meaning she has arrived for the purpose of delivering her husband's message."
With the intention that he is not merely a messenger but also a mediator,
he says: "The cloud, which is a bearer of water, with its deep and resonant sounds..."
By means of their roars; eager for the loosening—that is, the untying—of the braids of the weak ones, namely women;
for the multitudes of travelers (*pānthas*)—meaning those who are weary on the road, those who have fallen into distress, and those who are away from home—*proṣitas*. This is the sense.
He hastens the multitudes [of clouds]. The sense is: "What need is there to mention my helpfulness toward friends, when I am already helpful even to travelers? —96— Is it a water-bearer? A cloud?

When this has been told, O gentle one, she—her heart swelling with longing like Maithilī upon seeing the son of the Wind—will look up at you and honor you with her gaze; then, with rapt attention, that woman will listen to what follows from us. Thus ends the *Utsava* of women.
News of my beloved, brought by a friend, is but slightly less than the joy of union itself.
When you had spoken thus, she looked at you with an upward-turned gaze and,
reflecting in her mind that "this is appropriate for his role as a messenger," considered what should follow from this.
She will listen with focused attention,
for the news of her beloved brought by a friend—
namely, the account of her lover— is but slightly less than the joy of union itself when meeting the dear one.
The meaning is that it is like a reunion with a beloved because it produces consolation.
To whom did she look, and who was it? He says: just as Sītā, the daughter of Mithilā, formerly beheld Hanumān, the son of the Wind, and honored him as a messenger.
She whose heart has been made to heave with longing is described as such. || 97 ||
"O dear one,
it is indeed clockwise," thus [he said].
"Having honored Hanumān, the son of the Wind"— that is, having indeed paid him due respect; "she will not remain silent thinking, 'This is another person,' but rather,
recognizing him as her husband's friend, she will look upon you without any hesitation."
The particle *eva* is employed to indicate the meaning "and he honors [her]";
after this, following the statement "the husband's friend," he says "from meeting" (*saṅgamāt*) in response to the expectation: "What is the reason for further attention? || 33 ||
Mallinātha states that the purpose of making known [the king's] friendship with his master and so forth is as follows.

When this had been told, she— like Sītā, the daughter of Mithilā, upon seeing Hanumān, the son of the Wind— her heart swelling with the longing and eagerness of her desire for my beloved, and her mind blossoming with joy, beheld and honored you.

And having honored [him], she will listen to everything beyond this demonstration of her husband’s affection; being attentive and vigilant, she will certainly listen. This is evident from the narrative of Sītā and Hanumān.
Her devotion to her husband and the excellence of the cloud’s qualities as a messenger are revealed therein.
Those qualities are described in the *Rasākara* as follows:
"He is a celibate student, powerful, steadfast, illusory, and free from pride."
"A wise, noble, and fearless speaker would be an envoy to women.
Having raised the objection, "But what is the benefit for her from merely hearing this news?", he introduces another point: "O gentle and virtuous one! [Regarding] women, that is, wives..."

According to Amara, *nārī*, *sīmantinī*, and *vadhū* are synonyms for woman. "Having been brought" (*upanataḥ*) means having arrived by means of a friend (*suhṛdā*), that is, through the mouth of a friend; the word "friend" (*suhṛt*) is used here to dispel any suspicion of deception.
"News of the beloved" (*kāntodantaḥ*) refers to the report or tidings concerning the beloved; *vārtā* and *pravṛtti* are synonymous.

According to Amara, *vṛttānta* and *udanta* are synonyms. The meaning is that [the union] is "slightly less" (*kiñcidūna*) than from contact with a beloved (*kāntasaṃparkāt*), yet it produces joy in exactly the same manner. (40) Mallinātha typically employs the phrase *tathā hi* to introduce an *arthāntaranyāsa*.

"O long-lived one, speak thus to her on my behalf and for your own benefit: 'Your companion, staying at the hermitage of Rāmagiri, unharmed and well, asks after your welfare, O frail lady, though he is separated from you. (34) D;
For living beings who easily encounter calamities, this alone is what should be desired in the future: [the cultivation] of one's own speech and conduct.
98. 41 Ma; 107 Su; O Long-lived One! Da, Ma, Su; [the refinement of] the composition of speech. Su; of oneself. Da, Ma, Su;
To do her a favor, you, O long-lived one, should speak to her yourself with my words and for your own sake as well.
Thus you should speak, saying:
"Your companion, your husband, seated at Citrakūṭa, being unharmed and alive, inquires after your welfare."
Why, then, is the description of the welfare pertaining to both [this life and the next] given at the very beginning?
He says: because for embodied beings who are easily subject to calamities, this alone is what should be wished for first and what should be desired at the outset—namely, well-being (*svāsthya*).

In the word *āyuṣmān*, the term is the subject (*kartṛpada*) and not a vocative; this is because the first person is employed [in the corresponding verb]. Regarding the word *āśāsya*, there is no application of the suffix *kyap* (as in *etistuśāsvṛ...`), because it falls under the governing rule for prefixes (*anupasargādhikāra*).
{p3.1.109} || 98 || [The word] *tām* [is used] when separated by *ca*, *ca*, *abale*, or *viyukta*;
according to Dākṣiṇāvarta.
By the word "O long-lived one," it is said: "While you live, I too shall live.
The reading is *ātmanaścopakartuḥ*; that is, of the benefactor, the one who has done me a favor. And by my word, O long-lived one, and by the word of you, the benefactor, [speak] to her thus.
The meaning is that he should speak.

He states the manner of Megha’s speech as follows: "Your companion is staying at the hermitage on Mount Rāma. The word "hermitage" (*āśrama*) is used here specifically to indicate that the place is primarily inhabited by ascetics.
This has been introduced. Here, the following collection of sentences, beginning with "O companion" and ending with "said this through my mouth," constitutes the speech of the cloud.
From here on, the speech beginning with "Upon the dark limbs... belongs to the Yakṣa.

The meaning is this: that which is the very first thing to be prayed for by living beings to whom calamities are easily encountered—namely, that one who remains unharmed himself should inquire after the welfare of beloved ones—is precisely what is to be desired in the east by those prone to misfortune. (34) — Mallinātha.
Now he sends her this message.

"O venerable one!"—the suffix *matup* here denotes praise; thus the meaning is "one whose life is praiseworthy due to its service to others. "My word" refers to a request; and "in order to benefit yourself"—that is, to fulfill your own purpose through the service of others.

Even though [the self] is the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of benefiting, the genitive case in "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) is not contradictory when there is an intention to express a mere relationship—as in the expression "it benefits [him]" (*upakaroti*).
As Bhāravi said: "That is prosperity by which one benefits others."
Just as it was said that Śrīharṣa [intended] to assist the virtuous, to behold Lakṣmī,

and to travel through the sky; and likewise, because the accusative case is not seen in some instances, to claim that it is so for all cases is merely the word of one who has no master— it is simply the word of a non-authority.
You should speak thus to that beloved woman: "O frail one, your companion, your husband, dwells in the hermitages of Rāmagiri,
Citrakūṭa"— that is, while staying in the hermitages of Rāmagiri.
"Unharmed" means not dead. He states the reason for his not being dead:
"Separated"—having experienced separation and being thus suffering—he asks after your welfare.
Because the root *pṛcch* belongs to the class beginning with *duh*, it takes two objects.

For it is thus: for those living beings who easily encounter calamities and whose downfall is accomplished without effort, this very thing—this alone—is the wholesome matter that must necessarily be spoken first and inquired about at the outset.
The suffix *ṇyat* in the word *kṛtyāḥ* is used in the sense of necessity (*avaśyakārthe*). (41) —98—

Limb with limb, the slender with the slender, the intensely heated with the heated, the tearful with the flowing-tearful, the longing with the longing, and the one breathing hot sighs with the one sighing even more heavily—thus [he meets] while remaining far away. 35. Da;
With his path blocked by the enemy in the form of fate, he enters [the body] through your volitions.
Regarding those [objections], he says, "Then what? (tataḥ kim).
Your beloved, being far away, enters limb with limb through the power of longing born of his mental constructs;
he desires to enter your body—meaning he wishes to attain oneness with you. And the oneness of two distinct entities occurs through their similarity of form.
By using the distinct qualifiers "thin" (*tanu*) and "very thin" (*tanuni*) for those two limbs, he expresses their equal passion through the statement of their similarity.
"Flowing with tears" (*asradrava*) means that tears flow; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule beginning with "pada."

He asks: why does he not come in person? [The author] replies: because his path is blocked by adverse fate; for separation is to be experienced through the body. And as for the phrase "tanu ca tanunā," since there is no sense of duality, it should be read as "pratanu tanunā" (very slender with his slender [body]). 99.
"By means of the right-turning limb," [it is said]. This refers to an incomplete contradiction.

"By means of the body" (aṅgena) refers to the physical frame. In response to the expectation of what kind of body and what kind [of state], he says "but not by a thin one" (na tu ca tanunā). The particle *ca* is employed to connect each qualifying attribute with the verb.
He states the cause for the attenuation of the body with the words "heated by the intensely heated.
In response to the inquiry as to what manifests this heat, he says "with tears.
The reading is *āsradrutam*, which means "with flowing tears," according to the rule governing the *āhitāgni* group of compounds.
Its correctness is established by its inclusion in the lexicon (*pāṭha*).

In response to the inquiry as to what is the cause of the flow (*āsrava*), it says: "with longing" (*aviratotkaṇṭham*), meaning by one who is full of longing. Furthermore, although longing and the like are attributes of the self (*ātman*), they also exist in the body.
They are employed [in this way]. And it has been said by those who possess higher knowledge that "the fruit of agriculture depends upon you," referring to the movements of the eyebrows.
In response to the inquiry as to what manifests longing (*utkaṇṭhā*), he says:
Regarding the phrase "hot breath" (*uṣṇocchvāsam*):

there is a variant reading, *samadhikakharocchvāsinā*, meaning "one who breathes with an excessively harsh [breath]. Here, *kharam* means "hot. As it is said: "Harsh (*kharam*), intense (*tigam*), sharp (*tīvram*), pungent (*tīkṣṇam*), fierce (*caṇḍam*), hot (*uṣṇam*), and clever (*paṭu*) are recorded as synonyms."
Bhaṭṭahalāyudha [comments]: By the word "ucchvāsa" (exhalation), "niḥśvāsa" (inhalation) is intended.
"By those resolutions" means by those mental acts (*mānasakarma*), which consist of different bodily states characterized by emaciation, heat, and so forth.
Anticipating the question, "For what purpose does he act in this way?", [the author] says: "His path being blocked by a hostile fate" (verse 35). With what kind of body [does he do so]?
[Mallinātha] asks.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the limb":
Furthermore: he is far away, situated at a distance;
and since he cannot come, [the poet] says: his path is blocked and his way obstructed by hostile fate—that is, by adverse destiny—and thus your companion remains there, emaciated and thin.
By means of [the words] "intensely heated," "extremely tormented," "tearful," and "with tears," [it is shown that] a longing and a sensation of longing have arisen in him;
because he is thus longing, he is called "the longing one" (*utkaṇṭhita*).
The suffix *itac* is applied in this sense according to rules such as "that has arisen in him," or it is applied to the agent of the root *ut-kaṇṭh*.

*ktaḥ* [is the suffix]. *Samadhikatarocchvāsi* means "one who sighs more excessively"; that is to say, one who heaves long sighs. The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchilye*). *Aṅgena* refers to her own body; *pratanu* means thin or emaciated, and *taptaṃ* means scorched by the pain of separation.

"Filled with tears" means moistened by tears; according to Amara, *aśru* refers to the water of the eyes, weeping, and tears. "With incessant longing" means with uninterrupted pain, and "with hot sighs" means with intense gasps.

Halāyudha states that *tigma*, *tīvra*, *khara*, *tīkṣṇa*, *caṇḍa*, and *uṣṇa* are considered synonyms. Your limb—your body—enters into those volitions and mental desires which are self-perceived; the meaning is that it becomes one with them.
Here, in order to manifest their mutual passion, the hero has stated that he and the heroine are in the same state.
(35) -99- That which you indeed spoke in the presence of your friends...
Eager to speak at your ear out of a longing to touch your face,
he has now passed beyond the range of hearing and is no longer accessible to the eyes.
Thus, with words composed out of longing, he says this to you through my mouth.
109. He is unseen by the eyes of Locanā; [he is] invisible. (VALL)
Your beloved says this to you through my mouth, as follows:
who is he? He who, even regarding that which is expressible by words—that is, openly stated—was eager to whisper it into your ear, making a pretext while in the presence of his friends.
He was full of longing.
For what reason? Out of greed for the touch of her face. Indeed, whispering in her ear was for the sake of experiencing the pleasure of touching your face.

What is it like? It has transcended the range of hearing and is not reached because of its distance. For this very reason, it is inaccessible to the eyes, impossible to behold with the visual organs. It is that in which words—sounds—are produced by longing.
The specific qualification of the discourse. || 100 ||
"Right-turning sound," it is said.
"Expressible by words" (śabdākhyeya) means that for which words themselves are the expressible or denotable; the meaning is that it is devoid of meaning.
The phrase "in the presence of her friends" is used because of the crowded nature of the place.
It is said [this] because of the difficulty of obtaining a touch of the face that is free from artifice.
"Within the range of hearing" means the region of the ear, that is to say, the place for hearing each other's news. "With words composed of longing" means with reference to longing.

The meaning is "composed of words. It should be understood that these four diversions mentioned below—described in the *Kāmatantra* as looking at someone resembling the beloved, painting a picture of her, dreaming of union with her, and touching something she has touched—are hereby stated. As it says in the *Guṇapatākā*:
In separation and in union, following after those who resemble beloved ones; then, beholding them in a painting, or even seeing them at the time of sleep;
and the touch of those who have come and touched their limbs.
"Thus, some remedy has been prescribed for those whose minds are afflicted by desire. (36)
Now Mallinātha introduces [the following] in order to announce his own condition.
"It is expressible by words."
He who is dear to you,
out of greed— that is, out of longing— for the touch of the face, meaning the desire to drink from your lower lip,
[acts] even toward that which is "to be expressed by sound," meaning that which ought to be spoken aloud with a loud voice in the presence of his friends.
The word "even" (*api*) is to be understood as referring to "speech. He was indeed eager (*lola*), that is, longing (*lālasa*), to whisper it into his ear.
According to Yādava: "Lolupa, lolubha, lola, lālasa, and lampaṭa all mean [one who is] greedy."
He has passed beyond the range of hearing, transcending the path of the ears; likewise, he is unseen by the eyes. The sense is that, due to extreme distance, it is impossible to see or hear him.

That [person] is dear to you; he is described as such because his words—either individual words (*pada*) consisting of nouns and verbs (*suptiṅanta-śabda*), or sentences (*vākya*)—are composed out of longing for you. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "word" (*pada*) refers both to a single term and to a sentence. This refers to what is about to be said.
He speaks "śyāmāsvaṅgam" and so forth through my mouth; the meaning is that he himself speaks through my mouth. (43) —100— This is the sense; this is the intention:
[he says] "cast a glance upon the limbs of the dark-complexioned woman, with a look like that of a startled deer."
I perceive the shadow of your cheek in the moon, your tresses in the plumage of peacocks, and the play of your eyebrows in the slender ripples of rivers.
Alas, O timid one, there is not even a single instance where your likeness is found gathered together in one place.
Ma; 110 Su;
°hariṇī° Su; is it *prekṣite* or *prekṣaṇe*? Va; *prekṣaṇe* Da?, Ma; °pātān Su;
*vaktra* Da, Ma, Su; *barha* Da, Ma, Su; *°patākām* Da; *°patākās* (Ma);
*ekasmin* Ma; *caṇḍi* Da, Ma;
VALL.
To the question "What is this?", he says:
O timid one, O faint-hearted one, this miserable state of yours is concentrated in a single form; alas, it is not found anywhere else,
such that by beholding it I might find some consolation for myself.

For thus I imagine your body among the *śyāmā* creepers because of its slenderness; and I perceive your gaze in the eyes of startled deer because of your tremulous look, like that of a frightened antelope. In this manner, the comparison should be applied accordingly in what follows.
I perceive the beauty of her cheeks in the moon; the mass of her hair in the elaborate display of the peacocks' plumage;
and the play of her eyebrows in the ripples of the slender streams.
The name "Bhīrū" (the Timid One) given to women is truly significant; for indeed, a grammatical rule is preceded by its own designation.
The term *anitya* (non-eternal) here signifies the absence of the short vowel quality [as a governing rule]. || 101 ||
Regarding the right-turning [conch] among them, he describes the sight resembling that of a beloved with the words "among the *śyāmā*s.
Among the *śyāmā*s, which are *priyaṅgu* creepers; "I perceive" (*utpaśyāmi*) means I imagine. Among those that are slender (*pratanuṣu*).
"Exceedingly slender" means very thin. "The banner of the eyebrows" (*bhrūpatākā*): a banner (*patākā*) is a flag (*dhvaja*); thus, the eyebrows themselves are the banner, hence *bhrūpatākā*.
The metaphorical representation of the eyebrows as banners is due to their capacity to indicate internal states (*bhāva*) and so forth.
"Hanta" expresses dejection. "Ekastham" means situated in one place.
"Caṇḍi" means O excessively wrathful one! By this [statement], if a similar thing is found in one place, that alone is sufficient; what need have I for you? Thus, she becomes angry with me.
It was employed with the intention of jesting.
"Similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is indeed "that which is similar," because the previously cited examples possess the meaning of "similarity. —101— ? *mahyam* = "to me" / "me"?

Mallinātha states that there are four means of diversion for those separated from their beloveds: similarity, a likeness, seeing her in a dream, and touching something she has touched. Thus it is said in the *Guṇapatākā*:

In states of separation, the experience of something resembling a beloved person; furthermore, the marvelous power of karma which brings about even a vision during sleep; and even the sight of objects touched by that person's limbs as they happen to come near.
"A certain remedy has been declared for those whose minds are tormented by the pain of unfulfilled love.
In this context, he speaks of "beholding a similar object" with the words "In these dark nights... and so forth.

"Upon the dark *priyaṅgu* creepers"—for the *Amara-kośa* states: "The *śyāmā* is called *mahilā*; the creeper is *govandanī*, *gundrā*, *priyaṅgu*, *phalinī*, and *phalī*. "I perceive the limb"—the meaning is that, due to the similarity in qualities such as delicacy, I infer it to be a limb of the body (*aṅga*).
Likewise, you cast your glance upon the eyes of startled does; you perceive the reflection of your face in the moon, as well as the facial luster in the plumage of peacocks,
and your own fine hair in the slender ripples of rivers.

The suffix *enap* occurs after the word *dakṣiṇa* [to form the adverb *dakṣiṇena*] according to Pāṇini 5.3.35.

The word "by the southern path" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Furthermore, it is frequently employed [in the sense of a path], as in the phrase "again by the northern [path]" (*bhūya evottareṇa*).
In the phrase "guṇavati," the quality intended is the quality of touch that is pleasing to the body. This means that she is pleasant to the touch during embraces and so forth.

"Thine" (*tava*): the word *kila* is used here in the sense of probability. "By these winds from the snowy mountain" (*tuṣārādrivātaiḥ*):

"Set forth" means they have moved. O virtuous one!

By stating that there is no fault [in his view], the author of the Nirukta himself speaks like a madman and should be disregarded.

Mallinātha.
"It would be abbreviated."

*Dīrghayāmā* means that in which the watches (*yāma*) or hours (*prahara*) are long; the sense is that they are perceived as such due to the pain of separation. *Triyāmā* refers to the night, which is called "three-watch" because of the conventional usage of dividing it into three parts by means of the first, middle, and last watches.
Thus says Kṣīrasvāmī. How, by what means, could it be shortened or made light, even for a moment—that is, even for an instant? "Even the day" means at all times, in every state.
*Mandamanda* means "of a mild degree. The reduplication [of *manda*] occurs according to Pāṇini 8.1.12, which states that a word expressing a quality is repeated when it denotes a degree.

Because of the rule *karmadhārayavad uttareṣu*, which causes the subsequent compounds to behave like *karmadhārayas*, there is the elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*). How could there be a *mandamandātapa*—an extremely slight heat? It could not be so.
O you of tremulous eyes, O fickle-eyed one, in this manner my heart— whose desire is difficult to attain and unfulfilled— [is tormented] by [fevers] of intense heat.
"By the exceedingly intense agonies of separation from you, I have been rendered helpless and protectorless.
Indeed, though I reflect much upon myself by my own mind, I find no support; therefore, O blessed lady, you too must not fall into excessive despondency."
To whom has absolute happiness ever come, or to whom does suffering descend exclusively?
Conditions move upward and downward like the rim of a wheel.
But not [as in] Da, (Ma); thus [it is] Su; by the self alone [is it] Ma; most certainly Da, Ma;

"O auspicious one, O blessed lady, even there, surely while reckoning oneself in many ways and knowing [the truth] for oneself, do I not hold on? On the contrary, I do indeed hold on; this is the meaning."
O beloved, do not fall into a state of excessive timidity or lack of fortitude;
for to whom among those in the cycle of existence has eternal happiness ever truly arrived?
Or rather, it is exclusively and invariably suffering;
for these states and conditions, consisting of pleasure and pain, move like the rim of a wheel—
sometimes going downward, descending, and sometimes upward, rising to the top.
Moving by means of the spokes of the wheel, it revolves and proceeds gradually upward and downward;
thus it is said that pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence, gain and loss, and death [all arise].
And life itself—all these, in their various forms, one encounters here; therefore, a hero should neither rejoice nor grieve.
Indeed, in the sense of "making present," [the form] *mā gamaḥ* occurs; because the root has a *ḷ* as its penultimate letter, *aṅ* is substituted [for *luṅ*].

The meaning is as follows: he asks "of whom? to show that happiness and suffering occur in turn for every person, even one superior to me. "Eternal" (nityam) means that which has completely transcended its end.

Do not fall into extreme, absolute cowardice or timidity; do not go there. (In the phrase "mā gamaḥ," the *luṅ* suffix is used after the root *gam* with the particle *māṅ*, hence the absence of *am*; the absence of *aṅ* is due to its non-application.

Rather, it is the condition (*daśā*), the state, which is like the rim (*nemi*) of a wheel (*cakra*, the part of a chariot); that [state] is the rim.

The *cakra* is a wheel; its edge is the *nemi*, which is feminine, while the *pradhi* is masculine—so says Amara. By its sequence, that is, by its regular order (*krama*), as Viśva states that *krama* means "succession" (*paripāṭī*), it moves and proceeds both downward and upward. The meaning is that pleasure and pain revolve [alternately]. — 49 — But surely, is this not the reading "the end of the rim"? [No,] the end of my curse will come when the wielder of the Śārṅga bow has risen from his serpent-couch.

Ma; 117 Su; the remaining months Ma, Su; the calculation Da; two of them Su; VALL.

therefore, for the four months beginning today, I shall keep my eyes closed."
Pass the time somehow or other; then later, when union occurs,

on nights with fully ripened autumnal moonlight, may you fulfill each of your various personal desires and longings, which have become intense through being multiplied by the long period of separation.

"We two shall enjoy [it], that is, we shall consume it. Here, the reality of the matter is perceived by the closing of the eyes. *Tataḥ* means "afterwards. *Dvādaśa* [refers to] the right-turning [conch].
In response to the expectation, "When will our welfare come to pass?", he says:

Likewise, in the Kūrma Purāṇa:

"Hari shall recline upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, and He abandons His sleep on the full moon of Kārttika; during those two [periods], one should worship Hari. Thus, spend the other four months beginning with the month of Āṣāḍha.
The meaning is "until the end of the month of Āśvayuja.

But was it not stated that it is on the first day of Āṣāḍha? It is well known that Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa constitute the rainy season (prāvṛṭ), and what follows that is autumn (śarad). Therefore, how [is this so]?

It has been stated that the autumn season (*śaratkāla*) follows the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha. "We shall experience [it]; we shall endure it.
(43) Mallinātha explains that he says "until the end of the curse" because this suffering is not without limit.
He who has the Śārṅga bow in his hand is "Śārṅgapāṇi"; [this refers to] Viṣṇu.

The compound is a *bahuvrīhi* according to the rule beginning with "saptamīviśeṣaṇena" (Pāṇini 2.2.35). The Uttara-nipāta [states]:

"For the remaining four months that have not yet elapsed"—the meaning is from the appearance of the clouds until the day of Hari's awakening. The meaning is that one should pass [this time] with fortitude.

Afterwards, immediately thereafter, "you and I" refers to the two of us. According to the rule *tyadādīni sarvair nityam*, there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) compound; furthermore, when words beginning with *tyad* form a copulative compound (*dvandva*) among themselves, that which follows [last in the sequence] remains.
"He remains" (*śiṣyate*) means he is left behind; that is, he is excluded from "us.

Regarding "in separation," [the word] is repeated twice to express distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), as in "I shall act in this very way for each and every one. "The desire of ourselves" refers to the longing or aspiration of both of us.

On those nights in which the autumnal moonlight has fully spread, we two shall enjoy— that is, we shall experience pleasure— by means of the *lṛṭ* suffix from the root *viś*. According to Amara, "nirveśa" means both wages and enjoyment (*bhoga*).

Regarding this, some raise the objection that since only the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya constitute the rainy season (*vārṣika*), how can the four-month period beginning with Āṣāḍha be considered the rainy season?
They resolve this by resorting to the position that there are three seasons (*ṛtu*) [in a year], thereby avoiding the contradiction. All of that—

This is irrelevant. Here, the poet stated that "four months remain," but he did not say that those [months] belong to the rainy season (*varṣika*).
